All of these are ענין התנכרות וזרות, a sense of being disowned and strange.

מַיִם זָרִים קָרִים נוֹזְלִֽים (Yirmiyahu 18:14) are waters coming from a strange and distant place, as though strangers to the place they flow in. כְּמַהְפֵּכַת זָרִֽים (Yeshayahu 1:7) is the overturning by strange men from a far land, who when they come on a city and take it overturn and destroy everything, having no mind to stay in it, which neighbours do not do. In וְשִׁלַּחְתִּי לְבָבֶל זָרִים וְזֵרוּהָ (Yirmiyahu 51:2) one word plays on the other, וְזֵרוּהָ being from זְרֵה ־הָלְאָה (Bamidbar 17:2), scatter afar, and of that root; though it may be of this root, and then: I will send strangers to Bavel and they will treat her as a stranger in all she has, taking everything and plundering her.

דלה.sense: To draw water up, with דְּלִי for the bucket one draws with; and a second sense, to lift high, דָּֽלִיּוֹת being the high boughs.

more.t: וְגַם־ דָּלֹה דָלָה לָנוּ (Shemos 2:19), he even drew for us; וַתָּבֹאנָה וַתִּדְלֶנָה (Shemos 2:16); וְאִישׁ תְּבוּנָה יִדְלֶֽנָּה (Mishlei 20:5). The noun is כְּמַר מִדְּלִי (Yeshayahu 40:15), the vessel they draw with.

כִּי דִלִּיתָנִי (Tehillim 30:2), which he glosses רוממתני, You lifted me up. From this are the boughs: לִפְנוֹת דָּֽלִיּוֹתָיו אֵלָיו (Yechezkel 17:6) and בְּצֵל דָּֽלִיּוֹתָיו תִּשְׁכֹּֽנָּה (Yechezkel 17:23), ענפים הרמים והגבוהים, branches lifted and high.

יִֽזַּל־מַיִם מִדָּלְיָו, waters flow from his buckets, is the plural of דְּלִי, and by rule it should carry the short kamatz, on the pattern of חָפְנָיו, his handfuls, and אָזְנָיו, his ears, but it comes with the broad one, as בְּתוֹךְ הַדָּֽבְרוֹ (Michah 2:12). It may also belong with the boughs: from under his branches the waters flow.

more.h: Legs lifted off a lame man
more.t: דַּלְיוּ (דָּֽלְיוּ) שֹׁקַיִם מִפִּסֵּחַ (Mishlei 26:7), which he glosses גבהו, they are high. So Rabbi Yehudah Chayuj wrote it, among the past verbs of the light form; but we found a patach under the daled, and so Rabbi Yaakov ben Elazar wrote, and if so it is a command in the doubled form, with the lamed left soft where the rule would double it, and the sense is: lift the legs off a lame man, for what use are they to him, and so is a parable in the mouth of fools.

שׁאב.sense: To draw water, with מַשְׁאַבִּים for the places where water is drawn.

more.t: וּשְׁאַבְתֶּם ־מַיִם בְּשָׂשׂוֹן מִמַּֽעַיְנֵי הַיְשׁוּעָֽה (Yeshayahu 12:3), you shall draw water in joy from the wells of salvation; וַתִּשְׁאַב לְכָל־גְּמַלָּֽיו (Bereishis 24:20), she drew for all his camels; יִשְֽׁאֲבוּן הַנְּעָרִֽים (Rus 2:9), the lads draw; לְעֵת צֵאת הַשֹּֽׁאֲבֹֽת (Bereishis 24:11), the time the drawers of water go out; and the places where they draw, בֵּין מַשְׁאַבִּים (Shoftim 5:11).

שׁתה.sense: To drink, with מִשְׁתֶּה for a feast and שְׁתִיָּה for the drinking; and in the same letters שְׁתִי, the warp thread of a garment.

more.t: וּמַיִם לֹא שָׁתָה (Shemos 34:28), he drank no water; אֲשֶׁר יִשְׁתֶּה אֲדֹנִי בּוֹ (Bereishis 44:5), the cup my master drinks from; וַיֵּשְׁתְּ מִן־הַיַּיִן (Bereishis 9:21); and in the passive, וְכָל־מַשְׁקֶה אֲשֶׁר יִשָּׁתֶה (Vayikra 11:34), any drink that is drunk.

Chazal said שָׁתוּי אל יתפלל, one who has drunk should not pray. There שתוי is an adjective and not a passive, for it is the water or the wine that is drunk; and they used this word to keep him apart from the שִׁכּוֹר, the drunkard. The שתוי has not drunk as much as the drunkard, so if he prayed his prayer is a prayer, since he could still speak before a king; the drunkard has drunk so much that he could not speak before a king, so if he prayed his prayer is an abomination.

מִשְׁתֶּה וְשִׂמְחָֽה (Esther 9:22), feasting and joy; in the plural, וּמִיֵּין מִשְׁתָּיו (Daniel 1:5), the wine of his drinking, and וְיֵין מִשְׁתֵּיהֶם (Daniel 1:16); and with a heh, וְהַשְּׁתִיָּה כַדָּת (Esther 1:8).

בִּגְבוּרָה וְלֹא בַשְּׁתִֽי (Koheles 10:17): even at the hour they eat, their heart and mind are on strength and not on drinking. Others take it from אוֹ בִֽשְׁתִי אוֹ בְעֵרֶב (Vayikra 13:48), the thread that runs the length of the garment, the ערב, the woof, being the one that runs across it: not in confusion and mixture like the warp mixed with the woof, that is, their mind is not muddled with food and delights but clear in strength.
עַד שְׁתֽוֹתֵיהֶם (Shmuel II 10:4) he counts from this root, on the pattern of בְּנוֹתֵיהֶם and שְׁמוֹתֵיהֶם, and he has already explained it at the root שׁוּת.

גמא.sense: To give to drink, and so to swallow up; and גֹּמֶא, the exceedingly light wood small boats are made of.

more.t: הַגְמִיאִינִי נָא מְעַט־מַיִם מִכַּדֵּֽךְ (Bereishis 24:17), which he glosses השקיני, give me to drink.

more.h: The horse that drinks the ground
more.t: בְּרַעַשׂ וְרֹגֶז יְגַמֶּא ־אָרֶץ (Iyov 39:24): as though for his great lightness and speed he drinks up the ground.

His father explains מְגַמַּת פְּנֵיהֶם קָדִימָה (Chavakuk 1:9) from this, built like words weak in the heh: the east wind drinks their faces, that is, they come with a brazen face as though the east wind, which is fierce, had drunk their faces or given them to drink.

הֲיִגְאֶה־ גֹּמֶא בְּלֹא בִצָּה (Iyov 8:11), תֵּבַת גֹּמֶא (Shemos 2:3), וּבִכְלֵי־ גֹמֶא (Yeshayahu 18:2): a wood exceedingly light. They may also be explained from the word גמי that Chazal use, since small boats are made of it and coated with pitch so that the water should not come in, and they are light upon the face of the water.

הוה.sense: To be; and in the same letters a second sense, הַוַּת רְשָׁעִים, the ruin of the wicked, and the evil a man brings on another.

more.t: וְאַתָּה הוֶֹה לָהֶם לְמֶלֶךְ (Nechemiah 6:6), you will be a king to them; הֱוֵה גְבִיר לְאַחֶיךָ (Bereishis 27:29), be a lord to your brothers; כִּי מֶֽה־ הוֶֹה לָֽאָדָם (Koheles 2:22). In מְקוֹם שֶׁיִּפּוֹל הָעֵץ שָׁם יְהֽוּא (Koheles 11:3) the rule would have יֶהְוֶא, and the vav comes at rest as in וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ; and in כִּי לַשֶּׁלֶג יֹאמַר הֱוֵא אָרֶץ (Iyov 37:6), for to the snow He says be earth, the alef stands in place of a heh.

more.h: One root with היה, to be, or two
more.t: It is possible that the vav of this root stands in place of the yud of the root הָיָה, or they may be two roots; either way the sense is one.

הוָֹה עַל־ הוָֹה (Yechezkel 7:26), ruin upon ruin; and in another form, וְהַוַּת רְשָׁעִים יֶֽהְדֹּֽף (Mishlei 10:3) and הַוַּת נַפְשׁוֹ הוּא וַיְעַבְּתֽוּהָ (Michah 7:3). In the plural, עַד יַֽעֲבֹר הַוּֽוֹת (Tehillim 57:2), and הַוּוֹת תַּחְשֹׁב לְשׁוֹנֶךָ (Tehillim 52:4), which he reads as what you plot in your heart and bring out with your tongue. The sense of them all is breaking and evil things, and it may be that תְּהֽוֹתְתוּ עַל־אִישׁ (Tehillim 62:4) is of this root and this sense.

more.h: Strong in his ruin, or his wealth
more.t: יָעֹז בְּהַוָּתֽוֹ (Tehillim 52:9) he reads as ברעתו, in the evil he does to others. Rav Saadiah reads בהותו as in his wealth, from the first sense, the wealth that is his; and it may be so in וְהַוַּת רְשָׁעִים יֶֽהְדֹּֽף (Mishlei 10:3), which would then be the opposite of the same pasuk's saying that Hashem does not let the soul of the righteous hunger.

גזם.sense: A kind of locust; that is the whole of his entry.

more.t: One line, on יֶתֶר הַגָּזָם (Yoel 1:4), what the gazam left, of which he says הוא מין ארבה, it is a kind of locust.

שׁמן.sense: Oil; and to grow fat, שָׁמֵן being fat and, of ground, rich; and in the same letters שְׁמֹנֶה, eight.

more.t: שֶׁמֶן זַיִת (Shemos 27:20), olive oil; כַּשֶּׁמֶן הַטּוֹב עַל־הָרֹאשׁ (Tehillim 133:2). וְלֹא רֻכְּכָה בַּשָּֽׁמֶן (Yeshayahu 1:6) he takes of the dressing fit for a wound, called so because oil is put in it. שֶׁמֶן תּוּרַק שְׁמֶךָ (Shir HaShirim 1:3) is oil poured from vessel to vessel so that its scent spreads, that is, perfumer's oil, spoken of in the feminine; or תּוּרַק is an adjective on the pattern of תּוֹשָׁב.

שָׁמַנְתָּ עָבִיתָ כָּשִׂיתָ (Devarim 32:15), you grew fat and thick and gorged; וַיִּשְׁמַן יְשֻׁרוּן (Devarim 32:15), Yeshurun grew fat; וַיִּשְׂבְּעוּ וַיַּשְׁמִינוּ (Nechemiah 9:25), where nothing is done to anything else. Where it takes an object, הַשְׁמֵן לֵֽב־הָעָם הַזֶּה (Yeshayahu 6:10), which his father takes as an infinitive: that they made their own heart fat and their ear heavy and shut their eyes, so as not to see and not to understand.

וְהָיָה דָשֵׁן וְשָׁמֵן (Yeshayahu 30:23); מִרְעֶה שָׁמֵן וָטוֹב (Divrei HaYamim I 4:40), fat and good pasture; שְׁמֵנָה לַחְמוֹ (Bereishis 49:20), his land that brings out his bread; וַֽאֲדָמָה שְׁמֵנָה (Nechemiah 9:25). His father writes that in אוֹצָר נֶחְמָד וָשֶׁמֶן בִּנְוֵה חָכָם (Mishlei 21:20) the word is an adjective like שָׁמֵן. By way of borrowing, כָּל־ שָׁמֵן וְכָל־אִישׁ חָיִל (Shoftim 3:29) means sound and strong, and Targum Yonasan renders כָּל אֵימְתָן.

more.h: The fat hill, and the yoke broken
more.t: בְּקֶרֶן בֶּן־ שָֽׁמֶן (Yeshayahu 5:1): he calls the place a horn because it was high ground, and בן שמן, son of oil, because it was fat and rich; his father writes that Yerushalayim is called so because an anointed king and an anointed kohen were there, by the horn of the oil of anointing. וְחֻבַּל עֹל מִפְּנֵי־ שָֽׁמֶן (Yeshayahu 10:27) he reads as: through the fatness and strength of Chizkiyahu the yoke of Sancheriv will be broken; some explain the same words of the oil, of Chizkiyahu who was anointed with the oil of anointing.
עֲצֵי־ שָׁמֶן (Melachim I 6:31) and וַֽעֲלֵי־עֵץ שֶׁמֶן (Nechemiah 8:15): the tree called in the vernacular pine, because it is oily. Targum Yonasan renders אֲעֵי זֵיתָא, olive trees.

more.h: Eight, and a word for the graves
more.t: Another sense altogether: וּשְׁמֹנָה נְסִיכֵי אָדָֽם (Michah 5:4), שְׁמֹנֶה שָׁנִֽים (Shoftim 12:14), וּשְׁמֹנִים שָׁנָה (Bereishis 5:28), eight and eighty, which is known. בָּֽאַשְׁמַנִּים כַּמֵּתִֽים (Yeshayahu 59:10) has an added alef, and he explains it by its place as in graves; it may also be a four-letter word. His father writes that the alef is of the root and the nun added, and its sense is from תֶּאְשַׁם שֹֽׁמְרוֹן (Hoshea 14:1), a language of desolation, a place with no settlement, which is the graves.

צהר.sense: Noon, when the light is strong; צֹהַר, a window; and יִצְהָר, fresh oil, called by a word of light for its clearness.

more.t: כִּי אִתִּי יֹֽאכְלוּ הָֽאֲנָשִׁים בַּֽצָּֽהֳרָֽיִם (Bereishis 43:16), עֶרֶב וָבֹקֶר וְצָהֳרַיִם (Tehillim 55:18): the time when the day's light is strong. It is said as a pair because the day is divided in its light into two, from morning to midday going and brightening, and from midday on going and darkening, and the noon is the hour when the light is strong on both sides.
צֹהַר תַּֽעֲשֶׂה לַתֵּבָה (Bereishis 6:16): a window through which the light comes in.

דָּגָן תִּירוֹשׁ וְיִצְהָר (Devarim 28:51) and אֶרֶץ זֵית יִצְהָר וּדְבַשׁ (Melachim II 18:32): oil is called so at the time of its newness, straight after the treading. It is named by a word of light because it is so clear, as it is called gold in another place. The verb is בֵּין־שֽׁוּרֹתָם יַצְהִירוּ (Iyov 24:11), they tread the olives and make the oil.
שְׁנֵי בְנֵֽי הַיִּצְהָר (Zechariah 4:14) are Zerubavel ben Shealtiel and Yehoshua ben Yehotzadak, who were anointed with the oil of anointing, the one for kingship and the other for the kehunah.

להט.sense: To burn and blaze; לַהַט הַחֶרֶב, the flame of the sword; and perhaps בְּלַֽהֲטֵיהֶם, the arts of the sorcerers.

more.t: אֵשׁ לֹהֵֽט (Tehillim 104:4), blazing fire; וְלִהַט אֹתָם הַיּוֹם הַבָּא (Malachi 3:19), the day that comes will set them ablaze; וְלֶהָבָה לִֽהֲטָה (Yoel 1:19); וַתְּלַהֵט מֽוֹסְדֵי הָרִֽים (Devarim 32:22); וַתְּלַֽהֲטֵהוּ מִסָּבִיב (Yeshayahu 42:25). All of them are ענין שריפה, a sense of burning. אֶשְׁכְּבָה לֹֽהֲטִים (Tehillim 57:5) he reads as lying among ones that blaze.
וְאֵת לַהַט הַחֶרֶב (Bereishis 3:24), as וְלַהַב חֶרֶב וּבְרַק חֲנִית (Nachum 3:3), the blade of a sword and the glitter of a spear.
בְּלַֽהֲטֵיהֶם (Shemos 7:11) may well be of this root and this sense, since some of the work of sorcery is done with the flame of a sword.

לאט.sense: To cover over, as the king covered his face; and the words for the sorcerers' arts are set here, for those work by concealment.

more.t: וְהַמֶּלֶךְ לָאַט אֶת־פָּנָיו (Shmuel II 19:5), the king covered his face.

בְּלַהֲטֵיהֶם (Shemos 7:11) and בְּלָטֵיהֶם (Shemos 8:3), with their arts: the alef of לאט has turned to heh in the one and fallen silent in the other. What they do is done by hiding it and covering it from people, by contrivance and by illusion. He allows that בְּלַהֲטֵיהֶם may instead be from the root להט.
Rabbi Yehudah sets לָאַט under the root לוּט, the vav exchanged for an alef, so that the word stands whole; and Radak says that is correct.

הלם.sense: To strike so as to break and crush; and a second sense, הֲלֹם, here, in this place.

more.t: אָז הָלְמוּ עִקְּבֵי־סוּס (Shoftim 5:22), the horses' hooves were broken and battered, and הֲלוּמֵי יָיִן (Yeshayahu 28:1), men struck down by wine. The one who strikes is הוֹלֶם פָּעַם (Yeshayahu 41:6), and with a mem added, מַהֲלֻמוֹת, blows.
לְהַלְמוּת עֲמֵלִים (Shoftim 5:26), which he says is the מַקֶּבֶת, the workman's hammer.
אַל־תִּקְרַב הֲלֹם (Shemos 3:5), do not come near here, and כִּי הֲבִיאֹתַנִי עַד־הֲלֹם (Shmuel II 7:18), that You have brought me this far: in these the word is simply הנה, here.

At Tehillim 73:10 he takes הֲלֹם in this second sense: the people come back here again and again, to weigh and consider why the wicked have their ease, and why they drain a full cup, that is, that they are sated with every good of this world. Rabbi Yonah puts the pasuk in the first sense, that they come back broken at seeing that ease, and reads the full cup as the tears of their weeping.

In נֹפֶךְ סַפִּיר וְיָהֲלֹם (Shemos 28:18) the yud may be an addition, and the word is a precious stone. Rabbi Avraham ben Ezra writes there that a great Sephardi sage said it is the one Arabic names, which breaks every stone and pierces crystal, and that the name comes from הוֹלֶם פָּעַם (Yeshayahu 41:7), the one who strikes.

הן.sense: הֵן and הִנֵּה, behold, pointing at what is present and ready; it also stands for אם, if, and הֵנָּה for until now and for here.

more.h: Behold, and the thing at hand
more.t: הֵן־אֲנִי כְפִיךָ לָאֵל (Iyov 33:6), see, I am as your own mouth before Hashem. With a heh added it is הִנֵּה, and with the pronouns הִנְנִי and הִנֶּנִּי, here I am, הִנְנוּ and הִנֶּנּוּ, here we are. All of them, he says, point at the thing that stands ready.

הֵן הָיְתָה כָּזֹאת (Yirmiyahu 2:10) and הֵן נִזְבַּח (Shemos 8:22) are questions, yet הֵן keeps its plain force, since a question can be put without the interrogative heh, as אַתָּה זֶה בְּנִי עֵשָׂו (Bereishis 27:24), are you my son Esav. In these two the word also stands in place of אם, if.

עַד־הֵנָּה is of time, until now, as כִּי לֹא־שָׁלֵם עֲוֹן הָאֱמֹרִי עַד־הֵנָּה (Bereishis 15:16); הֵנָּה by itself is of place, וְהוֹרַדְתֶּם אֶת־אָבִי הֵנָּה (Bereishis 45:13), you shall bring my father down here. Some explain אֲשֶׁר־עֲדֶן לֹא הָיָה (Koheles 4:3), who has not yet been, as עד הן, and עֲדֶנָה (Koheles 4:2) as עד הנה.
הֵנָּה serves for women spoken of, כִּי טֹבֹת הֵנָּה (Bereishis 6:2), that they were fair, with להן, to them; and the nun form comes for men too, הֲלָהֵן תְּשַׂבֵּרְנָה (Rus 1:13).

כבד.sense: To be heavy, and so to be burdensome, to be many, or to be rich; from the same word כָּבוֹד, honour; and הַכָּבֵד, the liver.

more.t: כָּבְדָה מְאֹד יַד הָאֱלֹהִים שָׁם (Shmuel I 5:11), the hand of Hashem was heavy there; וַיִּכְבַּד לֵב פַּרְעֹה (Shemos 9:7), Paroh's heart grew heavy; וְעֵינֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כָּבְדוּ מִזֹּקֶן (Bereishis 48:10), his eyes were dim with age. A man is כָּבֵד in cattle, silver and gold (Bereishis 13:2), heavy with wealth.

יִכְבְּדוּ בָנָיו וְלֹא יֵדָע (Iyov 14:21), his sons grow many, or come to great and heavy wealth; the proof is the other half of the pasuk, וְיִצְעֲרוּ, and they are made small. So too וְהִכְבַּדְתִּים וְלֹא יִצְעָרוּ (Yirmiyahu 30:19), I will make them many. He holds all of it one thing, for the abundance of anything is its heaviness.
וְלֹא נִכְבַּד עָלֶיךָ (Shmuel II 13:25), we will not be a load and a burden on you, and תִּכְבַּד הָעֲבֹדָה עַל־הָאֲנָשִׁים (Shemos 5:9), let the work lie heavy on the men.

הִתְכַּבֵּד כַּיֶּלֶק (Nachum 3:15) he takes as multiplying like the locust. Others read it as sweeping away, in the sense of וְטֵאטֵאתִיהָ (Yeshayahu 14:23), I will sweep her, and from Chazal's מכבדין בין המטות, they sweep between the couches, and מכבדות של תמרה, palm-frond brooms; and they read כָּבֹד מִכֹּל כְּלִי חֶמְדָּה (Nachum 2:10) the same way.

כִּי־מְכַבְּדַי אֲכַבֵּד וּבֹזַי יֵקָלּוּ (Shmuel I 2:30), those who honour Me I honour and those who scorn Me are made light. Giving כָּבוֹד to Hashem (Yirmiyahu 13:16) he reads as honouring Him with praise and with confessing one's sins before Him.

The higher soul is called כָּבוֹד because it is the honour and worth of the body, שָׂמַח לִבִּי וַיָּגֶל כְּבוֹדִי (Tehillim 16:9). וּכְבוֹדִי לֶעָפָר יַשְׁכֵּן סֶלָה (Tehillim 7:6) he takes as a figure, since the soul does not dwell in dust, like דָּבְקָה לֶעָפָר נַפְשִׁי (Tehillim 119:25). At the end stands the organ, יֹתֶרֶת הַכָּבֵד (Vayikra 8:16), which he calls known.

יקר.sense: To be precious, dear or costly; and the noun יְקָר, honour and esteem.

more.t: וְלִי מַה־יָּקְרוּ רֵעֶיךָ אֵל (Tehillim 139:17): they are precious and too great to be grasped. אֲשֶׁר יָקַרְתִּי מֵעֲלֵיהֶם (Zechariah 11:13) he reads as, I was precious in myself and drew away from them, because I was not precious in their eyes.

מַה־יָּקָר חַסְדְּךָ אֱלֹהִים (Tehillim 36:8): Rabbi Yehudah recorded it as a past verb, and perhaps his own copy had the kuf with a patach; in our books it is all kamatz, so it stands as an adjective. At וְאֶת־יְקָר תִּפְאֶרֶת גְּדוּלָּתוֹ (Esther 1:4) Rabbi Yehudah wrote that the word is patach and Rabbi Yonah that it is kamatz, and the careful books were found both ways.
אֲבָנִים יְקָרוֹת לְיַסֵּד הַבָּיִת (Melachim I 5:31) means heavy stones; and as כבדות serves both for weight and for honour, so יקר serves for both.

לֹא־יִהְיֶה אוֹר יְקָרוֹת (Zechariah 14:6) is the clear light and קפאון the thick and clouded one: neither will there be, but something between, as לֹא־יוֹם וְלֹא־לָיְלָה (Zechariah 14:7), and he reads it as a figure for the redemption and for the troubles at its start. Targum Yonasan renders it, there will be no light but cold and ice.

בְּנוֹת מְלָכִים בִּיקְּרוֹתֶיךָ (Tehillim 45:10) is read so by Ben Naftali, the first letter of the root swallowed in the dagesh; Ben Asher reads the beis with a sheva and the yud with a chirik. The word is an adjective, among your honoured women, that is, kings' daughters were among them.

אגם.sense: אֲגַם, a pool where water gathers; and אַגְמוֹן, the rush that grows by it and the bent hook shaped like it.

more.t: לַאֲגַם־מַיִם (Tehillim 107:35) and וְהָיָה הַשָּׁרָב לַאֲגָם (Yeshayahu 35:7), the parched place will become a pool. אַגְמֵי־נָפֶשׁ (Yeshayahu 19:10) he takes as the pools where fish are caught. All of them are places where water is gathered.

הֲתָשִׂים אַגְמֹן בְּאַפּוֹ (Iyov 40:26) is a tool like an iron needle with which fish are taken, and the words beside it bear that out, וּבְחוֹחַ תִּקֹּב לֶחֱיוֹ, with a thorn you pierce his jaw. It is named so because its head is bent like the גומא, the rush.

הֲלָכֹף כְּאַגְמֹן רֹאשׁוֹ (Yeshayahu 58:5), to bow the head like a rush: the word is the גומא, which Chazal call גמי. So too וְאֶת־הָאֲגַמִּים שָׂרְפוּ בָאֵשׁ (Yirmiyahu 51:32), they burned the reeds that grow along the rivers, so that their thickness should not hold them back from reaching the towns. Rabbi Yonah explained that word as fortresses, likening it to the Arabic name for fortresses.
כִּפָּה וְאַגְמוֹן (Yeshayahu 40:14 in his edition): כפה is said of the strong and אגמון of the weak, who are like the rush. Or אגמון may be a title for a ruler, as Chazal have הגמון, an officer.

כְּדוּד נָפוּחַ וְאַגְמֹן (Iyov 41:12): some read אגמון here as the rush, some by the run of the pasuk as a pot, and one said it keeps its own sense of a pool, a hint at the vapour that rises off water in the winter.

שׁפת.sense: To set a pot on the fire, and so to set a thing in place; the שְׁפַתַּיִם are what a pot stands on.

more.t: תִּשְׁפֹּת שָׁלוֹם לָנוּ (Yeshayahu 26:12), You will set peace in order for us, and וְלַעֲפַר־מָוֶת תִּשְׁפְּתֵנִי (Tehillim 22:16), You lay me in the dust of death; he glosses both with תערוך, You set in order.

שְׁפֹת הַסִּיר שְׁפֹת (Yechezkel 24:3), set the pot on: the שְׁפַתַּיִם are the stones the pots stand on, or the iron frame. The word is dual because it is the place where two pots are set. אִם־תִּשְׁכְּבוּן בֵּין שְׁפַתָּיִם (Tehillim 68:14) he reads as, lying in a place as low as that, you will yet be overlaid with silver. On וְהַשְׁפַתַּיִם טֹפַח אֶחָד (Yechezkel 40:43) Targum Yonasan renders hooks projecting one handbreadth, the pegs on the pillars where the korbanos are hung and flayed.
רֹבֵץ בֵּין הַמִּשְׁפְּתָיִם (Bereishis 49:14), lying between the two loads that are set on him, one on this side and one on that; and he is strong enough to lie down under them and rise with them.

שֹפה.sense: שָׂפָה, the lip; from it the edge or brim of a thing; and שָׂפָה אֶחָת, one language.

more.t: Some of them are the lip itself, שְׂפָתַיִם יִשָּׁק (Mishlei 24:26), he kisses the lips, and some are a side or a brim: עַל שְׂפַת הַיְרִיעָה (Shemos 26:4), the edge of the curtain, עַל־שְׂפַת הַיְאֹר (Shemos 2:3), the bank of the river, and כְּמַעֲשֵׂה שְׂפַת־כּוֹס (Melachim I 7:26), the brim of a cup.
שָׂפָה אֶחָת (Bereishis 11:1) is one language, and וְשִׂפְתֵי רְנָנוֹת יְהַלֶּל־פִּי (Tehillim 63:6) he glosses as words of song.

שׁפה.sense: To rub down and wear away, so that a thing is crushed smooth; and a second sense, the bare high places.

more.t: וְשֻׁפּוּ עַצְמֹתָיו (Iyov 33:21), his bones are worn away and crushed. The Targum of וָאֶכֹּת אֹתוֹ טָחוֹן (Devarim 9:21), I beat it fine, uses this word for filing with a file, and Chazal speak of one who files down an idol.

וַיֵּלֶךְ שֶׁפִי (Bamidbar 23:3), אֶפְתַּח עַל־שְׁפָיִים נְהָרוֹת (Yeshayahu 41:18), I will open rivers on the bare places, and הַר־נִשְׁפֶּה (Yeshayahu 13:2), which he glosses as high. Rabbi Yehudah instead brought וַיֵּלֶךְ שֶׁפִי with the first sense, of being broken, that is, that he went with a broken spirit.

וּשְׁפוֹת בָּקָר (Shmuel II 17:29) he takes as cheeses of milk, and Targum Yonasan renders cheeses of cows' milk. Chazal said they were so smooth and fat that a fly could not stand on them but fell off at once, and he reckons it was the word שפות that drove them to it. He allows it may come from the first sense, since חריצים, another name for cheeses, is drawn the same way from a root of cutting; and others explain it as the udder of the cows.

שְׁפִיפֹן עֲלֵי־אֹרַח (Bereishis 49:17), what glides along the path, may belong here with the middle letter doubled, since the gliding of creatures is named from הוּא יְשׁוּפְךָ רֹאשׁ (Bereishis 3:15), so that שוף and שפה are one sense. He allows too that יָשְׁפֵה (Shemos 28:20) is of this root with an added yud, and that it is a stone whose Arabic name is close to the Hebrew.

לשׁן.sense: לָשׁוֹן, the tongue, and so a language; and the verb, to inform against a man behind his back.

more.t: The plural is used of peoples' languages, לְקַבֵּץ אֶת־כָּל־הַגּוֹיִם וְהַלְּשֹׁנוֹת (Yeshayahu 66:18), to gather all the nations and the tongues, and לִלְשֹׁנֹתָם בְּאַרְצֹתָם (Bereishis 10:20), by their tongues in their lands.
אַל־תַּלְשֵׁן עֶבֶד (Mishlei 30:10), do not denounce a servant to his master, and מְלָשְׁנִי בַסֵּתֶר רֵעֵהוּ (Tehillim 101:5), one who slanders his fellow in secret.

more.h: A tongue of gold, of fire, of sea
more.t: וּלְשׁוֹן זָהָב אֶחָד (Yehoshua 7:21) is a bar of gold shaped like a tongue; and by the same borrowing לְשׁוֹן אֵשׁ (Yeshayahu 5:24), a tongue of fire, לְשׁוֹן יָם (Yeshayahu 11:15), a tongue of sea, and מִן־הַלָּשֹׁן הַפֹּנֶה נֶגְבָּה (Yehoshua 15:2), a rock in the shape of a tongue, which Targum Yonasan renders as the rock.

צחק.sense: To laugh; and in the intensive, to make sport, whether in play and rejoicing, in mockery, or in abuse.

more.t: וַתִּצְחַק שָׂרָה בְּקִרְבָּהּ he reads as laughing and saying it within herself, with no word out of her mouth, which is why she could deny it out of fear; or that she laughed by herself, with nobody seeing her laugh. The noun צְחֹק, though, is laughter in the mouth.
וַיְצַחֵק לִפְנֵיהֶם (Shoftim 16:25) and וַיָּקֻמוּ לְצַחֵק (Shemos 32:6) he glosses as amusement and rejoicing, and מְצַחֵק אֵת רִבְקָה אִשְׁתּוֹ (Bereishis 26:8) is of that kind.
לְצַחֶק־בי (Bereishis 39:17) he glosses with להתעולל בי, to make sport of me for ill, and מְצַחֵק (Bereishis 21:9) as mocking. All of them, he says, come under the one sense of laughter.

שֹחק.sense: To laugh and to make merry; the word runs both to rejoicing and to derision.

more.t: וְשִׂחַקְתִּי לִפְנֵי (Shmuel II 6:21), I made merry before Hashem, and מְשַׂחֲקִים (Shmuel II 6:5), making merry; לִשְׂחוֹק עֹשִׂים לֶחֶם (Koheles 10:19), bread is made for merriment; and קִרְאוּ לְשִׁמְשׁוֹן וִישַׂחֶק־לָנוּ (Shoftim 16:25), call Shimshon that he may make sport for us.
וְרֹזְנִים מִשְׂחָק לוֹ (Chavakuk 1:10), rulers are a laughing matter to him, and וַיִּהְיוּ מַשְׂחִיקִים עֲלֵיהֶם (Divrei HaYamim II 30:10), they laughed them to scorn.

שׁחק.sense: To grind fine, which he says is more than treading down; and the noun שַׁחַק, the dust on the scales.

more.t: וְשָׁחַקְתָּ מִמֶּנָּה הָדֵק (Shemos 30:36), grind some of it fine, אֲבָנִים שָׁחֲקוּ מַיִם (Iyov 14:19), water wears stones away, and וְאֶשְׁחָקֵם כְּעָפָר עַל־פְּנֵי־רוּחַ (Tehillim 18:43), I ground them like dust before the wind.

וּכְשַׁחַק מֹאזְנַיִם (Yeshayahu 40:15), which he glosses as אבק, dust; and the same noun in כִּי מִי בַשַּׁחַק יַעֲרֹךְ (Tehillim 89:7) and וּבְגַאֲוָתוֹ שְׁחָקִים (Devarim 33:26), which he calls known.

צרע.sense: To be stricken with צָרַעַת, which he calls known; and the צִרְעָה, which some take as a stinging creature and some from צרעת itself.

more.t: וְהוּא צָרוּעַ אוֹ זָב (Vayikra 22:4) and מְצֹרַעַת כַּשָּׁלֶג (Bamidbar 12:10), leprous as snow; the noun is נֶגַע צָרַעַת (Vayikra 13:9), and he says the matter is known.

וְשָׁלַחְתִּי אֶת־הַצִּרְעָה (Shemos 23:28): they said it is a kind of flying swarming creature, which struck them in their eyes and cast its venom into them so that they died. Ibn Ezra explained the word from the sense of צרעת.

נגע.sense: To touch, and to touch so as to harm; to reach or arrive at; and נֶגַע, a plague, with נָגוּעַ, the man stricken.

more.t: כַּאֲשֶׁר לֹא נְגַעֲנוּךָ (Bereishis 26:29), that we did not touch you, he glosses as touching to do harm; so too הַנֹּגֵעַ בָּאִישׁ הַזֶּה (Bereishis 26:11), to do him harm.

עַד לַשָּׁמַיִם הִגִּיעַ (Divrei HaYamim II 28:9), it reached to heaven, and עֵת הַזָּמִיר הִגִּיעַ (Shir HaShirim 2:12), the time of singing has come; where it takes an object it is bringing one thing up against another, וְהִגַּעְתֶּם אֶל־הַמַּשְׁקוֹף (Shemos 12:22), and you shall touch it to the lintel.

וְאִם־לֹא תַגִּיעַ יָדוֹ (Vayikra 5:7) is that his hand does not reach to the money to buy a lamb with. Chazal explained that he has nothing to borrow against and no craft to work at, and that even one who had the lamb or its price but not the cost of the road brings the poor man's korban, as the pasuk says דֵּי שֶׂה, enough for a lamb.
נָגוּעַ מֻכֵּה (Yeshayahu 53:4), stricken and smitten; and the noun נֶגַע צָרַעַת (Vayikra 13:3) and אִישׁ נֶגַע לְבָבוֹ (Melachim I 8:38), each man and the plague of his own heart.

וַיִּנָּגְעוּ יְהוֹשֻׁעַ וְכָל־יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yehoshua 8:15) is that they made themselves out as men struck and beaten, fleeing so as to draw the people out of the city. He adds that they may well have been struck in truth, since men who flee and never turn to answer the fight are beaten; and had the sense been only that they made a show of it, the word would have stood as ויתנגעו, in the form for what one does to himself, for that is the rule.

כן.sense: The כִּנִּים of Shemos 8, a word he leaves as known; the single one is כִּנָּה, and הַכִּנָּם takes in the whole kind.

more.t: וַיַּעֲשׂוּ־כֵן הַחַרְטֻמִּים (Shemos 8:3), the magicians did so: that word he has already set down under the root כון, and with it וְכַנָּה אֲשֶׁר־נָטְעָה יְמִינֶךָ (Tehillim 80:16).

וְהָיָה לְכִנִּם (Shemos 8:12) and הָיָה כִנִּים (Shemos 8:13) are the many; the single one he found in Chazal's words with a feminine heh, one who kills a כנה on Shabbos. הַכִּנָּם, though, is a name for the whole kind.

לחך.sense: To lick up, as an ox licks up the green of the field; the sense, he says, is known.

more.t: A word and four pesukim: כִּלְחֹךְ הַשּׁוֹר אֵת יֶרֶק הַשָּׂדֶה (Bamidbar 22:4), עַתָּה יְלַחֲכוּ הַקָּהָל, now this company will lick up all around us, הַמַּיִם אֲשֶׁר־בַּתְּעָלָה לִחֵכָה (Melachim I 18:38), it licked up the water in the trench, and עָפָר יְלַחֵכוּ (Tehillim 72:9), they lick the dust.

טעה.sense: Straying, going wrong; the form that takes an object is leading a people astray.

more.h: Only the form with an object
more.t: In the pesukim there is הִטְעוּ אֶת־עַמִּי, they led my people astray, and not the plain verb. The plain verb is Biblical language all the same, since a people led astray are טועים, straying.
The Mishnah's case of one who goes before the teivah וטעה, and errs, is the word for an unwitting slip, שגגה.

more.h: The same word with a tav
more.t: טָעָה with a tet and תָּעָה with a tav are one word, formed at one place in the mouth, and Onkelos renders וַתֵּלֶךְ וַתֵּתַע, she went and strayed, with וַאֲזָלַת וְטָעַת.

ירק.sense: Two words here: spitting; and green, covering growing herbage, the garden herb people eat, and a greenish tinge in cloth, in gold and in a frightened face.

more.t: יָרֹק יָרַק בְּפָנֶיהָ, spitting in her face, and וְיָרְקָה בְּפָנָיו, she shall spit in his face, are the plain use. But רֻקִּי, my spittle, and יָרֹק הַזָּב, the spitting of the zav, belong to the root רָקַק, even if the matter is one.
יֶרֶק עֵשֶׂב, the green of herbage, יֶרֶק בָּעֵץ, the green on the tree, and in another form יְרַק דֶּשֶׁא, the green of grass. The adjective יָרוֹק means every green herb.
גַּן־יָרָק, a garden of herbs, and אֲרֻחַת יָרָק, a meal of herbs, use the word for the plant that is food for a man. So Chazal call such a plant ירק, and the plural is ירקות.

The doubled form, יְרַקְרַק אוֹ אֲדַמְדָּם, greenish or reddish, is for a deep green; בִּירַקְרַק חָרוּץ is gold whose colour leans a little towards green, or else the word names the saffron shade. In another form, יֵרָקוֹן is the green a face turns when trouble comes on a man suddenly.

כרפס.sense: One of the colours, and they say it is green.

more.t: חוּר כַּרְפַּס וּתְכֵלֶת, white, karpas and techeiles: the word is one of the colours, and they say it is green.

צעף.sense: A veil, the wrap with which women cover their faces.

more.t: וַתְּכַס בַּצָּעִיף, she covered herself with the tzaif, and וַתָּסַר צְעִיפָהּ מֵעָלֶיהָ, she took her tzaif off herself: it is the wrap women put over their faces.

רדד.sense: Spreading and beating flat, as gold is beaten into plate, and so beating a people down under one; the redid is a wrap of the same word.

more.t: The noun מַעֲשֵׂה מוֹרָד is a matter of spreading and beating out, and the form with an object is וַיָּרֶד עַל־הַכְּרוּבִים וְעַל־הַתִּמֹרוֹת אֶת־הַזָּהָב, he beat the gold out over the keruvim and the palm figures. The Targum renders וַיְרַקְּעוּ אֶת־פַּחֵי הַזָּהָב, they beat out the plates of gold, with וְרַדִּידוּ יָת טַסֵּי דַהֲבָא.

הָרוֹדֵד עַמִּי תַחְתָּי, who beats my people down under me; and of the same root and the same matter is לְרַד־לְפָנָיו גּוֹיִם, to beat nations down before him, which is an infinitive of the simple form.
נָשְׂאוּ אֶת־רְדִידִי מֵעָלַי, they took my redid from me. The redidim are like veils or wraps, called in Arabic al-arda; and some explain them as the silk braids women make to bind up the head.

מה.sense: The question word for what a thing is; with a lamed it asks for what reason, and the word also magnifies, belittles, laments, and leaves a thing unsaid.

more.t: The word asks what a thing is or how it is: מַה־תָּאֳרוֹ, what is his appearance, and מַה־זֶּה מִהַרְתָּ לִמְצֹא בְּנִי, what is this, that you found it so quickly, my son. It does not ask after a living speaker; מִי is the word for that.

It sometimes stands for מָתַי, as עַד־מָה, until when. With a lamed it asks the reason: לָמָּה זֶּה שְׁלַחְתָּנִי, for what did you send me on this way. A shin may join the lamed, שַׁלָּמָה, and the lamed may drop away with the sense of 'for what' still standing.

more.h: A reading of Rabbi Yonah refused
more.t: Rabbi Yonah read לָמָה אֶשְׁכַּל גַּם־שְׁנֵיכֶם and its like as 'lest'. There is no reason for that reading: they mean what their fellows mean, for what reason, and לָמָה אֶשְׁכַּל is why would you want that I be bereaved.

The word magnifies a thing, מָה רַב טוּבְךָ, how great is your goodness, and equally belittles it, מָה־אֱנוֹשׁ כִּי־תִזְכְּרֶנּוּ, what is man that you remember him. Of Aharon, מַה־הוּא, what is he, carries that the complaint was really against one greater than he.

וִיהִי מָה אָרֻצָה, let be what will be, I will run, leaves the thing unsaid, and so וְיַעֲבֹר עָלַי מָה, let come upon me what may. In some places it is a cry of grief, מָה אֲמֻלָה לִבָּתֵךְ, how faint is your heart.

With a kaf it asks quantity, כַּמָּה יְמֵי שְׁנֵי חַיֶּיךָ, how many are the days of the years of your life; it also magnifies, זֶה כַּמֶּה שָׁנִים, meaning many years. אֵיךְ asks after the manner of a thing, כַּמָּה after the thing itself.

מדע.sense: Why: it asks the reason of a thing, and some read it as two words, what knowledge, from the root for knowing.

more.t: וּמַדּוּעַ תִּתְנַשְּׂאוּ, and why do you raise yourselves, is the word in its use, and it means what לָמָּה means. Some say it is two words, מַה דַּוּעַ, from יָדַע, to know: what knowledge is in this thing, what is its matter.

ידע.sense: Knowing, and also feeling or noticing a thing; the word covers a man knowing his wife, making a thing known, and the kinsman the family knows.

more.t: Beyond knowing, the word is used of feeling a thing in oneself: לֹא יָדַעְתִּי נַפְשִׁי שָׂמַתְנִי is that he did not feel it in himself until his soul set him there, and הַמַּעְתִּיק הָרִים וְלֹא יָדָעוּ is that the mountains did not feel it until He moved them.
וְהָאָדָם יָדַע אֶת־חַוָּה, and Adam knew Chava, and אֲשֶׁר לֹא־יָדְעוּ אִישׁ, who had not known a man: this too is knowing, one sense following on another.

דֵּעָה and דַּעַת are the knowledge itself. מַדָּע is thought: וּמְבִינֵי מַדָּע are those who understood what was in a man's heart from a slight hint, and בְּמַדָּעֲךָ is in your thought. Its root may be נָדַע, on the showing of the Aramaic מִנְדַּע תִּנְדַּע, or else יָדַע.
Because a near relative knows a man, the kinsman is called מוֹדָע, and מֹדַעְתָּנוּ is of our family, a mem of connection missing from the word.

Rabbi Yehuda put וַיֹּדַע בָּהֶם אֵת אַנְשֵׁי סֻכּוֹת in another sense, and Rabbi Yonah likewise, of breaking and destroying, and so וִידוּעַ חֹלִי, broken by sickness. There is no need to take these words out of the sense of knowing: he made their sin and their guilt known to them, and וִידוּעַ חֹלִי is one known and marked to all as a man of sicknesses.
Chazal explained יִדְּעֹנִי as one who puts the bone of a yadua in his mouth and it speaks of itself, and יָדוּעַ is the name of an animal.

הוֹדִיעוּ בָעַמִּים (Tehillim 105:1), make it known among the peoples, and הוֹדַע אֶת יְרוּשָׁלַם (Yechezkel 16:2), make known to Yerushalayim. וּמוֹדִיעִים לְהַלֵּל (Divrei HaYamim II 23:13) he explains of those who knew how to sing and to praise well and taught the rest of their brothers the Leviim.

לֹא נוֹדַע מִי הִכָּהוּ (Devarim 21:1), it was not known who struck him, and כִּי נוֹדַע דָּוִד (Shmuel I 22:6), which he reads as word getting out and spreading of where they were. On וּמְעַקֵּשׁ דְּרָכָיו יִוָּדֵעַ (Mishlei 10:9) he sets the halves of the pasuk against each other: whoever walks in innocence walks secure and fears no man, while one who twists his ways becomes known to men, cannot keep his evil deeds hidden from them and cannot be secure. וְאַחֲרֵי הִוָּדְעִי סָפַקְתִּי עַל יָרֵךְ (Yirmiyahu 31:18) is after he came to know himself and knew the evil deeds he had done, and so regretted them and struck upon his thigh.
מָה אָדָם וַתֵּדָעֵהוּ (Tehillim 144:3), what is man that You should know him, he glosses as Your watching over him and turning to his sin.

On יִוָּדַע כְּמֵבִיא לְמָעְלָה (Tehillim 74:5) his father has the building of the House in view: whoever brought an axe into the thicket of the cedars of Levanon to hew them for it was known as one bringing them up before the Throne of Glory, and now the gold carvings on its walls are hammered with axe and hatchet by those who profane the dwelling of Your Name. His father reads וְגָבֹהַּ מִמֶּרְחָק יְיֵדָע (Tehillim 138:6) of Hashem being high in heaven and seeing the low upon earth, knowing hidden things from afar and making them known to whom He wishes. And וַיֵּדַע אַלְמְנוֹתָיו וְעָרֵיהֶם הֶחֱרִיב (Yechezkel 19:7) his father takes as the knowing of a wife, as וַיֵּדַע אָדָם עוֹד אֶת אִשְׁתּוֹ (Bereishis 4:25): he killed the men and lay with their widows, and the laying waste of their cities is said of him not because he pulled the cities down with his hands but because what he did was the ruin of the world.

Rabbi Yonah reads לִמְנוֹת יָמֵינוּ כֵּן הוֹדַע (Tehillim 90:12) by that other sense, as chastening: chasten us according to the days of our life, a request that our chastening not be multiplied, our days being few. Radak answers that there is no need to take the words out of knowing. It is according to the number of our days, which are short and have shrunk from a thousand years to seventy, as the pasuk says יְמֵי שְׁנוֹתֵינוּ בָּהֶם שִׁבְעִים שָׁנָה, the days of our years in them are seventy years: help us in the learning of wisdom and make its ways known to us, and then we shall acquire a heart of wisdom.

אלם.sense: Binding sheaves; and being dumb, which is where the widow has her name, since she cannot speak up against those who contend with her.

more.t: מְאַלְּמִים אֲלֻמִּים is tying and bundling sheaves, and the noun is אֲלֻמֹּתָיו, his sheaves. אֵלֶם צֶדֶק תְּדַבֵּרוּן is from this sense, a word for a multitude, or else from the word for one who is dumb.
אִלֵּם is one who cannot speak, and כְּלָבִים אִלְּמִים are dumb dogs; נֶאֱלַמְתִּי דוּמִיָּה, I was struck dumb in silence, and תֵּאָלַמְנָה שִׂפְתֵי שָׁקֶר, let lying lips be struck dumb.

more.h: Why the widow is called so
more.t: Rabbi Yonah wrote well that a woman whose husband has died is called אלמנה from this, because she cannot speak and contend with those who contend with her; the nun is an addition. Of the same word are אַלְמָן, שְׁכוֹל וְאַלְמֹן, bereavement and widowhood, and אַלְמְנוּת.

In פְּלֹנִי אַלְמֹנִי, since his name is not spoken he is called אַלְמֹנִי; and פְּלֹנִי is from פָלָא, that his name is hidden. The other suggestion, that he had a wife and she died, is set aside, since a place whose name is not given is called so as well.
וְאוּלָם חַי־אָנִי and its like mean truly. הָאוּלָם is a building like a lean-to, or a vault, and the plural forms are וְאֵלַמָּיו and וְאֵלַמּוֹת.

Rabbi Yonah read בְּאַלְמְנוֹתָיו as ארמנותיו, his palaces. That is possible, but not by an interchange of lamed and resh, for only the letters אהו"י interchange. The straight reading is the plain one, from the widow: ruined cities are called widows, since a city full of people is like a wife and when ruined is like a widow.

כרמל.sense: The fresh ear of grain while still soft and moist; also a colour said to be scarlet, and land of fields and fruit trees, which is how the mountain got the name.

more.t: וְלֶחֶם וְקָלִי וְכַרְמֶל: the ear of grain is called כַּרְמֶל while it is soft and still moist. The Sifra reads the word as רַךְ מָל, soft and full; the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught כַּר מָלֵא, a cushion full of down, the ear being full like it.
His father takes it as two words. כר is as in כרים וכסתות, cushions and covers, in the language of Chazal, and מל as in מילתא, which is a garment of silk.
רֹאשֵׁךְ עָלַיִךְ כַּכַּרְמֶל is a colour, and they say it is the colour of שָׁנִי, scarlet; with a yud, וְכַרְמִיל וּתְכֵלֶת.

כַּרְמֶל is a name anywhere for a place of fruit trees and fields of grain, and the mountain in Eretz Yisrael is called so because it was such a place. The pesukim that turn Levanon into karmel and karmel into forest are a parable: those high now like the cedars of Levanon will be low like the trees of the karmel, and those low now will be raised, a prophecy about the kingdom of Chizkiyahu. In the other prophecy, midbar becomes karmel and karmel a forest, that Yisrael go up from level to level.

נשׁה.sense: Forgetting; and a second word, lending and claiming a debt, which names the creditor and the debtor alike.

more.t: נָשִׁיתִי טוֹבָה, I have forgotten good, and תֶּשִׁי, you forgot; לֹא תִנָּשֵׁנִי is that you will not be forgotten by Me. אֶרֶץ נְשִׁיָּה is the place of the dead, so called because they are forgotten.

לֹא־נָשִׁיתִי וְלֹא־נָשׁוּ־בִי is a doubled saying: I asked nothing of them and they gave me nothing of themselves; or I did not lend to them and they did not lend to me, the lender being bound with a bet and the borrower without one.

It is not far off that נֹשֶׁה names lender and borrower alike, the bond of the bet parting them, as the one word שובר is used of the buyer and of the seller. Where the bet is missing, as in וְכָל־אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר־לוֹ נֹשֶׁא, the matter shows which is meant.

more.h: Laying an obligation on a man
more.t: כִּי־תַשֶּׁה בְרֵעֲךָ מַשַּׁאת מְאוּמָה is lending your fellow a loan, and the form also carries imposing something on a man: וְנָשָׁא־בוֹ אָלָה is that the judge lays an oath on him, and לֹא־יַשִּׁא אוֹיֵב בּוֹ is that no enemy will be over him as a creditor who takes his money.

Chazal said גִּיד הַנָּשֶׁה is called so because it slipped from its place and went up, as though it forgot its place and turned from it. It would be right to take it as the sinew that is severed, from נָשְׁתָה גְבוּרָתָם, their might failed, save that he would rather join that word to the root נָשַׁת.
נָשִׁים, women, and נְשֵׁיהֶם, their women, are not treated here but under the root אָנַשׁ.

דמה.sense: Being like, and likening one thing to another; also cutting off and destruction, thinking a thing out, and silence.

more.t: לֹא־דָמָה אֵלָיו בְּיָפְיוֹ, none was like him in his beauty, and with an object, דָּמִיתִי בַּת־צִיּוֹן, I have likened the daughter of Tzion. The noun is דְּמוּת, a likeness.

אִמְּךָ כַגֶּפֶן בְּדָמְךָ is like בדמותך, in your likeness, or else the noun is of another form. Rav Hai wrote that the word is the moisture of nature, since whatever comes out of another thing and blossoms from it holds some of that thing's moisture.

וְדָמִיתִי אִמֶּךָ, I will destroy your mother, and נִדְמְתָה אַשְׁקְלֹון, Ashkelon is cut off, are destruction, and בִּדְמִי יָמַי is the noun of that sense. עֵינִי נִגְּרָה וְלֹא תִדְמֶה, my eye runs and does not stop, belongs here too.

וְהוּא לֹא־כֵן יְדַמֶּה is he will think, and so אַל־תְּדַמִּי בְנַפְשֵׁךְ, do not think in yourself. For דִּמִּינוּ אֱלֹהִים חַסְדֶּךָ he also offers the sense of hope and expectation, that we looked to Your kindness.

אַל־דֳּמִי־לָךְ, have no silence, and דוּמִיָּה, stillness, are all silence; לְךָ דֻמִיָּה תְהִלָּה is that praise falls silent before deeds too great for it. Some read נִדְמֵיתִי from this, that I was silenced and cannot speak.

אנשׁ.sense: Man, the name that takes in all mankind; and a second word, grievous pain and sickness, which may be why man is called by it.

more.t: אֱנוֹשׁ כֶּחָצִיר יָמָיו is the name that takes in all of mankind, and sometimes it is said of one man in particular, וְאַתָּה אֱנוֹשׁ כְּעֶרְכִּי, and you, a man of my own rank.

אֲנָשִׁים standing alone does not say whether great men or lowly are meant, and the pasuk settles it: כֻּלָּם אֲנָשִׁים is known to mean great men only from what follows, ראשי בני ישראל המה, they are the heads of Bnei Yisrael; and זָקֵן בָּא בַאֲנָשִׁים means old men.
אִשָּׁה may be of this root, the dagesh standing for a missing nun, properly אנשה; and for the women the alef falls away, נָשִׁים בְּקִרְבֵּךְ, women in your midst.

אָנוּשׁ חִצִּי בְלִי־פָשַׁע, my arrow is grievous without transgression, and כִּי אֲנוּשָׁה מַכּוֹתֶיהָ, her blows are grievous: all of them pain, breaking and heavy sickness, and by a borrowing an evil thing in the thought of the heart, עָקֹב הַלֵּב מִכֹּל וְאָנֻשׁ הוּא. It may be that man is called אֱנוֹשׁ for this, since all his days are pains.

ידד.sense: Beloved, and the love of one's soul; under the same letters, casting lots, on whose root the authorities differ.

more.t: יְדִיד is one who is loved and יְדִידִי my beloved, as מֶה לִידִידִי בְּבֵיתִי, what is my beloved doing in My house; מַה־יְּדִידוֹת מִשְׁכְּנוֹתֶיךָ, how beloved are your dwellings. The noun יְדִדוּת נַפְשִׁי is the love of my soul.
יַדּוּ גוֹרָל is they cast lots. Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yonah put its root as יָדַד; his father wrote that the root is יָדָה, as in וַיַּדּוּ־אֶבֶן בִּי, they cast a stone at me.

קוא.sense: Vomiting, and the vomit itself; the land too is said to vomit out those in it.

more.t: כַּאֲשֶׁר קָאָה, as it vomited; and with an object, וְלֹא־תָקִיא אֶתְכֶם הָאָרֶץ, that the land not vomit you out, and וַיָּקֵא אֶת־יוֹנָה, it vomited Yonah out.
קִיא צֹאָה is vomit and filth, and שָׁב עַל־קֵאוֹ is returning to its vomit. The word is compounded with קלון, disgrace, in וְקִיקָלוֹן עַל־כְּבוֹדֶךָ.

עלק.sense: The leech, the worm that breeds in rivers and sucks the blood of man and beast until it is full, and never says enough.

more.t: Rav Saadiah Gaon took לַעֲלוּקָה שְׁתֵּי בָנוֹת as a matter of privation. Among living things it is of two kinds, the passing of what exists, which is שְׁאוֹל, the grave, and the not coming to be of what is not, which is עֹצֶר רָחַם, a closed womb; and so in plants, ground that drinks and grows nothing, and fire that consumes what has grown.

The root of the word looks to be the one in the words of Chazal, סכנת עלוקה, the danger of the leech: the worm that grows in rivers and fastens on the feet of man and beast as they cross, sucking their blood until it is full and swollen and drops off. The pasuk likens its subject to the leech, which never says enough of blood.

חבת.sense: The pan the meal offering was made in. He had filed מַֽחֲבַת, a pan, under a root ending in heh; here he allows the tav may belong to the root.

more.h: Why the tav may be a root letter
more.t: עַֽל־ מַֽחֲבַת בַּשֶּׁמֶן (Vayikra 6:14), on a pan with oil, he had treated under a root ending in heh; but בֶּאֱמוּנָה עַל מַֽעֲשֵׂה הַֽחֲבִתִּֽים (Divrei HaYamim I 9:31), in trust over the making of the pan offerings, keeps the tav, and for that he allows it may be a root letter.

Chachamim speak of חבתי כהן גדול, the Kohen Gadol's pan offerings (Menachos 96a), whose kneading and shaping are done inside: he offered a tenth of an eifah in a pan every day, half in the morning and half in the evening, as זֶה קָרְבַּן אַֽהֲרֹן וּבָנָיו (Vayikra 6:13), this is the offering of Aharon and his sons.

נדר.sense: To vow. Of the sense he says only that it is known; the entry is five pesukim and a note that נֶדֶר, a vow, is pointed one way in five places and another in the rest.

more.t: כִּֽי־ נֵדֶר נָדַר עַבְדְּךָ (Shmuel II 15:8), for your servant vowed a vow; אִישׁ כִּֽי־ יִדֹּר נֶדֶר (Bamidbar 30:3), a man who vows a vow; וַיִּדַּר יַֽעֲקֹב נֶדֶר לֵאמֹר (Bereishis 28:20), and Yaakov vowed a vow, saying; וַיִּדְּרוּ נְדָרִֽים (Yonah 1:16), and they vowed vows; and וְכִי תֶחְדַּל לִנְדֹּר (Devarim 23:23), and if you refrain from vowing. Of all of them, ענינם ידוע, their sense is known.

נדב.sense: To give willingly, of a heart that moves a man to give; and the נָדִיב, the generous man, whose soul is broad to give of his own where it is fitting.

more.t: וענין הנדיבות ידוע, the sense of generosity is known: he is the man whose soul is broad to give of his own in the fitting place and in the measure that befits him. What moves him is his heart, אֲשֶׁר נָדַב לִבָּם אֹתָם (Shemos 35:29), whose heart moved them, and אֲשֶׁר יִדְּבֶנּוּ לִבּוֹ (Shemos 25:2), whom his heart moves.

more.h: The noble man and his qualities
more.t: וְנָדִיב נְדִיבוֹת יָעָץ (Yeshayahu 32:8), the noble man counsels noble things; כֹּל נְדִיב לֵב (Shemos 35:22), everyone generous of heart; לְהוֹשִׁיבִי עִם־ נְדִיבִים (Tehillim 113:8), to seat him with princes. In וְהוּא עַל־נְדִיבוֹת יָקֽוּם, the נְדִיבוֹת are noble qualities, and it is for their sake that he stands.

more.h: The freewill gift, and offering oneself
more.t: The noun is a gift given freely: גֶּשֶׁם נְדָבוֹת (Tehillim 68:10), a rain of bounty, and נִדְבוֹת פִּי רְצֵה (Tehillim 119:108), accept the freewill offerings of my mouth. Where a man offers himself, הַמִּֽתְנַדְּבִים בָּעָם (Shoftim 5:9), those who offered themselves among the people, and אֲנִי בְּיֹשֶׁר לְבָבִי הִתְנַדַּבְתִּי (Divrei HaYamim I 29:17), in the uprightness of my heart I have given willingly.

לְבַד עַל־כָּל־ הִתְנַדֵּֽב (Ezra 1:6), besides all that was freely offered, carries two particles where one would have done: either לְבַד, apart from, or עַל, over, would have sufficed on its own, and the second is added to make the sense plain. Lashon Hakodesh does this in many places, as הֲמִבְּלִי אֵין־קְבָרִים (Shemos 14:11), is it for want of there being no graves.

תִּרְדֹּף כָּרוּחַ נְדִֽבָתִי (Iyov 30:15), it pursues my nobility like the wind. He takes the word of the soul, as וְרוּחַ נְדִיבָה תִסְמְכֵֽנִי (Tehillim 51:14), let a willing spirit uphold me, since it is the soul that has nobility in it; or else of a high station that was due to come to him, as the pasuk goes on, וּכְעָב עָֽבְרָה יְשֻֽׁעָתִֽי, and my deliverance passed away like a cloud.

מלץ.sense: To be sweet on the palate: he glosses נִּמְלְצוּ as sweetened and forceful at once, the sweetness at its full strength. The words for a spokesman may belong here too.

more.t: מַה־ נִּמְלְצוּ לְחִכִּי אִמְרָתֶךָ (Tehillim 119:103), how sweet Your word is to my palate, he glosses מה נמתקו ומה נמרצו, how sweet they are and how forceful, meaning that the sweetness was at its full strength.

He allows that מְלִיצָה may be of this root, and with it בִּמְלִיצֵי שָׂרֵי בָבֶל (Divrei HaYamim II 32:31), with the spokesmen of the princes of Bavel, and וּמְלִיצֶיךָ פָּשְׁעוּ בִֽי (Yeshayahu 43:27), and your spokesmen rebelled against Me; מליצי and מְלִיצֶיךָ would then stand to it as שָֹרֵי, the princes of, and שָֹרֶיךָ, your princes, stand to theirs.

לוץ.sense: To scoff, the לֵץ being the scoffer; and in another sense to put a case, the מֵלִיץ being the one who sets out the matter and the plea for it.

more.t: וְלַצְתָּ לְֽבַדְּךָ תִשָּֽׂא (Mishlei 9:12), if you scoff, you alone will bear it; אִם־לַלֵּצִים הוּא יָלִיץ (Mishlei 3:34), if it is the scorners, He scorns them; זֵדִים הֱלִיצֻנִי (Tehillim 119:51), the insolent have scorned me; and וְעַתָּה אַל־ תִּתְלוֹצָצוּ (Yeshayahu 28:22), and now do not scoff. Of the thing itself he says only ענין הליצנות ידוע, the sense of scoffing is known.

לֵץ תַּכֶּה וּפֶתִי יַעְרִם (Mishlei 19:25), strike a scoffer and the simple grows shrewd; זֵד יָהִיר לֵץ שְׁמוֹ (Mishlei 21:24), proud and haughty, scoffer is his name. לֵץ הַיַּין (Mishlei 20:1) he reads as the man who drinks the wine.
מָשַׁךְ יָדוֹ אֶת־ לֹֽצְצִֽים (Hoshea 7:5), he stretched out his hand with scoffers. The word is a noun and not a verb, for a verb shaped so would have to come from a root whose last letter doubles.

כִּי הַמֵּלִיץ בֵּֽינֹתָֽם (Bereishis 42:23), for the go-between was between them; אִם־יֵשׁ עָלָיו מַלְאָךְ מֵלִיץ (Iyov 33:23), if there is an angel to speak for him; מְלִיצַי רֵעָי (Iyov 16:20), my friends are the ones who plead for me; אֱוִלִים יָלִיץ אָשָׁם (Mishlei 14:9); and the noun לְהָבִין מָשָׁל וּמְלִיצָה (Mishlei 1:6), to understand a parable and a saying. Of all of them: ענינם תוכן הדבר והטענה, their sense is the substance of the matter and the plea made for it.

עֵד בְּלִיַּעַל יָלִיץ מִשְׁפָּט (Mishlei 19:28): the worthless witness dresses his testimony up in his best words, and false though it is, sets it out in judgment as though it were true. So the pasuk goes on, וּפִי רְשָׁעִים יְבַלַּע־אָֽוֶן, the mouth of the wicked swallows iniquity, that is, he covers the lie over with his finest arguments.

לוז.sense: To turn aside, and so to be crooked; and separately the לוּז, a tree, which Rav Saadiah Gaon takes for the almond.

more.t: אַל־ יָלֻזוּ מֵעֵינֶיךָ נְצֹר תֻּשִׁיָּה (Mishlei 3:21), which he glosses as let them not depart and not turn away from before your eyes; and again אַל־ יַלִּיזוּ מֵֽעֵינֶיךָ שָׁמְרֵם בְּתוֹךְ לְבָבֶֽךָ (Mishlei 4:21), let them not slip from your eyes, keep them within your heart, where the dagesh stands in place of a quiescent letter, as in וַיַּלִּינוּ (Bamidbar 14:36).

The one who turns aside is crooked: נָלוֹז (Mishlei 3:32) is an abomination to Hashem, and וּנְלוֹזִים בְּמַעְגְּלוֹתָֽם (Mishlei 2:15), crooked in their paths. וַתִּבְטְחוּ בְּעֹשֶׁק וְנָלוֹז (Yeshayahu 30:12), you trusted in oppression, he reads as trust in a crooked thing, that is, in bent judgment, on the model of וְהָעִיר מָֽלְאָה מֻטֶּה (Yechezkel 9:9), the city is full of perversion. Rabbi Yonah takes וְנָלוֹז there as a noun.

more.h: A word from a neighbouring root
more.t: From the same sense he takes the noun in וּלְזוּת שְׂפָתַיִם הַרְחֵק מִמֶּֽךָּ (Mishlei 4:24), put crookedness of lips far from you, which he files under a root of its own.

more.h: The tree, and whether it is the almond
more.t: וְלוּז (Bereishis 30:37) is a tree, the one the vernacular calls avellanier. Rav Saadiah Gaon explained it as שְׁקֵדִים, almonds, because that is their name in the language of Yishmael, and the Targum Yerushalmi renders שְׁקֵדִֽים (Bamidbar 17:23), almonds, by the plural of this word.

שׁקד.sense: To be quick and constant at a thing, to watch over it; the שָׁקֵד, the almond, carries the name because its tree is the first to blossom.

more.t: שָׁוְא שָׁקַד שׁוֹמֵֽר (Tehillim 127:1), in vain the watchman keeps watch; נָמֵר שֹׁקֵד עַל־עָרֵיהֶם (Yirmiyahu 5:6), a leopard watching over their cities; לִשְׁקֹד עַל־דַּלְתֹתַי (Mishlei 8:34), to watch at my doors; וְנִכְרְתוּ כָּל־ שֹׁקְדֵי אָֽוֶן (Yeshayahu 29:20), all who are quick after iniquity will be cut off; שִׁקְדוּ וְשִׁמְרוּ (Ezra 8:29), be watchful and guard them. The sense, he says, is ענין המהירות וההשתדלות וההתמדה על הדבר, speed, effort, and staying constantly at the thing.

more.h: Why the almond carries the name
more.t: וּשְׁקֵדִֽים (Bereishis 43:11), and almonds, and וַיִּגְמֹל שְׁקֵדִֽים (Bamidbar 17:23), it ripened almonds, he calls known; but the name is taken from the first sense, because the almond tree hastens to blossom before the other trees. So with מַקֵּל שָׁקֵד (Yirmiyahu 1:11), an almond rod, and the answer given to it, הֵיטַבְתָּ לִרְאוֹת כִּֽי־ שֹׁקֵד אֲנִי עַל־דְּבָרִי (Yirmiyahu 1:12), you have seen well, for I am watchful over My word.
שְׁלֹשָׁה גְבִעִים מְשֻׁקָּדִים (Shemos 25:33), three cups made almond-shaped, which he glosses as carved in the likeness of almonds.
וְיָנֵאץ הַשָּׁקֵד (Koheles 12:5), the almond blossoms, he takes by way of figure for white hair, which is white like the almond's blossom.

more.h: Two other readings of that pasuk
more.t: Some read הַשָּׁקֵד there as the member of intercourse, and then וְיָנֵאץ is like וַיִנְאַץ בְּזַֽעַם־אַפּוֹ (Eichah 2:6), He spurned in the heat of His anger: a man comes to loathe the bed out of his weakness, as the pasuk goes on, וְתָפֵר הָֽאֲבִיּוֹנָה, and desire fails. Chachamim (Shabbos 152a) read it as the bone above the buttocks, and then וְיָנֵאץ is its growing large, for it stands out in old age as the flesh wastes and the moisture dries.

שֹקד.sense: Bound or joined: so he takes נִשְׂקַד עֹל פְּשָׁעַי (Eichah 1:14), the yoke of my transgressions is bound fast, from what its place requires.

more.t: One pasuk, whose sense in its place is bound or joined. Vayikra Rabbah takes Hashem's promise to teach a man as a promise to stay bound to him, as the goad stays always by the cow to drive her, meaning I shall be with you always to lead you. Rabbeinu Hai brought a further proof for the sense from the language of Chachamim.

כסא.sense: A throne or a seat, the heavens being called Hashem's throne; and separately הַכֶּסֶא, a set time, whose heh stands in place of an alef.

more.t: כִּסֵּא כָבוֹד (Yirmiyahu 17:12), a throne of glory; הַיֹּשֵׁב עַל־ כִּסְאוֹ (Shemos 11:5), the one who sits on his throne; הַשָּׁמַיִם כִּסְאִי (Yeshayahu 66:1), the heavens are My throne. The plural is feminine, כִסְאוֹת לְמִשְׁפָּט כִּסְאוֹת לְבֵית דָּוִֽד (Tehillim 122:5), thrones for judgment, thrones of the house of David. Where Shlomo sat on Hashem's throne (Divrei HaYamim I 29:23), he means for judgment, since judgment belongs to Hashem.

more.h: Written with a heh, and shortened
more.t: שֵׁשׁ מַֽעֲלוֹת לַכִּסֵּה (Melachim I 10:19), six steps to the throne, and וְרֹאשׁ־עָגֹל לַכִּסֵּה, the top of the throne round behind, are written with a heh. In Shemos 17:16 the word stands as כֵּס, a throne, without its alef, because it joined to the name after it and the two became one word.

more.h: Grasping the face of the throne
more.t: מְאַחֵז פְּנֵי־ כִסֵּה (Iyov 26:9): Hashem holds fast the face of the heavens, which are called a throne, that is, by His power they stand, and He spreads His cloud over them.

לְיוֹם הַכֶּסֶא יָבֹא בֵיתֽוֹ (Mishlei 7:20), at the appointed day he will come home, where the word is a set time; and so בַּכֵּסֶה לְיוֹם חַגֵּֽנוּ (Tehillim 81:4), at the appointed time for our festival day. The heh stands in place of an alef.

כרשֹ.sense: The belly: מִלָּא כְרֵשֹׂו מֵֽעֲדָנָי (Yirmiyahu 51:34), he filled his belly with my delicacies. The word, he says, is known from the language of Chachamim.

more.t: One pasuk, and the word as Chachamim use it (Chullin 42a), where they speak of the inner כרס, the belly, being pierced, or most of the outer one torn, and much else besides.

ילד.sense: To bear a child, and to beget; the יֶלֶד is the child, and תולדות is sometimes a man's offspring and sometimes what befell him.

more.t: The lighter form is used of the woman and the heavier of the man, for the most part: וְיָֽלְדָה ־לּוֹ בָנִים אוֹ בָנוֹת (Shemos 21:4), she bears him sons or daughters, against וְהוֹלִיד בֵּן־פָּרִיץ (Yechezkel 18:10), he begets a violent son. Sometimes the lighter form is used of the man too, וְכוּשׁ יָלַד (Bereishis 10:8) and שְׁמַע לְאָבִיךָ זֶה יְלָדֶךָ (Mishlei 23:22), listen to your father who begot you. אֲנִי הַיּוֹם יְלִדְתִּֽיךָ (Tehillim 2:7), today I have borne you, he reads as though today I bore you for a king.

The male child is יֶלֶד, הַיֶּלֶד אֵינֶנּוּ (Bereishis 37:30), the boy is gone; the female קַח־לִי אֶת־ הַיַּלְדָּה הַזֹּאת (Bereishis 34:4), take me this girl. With a vav for the yud, אֵין לָהּ וָלָֽד (Bereishis 11:30), she had no child; and in another pattern יְלִיד בָּיִת (Bereishis 17:12), one born in the house. The days of childhood are יַלְדוּת, כִּֽי־ הַיַּלְדוּת וְהַֽשַּֽׁחֲרוּת הָֽבֶל (Koheles 11:10), for childhood and youth are vanity.

more.h: The midwife, and the day of birth
more.t: הַֽמְיַלֶּדֶת (Bereishis 38:28) is the midwife, so called because she helps the woman in labour to give birth. יוֹם הֻלֶּדֶת אֶת־פַּרְעֹה (Bereishis 40:20) is either the day a son was born to Pharaoh, or the day he himself was born, on which he made a feast every year.

more.h: Born in the house or outside it
more.t: מוֹלֶדֶת בַּיִת אוֹ מוֹלֶדֶת חוּץ (Vayikra 18:9) is best taken as an adjective. By the plain sense it explains the daughter of your father or the daughter of your mother: born to your father from another woman, which is מוֹלֶדֶת בַּיִת, or born to your mother from another man, which is מוֹלֶדֶת חוּץ, and so Onkelos renders it. Chachamim expounded it (Yevamos 23a) of whether your father is told to keep her mother or to send her away, as with the daughter of a mamzeres or of a nesinah.

more.h: What a day gives birth to
more.t: Because time gives birth to what happens, the events of time are called its children: כִּי לֹא־תֵדַע מַה־ יֵּלֶד יֽוֹם (Mishlei 27:1), you do not know what a day will bring forth. So אֵלֶּה תֹּֽלְדוֹת יַֽעֲקֹב (Bereishis 37:2) is what befell Yaakov in the matter of Yosef and the cause of his going down to Mitzrayim, while אֵלֶּה תּֽוֹלְדֹת נֹחַ (Bereishis 6:9) takes in his children and what befell him both. Wherever the word stands, its place shows which of the two is meant.

Because the heart gives birth to thoughts, its thoughts and counsels are called its children: וּבְיַלְדֵי נָכְרִים יַשְׂפִּֽיקוּ (Yeshayahu 2:6). Some read that of men contenting themselves with outside wisdoms and busying themselves with those rather than with the statutes of Hashem and His Torah, and others of idols made new every day.

טלא.sense: Marked with broad spots, and so a patch; and the טָלֶה, the lamb, which he holds belongs here too, since its plural is written with an alef.

more.t: נָקֹד וְטָלוּא בָּֽעִזִּים (Bereishis 30:33), speckled and spotted among the goats, and הָֽעֲקֻדִּים וְהַטְּלֻאִים (Bereishis 30:35), the streaked and the spotted. טָלוּא marks the large spots, while נָקֹד marks the small ones, dots upon dots; the spotted one is the one whose spots are broad.

וּנְעָלוֹת בָּלוֹת וּמְטֻלָּאוֹת (Yehoshua 9:5), worn and patched shoes: mended with pieces of leather set on where they wore through. Chachamim say of a piece of leather טלאי על גבי טלאי, patch upon patch (Shabbos 114a), and of a piece of cloth מטלית, a rag (Niddah 56a). So too וַתַּֽעֲשִׂי־לָךְ בָּמוֹת טְלֻאוֹת (Yechezkel 16:16), which he takes as garments of many colours, the patches of colour being like pieces.

more.h: Why the lamb belongs to this root
more.t: זְאֵב וְטָלֶה (Yeshayahu 65:25), wolf and lamb, and טְלֵה חָלָב אֶחָד (Shmuel I 7:9), one suckling lamb, are written with a heh, but the plural has an alef, בִּזְרֹעוֹ יְקַבֵּץ טְלָאִים (Yeshayahu 40:11), He gathers lambs in His arm. By rule the last root letter of טְלָאִים should carry a tzeirei, as in צָמֵא צְמֵאִים, thirsty, and טָמֵא טְמֵאִים, unclean; it carries a kamatz instead, as נְכָאִֽים (Yeshayahu 16:7) does beside נְכֵה רַגְלָיִם (Shmuel II 4:4), stricken in his feet. טְלֵה חָלָב he explains as one still sucking milk that had not yet eaten grass, and that is the choicest.

more.h: Against a root ending in heh
more.t: One might hold the root ends in heh and that the alef of טְלָאִים replaces a yud, as the alef does in וְעַמִּי תְלוּאִים (Hoshea 11:7); he calls that far-fetched. The root with alef is found in many words and with heh is not found at all, and a root ending in heh would have given the plural טָלִים, lambs, as קָנֶה, a reed, gives קָנִים, reeds.

וַֽיִּפְקְדֵם בַּטְּלָאִים (Shmuel I 15:4), he mustered them with the lambs. Chachamim (Yoma 22b) took the word as a place name; the right reading, he holds, is the plain one, from the lamb: he knew their number because each man brought a lamb, the season being Pesach. So Targum Yonasan renders it בְּאִימְרֵי פִסְחַיָא, with the Pesach lambs.

קור.sense: To come to the source of water: מְקוֹר מַֽיִם־חַיִּים, a spring of living water; and from the same root the spider's web.

more.t: On אֲנִי קַרְתִּי וְשָׁתִיתִי מַיִם (Melachim II 19:24), he takes the verb as having come as far as the source: the speaker drank all the waters of the rivers and the streams until he came to their springs and drank their water. Targum Yonasan renders it as digging wells and drinking water.

more.h: The spring, and making water flow
more.t: מְקוֹר מַֽיִם־חַיִּים (Yirmiyahu 2:13), a spring of living water; and as a well makes its waters flow (Yirmiyahu 6:7), so כֵּן הֵקֵרָה רָעָתָהּ, she makes her evil flow.

וְקוּרֵי עַכָּבִישׁ יֶאֱרֹגוּ (Yeshayahu 59:5), they weave spiders' webs, and קֽוּרֵיהֶם לֹא־יִהְיוּ לְבֶגֶד (Yeshayahu 59:6), their webs will not serve for a garment; he glosses them as sheets. His father takes them from קֹרוֹת בָּתֵּינוּ (Shir HaShirim 1:17), the beams of our houses: the spider weaves a covering as the beams cover a house.

צנן.sense: Coldness, as the cold of snow in harvest; and in other senses a thorn, and the צִנָּה, the long shield carried before a warrior.

more.t: כְּצִנַּת ־שֶׁלֶג בְּיוֹם קָצִיר (Mishlei 25:13), like the cold of snow in the day of harvest. Chachamim use the doubled form of it, of hot food put into cold so that it should not cool (Pesachim 76a), and of separating from the warm for the cold and from the cold for the warm (Demai 5:6).

וְלִצְנִינִם בְּצִדֵּיכֶם (Bamidbar 33:55), and for thorns in your sides, and וְלִצְנִנִים בְּעֵֽינֵיכֶם (Yehoshua 23:13), and for thorns in your eyes: the sense is a thorn, explained as a hedge of thorns set round about to shut you in, so that none goes out and none comes in; or else it is a figure, like לְשִׂכִּים בְּעֵינֵיכֶם (Bamidbar 33:55), for pricks in your eyes.

וְאֶל־ מִצִּנִּים יִקָּחֵהוּ (Iyov 5:5), and the thorns take it away, and צִנִּים פַּחִים בְּדֶרֶךְ עִקֵּשׁ (Mishlei 22:5), thorns and snares in the crooked way; and in the feminine וְנִשָּׂא אֶתְכֶם בְּצִנּוֹת (Amos 4:2). The Mishlei phrase may also be read from the cold: the cold is like snares in a crooked way.

וְנֹשֵׂא הַצִּנָּה הֹלֵךְ לְפָנָֽיו (Shmuel I 17:7), the bearer of the shield went before him; עֹֽרְכֵי צִנָּה וָרֹמַח (Divrei HaYamim I 12:8), men handling shield and spear; צִנָּה וְֽסֹחֵרָה אֲמִתּֽוֹ (Tehillim 91:4), His truth is a shield and a buckler; and the plural צִנּוֹת וּרְמָחִים (Divrei HaYamim II 11:12), shields and spears. It is a weapon of war like a shield, targa in the vernacular and al-daraqa in Arabic.

וְנִשָּׂא אֶתְכֶם בְּצִנּוֹת (Amos 4:2) may belong here as well: the small boats made in the shape of a shield. Chachamim read the rest of that pasuk so (Bava Basra 73a), that Sumchos, being of Eretz Yisrael, calls a ship's dinghy by the word the pasuk uses. Targum Yonasan takes בְּצִנּוֹת from the shield: the nations will carry you off on their shields, and your daughters in fishermen's boats.

כרת.sense: To cut; to cut a covenant, which is to make one; and in the passive to be cut off from among the people.

more.t: וַיִּכְרְתוּ בְרִית בִּבְאֵר שָׁבַע (Bereishis 21:32), they made a covenant at Be'er Sheva; הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי כֹּרֵת בְּרִית (Shemos 34:10), I am making a covenant; כְּרָת ־לָנוּ בְרִית (Shmuel I 11:1), make a covenant with us; and אָלוֹת שָׁוְא כָּרֹת בְּרִית (Hoshea 10:4), swearing falsely in making a covenant. From the same cutting comes סֵפֶר כְּרִיתֻת, a bill of divorce, and its plural, וָאֶתֵּן אֶת־סֵפֶר כְּרִֽיתֻתֶיהָ אֵלֶיהָ (Yirmiyahu 3:8), I gave her her bill of divorce.

more.h: A dispute over one word in Yirmiyahu
more.t: In כָּֽרְתוּ יַעְרָהּ (Yirmiyahu 46:23) some read the word as a command, cut down her forest; others read it as a past with a pause on the first letter, and the accurate books have a ga'ya there. That, he holds, is the right one, and the past stands for a future, יִכְרְתוּ יַעְרָהּ, they will cut down her forest, as Scripture does in many places and most of all in prophecy. That נְאֻם, the declaration, should follow a past verb is not the way of prophecy either, but יָֽרְדוּ לַטָּבַח (Yirmiyahu 48:15), they have gone down to the slaughter, is one like it, and so in words of rebuke, כֻּלְּכֶם פְּשַׁעְתֶּם בִּי (Yirmiyahu 2:29), all of you have rebelled against Me.

more.h: Being cut off, and cutting off
more.t: וְנִכְרַת מֵֽעַמָּֽיו (Shemos 30:33), he is cut off from his people; וְנִכְרְתָה הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַהִוא (Vayikra 7:20), that soul is cut off; הִכָּרֵת תִּכָּרֵת (Bamidbar 15:31), it is surely cut off; אַֽחֲרִית רְשָׁעִים נִכְרָֽתָה (Tehillim 37:38), the end of the wicked is cut off. Where another does the cutting, וְהִכְרַתִּי לְאַחְאָב (Melachim II 9:8), I will cut off from Achav, and לְהַכְרִית הַֽצְפַרְדְּעִים (Shemos 8:5), to cut off the frogs. וְלוֹא נַכְרִית מֵהַבְּהֵמָֽה (Melachim I 18:5) he reads as not cutting the city off from its beasts.
וּכְרוּת שָׁפְכָה he explains as one whose member is cut, so that it no longer shoots the seed out like an arrow in a stream but pours and dribbles, and he does not beget.

וְהַכְּרֵתִי וְהַפְּלֵתִי (Melachim I 1:38) were two families in Israel whose name was so, and Targum Yonasan renders them as archers and slingers. But נֶגֶב הַכְּרֵתִי (Shmuel I 30:14), the Negev of the Kereisi, is of the Pelishtim, as it says of them גּוֹי כְּרֵתִים (Tzefaniah 2:5), the nation of the Kereisim.
כְּרֻתֹת אֲרָזִֽים (Melachim I 6:36), which he explains as beams of cedar, cut and well hewn; and כִּרְתוּ עֵצָה (Yirmiyahu 6:6), cut down timber, has a chirik under its first root letter.

ערר.sense: Childless: the עֲרִירִי is a man alone, with no children.

more.t: וְאָֽנֹכִי הוֹלֵךְ עֲרִירִי (Bereishis 15:2), and I go childless, which he glosses as alone, without children, and so כִּתְבוּ אֶת־הָאִישׁ הַזֶּה עֲרִירִי (Yirmiyahu 22:30), write this man down childless. On עֲרִירִים יִֽהְיֽוּ (Vayikra 20:21) Chachamim said (Yevamos 55a) that even if he has children he buries them and is left without them; עֲרִירִים יָמֻֽתוּ (Vayikra 20:20) is that they will have no children.

חשֹך.sense: To hold back, to withhold or to spare: וְלֹֽא־ חָשַׂךְ מִמֶּנִּי מְאוּמָה, he withheld nothing from me.

more.t: וְלֹֽא־ חָשַׂךְ מִמֶּנִּי מְאוּמָה (Bereishis 39:9), he withheld nothing from me; וְאֶת־עַבְדּוֹ חָשַׂךְ מֵֽרָעָה (Shmuel I 25:39), He kept His servant back from evil; גַּם מִזֵּדִים חֲשׂךְ עַבְדֶּךָ (Tehillim 19:14), keep Your servant back from the insolent; וְחוֹשֵׂךְ שְׂפָתָיו מַשְׂכִּֽיל (Mishlei 10:19), the one who holds his lips back is wise. מֻרְדָּף בְּלִי חָשָֽׂךְ (Yeshayahu 14:6) he reads as a pursuer who did not hold himself back from pursuing. All of them, he says, are the sense of holding back.

קְרָא בְגָרוֹן אַל־ תַּחְשֹׂךְ (Yeshayahu 58:1), call out and do not hold back, means do not hold the call back, and וְצַדִּיק יִתֵּן וְלֹא יַחְשֹֽׂךְ (Mishlei 21:26), the righteous gives and does not hold back, means he does not hold the gift back: all of these carry an object. But וְנִיד שְׂפָתַי יַחְשֹֽׂךְ (Iyov 15:5) looks to him like a verb that stands on its own. חָשַׂכְתָּֽ לְמַטָּה מֵֽעֲוֹנֵנוּ (Ezra 9:13) he reads as having held back from bringing us low and from repaying us as our sins deserved.

וּבִתְחַפְנְחֵס חָשַׂךְ הַיּוֹם (Yechezkel 30:18). Rabbi Yonah read חָשַׂךְ here as the sun going dark; but such an exchange of letters, he says, is not found in Lashon Hakodesh, and the word means what it says, holding back, with a word left unsaid, אוֹרוֹ, its light: the day held its light back. He says it of the greatness of the trouble that was to come upon them.

חשׁך.sense: To grow dark; חשֶׁךְ is darkness and מַחְשָׁךְ a dark place, and the חֲשֻׁכִּֽים are the low among men, who sit in the dark.

more.t: חָשַׁךְ הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ בְּצֵאתוֹ (Yeshayahu 13:10), the sun is darkened as it goes forth; וַתֶּחְשַׁךְ הָאָרֶץ (Shemos 10:15), the land was darkened; וְחָשְׁכָה לָכֶם מִקְּסֹם (Michah 3:6), it will be dark for you, with no divining; and תֶּחְשַׁכְנָה עֵינֵיהֶם מֵרְאוֹת (Tehillim 69:24), let their eyes grow too dark to see.

וְחשֶׁךְ עַל־פְּנֵי תְהוֹם (Bereishis 1:2), darkness on the face of the deep, and יַגִּיהַּ חָשְׁכִּֽי (Tehillim 18:29), He lights up my darkness. With a mem added, וְהָיָה בְמַחְשָׁךְ מַֽעֲשֵׂיהֶם (Yeshayahu 29:15), their deeds are in the dark, and מְֽיֻדָּעַי מַחְשָֽׁךְ (Tehillim 88:19), which he reads as my friends being as though in a dark place, where I cannot see them and they do not come to visit me in my illness. Also בְּמַֽחֲשַׁכִּים הוֹשִׁיבַנִי (Eichah 3:6), He has set me in dark places, כַּֽחֲשֵׁיכָה כָּאוֹרָֽה (Tehillim 139:12), the dark as the light, and the construct חֶֽשְׁכַת ־מַיִם (Tehillim 18:12), a darkness of waters.

כִּי־מָלְאוּ מַֽחֲשַׁכֵּי ־אֶרֶץ (Tehillim 74:20), the dark places of the land are full: these are the lowly of men, who sit in the dark. So בַּל־יִתְיַצֵּב לִפְנֵי חֲשֻׁכִּֽים (Mishlei 22:29), he will not stand before mean men, where the word is an adjective on the pattern of עֲרֻמִּים, naked; and the masculine plural אֲשֶׁר הָלַךְ חֲשֵׁכִים (Yeshayahu 50:10), who has walked in darkness. The Targum bears it out, rendering הָעָם הַדַּלִּים (Yirmiyahu 39:10), the poor of the people, with a word of this root, and rendering דַּלּוֹת וְרָעוֹת (Bereishis 41:19), lean and ill favoured, in the same way.

גַּם־חשֶׁךְ לֹֽא־ יַחְשִׁיךְ מִמֶּךָ (Tehillim 139:12), even darkness is not dark to You, which he reads as its not darkening anything from You; שָׁלַֽח חשֶׁךְ וַיַּחְשִׁךְ (Tehillim 105:28), He sent darkness and made it dark; and בְּטֶרֶם יַחְשִׁךְ (Yirmiyahu 13:16), before it grows dark.

פרעשׁ.sense: The flea, whose sense he calls known; David names himself one before the king, for how slight and weak he is.

more.h: A flea, and why David says it
more.t: אַֽחֲרֵי פַּרְעֹשׁ אֶחָֽד (Shmuel I 24:15), after a single flea, which he says is a known word. For his slightness and his weakness against the king, he explains, David called himself a dog and a flea. Targum Yonasan renders the words בָּתַר חֲלַשׁ חָד, after one weak man, and again הֶדְיוֹט חָד, one common man; and at לְבַקֵּשׁ אֶת פַּרְעֹשׁ אֶחָד (Shmuel I 26:20), to seek a single flea, he renders יַת חֲלָשׁ חַד, the one weak man. It is also a man's name (Ezra 2:3).

קרן.sense: A horn; and by figure, strength. The same word is a corner of the mizbeach, and in another sense a shining of light.

more.t: רָמָה קַרְנִי (Shmuel I 2:1), my horn is lifted, and וְיָרֵם קֶרֶן מְשִׁיחוֹ (Shmuel I 2:10), He will raise the horn of His anointed; וְכָל קַרְנֵי רְשָׁעִים אֲגַדֵּעַ (Tehillim 75:11), I will cut off all the horns of the wicked, he marks as a figure. The sense in all of them is might.

more.h: His father on the sprouting horn
more.t: אַצְמִיחַ קֶרֶן לְבֵית יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yechezkel 29:21), I will make a horn sprout for the house of Yisrael, his father sets inside the seventy years that the kingdom of Nevuchadnetzar, his son and his son's son stood. The horn is Koresh, born fifty years from the exile, the fifty of עַד מָשִׁיחַ נָגִיד שָׁבֻעִים שִׁבְעָה (Daniel 9:25), seven weeks until an anointed leader. He is called a horn as the pasuk says לִמְשִׁיחוֹ לְכוֹרֶשׁ (Yeshayahu 45:1), to His anointed, to Koresh, for by him they came out of exile.

עַל קַרְנֹת הַמִּזְבֵּחַ (Shemos 29:12), on the corners of the mizbeach, and וְעָשִׂיתָ קַרְנֹתָיו (Shemos 27:2), you shall make its corners: these are angles, and in the vernacular too a corner is named by the word for a horn.

כִּי קָרַן עוֹר פְּנֵי מֹשֶׁה (Shemos 34:35), the skin of Moshe's face shone, is another sense, and so קַרְנַיִם מִיָּדוֹ לוֹ (Chavakuk 3:4), rays from His hand. He holds it near the first: a man who looks hard at the sun or at any light sees the brightness make horns. From this also וְעֹלַלְתִּי בֶעָפָר קַרְנִי (Iyov 16:15), my brightness and my honour laid in the dust.

חצר.sense: A courtyard; also the unwalled villages that are like one, grass of the field, and the leek. In another use, to sound the trumpets.

more.t: At Divrei HaYamim II 5:13 and 5:12 the word is those who blow the trumpets, standing beside the singers. The tzadi in the verb is doubled because it is doubled in חֲצֹצְרוֹת, trumpets.

הֶחָצֵר הַפְּנִימִית (Yechezkel 10:3), the inner court, and הֶחָצֵר הַחִיצֹנָה (Yechezkel 10:5), the outer. Most of them are feminine, but some are masculine: הֶחָצֵר הַפְּנִימִי (Yechezkel 40:19), and בֶּחָצֵר הָעֶלְיוֹן (Yirmiyahu 36:10), in the upper court. The plural is both בְּחַצְרוֹת בֵּית (Tehillim 116:19), in the courts of the house, and רְמֹס חֲצֵרָי (Yeshayahu 1:12), to trample My courts.

וּבָתֵּי הַחֲצֵרִים (Vayikra 25:31), the houses of the villages, בְּחַצְרֵיהֶם וּבְטִירֹתָם (Bereishis 25:16), in their villages and encampments, and חֲצֵרִים תֵּשֵׁב קֵדָר (Yeshayahu 42:11), the villages where Kedar dwells: these are the hamlets and open places with no wall around them, being like a courtyard. So too חָצִיר לִבְנוֹת יַעֲנָה (Yeshayahu 34:13) and חָצִיר לְקָנֶה וָגֹמֶא (Yeshayahu 35:7), which he takes in the sense of a courtyard.

חָצִיר כַּבָּקָר יֹאכֵל (Iyov 40:15), he eats grass like an ox, and מַצְמִיחַ חָצִיר לַבְּהֵמָה (Tehillim 104:14), who makes grass grow for the cattle: herbage. Rabbi Yonah takes וְצָמְחוּ בְּבֵין חָצִיר (Yeshayahu 44:4) in the first sense instead, as a courtyard. And וְאֶת הֶחָצִיר וְאֶת הַבְּצָלִים (Bamidbar 11:5), the leeks and the onions, is what Chazal call כרתי, the leek, and Targum Yonasan renders it so as well.

מנע.sense: To withhold a thing, to keep it back from someone; and in the passive, to be withheld.

more.t: אֲשֶׁר מָנַע מִמֵּךְ פְּרִי בָטֶן (Bereishis 30:2), who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb; לֹא יִמְנַע טוֹב לַהֹלְכִים בְּתָמִים (Tehillim 84:12), He withholds no good from those who walk whole; מֹנֵעַ בָּר יִקְּבֻהוּ לְאוֹם (Mishlei 11:26), the people curse one who withholds grain; וָאֶמְנַע נַהֲרוֹתֶיהָ (Yechezkel 31:15), I held back its rivers.

כִּי נִמְנַע מִבֵּית אֱלֹהֵיכֶם (Yoel 1:13), it is withheld from the house of your God, and וַיִּמָּנְעוּ רְבִבִים (Yirmiyahu 3:3), the showers were withheld. His ruling on the whole root is one line: the sense of withholding is known.

כלא.sense: To hold a thing back or shut it in; from it the prison, the sheepfold, and the forbidden mixtures.

more.t: כָּלְאוּ שָׁמַיִם מִטָּל וְהָאָרֶץ כָּלְאָה יְבוּלָהּ (Chaggai 1:10), the heavens have held back their dew and the earth her produce; הִנֵּה שְׂפָתַי לֹא אֶכְלָא (Tehillim 40:10), I do not hold back my lips; and וַיִּכָּלֵא הַגֶּשֶׁם (Bereishis 8:2), the rain was held back. He glosses them all as withholding and restraining.

בֵּית הַכֶּלֶא (Yirmiyahu 37:18), the prison house, אֵת בִּגְדֵי כִלְאוֹ (Yirmiyahu 52:33), his prison clothes, and וּבְבָתֵּי כְלָאִים הָחְבָּאוּ (Yeshayahu 42:22), they are hidden away in prison houses.

גָּזַר מִמִּכְלָה צֹאן (Chavakuk 3:17), the flock cut off from the fold: the place where the sheep are held inside the walls around it, so that they can go out only through the opening. The heh there stands for an alef, as its plural מִמִּכְלְאֹת צֹאן (Tehillim 78:70), from the sheepfolds, shows.

וּבֶגֶד כִּלְאַיִם (Vayikra 19:19) is cloth mixed of wool and linen; לֹא תִזְרַע כַּרְמְךָ כִּלְאָיִם (Devarim 22:9) is two kinds of seed together with the grape; שָׂדְךָ לֹא תִזְרַע כִּלְאָיִם (Vayikra 19:19) is two kinds of seed, and grafting a tree is included in it.

כלם.sense: To be put to disgrace, and to put another to it; the noun is כְּלִמָּה, disgrace.

more.t: He holds it more than בושה, shame, and the proof is the pesukim that pair the two: בּוֹשׁוּ וְגַם נִכְלְמוּ (Yeshayahu 45:16), they were ashamed and disgraced besides, and בֹּשְׁתִּי וְגַם נִכְלַמְתִּי (Yirmiyahu 31:18), I was ashamed and disgraced besides.
כְּלִמָּה is always from the side of disrepute, while shame is at times from the side of praise, coming from a man's humility.
