A short entry: וְהִנֵּה־גֶפֶן לְפָנָי (Bereishis 9:9), and behold a vine before me; לְגֶפֶן אַדָּרֶת (Yechezkel 17:8), a splendid vine; גֶּפֶן בּוֹקֵק יִשְׂרָאֵל (Hoshea 10:1), Yisrael is an emptied vine; and the plural, וְהַגְּפָנִים סְמָדַר (Shir HaShirim 2:13), the vines are in blossom.

וַיִּמְצָא גֶּפֶן שָׂדֶה (Melachim II 4:39), and he found a vine of the field, from which he gathered wild gourds. Some say גפן שדה is a particular tree on which the gourds grow, and it is called a vine of the field because it is like a vine.

לקשׁ.sense: The late rain and the late growth: יוֹרֶה is the rain that comes first in the season, מַלְקוֹשׁ the one that comes last, and לֶקֶשׁ the grass that comes up late.

more.h: The first rain and the last
more.t: יוֹרֶה וּמַלְקוֹשׁ (Devarim 11:14), the early rain and the late rain: the yoreh is the rain that comes first and the malkosh is the later one.

The same word is used of grass that comes up late, בִּתְחִלַּת עֲלוֹת הַלָּקֶשׁ (Amos 7:1), at the beginning of the coming up of the late growth, and in that same pasuk וְהִנֵּה־ לֶקֶשׁ אַחַר גִּזֵּי הַמֶּֽלֶךְ, and behold, a late growth after the king's mowings. The noun carries six points.

The verb of holding back, וְכֶרֶם רָשָׁע יְלַקֵּֽשׁוּ (Iyov 24:6), and they leave the wicked man's vineyard late. His father explains it rightly: they delay the vineyard for the wicked man's need, leaving the grapes on the vines after the other vineyards have been picked, so that the grapes ripen well and make the finest wine; and out of dread of the wicked man they are afraid, and no one touches them, though every other vineyard has been harvested.

מרד.sense: To rebel, to throw off the rule of a king or of Hashem; and in another sense, the wandering of a man in poverty and lowliness.

more.t: וְגַם בַּמֶּלֶךְ נְבֽוּכַדְנֶאצַּר מָרָד (Divrei HaYamim II 36:13), and he also rebelled against king Nevuchadnetzar; and וּשְׁלשׁ־עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה מָרָֽדוּ (Bereishis 14:4), thirteen years they rebelled, which he reads as, and in the thirteenth year.
אַל־ תִּמְרֹדוּ (Bamidbar 14:9), do not rebel, said of rebelling against Hashem, and וְאֹתָנוּ אֶל־ תִּמְרֹדוּ (Yehoshua 22:19), and do not rebel against us.

הֵמָּה הָיוּ בְּֽמֹרְדֵי ־אוֹר (Iyov 24:13), they were among those who rebel against the light, that is, they rebel against the light and do not know it. He allows a second reading, that the mem is added and the root is יָרַד, to go down, so that they were in the going down of the light: they go about at evening and dig through the walls of houses in the dark.

אִם־ בְּמֶרֶד וְאִם־בְּמַעַל (Yehoshua 22:22), whether in rebellion or in treachery, which carries six points; and in another pattern בֶּֽן־נַֽעֲוַת הַמַּרְדּוּת (Shmuel I 20:30), son of a perverse rebelliousness.

מְרוּדִים תָּבִיא בָיִת (Yeshayahu 58:7), bring the wandering poor into your house; and the noun יְמֵי עָנְיָהּ וּמְרוּדֶיהָ (Eichah 1:7), the days of her affliction and her wanderings, which he reads as, in the days of her affliction; and זְכָר־עָנְיִי וּמְרוּדִי (Eichah 3:19), remember my affliction and my wandering. Their sense is poverty and lowliness.

מרה.sense: To defy a word or a command and refuse it; he sums them all as a matter of changing and altering what was said or commanded.

more.t: אֲשֶׁר מָרָה אֶת־פִּי (Melachim I 13:26), who defied the mouth of Hashem; כִּי מָרוּ בָֽךְ (Tehillim 5:11), for they rebelled against You; and כִּֽי־אֹתִי מָרָתָה (Yirmiyahu 4:17), for she defied Me.

more.h: They did not defy His word
more.t: וְלֹֽא־ מָרוּ אֶת־דְּבָרֹֽיו (Tehillim 105:28), and they did not defy His words: the signs He set among them were as He commanded, and so the frogs and the wild beasts came. Or the meaning is that Moshe and Aharon, whom He sent over the plagues, did not defy His word.
כִּי מָרוֹ מָרִיתִי (Eichah 1:20), for I have grievously defied; סוֹרֵר וּמוֹרֶה (Devarim 21:18), wayward and defiant; and שִׁמְעוּ־נָא הַמֹּרִים (Bamidbar 20:10), hear now, you defiant ones.

מֹרַת רוּחַ (Bereishis 26:35), a defiance of spirit, said of Esav's wives: each one of them was defying their spirit, that is, altering and changing their will. Or it is a noun on the pattern of תּוֹעָה, error, at Yeshayahu 32:6.

כִּי בֵּית מְרִי הֵמָּה (Yechezkel 2:5), for they are a house of defiance; גַּם־הַיּוֹם מְרִי שִׂחִי (Iyov 23:2), even today my complaint is defiant; אֶֽת־ מֶרְיְךָ (Devarim 31:27), your defiance, with a segol under the mem; and לָשׁוּב לְעַבְדֻתָם בְּמִרְיָם (Nechemiah 9:17), to return to their bondage in their defiance, with a chirik under the mem.

וְאָמַרְתָּ אֶל־ מֶרִי (Yechezkel 44:6), and you shall say to the defiant one, and אַל־תְּהִי־ מֶרִי כְּבֵית הַמֶּרִי (Yechezkel 2:8), do not be defiant like the house of defiance. He takes the first as a description and the second as a noun; or both are nouns and the first is short a word, the right reading being, do not be a man of defiance. So too וַֽאֲנִי תְפִלָּֽה (Tehillim 109:4), and I am prayer, meaning I am a man of prayer; and so אַךְ־ מְרִי יְבַקֶּשׁ־רָע (Mishlei 17:11), a defiant man seeks only evil, a description or a noun short the word man.

כִּֽי־ הִמְרוּ אֶת־רוּחוֹ (Tehillim 106:33), for they defied His spirit: Moshe and Aharon defied the word of Hashem, and His spirit here is His word, since He pronounced with His lips that they should not enter the land. So וַיַּמְרוּ ־בִי (Yechezkel 20:13), and they defied Me; מַמְרִים הֱיִתֶם (Devarim 31:27), you have been defiant; כַּמָּה יַמְרוּהוּ בַמִּדְבָּר (Tehillim 78:40), how often they defied Him in the wilderness; and וַתֶּמֶר אֶת־מִשְׁפָּטַי לְרִשְׁעָה (Yechezkel 5:6), and she changed My laws into wickedness.
לַמְרוֹת עֵנֵי כְבוֹדֽוֹ (Yeshayahu 3:8), to defy the eyes of His glory, whose proper form is לְהַמְרוֹת; and so לַמְרוֹת עֶלְיוֹן בַּצִּיָּֽה (Tehillim 78:17), to defy the Most High in the desert.

עַל־הָאָרֶץ מְרָתַיִם (Yirmiyahu 50:21), against the land of Merasayim, Targum Yonasan renders עַל אַרְעָא דְעַמָא סַרְבָן, against the land of a defiant people, which he brings as belonging to this same sense.

אֶת־עֳנִי יִשְׂרָאֵל מֹרֶה מְאֹד (Melachim II 14:26), the affliction of Israel was very bitter, he takes from this sense too, that is, much changed and altered. But וּמוֹרָה לֹא־יַעֲלֶה עַל־רֹאשׁוֹ (Shoftim 13:5), and no razor shall come upon his head, is the razor.

מרר.sense: Bitter, and bitterness: of taste, of grief, and of a life made bitter; in another sense to alter or exchange, and in another a tall heap set up as a marker.

more.h: Bitter in taste and in soul
more.t: מַר ־נֶפֶשׁ (Shmuel I 22:2), bitter of soul; כִּי מָרִים הֵם (Shemos 15:23), for they are bitter, said of the waters; צְעָקָה גְּדֹלָה וּמָרָה (Bereishis 27:34), a great and bitter cry; and מָרָה כַלַּֽעֲנָה (Mishlei 5:4), bitter as wormwood. The alef comes in place of the hei in קְרֶאןָ לִי מָרָא (Rus 1:20), call me Mara, and so וְהִיא מָרַת נָפֶשׁ (Shmuel I 1:10), and she was bitter of soul, and כִּי־רַע וָמָר עָזְבֵךְ (Yirmiyahu 2:19), that it is evil and bitter that you forsook Hashem your God.

כִּֽי־ מָרָה נֶפֶשׁ כָּל־הָעָם (Shmuel I 30:6), for the soul of all the people was bitter, is a past verb, since the stress falls back and it carries two peshatin. כִּֽי־ מַר ־לִי מְאֹד מִכֶּם (Rus 1:13), for it is far more bitter for me than for you, may likewise be a past verb because of its patach, or it may be a noun and not a description, since patach is found in descriptions of doubled roots only rarely.

עַל־ מַר נַפְשִֽׁי (Yeshayahu 38:15), over the bitterness of my soul, is a noun, that is, that You saved me from my soul's bitterness; and Targum Yonasan there renders דְאוֹסִיף עַל חַיַי וְשֵׁיזֵיב מִמְרִיר נַפְשִׁי, who added to my life and delivered me from the bitterness of my soul. So also הִנֵּה לְשָׁלוֹם מַר ־לִי מָר (Yeshayahu 38:17), behold, for peace I had great bitterness; and with the feminine hei, in the bound form, לֵב יוֹדֵעַ מָרַּת נַפְשׁוֹ (Mishlei 14:10), the heart knows its own bitterness, the resh taking a dagesh.

Rabbi Yonah brought מֹרַת רוּחַ (Bereishis 26:35), a bitterness of spirit, under this root; but it would then have needed a dagesh and a short vowel under the mem, and the right view is that it belongs to the root מָרָה.

The noun in full is מָרוֹר, and in the plural עַל־מַצּוֹת וּמְרֹרִים (Bamidbar 9:11), with matzos and bitter herbs, and הִשְׂבִּיעַנִי בַמְּרוֹרִים (Eichah 3:15), He has filled me with bitterness. In the feminine plural כִּֽי־תִכְתֹּב עָלַי מְרֹרוֹת (Iyov 13:26), for You write bitter things against me, and אַשְׁכְּלֹת מְרֹרֹת (Devarim 32:32), clusters of bitterness.

בְּשִׁבְרוֹן מָתְנַיִם וּבִמְרִירוּת (Yechezkel 21:11), with breaking of loins and with bitterness; בְּכִי תַמְרוּרִים (Yirmiyahu 31:14), bitter weeping; וּמֶמֶר לְיֽוֹלַדְתּֽוֹ (Mishlei 17:25), and bitterness to her who bore him; and כִּי יַשְׂבִּעַנִי מַמְּרֹרִֽים (Iyov 9:18), for He fills me with bitterness.

וְקֶטֶב מְרִירִי (Devarim 32:24), and bitter destruction, whose sense is the force of the heat, like a deadly poison. כִּמְרִירֵי יֽוֹם (Iyov 3:5), which he reads as, like those who are bitter of day and ill starred, that they should terrify that day with their curses. Others take the kaf as added, as in כַּֽחֲצֹת הַלַּיְלָה (Shemos 11:4), about midnight, and כְּמַסִּיגֵי גְּבוּל (Hoshea 5:10), like those who move a boundary.

יֵמַר שֵׁכָר לְשֹׁתָֽיו (Yeshayahu 24:9), strong drink turns bitter to those who drink it; אֲמָרֵר בַּבֶּכִי (Yeshayahu 22:4), I will weep bitterly, which he reads as embittering myself, or those who hear me; וַיְמָֽרֲרוּ אֶת־חַיֵּיהֶם (Shemos 1:14), and they made their lives bitter; and כִּי־ הֵמַר שַׁדַּי לִי (Rus 1:20), for Shakai has dealt bitterly with me.

אַל־ תַּמֵּר בּוֹ (Shemos 23:21), do not defy him, is another sense in this verb, and because it is bound with a beis it is like תְּמָרֵר. And וְרֵיחוֹ לֹא נָמָֽר (Yirmiyahu 48:11), and its scent was not changed, is in the sense of not being exchanged. His father writes that אֶדַּדֶּה כָל־שְׁנוֹתַי (Yeshayahu 38:16), I shall go softly all my years, belongs here too: I shall take my ease all my days over what He exchanged for me, in adding to my years.

שִׂמִי לָךְ תַּמְרוּרִים (Yirmiyahu 31:20), set up markers for yourself, are the tall signposts; and so הִכְעִיס אֶפְרַיִם תַּמְרוּרִים (Hoshea 12:15), Ephraim provoked with the markers he made, though it may also belong to the first sense, that Ephraim provoked with a provocation of bitterness. וַיִּתְמַרְמַר אֵלָיו (Daniel 8:7), he raged against him, he takes as rising and lifting himself up against him. And the right view is that כְּמַר מִדְּלִי (Yeshayahu 40:15), like a drop from a bucket, is from this root and this sense of height, the bucket's drip being so called because it falls from a height.

יִשְׁפֹּךְ לָאָרֶץ מְרֵֽרָֽתִי (Iyov 16:13), He pours out my gall on the ground; מְרוֹרַת פְּתָנִים בְּקִרְבּֽוֹ (Iyov 20:14), the gall of asps within him; and וּבָרָק מִמְּרֹֽרָתוֹ יַֽהֲלֹךְ (Iyov 20:25), and a glittering point comes out of his gall. This is the gall bladder, and some read אַשְׁכְּלֹת מְרֹרֹת (Devarim 32:32) the same way. So וַֽיְמָֽרֲרֻהוּ וָרֹבּוּ (Bereishis 49:23), and they embittered him and shot at him, that is, they shot their arrows as far as the gall.

קדד.sense: To bow the head low; and from it קָדְקֹד, the crown of the head, whose first letter is doubled. Another word under these letters is the spice קִדָּה.

more.t: וַיִּקֹּד דָּוִד אַפַּיִם (Shmuel I 24:8), and David bowed with his face to the ground, and וַֽיִּקְּדוּ (Bereishis 43:28), and they bowed low and prostrated themselves. Their sense is the bending and lowering of the crown of the head.

קדקד is from the root קָדַד with its first letter doubled: וְטָרַף זְרוֹעַ אַף־ קָדְקֹֽד (Devarim 33:20), and he tears the arm, yes, the crown of the head; וּלְקָדְקֹד נְזִיר אֶחָֽיו (Bereishis 49:26), and on the crown of the head of him who was set apart from his brothers; וְעַֽל־ קָדְקֳדוֹ חֲמָסוֹ יֵרֵֽד (Tehillim 7:17), and his violence comes down on his own crown; and וְעַד קָדְקֳדֶֽךָ (Devarim 28:35), and to the crown of your head. קָדְקֹד שֵׂעָר (Tehillim 68:22), the hairy crown, is so called because at the crown the hair of the head divides, half to the right and half to the left.

וְקִדָּה חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת (Shemos 30:24), and five hundred of kidah, Onkelos renders וּקְצִיעֲתָא, cassia. So it is named in the words of Chazal in the compounding of the ketores, myrrh and cassia; and so it is called in Arabic and in Greek, קציעה. Rav Saadiah Gaon wrote that it is costus.

כרע.sense: To kneel and to be brought low; and from it כְּרָעַיִם, the legs of an animal, so called because they bend in kneeling.

more.t: כָּרַע רָבַץ כְּאַרְיֵה (Bereishis 49:9), he crouched, he lay down like a lion; כָּֽרְעוּ עַל־בִּרְכֵיהֶם (Shoftim 7:6), they knelt on their knees; מִכְּרֹעַ עַל־בִּרְכָּיו (Melachim I 8:54), from kneeling on his knees; וּבִרְכַּיִם כֹּֽרְעוֹת תְּאַמֵּֽץ (Iyov 4:4), you strengthened the buckling knees; and וְכֻלְּכֶם לַטֶּבַח תִּכְרָעוּ (Yeshayahu 65:12), and all of you shall bow down to the slaughter.

בִּלְתִּי כָרַע תַּחַת אַסִּיר (Yeshayahu 10:4), without bowing under the prisoner. Ibn Ezra explains that none escapes except one who bows and hides himself beneath a prisoner, and beneath the slain they fall so as to escape. His brother Rabbi Moshe explains it otherwise: apart from this bowing they now have in their own land, where the nations bring them low, they shall go as prisoners and fall as slain; and תַּחַת here means in the place of, as in שְׁבוּ אִישׁ תַּחְתָּיו (Shemos 16:29), let every man stay in his place.

וּבַחוּרֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הִכְרִֽיעַ (Tehillim 78:31), and He brought down the young men of Israel; תַּכְרִיעַ קָמַי תַּחְתָּֽי (Tehillim 18:40), You bring my foes down under me; and הַכְרֵעַ הִכְרַעְתִּנִי (Shoftim 11:35), you have brought me very low. Their sense is being brought low.

From this the legs of a beast are called כרעים, because they bend in kneeling: שְׁתֵּי כְרָעַיִם אוֹ בְדַל־אֹזֶן (Amos 3:12), two legs or a piece of an ear, and וְהַקֶּרֶב וְהַכְּרָעַיִם יִרְחַץ בַּמָּיִם (Vayikra 1:13), and the innards and the legs he washes in water.

But כְרָעַיִם מִמַּעַל לְרַגְלָיו (Vayikra 11:21), legs above its feet, are the extra joints above the four legs that the locust has near its head, with which it braces itself when it wants to spring; and that is what the pasuk means by לְנַתֵּר בָּהֵן עַל־הָאָֽרֶץ, to leap with them upon the ground.

סגד.sense: To bow down before an idol; the word is the Targum's for prostrating oneself, and his entry gives no gloss of its own.

more.t: יִסְגָּד ־לוֹ וְיִשְׁתַּחוּ (Yeshayahu 44:17), he bows to it and prostrates himself, and לְבוּל עֵץ אֶסְגּֽוֹד (Yeshayahu 44:19), shall I bow down to a block of wood. The Targum renders וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ (Bereishis 18:2), and he bowed himself, with וּסְגִיד. That is the whole of the entry.

צעק.sense: To cry out, to shout aloud, and the cry itself; he holds the sense is the same as that of זעקה spelled with a zayin.

more.t: צָעַק לִבָּם (Eichah 2:18), their heart cried out; צָֽעֲקוּ (Tehillim 34:18), they cried out and Hashem heard; עַל־כֵּן הֵם צֹֽעֲקִים (Shemos 5:8), therefore they cry out; and עֲלִי הַלְּבָנוֹן וּֽצְעָקִי (Yirmiyahu 22:20), go up to Levanon and cry out, where the first root letter takes a kamatz chatuf. The doubled form כִּי אִם־ צָעֹק יִצְעַק (Shemos 22:22), if he cries out at all to Me.

וַיִּצְעַק צְעָקָה גְּדֹלָה (Bereishis 27:34), and he cried a great cry; הַכְּצַֽעֲקָתָהּ הַבָּאָה אֵלַי (Bereishis 18:21), whether they have done according to the cry of it that has come to Me; and וְאֶת־ צַֽעֲקָתָם שָׁמַעְתִּי (Shemos 3:7), and I have heard their cry.

more.h: Summoned by a cry, and crying aloud
more.t: In the form where the crying falls upon those called: וַיִּצָּֽעֲקוּ מִכֹּל חֹגֵר חֲגֹרָה (Melachim II 3:21), and they were called out, everyone who could gird on armour, and וַיִּצָּעֵק אִישׁ־יִשְׂרָאֵל (Shoftim 7:23), and the men of Israel were called together. And in the form of crying aloud, וְהוּא מְצַעֵק אָבִי אָבִי (Melachim II 2:12), and he cried out, my father, my father. He glosses none of them, saying only that their sense throughout is that of זעקה with a zayin.

זעק.sense: To cry out, a calling in a loud voice; and in the form where men are called out, the mustering of a crowd at that cry.

more.t: אֵלֶיךָ זָֽעֲקוּ וְנִמְלָטוּ (Tehillim 22:6), to You they cried out and were delivered; וַתֵּלֶךְ הָלוֹךְ וְזָעָֽקָה (Shmuel II 13:19), and she went on and cried out, where the past stands for the present, that is, she was going and crying; לִי יִזְעָקוּ (Hoshea 8:2), to Me they cry, my God, we know You; זְעַק וְהֵילֵל בֶּן־אָדָם (Yechezkel 21:17), cry out and wail, son of man; and וַיָּשׁוּבוּ וַיִּזְעָקוּךָ (Nechemiah 9:28), and they turned back and cried to You, which he reads as, and they cried to You.

וּזְעָקָה בַּגּוֹיִם נִשְׁמָֽע (Yirmiyahu 50:46), and a cry is heard among the nations; וְאֶת־ זַֽעֲקָתָם שָׁמַעְתָּ עַל־יַם־סֽוּף (Nechemiah 9:9), and You heard their cry at the Sea of Reeds; and וְֽאַל־יְהִי מָקוֹם לְזַֽעֲקָתִֽי (Iyov 16:18), and let there be no place for my cry. The sense of the noun is calling out in a loud voice.

more.h: His father on a double object
more.t: מֵרֹב עֲשׁוּקִים יַזְעִיקוּ (Iyov 35:9), his father takes as a verb governing two objects: the wicked and the robbers make the poor cry out, and the poor cry to Hashem.

הַזְעֶק ־לִי אֶת־אִֽישׁ־יְהוּדָה (Shmuel II 20:4), call out the men of Yehudah for me, and וַיַּזְעֵק בָּרָק אֶת־זְבוּלֻן וְאֶת־נַפְתָּלִי (Shoftim 4:10), and Barak called out Zevulun and Naftali. In the form where the men are the ones called: נִֽזְעֲקוּ וַיַּדְבִּיקוּ אֶת־בְּנֵי־דָֽן (Shoftim 18:23), they were called together and overtook the sons of Dan, מַה־לְּךָ כִּי נִזְעָֽקְתָּ (Shoftim 18:23), what ails you that you were called out, and וַיִּזָּֽעֲקוּ כָּל־הָעָם (Yehoshua 8:16), and all the people were called together.

more.h: Why a cry gathers a crowd
more.t: בְּזַֽעֲקֵךְ יַצִּילֻךְ קִבּוּצַיִךְ (Yeshayahu 57:13), when you cry out, let your gathered ones save you. Their sense is the gathering and assembling of the people, and these too belong to the first sense, since a people is not gathered without a herald who goes about and cries to them to assemble; or when a man cries out at a wrong done him, the people gather at the sound of his cry, so that he is the one who summons them.

שׁוע.sense: To cry out for help, and the cry itself; in other senses, to shut the eyes or to smear over, and a man of standing open handed with his money.

more.t: הִנֵּה־קוֹל שַֽׁוְעַת בַּת־עַמִּי (Yirmiyahu 8:19), behold the sound of the cry of the daughter of my people, and וְשַׁוְעָתִי לְפָנָיו תָּבוֹא בְאָזְנָֽיו (Tehillim 18:7), and my cry before Him came into His ears. The verb: שִׁוַּעְתִּי שָׁמַעְתָּ קוֹלִֽי (Yonah 2:3), I cried out and You heard my voice; יְשַׁוְּעוּ וְאֵין מוֹשִׁיעַ (Tehillim 18:42), they cry out and there is none to save; and קַמְתִּי בַקָּהָל אֲשַׁוֵּֽעַ (Iyov 30:28), I stood up in the assembly and cried out. Their sense is crying out.

Some explain הֲיַֽעֲרֹךְ שׁוּֽעֲךָ לֹא בְצָר (Iyov 36:19), will your cry avail you without distress, in this sense; and Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Yonah brought with them אִם־בְּפִידוֹ לָהֶן שֽׁוּעַ (Iyov 30:24), whether in his calamity there is a cry for them. They also brought under this root and this sense הַנּוֹתֵן תְּשׁוּעָה לַמְּלָכִים (Tehillim 144:10), who gives salvation to kings.

more.h: His father on the word for salvation
more.t: His father writes in Sefer HaGalui that the sense of תשועה in Arabic is א"ל גאת"ה, which is the receiving of a cry.

From the same source וְעֵינָיו הָשַׁע (Yeshayahu 6:10), and shut his eyes, which he explains as, close his eyes so that he not see. The Targum renders וְטָח אֶת־הַבָּֽיִת (Vayikra 14:42), and he plasters the house, with וִישׁוּעַ יָת בֵּיתָא.

His father takes וּבְמַיִם לֹֽא־רֻחַצְתְּ לְמִשְׁעִי (Yechezkel 16:4), and you were not washed in water for smoothing, in the sense of anointing, since the plastering of a house is done by drawing the hand over it as anointing is, the yod standing for a hei. It may instead carry the sense of smoothness, the yod standing for the doubled letter and the root being שָׁעַע, from the Targum of חֶלְקַת צַוָּארָֽיו (Bereishis 27:16), the smooth of his neck, which is שְׁעִיעוּת צַוְרֵיהּ, and of וְאָֽנֹכִי אִישׁ חָלָֽק (Bereishis 27:11), and I am a smooth man, which is גבר שעיע; so the pasuk would mean, to make your flesh smooth, since washing in water smooths the flesh and makes it soft. His father writes a further gloss, for cleansing, since in Arabic טהרה, cleanness, is א"ל תמשי"ע.

Rabbi Yonah explains הָשַׁע מִמֶּנִּי וְאַבְלִיגָה (Tehillim 39:14) from the sense of shutting the eyes: turn your eyes from me, as though it said, leave off from me. Others read it as, let go of me, like שְׁעֵה מֵעָלָיו וְיֶחְדָּל (Iyov 14:6), look away from him that he may rest, שוע and שעה being one sense.

הִשְׁתַּֽעַשְׁעוּ וָשֹׁעוּ (Yeshayahu 29:9) he takes from the first sense, that is, they cried out and cried for help, and so וְשׁוֹעַ אֶל־הָהָֽר (Yeshayahu 22:5), and crying to the mountain. His father explains them from the sense of shutting the eyes, as the next pasuk says וַיְעַצֵּם אֶת־עֵֽינֵיכֶם, and He has closed your eyes, and said this of the false prophet; so the meaning is that the false prophets were blinded and blinded others. Both words are past tense.

Another sense: וּלְכִילַי לֹא יֵֽאָמֵר שֽׁוֹעַ (cited with a book name his edition prints wrongly), and of the churl it shall not be said that he is noble. He is the honoured man, open handed with his money, who gives more than is fitting for him. The noun from this is הֲיַֽעֲרֹךְ שׁוּֽעֲךָ לֹא בְצָר (Iyov 36:19), that is, will your money set you beyond distress, and וְכֹל מַֽאֲמַצֵּי־כֹֽחַ, and all the forces of strength: money and strength cannot save you from the trouble fated to come upon you.

גאל.sense: To redeem, to buy back what was sold and to act as the near kinsman; and in another sense, spelled the same, to defile and to be defiled.

more.t: גְּאַל ־לְךָ אַתָּה אֶת־גְּאֻלָּתִי (Rus 4:6), redeem for yourself my right of redemption; וּבָא גֹֽאֲלוֹ הַקָּרֹב אֵלָיו (Vayikra 25:25), and his kinsman who is near to him comes and redeems; and מִֽגֹּֽאֲלֵנוּ הֽוּא (Rus 2:20), he is one of our redeeming kinsmen: because the right of redemption belongs to the near relative, he is called גואל. Hashem redeeming His servant Yaakov is the same verb at Yeshayahu 48:20.

אֽוֹ־הִשִּׂיגָה יָדוֹ וְנִגְאָֽל (Vayikra 25:49), or if his means suffice, he is redeemed; וְאִם־לֹא יִגָּאֵל בְּאֵלֶּה (Vayikra 25:54), and if he is not redeemed by these; and the noun וּלְךָ הַגְּאֻלָּה (Yirmiyahu 32:8), and the right of redemption is yours.

more.h: Buying from a Levi, or redeeming
more.t: Some explain וַֽאֲשֶׁר יִגְאַל מִן־הַֽלְוִיִּם (Vayikra 25:33) as, who buys from them: if a man buys a house in a walled city from the Leviim, it is not made his outright after a year as one bought from an Israel would be, but goes out at the yovel if he did not redeem it. It may also be read as redemption, since the pasuk says גְּאֻלַּת עוֹלָם תִּהְיֶה לַֽלְוִיִּֽם (Vayikra 25:32), the Leviim shall have a perpetual right of redemption. One might have thought the pasuk speaks only of an Israel who took from a Levi, so that a Levi may redeem forever but a Levi who took from a Levi could not; therefore it says that a Levi redeems from the hand of a Levi with a perpetual redemption, and if he did not redeem it, the sale of the house and of the city of his holding goes out at the yovel.

Another sense: הוֹי מֹֽרְאָה וְנִגְאָלָה (Tzefaniah 3:1), woe to her that is filthy and defiled; בַּמֶּה גֵֽאַלְנוּךָ (Malachi 1:7), wherein have we defiled You, and in that same pasuk לֶחֶם מְגֹאָל, defiled bread; וַיְגֹֽאֲלוּ מִן־הַכְּהֻנָּֽה (Nechemiah 7:64), and they were put out of the priesthood as defiled; נְגֹֽאֲלוּ בַדָּם (Yeshayahu 59:3), they are defiled with blood; גָּֽאֳלֵי הַכְּהֻנָּה (Nechemiah 13:29), those who defiled the priesthood; and אֲשֶׁר לֹֽא־ יִתְגָּאַל בְּפַת־בַּג הַמֶּלֶךְ (Daniel 1:8), that he would not defile himself with the king's food. All of them are a matter of filth and befouling.

יִגְאָלֻהוּ חשֶׁךְ וְצַלְמָוֶת (Iyov 3:5), in the sense of filth, means, let darkness and the shadow of death defile it. Others read it from מִֽגֹּֽאֲלֵנוּ הֽוּא (Rus 2:20), that is, let darkness and the shadow of death be its near kin. And some read וַיְגֹֽאֲלוּ מִן־הַכְּהֻנָּֽה (Nechemiah 7:64) as the priesthood having redeemed them, the word carrying its own opposite, as משריש, taking root, stands against משרש, uprooting: a גואל is the near kinsman and a מגאל one put far from kinship and family, and these were put far off because they could not find their book of genealogy.
וְכָל־מַלְבּוּשַׁי אֶגְאָֽלְתִּי (Yeshayahu 63:3), and I have stained all my raiment, whose proper form is הִגְאָלְתִּי, the alef standing in place of the hei of the form.

פדה.sense: To ransom, to redeem by payment; and the nouns of the ransom and of the one ransomed.

more.t: פָּדָה בְשָׁלוֹם נַפְשִׁי (Tehillim 55:19), He has redeemed my soul in peace, and וְהוּא יִפְדֶּה אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל (Tehillim 130:8), and He will redeem Israel.

פְּדוּת שָׁלַח לְעַמּוֹ (Tehillim 111:9), He sent redemption to His people; in another pattern וְיֵקַר פִּדְיוֹן נַפְשָׁם (Tehillim 49:9), and the ransom of their soul is costly; with a mem, אֵת כֶּסֶף הַפִּדְיוֹם (Bamidbar 3:49), the ransom money; and וְאֵת פְּדוּיֵי הַשְּׁלֹשָׁה (Bamidbar 3:46), and the redeemed of the three, one of whom is a פְּדוּי, a redeemed one.

לֹא נִפְדָּתָה (Vayikra 19:20), she was not redeemed; and יְעָדָהּ וְהֶפְדָּהּ (Shemos 21:8), he designated her and let her be redeemed. He explains that he helps in her redemption, deducting from her redemption price the years she was with him, as though she had been hired to him, and she pays him the rest and goes free. The infinitive of the passive is וְהָפְדֵּה לֹא נִפְדָּתָה (Vayikra 19:20), and she was not redeemed at all.

וְשַׂמְתִּי פְדֻת בֵּין עַמִּי וּבֵין עַמֶּךָ (Shemos 8:19), and I will set a redemption between My people and your people: the redemption is that they shall be ransomed and saved from the wild beasts, and it is the separation and the distinction between My people and your people.

פדע.sense: One word only, to deliver, which he glosses as the same as פדה, to redeem.

more.t: פְּדָעֵהוּ מֵרֶדֶת שָׁחַת (Iyov 33:24), deliver him from going down to the pit, which he glosses as the same as פדהו, redeem him. That is the whole of the entry.

בזה.sense: To despise and hold in contempt, and the noun contempt; in another sense, spelled with an alef at the end, to plunder.

more.t: בָּזָה (Bamidbar 15:31), he despised, said of despising the word of Hashem, and מַדּוּעַ בָּזִיתָ אֶת־דְּבַר (Shmuel II 12:9), why have you despised the word of Hashem. In the passive נִבְזֶה בְּֽעֵינָיו נִמְאָס (Tehillim 15:4), a vile man is despised in his eyes; and causing contempt, לְהַבְזוֹת בַּעְלֵיהֶן בְּעֵינֵיהֶן (Esther 1:17), to make their husbands contemptible in their eyes. The noun is בִּזָּיוֹן וָקָֽצֶף (Esther 1:18), contempt and wrath, and the sense of contempt is plain.

לִבְזֹה ־נֶפֶשׁ (Yeshayahu 49:7), to him despised of soul, is a description or an infinitive on the pattern of קְֽנֹה־חָכְמָה מַה־טּוֹב (Mishlei 16:16), how much better it is to get wisdom; the meaning is, to one whom every soul is ready to despise and every nation to abhor. Or it stands for the passive, as though it said לבזוי נפש, despised of soul. From this sense also נְמִבְזָה וְנָמֵס (Shmuel I 15:9), despised and worthless, with an added nun and mem.

אֲשֶׁר־ בָּֽזְאוּ נְהָרִים אַרְצֽוֹ (Yeshayahu 18:2), whose land the rivers have spoiled. In his view it is from this root, the alef standing in place of the hei of the last letter, as a yod came in place of the hei in the word חֲסָיוּ; its sense is plunder and spoil, and the two roots are one sense. Most of the grammarians say the alef stands for the doubled letter, and that it is like בזזו, they plundered.

קלה.sense: To parch or roast in fire; and in another sense to be held cheap, with the noun קלון, disgrace.

more.t: אֲשֶׁר־ קָלָם מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶל (Yirmiyahu 29:22), whom the king of Bavel roasted in the fire; אָבִיב קָלוּי בָּאֵשׁ (Vayikra 2:14), fresh ears parched with fire; and מַצּוֹת וְקָלוּי (Yehoshua 5:11), matzos and parched grain. The description is וְלֶחֶם וְקָלִי וְכַרְמֶל (Vayikra 23:14), bread and parched grain and fresh ears; and it is written with an alef in אֵיפַת הַקָּלִיא הַזֶּה (Shmuel I 17:17), this ephah of parched grain.

His father takes כִּֽי־כְסָלַי מָלְאוּ נִקְלֶה (Tehillim 38:8), for my loins are filled with burning, and מַלֵּא פְנֵיהֶם קָלוֹן (Tehillim 83:17), fill their faces with shame, from this root; their sense there is burning and roasting.

Another sense: מַקְלֶה אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ (Devarim 27:16), he who holds his father and his mother cheap; and where the man is the one brought low, וְנִקְלָה כבוד מואב (Yeshayahu 16:14), the glory of Moav shall be brought low, and אִישׁ־רָשׁ וְנִקְלֶֽה (Shmuel I 18:23), a poor man and lightly esteemed. Here he glosses כִּֽי־כְסָלַי מָלְאוּ נִקְלֶה (Tehillim 38:8) as a contemptible affliction.

שָׂבַעְתָּ קָלוֹן מִכָּבוֹד (Chavakuk 2:16), you are filled with shame instead of honour, and in that same pasuk וְקִֽיקָלוֹן עַל־כְּבוֹדֶֽךָ, and foul shame upon your glory, a word compounded of קיא, vomit, and קלון, shame. Their sense is contempt.

נחם.sense: Consolation and comforting through most of its forms, and in a second set of pesukim regret, a turn of heart over what was done.

more.t: מֵֽאֲנָה לְהִנָּחֵם עַל־בָּנֶיהָ (Yirmiyahu 31:15), she refused to be comforted for her children; נַֽחֲמוּ עַמִּי (Yeshayahu 40:1), comfort My people; כְּאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר אִמּוֹ תְּנַֽחֲמֶנּוּ (Yeshayahu 66:13), as a man whom his mother comforts. All of these, he says, are the matter of consolation, and the sense is known.

כּוֹס תַּנְחוּמִים (Yirmiyahu 16:7), a cup of consolations; תַּנְחוּמֶיךָ יְֽשַֽׁעַשְׁעוּ נַפְשִֽׁי (Tehillim 94:19), Your consolations delight my soul; זֹאת נֶחָמָתִי בְעָנְיִי (Tehillim 119:50), this is my comfort in my affliction. On דְּבָרִים נִֽחֻמִֽים (Zechariah 1:13), comforting words, he says the governed word has dropped out and the full phrase is דברים דברי ניחומים, words that are words of consolation.

more.h: Against Rabbi Yonah on a form
more.t: הוֹי אֶנָּחֵם מִצָּרַי (Yeshayahu 1:24), I will be eased of My foes. Rabbi Yonah wrote that the word may stand for אֶתְנָחֵם. Radak holds otherwise, since the nun carries a kamatz and the form is therefore the passive one; had it been the reflexive the nun would carry a patach, because with a ches the doubling is not made good.

אֵין אִישׁ נִחָם עַל־רָעָתוֹ (Yirmiyahu 8:6), no man regrets his wickedness; וְנִחָם עַל־הָֽרָעָֽה (Yonah 4:2), and relents of the evil; כִּי נִחַמְתִּי כִּי עֲשִׂיתִֽם (Bereishis 6:7), for I regret that I made them. All of these, he says, are regret. יַחַד נִכְמְרוּ נִֽחוּמָֽי (Hoshea 11:8) he reads as נתגלגלו חרטותי, my regrets turned over within me, when I had thought to overturn them and destroy them.

חלב.sense: Milk; and with other vowels chelev, the fat, which by a borrowing becomes the choicest part of anything.

more.t: וּבְלוֹא מְחִיר יַיִן וְחָלָֽב (Yeshayahu 55:1), and without price wine and milk; לֹֽא־תְבַשֵּׁל גְּדִי בַּֽחֲלֵב אִמּֽוֹ (Shemos 34:26), you shall not cook a kid in its mother's milk; וְהֵמָּה יִשְׁתּוּ חֲלָבֵֽךְ (Yechezkel 25:4), and they shall drink your milk. The word, he says, is known.

וְחֵלֶב נְבֵלָה וְחֵלֶב טְרֵפָה (Vayikra 7:24), the fat of a carcass and the fat of a torn beast, and in the plural עַל אִשֵּׁי הַֽחֲלָבִים (Vayikra 10:15), upon the fire offerings of the fats. Radak holds it right that וּמֵֽחֶלְבֵהֶן (Bereishis 4:4), and of their fat, is a describing word, as the Targum renders it וּמִשַּׁמִּנְהוֹן, of their fattest; and fat itself is called chelev on the pattern of מֶלֶךְ and עֶבֶד.

Since the fat is the choicest of the flesh, the choicest of anything came to be called chelev: כֹּל חֵלֶב יִצְהָר וְכָל־ חֵלֶב תִּירוֹשׁ וְדָגָן (Bamidbar 18:12), all the best of the oil and all the best of the wine and the grain, and וְאִכְלוּ אֶת־ חֵלֶב הָאָֽרֶץ (Bereishis 45:18), and eat the fat of the land.

וּשְׁחֵלֶת וְחֶלְבְּנָה (Shemos 30:34), onycha and galbanum: he describes it as a spice whose smell is foul, the resin of a tree found in the cities of Greece, like a black honey, and in Arabic מיעה. And בְּיֵין חֶלְבּוֹן (Yechezkel 27:18), wine of Chelbon, which Targum Yonasan renders בַּחֲמַר חֵילַת מְבַשֵׁל.

צחר.sense: White: אֲתֹנוֹת צְחֹרוֹת (Shoftim 5:10), white she-donkeys, and וְצֶמֶר צָֽחַר (Yechezkel 27:18), white wool.

גנן.sense: To shield or cover over; and the noun magen, a shield, so called because it shields the one who carries it.

more.t: וְגַנּוֹתִי עַל־הָעִיר הַזֹּאת (Melachim II 20:6), and I will shield this city, and גָּנוֹן וְהִצִּיל (Yeshayahu 31:5), shielding and rescuing.

מָגֵן גִּבֹּרֵיהוּ מְאָדָּם (Nachum 2:4), the shield of his mighty men is reddened; אֶלֶף הַמָּגֵן תָּלוּי עָלָיו (Shir HaShirim 4:4), a thousand shields hung upon it; and in the feminine וְאֶת־ הַמָּגִנּוֹת (Divrei HaYamim II 23:9), and the shields. It is called magen, he says, because it shields the one who bears it.
The great men of a people are called shields as well, because they shield the people, as in אָֽהֲבוּ הֵבוּ קָלוֹן מָֽגִנֶּֽיהָ (Hoshea 4:18), her shields have loved, give shame.

מְגִנַּת ־לֵב (Eichah 3:65) he glosses as דאבון, sorrow. Radak allows that it may belong with the first sense, a covering of the heart, on the model of הַשְׁמֵן לֵֽב־הָעָם הַזֶּה (Yeshayahu 6:10), make the heart of this people fat; and his father explains a covering of the heart as a known sickness among the sicknesses of the brain, called in Arabic gashit al kalb.

פרדס.sense: An orchard: פַּרְדֵּס רִמּוֹנִים (Shir HaShirim 4:13), an orchard of pomegranates. He glosses it as a garden of fruit trees.

רעב.sense: To be hungry, and the noun ra'av, famine; and in the causative form, to leave a man hungry.

more.t: רָשׁוּ וְרָעֵבוּ (Tehillim 34:11), they wanted and were hungry; לֹא יִרְעָבוּ וְלֹא יִצְמָאוּ (Yeshayahu 49:10), they shall not hunger nor thirst; the noun וַיְהִי רָעָב בָּאָרֶץ (Bereishis 12:10), and there was a famine in the land; and in another form וּבִימֵי רְעָבוֹן יִשְׂבָּֽעוּ (Tehillim 37:19), in days of famine they shall be satisfied.

On רַֽעֲבוֹן בָּֽתֵּיכֶם (Bereishis 42:33), the hunger of your households, he gives two readings. A word is missing, and the sense is the grain for the hunger of your households; or it is as it sounds, take what is רַֽעֲבוֹן בָּֽתֵּיכֶם and go, that is, the bread they are hungry for, and so it is their hunger.
וַֽיְעַנְּךָ וַיַּרְעִבֶךָ (Devarim 8:3), and He afflicted you and let you hunger.

כפן.sense: Two things under these letters: a word for gathering in, and kafan, hunger, which his father reads instead as want of money.

more.t: כָּֽפְנָה שָֽׁרֳשֶׁיהָ עָלָיו (Yechezkel 17:7), it gathered its roots toward him. He glosses אספה, it gathered, and says the word is the reverse of its like in the language of Chazal, who call a gathering of people כנופיא (Yoma 51a).

לְשֹׁד וּלְכָפָן תִּשְׂחָק (Iyov 5:22), at destruction and at kafan you shall laugh. He notes that the Targum renders רָעָב as כַפְנָא. His father explains kafan well, as emptiness of the purse, want of money at a time when money is dear, since there is no need to mention famine twice, famine having been named already at the head of them all in בְּרָעָב פָּֽדְךָ מִמָּוֶת, in famine He redeemed you from death.

רחשׁ.sense: To stir or set moving; and from it the marcheshes, the deep pan whose contents stir about in it.

more.t: רָחַשׁ לִבִּי דָּבָר טוֹב (Tehillim 45:2), my heart stirred a goodly word. He glosses הוציא והניע, brought forth and set moving, since in the language of Chazal the word is used of the movement of the lips, רחושי מרחשן שפוותיה (Sanhedrin 90b).

From this sense comes וְאִם־מִנְחַת מַרְחֶשֶׁת (Vayikra 2:7), and if your offering is a marcheshes offering, which he says is a deep vessel. Chazal taught that the marcheshes is deep and what is made in it stirs, while the machavas is flat and what is made in it is hard. Radak explains that because the pan is deep the oil gathers in it and the fire does not burn it, so the meal offerings made inside it stir and move.

גשׁם.sense: Rain, and the strong rain in particular; in the plural, the rains given in their season.

more.t: הַגֶּשֶׁם וְהַשֶּׁלֶג (Yeshayahu 55:10), the rain and the snow; גֶּשֶׁם שׁוֹטֵף (Yechezkel 13:11), an overflowing rain; וַיּוֹרֶד לָכֶם גֶּשֶׁם (Yoel 2:23), and He brought down rain for you. It is the heavy rain. In the plural, וְנָֽתַתִּי גִשְׁמֵיכֶם בְּעִתָּם (Vayikra 26:4), and I will give your rains in their season.

On נָטַע אֹרֶן וְגֶשֶׁם יְגַדֵּֽל (Yeshayahu 44:14), he planted an oren and the rain makes it grow, the Targum says וּמִטְרָא יְרַבֵּי, and the rain makes it grow. Some explain geshem here as the name of a tree, and some as a body, from the Aramaic גִּשְׁמֵהּ יִצְטַבַּע (Daniel 4:30), his body was drenched. Radak holds the right reading is rain.

more.h: Why the pasuk says the rain grows it
more.t: It is plain that rain makes everything grow, so the pasuk comes to say that although a man plants the tree for avodah zarah, the rain grows it; and though the rain comes on Hashem's errand and by His will, the world goes on in its way. So Chazal said on this matter that one who stole a se'ah of wheat and sowed it, by right it should not sprout, yet the world goes on in its way, and the fools who spoiled it will one day give account.

לֹא גֻשְׁמָהּ בְּיוֹם זָֽעַם (Yechezkel 22:24), it was not rained upon in the day of wrath, which he reads as its rain did not come down in the day of wrath. He allows that the word is a noun, and also that it is a passive verb whose closing heh is sounded for the beauty of the reading and not out of need, like וְתַֽעֲלֻמָהּ יֹצִא אֽוֹר (Iyov 28:11), and He brings the hidden thing out to light.

שׁנה.sense: Change; and from it second, doing a thing again, and the year that comes round a second time. Scarlet he sends to the root shen.

more.t: עִם־ שׁוֹנִים אַל־תִּתְעָרָֽב (Mishlei 24:21), do not mix with those who change; וְדָתֵיהֶם שֹׁנוֹת מִכָּל־עָם (Esther 3:8), their laws are different from every people; וְשִׁנָּא אֵת בִּגְדֵי כִלְאוֹ (Melachim II 25:29), and he changed his prison garments; קוּמִי נָא וְהִשְׁתַּנִּית (Melachim I 14:2), rise now and change your appearance. The sense of change, he says, is known.

יוֹם שֵׁנִֽי (Bereishis 1:8), a second day. On וּפַר הַשֵּׁנִי שֶׁבַע שָׁנִים (Shoftim 6:25), and the second bull of seven years, some explain second to the womb, while Radak holds the right reading is second to the bull just named, קַח אֶת־פַּר־הַשּׁוֹר אֲשֶׁר לְאָבִיךָ, take the bullock of the ox that is your father's. The seven years Targum Yonasan renders דְאִתְפַּטִים שְׁבַע שְׁנִין, that had been fattened seven years.

more.h: Mishneh, a second of a thing
more.t: וְכֶסֶף מִשְׁנֶה (Bereishis 43:12), double money; כִּי מִשְׁנֶה שְׂכַר שָׂכִיר (Devarim 15:18), double the hire of a hired man, which he takes as a second hired man's wage, since your servant worked six full years by day and by night, while a hired man who works by day does not work by night. אֶת־ מִשְׁנֵה הַתּוֹרָה הַזֹּאת (Devarim 17:18) he reads as writing it a second time, so that the king has two, and Chazal learned from here that a king needs two, one that goes out and comes in with him and one laid up in his treasury. כֹּֽהֲנֵי הַמִּשְׁנֶה (Melachim II 23:4) are the deputies of the kohanim, second to the kohanim gedolim.

שָׁנָה תְמִימָה (Vayikra 25:30), a full year, is called so because the sun has returned a second time to the point from which it began. שְׁנָתַיִם יָמִים (Bereishis 41:1) he explains as two full years.

Rav Saadiah Gaon explained עִם־ שׁוֹנִים אַל־תִּתְעָרָֽב (Mishlei 24:21) of those who say there are שְׁנַיִם אלהים, two powers, in the world; and he gave a second explanation, better than that one, that the shonim are men who go back a second time to their wickedness after they have done teshuvah.

כִּי כָל־בֵּיתָהּ לָבֻשׁ שָׁנִֽים (Mishlei 31:21), for all her household is clothed in shanim. His father reads the word from this root, בגדים שונים, garments of several kinds, and so she has no fear of the snow for her household.

וְתוֹלַעַת שָׁנִי (Shemos 25:4), scarlet worm, and אִם־יִֽהְיוּ חֲטָֽאֵיכֶם כַּשָּׁנִים (Yeshayahu 1:18), though your sins be as scarlet, come from this root, and he says he has already written of them under the root shen.

אמץ.sense: To be strong, and to strengthen another; and in one place amutzim, a shade of red that is not the full red.

more.t: כִּי אָֽמְצוּ מִמֶּֽנִי (Tehillim 142:6), for they are stronger than I; חֲזַק וֶֽאֱמָץ (Yehoshua 1:6), be strong and resolute; וּלְאֹם מִלְאֹם יֶֽאֱמָץ (Bereishis 25:23), one people shall be stronger than the other; וְאַמִּיץ כֹּחַ (Iyov 9:4), mighty in strength. All of these and their like, he says, are the matter of strength.

וְאִמֵּץ אֶת־לְבָבוֹ (Devarim 2:30), and He hardened his heart; וּבִרְכַּיִם כֹּֽרְעוֹת תְּאַמֵּֽץ (Iyov 4:4), you strengthened bowing knees; וְיַֽאֲמֵץ לְבַבְכֶם (Tehillim 31:25), and He will strengthen your heart; and of a man gathering his own strength, הִתְאַמֵּץ לַֽעֲלוֹת בַּמֶּרְכָּבָה (Melachim I 12:18), he forced himself to mount the chariot.

בְּרֻדִּים אֲמֻצִּֽים (Zechariah 6:3), speckled amutzim. Radak reads amutzim as חמוצים, from חֲמוּץ בְּגָדִים (Yeshayahu 63:1), crimsoned in garments, that is to say red; and although reds had been named already, there were two shades of redness, one truly red and one not strong in its redness. Some explain amutzim as the colour of ashes, and Targum Yonasan renders קִטְמָנִין.

חום.sense: Chum, said of a sheep, which he glosses as black; Radak holds the word belongs to the root chamam, where he will explain it.

more.t: וְכָל־שֶֽׂה־ חוּם בַּכְּשָׂבִים (Bereishis 30:32), and every chum lamb among the sheep, which he glosses as black. The right view in his own eyes is that chum comes from the root חָמַם, and he says he will explain it there.

יסף.sense: To add; and to do a thing again or go on doing it; in the passive, to be added on to something.

more.t: וְלֹא־ יָֽסְפָה שׁוּב־אֵלָיו עֽוֹד (Bereishis 8:12), and it did not return to him again; לֹא אֹסֵף לִשְׁמֹעַ (Devarim 18:16), I will not hear again. קוֹל גָּדוֹל וְלֹא יָסָף (Devarim 5:22), a great voice that did not go on, he glosses as there came no other great voice like it.

וַיִּֽתְנַבְּאוּ וְלֹא יָסָֽפוּ (Bamidbar 11:25), and they prophesied and did not go on, which he glosses as they did not prophesy again, as Chazal said that they prophesied that day alone. The Targum took the words in another sense, rendering וְלָא פָּסְקָן, and they did not cease.

יָסַפְתָּ עַל־הַשְּׁמוּעָה אֲשֶׁר שָׁמָֽעְתִּי (Divrei HaYamim II 9:6), you have added to the report that I heard; אַל־ תּוֹסְףְ עַל־דְּבָרָיו (Mishlei 30:6), do not add to His words; and in the passive וְנוֹסַף גַּם־הוּא עַל־שֹׂנְאֵינוּ (Shemos 1:10), and he too will be added to our enemies.

On כִּי לֹא תוֹסִיפִי יִקְרְאוּ־לָךְ רַכָּה וַֽעֲנֻגָּֽה (Yeshayahu 47:1), you shall no more be called tender and delicate, and כִּי לֹא תוֹסִיפִי יִקְרְאוּ־לָךְ גְּבֶרֶת מַמְלָכֽוֹת (Yeshayahu 47:5), you shall no more be called mistress of kingdoms, he says both carry the stress on the last syllable, and so the Mesorah marks them. Rabbi Yonah separated the two; Radak says there is no need, and the whole root is one sense.

ברך.sense: To bless, and berachah; also a gift brought to another, a greeting of peace, the knee, and a pool of gathered water.

more.t: בְּרָכָה בְּקֶרֶב הָאָֽרֶץ (Yeshayahu 19:24), a blessing in the midst of the earth; בְרָכוֹת לָעַד (Tehillim 21:7), blessings for ever; בִּרְכֹת שָׁמַיִם מֵעָל בִּרְכֹת תְּהוֹם רֹבֶצֶת תָּחַת (Bereishis 49:25), blessings of heaven above, blessings of the deep couching beneath; בֵּרַךְ אֶת־אַבְרָהָם בַּכֹּֽל (Bereishis 24:1), He blessed Avraham in all. The baruch forms, he says, are describing words, since the simple verb was never built from this root; and where created beings bless Hashem the word carries the sense of praise.
בֵּרַךְ נָבוֹת אֱלֹהִים (Melachim I 21:13), Navos blessed Hashem, and בָּרֵךְ אֱלֹהִים וָמֻֽת (Iyov 2:9), bless Hashem and die, and their like, are a way of speaking around a curse.

קַח־נָא אֶת־ בִּרְכָתִי (Bereishis 33:11), take my berachah, he glosses מנחתי, my gift, and so קַח־נָא בְרָכָה מֵאֵת עַבְדֶּֽךָ (Melachim II 5:15), take a gift from your servant. He allows that מְבָרֵֽךְ אָוֶן (Yeshayahu 66:3) is of this sort, one who brings the offering.

וְאָֽרוֹתִי אֶת־ בִּרְכֽוֹתֵיכֶם (Malachi 2:2), and I will curse your blessings, is not of that sort, against what Rabbi Yonah wrote. Radak says it is blessing in the plain sense, and the proof is the word וְאָֽרוֹתִי, since the curse is the opposite of the blessing: a blessing adds to the good and a curse takes from it.

עֲשׂוּ־אִתִּי בְרָכָה (Yeshayahu 36:16) he glosses פשרה ושלום, a settlement and peace, like וַיְבָרֶךְ יַֽעֲקֹב אֶת־פַּרְעֹֽה (Bereishis 47:7), and Yaakov greeted Pharaoh, and כִּי תִמְצָא־אִישׁ לֹא תְבָֽרֲכֶנּוּ (Melachim II 4:29), if you meet a man do not greet him, which are the asking after another's peace.

תִּכְרַע כָּל־ בֶּרֶךְ (Yeshayahu 45:23), every knee shall bow; וַיִּבְרַךְ עַל־ בִּרְכָּיו (Divrei HaYamim II 6:13), and he knelt upon his knees; כָּֽרְעוּ עַל־ בִּרְכֵיהֶם (Shoftim 7:6), they knelt upon their knees, which the Mesorah marks as one of the two places where the word is left soft.

הַבְּרֵכָה הָֽעֶלְיוֹנָה (Yeshayahu 7:3), the upper pool. Some explain bereichah as a spring; the truth, he says, is that it is water gathered together and not a spring. So too in the words of Chazal, where the pesakos and the berechos that filled with water before yom tov may not be watered from on chol hamoed: the pesakos are ditches not built up with stones, and the berechos ditches built with stones and plaster, into which rainwater is gathered, or water is gathered, or water is drawn to them from the spring. So בְּרֵכוֹת מָיִם (Koheles 2:6), pools of water.

רכך.sense: Soft or tender: a soft heart, words softer than oil, a tender child, weak eyes; and the noun morech, faintness.

more.t: יַעַן רַךְ ־לְבָבְךָ (Melachim II 22:19), because your heart was soft; רַכּוּ דְבָרָיו מִשֶּׁמֶן (Tehillim 55:22), his words were softer than oil; רַךְ וָטוֹב (Bereishis 18:7), tender and good; כִּֽי־הַיְלָדִים רַכִּים (Bereishis 33:13), that the children are tender; וְעֵינֵי לֵאָה רַכּוֹת (Bereishis 29:17), and Leah's eyes were weak.
רַךְ וּמָשׁוּחַ מֶלֶךְ (Shmuel II 3:39), soft and an anointed king, he explains to mean that in the matter of kingship he was still soft, as a lad is soft.

אַל־ יֵרַךְ לְבַבְכֶם (Devarim 20:3), let not your heart grow faint; וְאֵל הֵרַךְ לִבִּי (Iyov 23:16), and Hashem made my heart faint; וְלֹא רֻכְּכָה בַּשָּֽׁמֶן (Yeshayahu 1:6), nor softened with oil; and the noun וְהֵבֵאתִי מֹרֶךְ (Vayikra 26:36), and I will bring faintness.

שׁדם.sense: Vineyards, and perhaps a field of grain; in the Kidron pesukim the Targum makes it the valley plain, and in one pasuk the word is blight.

more.t: וּמִשַּׁדְמֹת עֲמֹרָה (Devarim 32:32), and of the vineyards of Amorah, he glosses as vines, and so כִּי שַׁדְמוֹת חֶשְׁבּוֹן אֻמְלָל (Yeshayahu 16:8), for the vineyards of Cheshbon are withered, and וּשְׁדֵמוֹת לֹא־עָשָׂה אֹכֶל (Chavakuk 3:17), the vineyards have made no food.
He allows that the sense may be a field of seed, since the pasuk has already said וְאֵין יְבוּל בַּגְּפָנִים, that there is no produce in the vines.

For בְּשַׁדְמוֹת קִדְרוֹן (Melachim II 23:4), in the fields of Kidron, the Targum gives נַחְלָא בְמֵישַׁר קִדְרוֹן, the wadi in the plain of Kidron, and Radak reads הַשְּׁדֵמוֹת עַד־נַחַל קִדְרוֹן (Yirmiyahu 31:39), the fields as far as the brook of Kidron, the same way, though another Targum reads it otherwise.

But וּשְׁדֵמָה לִפְנֵי קָמָֽה (Yeshayahu 37:27), blasted before it is grown, he takes as though it were וּשְׁדֵפָה, from שִׁדָּפוֹן, blight, the mem and the peh coming from one place in the mouth; and the parallel pasuk in Melachim II 19:26 prints וּשְׁדֵפָה לִפְנֵי קָמָֽה.

שֹרג.sense: A tendril or shoot of the vine; the verb from it is to be twined and tangled together.

more.t: וּבַגֶּפֶן שְׁלֹשָׁה שָֽׂרִיגִם (Bereishis 40:10), and on the vine were three tendrils, which he glosses as branches, and הִלְבִּינוּ שָֽׂרִיגֶֽיהָ (Yoel 1:6), its branches are made white.

The reflexive form יִשְׂתָּרְגוּ עָלוּ עַל־צַוָּארִי (Eichah 1:14), they are knit together and come up upon my neck, he explains as יסתבכו, they become entangled; so too פַֽחֲדָיו יְשׂרָֽגוּ (Iyov 40:17), the sinews of his thighs are interwoven.
The Targum of מַֽעֲשֵׂה שְׂבָכָה (Melachim I 7:17), lattice work, is עוֹבַד סְרִיגָא, and the Mishnah in Moed Katan uses the verb in ומסרגין את המטות, and one plaits the cords of the beds.

סוד.sense: Counsel and a matter kept hidden, and from there the company of those who sit together.

more.t: He glosses the word ענין עצה ודבר סתר, a matter of counsel and of a hidden thing: כִּי אִם־גָּלָה סוֹדוֹ (Amos 3:7), unless He has revealed His secret, and וְסוֹד אַחֵר אַל־תְּגָֽל (Mishlei 25:9), do not reveal another man's secret.

From the same sense לֹֽא־יָשַׁבְתִּי בְסוֹד־מְשַֽׂחֲקִים (Yirmiyahu 15:17), I have not sat in the company of merrymakers, which he explains בעצתם, in their counsel, when they join together for play and for the vanities of the world; and so וְעַל סוֹד בַּחוּרִים יַחְדָּו (Yirmiyahu 6:11), upon the gathering of young men together, and בְּסוֹד יְשָׁרִים וְעֵדָֽה (Tehillim 111:1), in the company of the upright and the congregation.
Rabbi Yonah divided these into two senses. Radak holds the correct view is that the whole of it is one sense.

הוּסַד שְׁלֹמֹה לִבְנוֹת אֶת־בֵּית הָֽאֱלֹהִים (Divrei HaYamim II 3:3), Shlomo was founded to build the house of Hashem, he puts in this root and this sense: נתיעץ ועמד בסוד בנין עם דוד אביו, he took counsel and stood in the council of the building with Dovid his father.
For וְתָשֵׂם בַּסַּד רַגְלַי (Iyov 13:27), and You put my feet in the stocks, there are those who explain it as the wood in which the feet of prisoners are set.

כמס.sense: Stored away and kept out of sight; he glosses כָּמֻס עִמָּדִי (Devarim 32:34), laid up with Me, as גנוז, put away in store.

רזם.sense: To signal with the eyes; he takes it as the letters of רמז, to hint, turned about, as the Chachamim use the word.

more.t: וּֽמַה־יִּרְזְמוּן עֵינֶֽיךָ (Iyov 15:12), and what do your eyes signal, he explains from the Chachamim's usage חרש רומז ונרמז, a deaf man signals and is signalled to, and מרמוזי רמוזי להדדי, they hint one to another.

קֹרֵֽץ עַיִן (Mishlei 10:10), he who winks the eye, the Targum renders דְרָמֵז בְּעַיְנוֹהִי, who hints with his eyes, and שְׁלַח אֶצְבַּע (Yeshayahu 58:9), the pointing of the finger, it renders מִרְמַז בְּאֶצְבַּע, hinting with the finger.

דון.sense: To judge and to plead a case: the noun דִּין is a judgment and דַּיָּן a judge, and מָדוֹן, strife, belongs to the same root.

more.t: דָּן דִּין־עָנִי וְאֶבְיוֹן (Yirmiyahu 22:16), he judged the cause of the poor and needy, דָּנַנִּי אֱלֹהִים (Bereishis 30:6), Hashem has judged me, and לֹֽא־יָדוֹן רוּחִי (Bereishis 6:3), My spirit shall not judge.

The noun is a judgment: לֹֽא־דָנוּ דִּין יָתוֹם (Yirmiyahu 5:28), they did not judge the cause of the orphan; and the title is a judge: אֲבִי יְתוֹמִים וְדַיַּן אַלְמָנוֹת (Tehillim 68:6), father of orphans and judge of widows.

The word for a quarrel he puts here too: אִישׁ חֵמָה יְגָרֶה מָדוֹן (Mishlei 15:18), a man of wrath stirs up strife, and מִדְיָנִים יְשַׁלֵּֽחַ (Mishlei 6:14), he sends out quarrels; and Radak allows that וַיְהִי אִישׁ מָדֹין (Shmuel II 21:20) be explained from this, איש ריב ומלחמה, a man of quarrel and of war.

more.h: A sheath, on a second reading
more.t: For לֹֽא־יָדוֹן רוּחִי he offers another possibility, that the first root letter is a nun that has dropped, and the root is נָדַן, as in וַיָּשֶׁב חַרְבּוֹ אֶל־נְדָנָֽהּ (Divrei HaYamim I 21:27), he returned his sword to its sheath.

more.h: A sense of quarrel on its own
more.t: The chacham Rabbi Yehudah brought לֹֽא־יָדוֹן רוּחִי and כָל־הָעָם נָדוֹן together with יְגָרֶה מָדוֹן as a sense standing on its own, that of strife. Radak's father explained the pasuk that way: the higher spirit blown into man shall not be at strife with the body forever, since the spirit takes no pleasure in the body's desires while the body is drawn after them, and his days are set at a hundred and twenty years if they repent.

תקע.sense: To sound a shofar; also to drive a thing in so that it stands fast, and to strike the palm in pledge or in joy.

more.t: וְשָׁאוּל תָּקַע בַּשּׁוֹפָר (Shmuel I 13:3), and Shaul blew the shofar, with the noun בְּתֵקַע שׁוֹפָר (Tehillim 150:3), with the blast of the shofar. The shofar itself is called תָּקוֹעַ, as in תָּֽקְעוּ בַתָּקוֹעַ (Yechezkel 7:14), they have blown the trumpet.

But וּבִתְקוֹעַ תִּקְעוּ שׁוֹפָר (Yirmiyahu 6:1), in Tekoa blow the shofar, he takes as a place name, said as a turn of speech with one word falling on another, as in וְעֶקְרוֹן תֵּֽעָקֵֽר (Tzefaniah 2:4), and Ekron shall be uprooted.

Another sense: ויעקב תָּקַע אֶת־אָֽהֳלוֹ (Bereishis 31:25), Yaakov pitched his tent, and וְלָבָן תָּקַע אֶת־אֶחָיו, Lavan stationed his brothers there. So וְאֶת־גְּוִיָּתוֹ תָּֽקְעוּ בְּחוֹמַת בֵּית שָֽׁן (Shmuel I 31:10), they fastened his body to the wall of Beis Shan, with nails or otherwise, and וַתִּתְקַע אֶת־הַיָּתֵד בְּרַקָּתוֹ (Shoftim 4:21), she drove the peg into his temple.

Near to this is אַל־תְּהִי בְתֹֽקְעֵי־כָף (Mishlei 22:26), be not of those who strike hands, which he explains as הכות כף האדם אל כף חבירו בערבון, a man striking his palm against his fellow's in surety; and for joy תָּקְעוּ כַף עָלֶיךָ (Nachum 3:19), they have clapped hands over you.

רוע.sense: Evil, and what is bad to look upon; under other senses a shout, thunder, a friend, and the breaking of a thing.

more.t: וּבְעֵינֵי מֹשֶׁה רָֽע (Bamidbar 11:10), and it was evil in the eyes of Moshe, כַּדָּבָר הָרָע הַזֶּה (Devarim 19:20), this evil thing, and the noun רֹעַ לֵב (Nechemiah 2:2), badness of heart. Radak holds there is no dividing this from רַבּוֹת רָעוֹת צַדִּיק (Tehillim 34:20), many are the evils of the righteous, for an evil that comes from a man and an evil that comes upon him from Hashem are alike evil, with no difference between them.

הֵרֵעוּ מַֽעַלְלֵיהֶֽם (Michah 3:4), they made their deeds evil, and לָמָה הֲרֵֽעֹתֶם לִי (Bereishis 43:6), why did you deal ill with me. In זֶרַע מְרֵעִים (Yeshayahu 1:4), a seed of evildoers, he says the word is said not of the fathers but of the sons, a seed who are your evildoers and children who corrupt their doings.

The same word for a body run down and a face fallen: רָעוֹת הַמַּרְאֶה (Bereishis 41:4), ugly of appearance, and מַדּוּעַ פְּנֵיכֶם רָעִים (Bereishis 40:7), why are your faces downcast. So וְלֹֽא־הָיִיתִי רַע לְפָנָֽיו (Nechemiah 2:1): until that day he had not been downcast before the king but glad of heart, and when the king saw him so he asked why his face was sad.

Another sense: תִּתְקְעוּ וְלֹא תָרִֽיעוּ (Bamidbar 10:7), you shall blow but not sound a teruah, with the noun וּתְקַעְתֶּם תְּרוּעָה (Bamidbar 10:16), you shall sound a teruah. All of them are the sounding of the voice in a shout, whether for joy or for mourning, as לָמָּה תָרִיעִי רֵעַ (Michah 4:9), why do you cry aloud.
יַגִּיד עָלָיו רֵעוֹ (Iyov 36:33), which he explains: the thunder tells of the rain and points to it.
Another sense is a companion: אִישׁ רֵעִים לְהִתְרוֹעֵעַ (Mishlei 18:24), a man of friends to keep company with, and וְרֵעַ אָבִיךָ (Mishlei 27:10), and your father's friend.

Another sense is shattering: תְּרֹעֵֽם בְּשֵׁבֶט בַּרְזֶל (Tehillim 2:9), You shall break them with a rod of iron, and רֹעוּ עַמִּים וָחֹתּוּ (Yeshayahu 8:9), be broken, you peoples, and be dismayed. הֲיָרֹעַ בַּרְזֶל (Yirmiyahu 15:12) he reads of Nevuchadnetzar: if they are strong, one stronger than they will come upon them to break them and crush them. Radak holds this whole sense belongs to the doubled roots, and points to בכותל רעוע in the words of the Chachamim, a cracked wall.

חנן.sense: To show favour and to give freely out of grace; from it חֵן, favour, and תְּחִנָּה, the plea that asks for it.

more.t: וְחַנֹּתִי אֶת־אֲשֶׁר אָחֹן (Shemos 33:19), I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, which he glosses אתן חִנִּי, I will give My favour; and so כִּֽי־חַנַּנִי אֱלֹהִים (Bereishis 33:11), for Hashem has been gracious to me.

אֲשֶׁר־חָנַן אֱלֹהִים אֶת־עַבְדֶּֽךָ (Bereishis 33:5), whom Hashem has graciously given your servant, which he takes of the children, and חָנּוּנוּ אוֹתָם (Shoftim 21:22), which he explains חנו אותנו מהם, be gracious to us with them. These, he says, are close to the sense of מתנה, a gift.

וָֽאֶתְחַנַּן (Devarim 3:23), I pleaded, he explains בקשתי מלפניו שיחנני, I asked before Him that He favour me; and כִּֽי־יְחַנֵּן קוֹלוֹ (Mishlei 26:25) is ישא קולו בדרך תחינה, he raises his voice in the manner of supplication. These he calls close to the sense of תפלה ובקשה, prayer and request.
He holds כלם ענין חֵן, that all of them are the sense of favour, adding that one who understands can tell a little between each of them according to its place.

more.h: Free, which is to say in favour
more.t: וְיָֽצְאָה חִנָּם (Shemos 21:11), she shall go out free: the mem is an addition, as the mem of רֵיקָם, empty, and the sense is that she goes out בחן מאין כסף, in favour and without money; Radak holds every חנם in Scripture is to be explained in this way.

חוס.sense: To spare and to take pity, most often said of the eye that spares; he gives the root the sense of חמלה, compassion.

more.t: אַתָּה חַסְתָּ עַל־הַקִּיקָיוֹן (Yonah 4:10), you took pity on the gourd, לֹֽא־חָסָה עָלַיִךְ עַיִן (Yechezkel 16:5), no eye pitied you, and יָחֹס עַל־דַּל וְאֶבְיוֹן (Tehillim 72:13), he shall spare the poor and the needy.

more.h: Where the eye is left out
more.t: וַתָּחָס עֵינִי עֲלֵיהֶם מִשַּֽׁחֲתָם (Yechezkel 20:17), my eye spared them from destroying them; and where the pasuk says only וַתָּחָס עָלֶיךָ (Shmuel I 24:11), it spared you, he supplies ותחס עיני או נפשי, my eye or my soul spared.
The forms all come with cholam, and one stands alone with shuruk, לֹֽא־תָחוּס עֵינָֽם (Yeshayahu 13:18), their eye shall not spare, as does every אָחוּס, I will spare.

חמל.sense: To have compassion, and so to spare; he resists taking any of its pesukim out of that sense.

more.t: מִֽי־יַחְמֹל עָלַיִךְ יְרוּשָׁלַם (Yirmiyahu 15:5), who will pity you, Yerushalayim, and וְלֹֽא־תַחְמֹל וְלֹֽא־תְכַסֶּה עָלָֽיו (Devarim 13:9), you shall not spare him nor cover for him; a further form of the noun is וּמַחְמַל נַפְשְׁכֶם (Yechezkel 24:21), that on which your soul has pity.

Some explain וַיַּחְמֹל הַמֶּלֶךְ עַל־מְפִיבֹשֶׁת (Shmuel II 21:7) as וישמח, the king rejoiced, and so וְחָֽמַלְתִּי עֲלֵיהֶם כַּֽאֲשֶׁר יַחְמֹל אִישׁ עַל־בְּנוֹ (Malachi 3:17). Radak says there is no need to take them out of the sense of pity: the king spared him, that he not be taken with the others, or, as the Chachamim explain it, he asked mercy for him that the aron not take him in.

לְחֻמְלָה עָלָיִךְ (Yechezkel 16:5), to have pity on you, is an infinitive whose first root letter carries shuruk, and another comes in that same measure, מִלּוּשׁ בָּצֵק עַד־חֻמְצָתֽוֹ (Hoshea 7:4), from the kneading of the dough until it is leavened.

אהב.sense: To love: a father for his son, a man for Hashem, a lover for his beloved; the noun is אַהֲבָה, love.

more.t: וְיִשְׂרָאֵל אָהַב אֶת־יוֹסֵף (Bereishis 37:3), and Yisrael loved Yosef, וַיֶּֽאֱהַב יִצְחָק אֶת־עֵשָׂו (Bereishis 25:28), and Yitzchak loved Esav, and וָֽאֹהַב אֶֽת־יַֽעֲקֹֽב (Malachi 1:2), and I loved Yaakov.

לְזֶרַע אַבְרָהָם אֹֽהַבְךָ (Divrei HaYamim II 20:7), the seed of Avraham who loved You, carries its suffix as בֹּרַֽאֲךָ יַֽעֲקֹב (Yeshayahu 43:1), your Creator, Yaakov, and חֲמוֹר שֹׂנַֽאֲךָ (Shemos 23:5), the donkey of one who hates you, do.
וְרִדְּפָה אֶת־מְאַֽהֲבֶיהָ (Hoshea 2:7), and she shall pursue her lovers, and תְּֽאֵֽהֲבוּ פֶתִי (Mishlei 1:22), you love simplicity, where the tzeirei stands in place of a patach.

In the feminine: אִם־תָּעִירוּ וְֽאִם־תְּעֽוֹרְרוּ אֶת־הָאַֽהֲבָה (Shir HaShirim 2:7), that you not stir up love. In the masculine the noun is אַהַב, whose plural forms are אַיֶּלֶת אֲהָבִים (Mishlei 7:18), a hind of loves, and נִתְעַלְּסָה בָּֽאֳהָבִֽים (Mishlei 7:18), let us delight ourselves with loves.

more.h: A neighbouring word that is not his
more.t: In אָֽהֲבוּ הֵבוּ (Hoshea 4:18) he notes that הבו is not of this root but of יהב, which he will explain in its own place.

חבב.sense: Affection, holding a thing dear; he reads בְּחֻבִּי (Iyov 31:33) as in my love for it, not as a fold of the garment.

more.t: אַף חֹבֵב עַמִּים (Devarim 33:3), He loves the peoples, and לִטְמוֹן בְּחֻבִּי עֲוֹֽנִי (Iyov 31:33), to hide my sin in my bosom, he gives the sense ענין אהבה וחיבה, love and affection.

The Chachamim use this word a great deal, as in חביבין ישראל שנקראו בנים למקום, beloved are Yisrael, who are called sons of the Omnipresent, and חיבה יתירה נודעת להם, an extra affection was made known to them.

more.h: Hiding a sin out of love
more.t: לִטְמוֹן בְּחֻבִּי עֲוֹֽנִי he explains לטמן עוני באהבתי אותו, to hide my sin out of my love for it, and continues רק גליתי אותו ושנאתיו והרחקתיו ממני, rather I uncovered it and hated it and put it far from me.

עגב.sense: Doting love and words of desire, said of harlotry; the same letters also give עוגב, a pipe played in song.

more.t: וּבְכֹל אֲשֶׁר־עָֽגְבָה (Yechezkel 23:7), all upon whom she doted, מָֽאֲסוּ־בָךְ עֹֽגְבִים (Yirmiyahu 4:30), your lovers despise you, and וַתַּעְגַּב עַל־מְאַֽהֲבֶיהָ (Yechezkel 23:5), she doted upon her lovers; he gives them the sense ענין אהבה ודברי חשק, love and words of desire.

כִּֽי־עֲגָבִים בְּפִיהֶם הֵמָּה עֹשִׂים (Yechezkel 33:31) he explains מדמים בפיהם ובדבריהם כי דברי חשק להם דבריך ולא כן לבם, with their mouths and their words they make it seem that your words are words of desire to them, but their heart is not so. Targum Yonasan renders the phrase as mockery and derision, אֲרֵי תּוּלְעָבָא בְּפוּמְהוֹן אִינוּן עָבְדִין.

בְּמִנִּים וְעוּגָֽב (Tehillim 150:4), with strings and pipe, and וְעֻגָבִי לְקוֹל בֹּכִֽים (Iyov 30:31), my pipe to the voice of those who weep. Targum Yonasan renders כְּשִׁיר עֲגָבִים (Yechezkel 33:32) as כִּזְמַר אֲבּוּבִין, and Radak says this is one of the instruments of music.

מטר.sense: Rain, and the verb that rains a thing down; the one that rains can be Hashem or the cloud itself.

more.t: יַֽעֲרֹף כַּמָּטָר לִקְחִי (Devarim 32:2), my teaching shall drop as the rain, and וְנָֽתַתִּי מְטַֽר־אַרְצְכֶם בְּעִתּוֹ (Devarim 11:14), I will give the rain of your land in its season; the plural in the feminine is מִטְרוֹת עֻזּֽוֹ (Iyov 37:6), the rains of His strength.

more.h: Bound to the word for shower
more.t: וּמְטַֽר־גֶּשֶׁם יִתֵּן לָהֶם (Zechariah 10:1), He will give them showers of rain, a pair he likens to אַדְמַת עָפָר (Daniel 12:2), the dust of the earth, and מִטִּיט הַיָּוֵן (Tehillim 40:3), out of the miry clay.

The heavier form takes a further object: הִנְנִי מַמְטִיר לָכֶם לֶחֶם (Shemos 16:4), I will rain down bread for you, and יַמְטֵר עַל־רְשָׁעִים פַּחִים (Tehillim 11:6), He will rain snares upon the wicked.

In וְחֶלְקָה אֲשֶֽׁר־לֹֽא־תַמְטִיר עָלֶיהָ תִּיבָֽשׁ (Amos 4:7), and the field on which it does not rain shall wither, he says the one that does not rain upon it is the cloud, and so the verb is used of clouds in וְעַל הֶֽעָבִים אֲצַוֶּה מֵֽהַמְטִיר עָלָיו מָטָֽר (Yeshayahu 5:6), and I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it.

זהם.sense: Filth, and food gone foul: a man's appetite reckons the bread loathsome, and Chazal use the word of dirty hands and of a body's own filth.

more.t: וְזִֽהֲמַתּוּ חַיָּתוֹ לָחֶם (Iyov 33:20), his appetite makes bread loathsome to him. Radak explains that the man's soul comes to reckon the food as zuhama, filth.
The zuhama is הזיעה המאוסה, the loathsome sweat, whether it comes off a man's body or off the food.

more.h: The word in Chazal, of food
more.t: Chazal use it of food, להעביר הזהומה, to take off the filth (Chullin 105a), and בידים מזהמות, with filthy hands (Berachos 47b).

more.h: The word in Chazal, of the body
more.t: Of the body, ישֹראל שעמדו על הר סיני פסקה זוהמתן, that the filth of those who stood at Har Sinai ceased (Avodah Zarah 22b).

טנף.sense: To soil or dirty something. The one pasuk asks how I shall soil them, and Chazal use the word of filthy places.

more.t: אֵיכָכָה אֲטַנְּפֵֽם (Shir HaShirim 5:3), how shall I soil them. Radak glosses it אלכלכם, I shall dirty them.
Chazal speak of dirt in this word, במבואות המטונפות, in the filthy alleyways (Berachos 24b). Radak adds that there are many more like it.

אלח.sense: To be foul, gone rotten. Radak gives the sense as stinking, and holds the root a transposition of the letters behind a pot's scum.

more.t: אַף כִּֽי־נִתְעָב וְֽנֶאֱלָח (Iyov 15:15 in his edition), all the more one abhorrent and foul, and יַחְדָּו נֶאֱלָחוּ (Tehillim 14:3), together they have turned rotten. Radak gives the sense of both as נבאש, stinking.
Radak holds the word a transposition of the letters in סִיר אֲשֶׁר חֶלְאָתָה בָהּ (Yechezkel 24:6), a pot whose scum is in it.

בהן.sense: The thumb. Radak glosses the word as the thick one, and its plural covers the thumbs and big toes of hands and feet alike.

more.t: וְעַל־ בֹּהֶן יָדוֹ הַיְמָנִית (Vayikra 14:17), on the thumb of his right hand. Radak glosses the word as גודל, the thick one.

בְּֽהֹנוֹת יְדֵיהֶם וְרַגְלֵיהֶם מְקֻצָּצִים (Shoftim 1:7), the thumbs of their hands and the big toes of their feet cut off. Radak allows that this plural may stand on a different pattern of the noun.

זקף.sense: To raise up, to set upright. Hashem raises those who are bent over, and the Targum uses the word for lifting the eyes.

more.t: זֹקֵף כְּפוּפִים (Tehillim 146:8), Hashem raises up those who are bent over. Radak gives the sense as מרים, lifting.
The Targum renders וַיִּשָּׂא עֵינָיו וַיַּרְא (Bereishis 18:2), he lifted his eyes and saw, as וּזְקַף עֵינוֹהִי וַחֲזָא, putting this root where the pasuk has lifting.

רבב.sense: Many, much, great. From it come the number ten thousand, the great man called rav, the heavy rain, and in one place the shooting of arrows.

more.t: רַבּוּ מִשַּֽׂעֲרוֹת רֹאשִׁי (Tehillim 49:5), they are more than the hairs of my head, and as a description, עוֹד הָעָם רָב (Shoftim 7:4), the people are still too many.

In some places the word is enough: רַב ־לָכֶם בְּנֵי לֵוִֽי (Bamidbar 16:7), enough for you, sons of Levi, and רַב עַתָּה הֶרֶף יָדֶךָ (Shmuel II 24:16), it is enough, now stay your hand. Radak glosses the group די, sufficient.
As a number the word is ten thousand, which Radak calls the great reckoning: רִֽבֲבוֹת אַלְפֵי יִשְׂרָאֵֽל (Bamidbar 10:36), the ten thousands of the thousands of Yisrael.

A man of standing is called rav because his merits are many: עַל כָּל־ רַב בֵּיתוֹ (Esther 1:8), over every officer of his house. Radak reads קִרְיַת מֶלֶךְ רָֽב (Tehillim 48:3), the city of a great king, of Dovid.
From the same root and sense, וְכִרְבִיבִים עֲלֵי־עֵֽשֶׂב (Devarim 32:2), like showers upon grass, which Radak explains as המטר החזק, the hard rain.
Radak sets aside יָסֹבּוּ עָלַי רַבָּיו (Iyov 16:13), his archers surround me, as ענין הורות החצים, the shooting of arrows.

טטף.sense: The totafos of the Shema: an ornament bound on the forehead, which Chazal identify as the tefillin of the head.

more.t: וְהָיוּ לְטֽוֹטָפֹת בֵּין עֵֽינֵיכֶֽם (Devarim 11:18), they shall be for totafos between your eyes. Radak explains the word as a ציץ, a plate or band tied on the forehead.

Chazal bar going out לא בטוטפת ולא בסנביטין, not with a totefes and not with sanvutin (Shabbos 57a), and ask מאי טוטפת, what is a totefes; Rabbi Abahu answers המקפת מאזן לאזן, the one that reaches round from ear to ear.
The Targum renders וְאֶצְעָדָה אֲשֶׁר עַל־זְרֹעוֹ (Shmuel II 1:10), the armlet that was on his arm, as וְטוֹטַפְתָּא דְעַל דַרְעֵיהּ, so a totefes is sometimes tied on the arm.

Radak says the totefes written in the Torah is what Chazal call tefillin, and that the head tefillin holds four compartments; following the received tradition they rest this on the word itself, טט בכתפי שתים פת באפרקי שתים, tat is two in Kaftori and pat is two in Afriki (Menachos 34b).

They explain בין עיניך, between your eyes, as בגובה הראש, the high part of the head, the place where an infant's brain is soft, which lies opposite the space between the eyes (Menachos 36a), and Radak reads לֹֽא־תָשִׂימוּ קָרְחָה בֵּין עֵֽינֵיכֶם (Devarim 14:1), you shall not make a bald patch between your eyes, the same way.

תפל.sense: Something with nothing in it: plaster that will not hold, food without salt, and by extension empty prophecy and words of no worth.

more.t: וְהִנָּם טָחִים אֹתוֹ תָּפֵֽל (Yechezkel 13:10), they daub it with tafel, which Radak takes as a building that has no standing. The Targum renders it טִין פַּטִיר דְלָא תֲבָן, clay without straw.
הֲיֵֽאָכֵל תָּפֵל מִבְּלִי־מֶלַח (Iyov 6:6), can what is tafel be eaten without salt. Radak explains it as raw meat or raw fish, which is not eaten raw unless it is heavily salted.
נְבִיאַיִךְ חָזוּ לָךְ שָׁוְא וְתָפֵל (Eichah 2:14), your prophets saw for you emptiness and tafel.

more.h: Tiflah, a thing of no worth
more.t: וְלֹֽא־נָתַן תִּפְלָה לֵֽאלֹהִֽים (Iyov 1:12 in his edition), he ascribed no tiflah to Hashem, and וֶאֱלוֹהַּ לֹא־יָשִׂים תִּפְלָֽה (Iyov 24:12). Radak glosses tiflah as דבר גרועה שאין לו טעם, a poor thing with no sense to it, and reads the second pasuk as saying that Hashem sets them no obstacle and no restraint upon their deeds.

פסח.sense: Lame, and in a sense near it to skip over: Hashem passing over the doorways in Mitzrayim, and the korban named for that passing over.

more.t: אִישׁ עִוֵּר אוֹ פִסֵּחַ (Vayikra 21:18), a blind man or a lame one, and פִּסֵּחַ שְׁתֵּי רַגְלָֽיו (Shmuel II 9:13), lame in both his legs. In the plural, פִּסְחִים בָּזְזוּ בַֽז (Yeshayahu 33:23), the lame plunder spoil; and וַיִּפֹּל וַיִּפָּסֵחַ (Shmuel II 4:4), he fell and was made lame.

A sense close to it is skipping over: וּפָֽסַחְתִּי עֲלֵכֶם (Shemos 12:13), I shall pass over you. Radak explains that Hashem skips over the doorway when He sees the blood, and the destroyer does not come in.
So that offering is called pesach: וַֽאֲמַרְתֶּם זֶֽבַח־ פֶּסַח הוּא (Shemos 12:27), you shall say that it is a pesach offering, because He passed over the houses of Bnei Yisrael and skipped them.

גָּנוֹן וְהִצִּיל פָּסוֹחַ וְהִמְלִֽיט (Yeshayahu 31:6 in his edition), shielding and saving, passing over and rescuing. Radak says Hashem passed over Yerushalayim when the destroying angel came upon the camp of Ashur.

עַד־מָתַי אַתֶּם פֹּֽסְחִים עַל־שְׁתֵּי הַסְּעִפִּים (Melachim I 18:21), how long will you skip between the two boughs. Radak explains that they do not stand firm on either one but skip and leap over both.

וַיְפַסְּחוּ עַל־הַמִּזְבֵּחַ אֲשֶׁר עָשָֽׂה (Melachim I 18:26), they limped about the mizbeach that he made. Radak says they went over it in skips, their minds settling on nothing. Targum Yonasan renders וְאִשְׁתַּטוּ עַל אֱגוֹרָא דַעֲבָד, and Radak takes that to mean they were dancing after their custom on their altars, and that the one who made it was Achav or another who made it for the Baal.

דלג.sense: To leap or skip over. The lame man will leap like a deer, and the beloved comes skipping over the mountains.

more.t: עַל כָּל־ הַדּוֹלֵג עַל־הַמִּפְתָּן (Tzefaniah 1:9), everyone who leaps over the threshold. Targum Yonasan renders it עַל כָּל דִמְהַלְכִין בְּנִימוּסֵי פְּלִשְׁתָּאֵי, all who walk in the customs of the Pelishtim.
Radak ties it to עַל־כֵּן לֹֽא־יִדְרְכוּ כֹֽהֲנֵי דָגוֹן (Shmuel I 5:5), that the priests of Dagon do not tread on Dagon's threshold.

אָז יְדַלֵּג כָּֽאַיָּל פִּסֵּחַ (Yeshayahu 35:6), then the lame man will leap like a deer, and מְדַלֵּג עַל־הֶהָרִים (Shir HaShirim 2:8), leaping over the mountains. Radak gives the sense as מקפץ, springing.

קפץ.sense: To shut and hold back: a closed hand, a shut mouth. In a second use it is springing, leaping over the hills.

more.t: וְלֹא תִקְפֹּץ אֶת־יָדְךָ (Devarim 15:7), you shall not close your hand; יִקְפְּצוּ מְלָכִים פִּיהֶם (Yeshayahu 52:15), kings will shut their mouths; אִם־ קָפַץ בְּאַף רַֽחֲמָיו סֶֽלָה (Tehillim 77:10), has He in anger shut up His mercies; וְעֹלָתָה קָפְצָה פִּֽיהָ (Iyov 5:16), wrongdoing shuts its mouth. Radak gives the sense of all of them as סתימה ומניעה, closing and withholding.
מְקַפֵּץ עַל־הַגְּבָעֽוֹת (Shir HaShirim 2:8), springing over the hills, which Radak takes as leaping and hurrying along.
כַּכֹּל יִקָּפְצוּן (Iyov 24:24), they are gathered in like all the rest. Radak explains that they are finished off quickly and their place is not known, like one who leaps away.
Chazal use the word of jumping in, קפץ ונשבע, he jumped and swore (Yevamos 32b).

כלה.sense: To come to an end, to finish, and to long for. From it the kidneys, which some name for their part in desire, and kli, any vessel, garment or weapon.

more.t: כִּי לֹא־ כָלוּ רַֽחֲמָֽיו (Eichah 3:22), His mercies are not spent, and כָּלוּ עֵינַי מְיַחֵל (Tehillim 69:4), my eyes are spent with waiting. Radak gives this group the sense of כליון והשחתה, wasting away and ruin.

A sense near the first is completion: כָּלָה הַבַּיִת לְכָל־דְּבָרָיו (Melachim I 6:38), the house was finished in all its details, and וַתְּכַל לְהַשְׁקֹתוֹ (Bereishis 24:19), she finished giving him drink.

On לְֽכָל תִּכְלָה רָאִיתִי קֵץ (Tehillim 119:96), to every completion I have seen an end, Radak says that whoever derives תִּכְלָה from וְכָל בַּשָּׁלִשׁ (Yeshayahu 40:12), and measured in a measure, has erred on both counts, since both words come from roots ending in a heh. Others explain רְחָבָה מִצְוָתְךָ מְאֹֽד, Your commandment is exceedingly broad, of the mitzvos of the heart, while the mitzvos of the body have a limit, and Radak holds that explanation the true one.

נִכְסְפָה וְגַם־ כָּלְתָה נַפְשִׁי (Tehillim 84:3), my soul yearned and pined. In וַתְּכַל דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ (Shmuel II 13:39) Radak supplies the missing word, the soul of Dovid longed. Ibn Ezra takes the word as carrying an object, of Avshalom's mother, who longed for Dovid until he wished to go out from his place to his son; Radak adds that the pasuk does not mention her.

Close to כלה with an alef: וְאֶת־בְּנֵיהֶם כָּלוּ בַבָּֽיִת (Shmuel I 6:10), they shut their young up in the house, and לֹֽא־ יִכְלֶה מִמְּךָ (Bereishis 23:6), none will withhold from you. Radak says all of these are מניעה ועצירה, holding back and restraining.

From this root וְאֵת שְׁתֵּי הַכְּלָיֹת (Vayikra 3:4), the two kidneys, which Radak calls well known. Some say they are named so because they have power in desire, from the sense of כָּלְתָה נַפְשִׁי, my soul pined. By borrowing, כִּלְיוֹת חִטָּה (Devarim 32:14), kidneys of wheat, since the grains of wheat are shaped like kidneys.

From the same root כָּל־ כְּלִי יוּצַר עָלַיִךְ (Yeshayahu 54:17), no weapon formed against you. Radak says the word serves for any article of use, for weapons, and for clothing, as in וְכַכַּלָּה תַּעְדֶּה כֵלֶֽיהָ (Yeshayahu 61:10), like a bride who puts on her ornaments, which he explains as her garments and her jewellery.

עצה.sense: To shut the eyes, and as a noun the end of the spine. Chazal put the word instead under the root of counsel.

more.t: עֹצֶה עֵינָיו לַחְשֹׁב תַּהְפֻּכוֹת (Mishlei 16:30), he shuts his eyes to devise perverse things. Radak glosses it סותם, closing, and explains that a man thinks better with his eyes shut than open, since he does not turn this way and that and his heart is on nothing but the matter he is thinking about.
לְעֻמַּת הֶֽעָצֶה יְסִירֶנָּה (Vayikra 3:9), he shall remove it opposite the atzeh, which Radak says is the end of the spine.
Chazal put this word under the root of counsel, saying מקום שהכליות יועצות, the place where the kidneys give counsel (Chullin 11a), and that it was taken off above the kidneys.

טוח.sense: To plaster or smear over: daubing a wall, and eyes smeared over so they cannot see. The tuchos of two pesukim he takes as the kidneys.

more.t: וְטָח אֶת־הַבָּֽיִת (Vayikra 14:42), he shall plaster the house, and אַיֵּה הַטִּיחַ אֲשֶׁר טַחְתֶּֽם (Yechezkel 13:12), where is the daubing you daubed. Radak explains the tiach as plastering the walls of a house with lime or clay, between one stone and the next on the outside, or over the whole wall.

כִּי טַח מֵֽרְאוֹת עֵֽינֵיהֶם (Yeshayahu 44:18), for their eyes are smeared over from seeing. Radak allows that טַח here stands without an object, or that it carries one like its fellows, the smearer being the false prophet or the heart, as in לֵב הוּתַל הִטָּהוּ (Yeshayahu 44:20), a deluded heart has turned him aside.
וְהִנָּם טָחִים אֹתוֹ תָּפֵֽל (Yechezkel 13:10), they daub it with untempered plaster, and אֱמֹר אֶל־ טָחֵי תָפֵל וְיִפֹּל (Yechezkel 13:11), say to those who daub with tafel that it shall fall.

הֵן־אֱמֶת חָפַצְתָּ בַטֻּחוֹת (Tehillim 51:8), You desire truth in the tuchos, and מִי־שָׁת בַּטֻּחוֹת חָכְמָה (Iyov 38:36), who put wisdom in the tuchos. Radak explains both as the kidneys, and reports that they are called so because they are plastered over and covered with fat.

סחר.sense: To go round about. A trader is called socher because he travels the lands and returns, and from it come trade, wares, a round shield and a stone.

more.t: סָֽחֲרוּ אֶל־אֶרֶץ וְלֹא יָדָֽעוּ (Yirmiyahu 14:18), which Radak glosses סבבו, they went round, to a land they did not know. And לִבִּי סְחַרְחַר (Tehillim 38:11), my heart goes round and round and will not settle, from the weight of troubles.
The Targum renders סָבִיב סָבִיב (Yechezkel 37:2), round about, as סְחוֹר סְחוֹר, and וַיִּסֹּב מֵֽעֲלֵיהֶם (Bereishis 42:24), he turned away from them, as וְאִסְתַּחַר מֵעִלָּוֵיהוֹן.

more.h: Why a trader is a socher
more.t: Radak says the dealer is called socher because he is always going round the lands, out and back: אֲנָשִׁים מִדְיָנִים סֹֽחֲרִים (Bereishis 37:28), Midianite traders, and אֲשֶׁר סֹֽחֲרֶיה שָׂרִים (Yeshayahu 23:8), whose merchants are princes.

שְׁבוּ וּסְחָרוּהָ (Bereishis 34:10), settle and trade in the land, and תַּרְשִׁישׁ סֹֽחַרְתֵּךְ (Yechezkel 27:12), Tarshish was your merchant, which Radak reads as bringing her wares to you. As a noun, אִיִּים רַבִּים סְחֹרַת יָדֵךְ (Yechezkel 27:15), many islands were the market of your hand, and טוֹב סַחְרָהּ (Mishlei 3:14), her profit is good.
From the same sense the shield that is round on every side is called sochera: צִנָּה וְֽסֹחֵרָה אֲמִתּֽוֹ (Tehillim 91:4), His truth is a shield and a buckler.

וְדַר וְסֹחָֽרֶת (Esther 1:6), dar and sochares, which Radak says is a precious stone, perhaps called sochares because it is always in the hands of traders. Chazal say of the pasuk that it is one stone, and that it calls out dror, freedom, to everyone who deals in wares (Megillah 12a).

פתה.sense: Being drawn aside: the heart leaning off the way of truth and sense; the fool is a פתי for leaning at anything, and פתאום is what is on you before you feel it.

more.h: A heart leaning where it should not
