more.t: פֶּן־ יִפְתֶּה לְבַבְכֶם (Devarim 11:16), lest your heart be drawn away, and וַיִּפְתְּ בַּסֵּתֶר לִבִּי (Iyov 31:27), and my heart was secretly drawn: the sense is the heart inclining toward another, not along the way of truth and understanding. So וּלְפֹתֶה שְׂפָתָיו לֹא תִתְעָרָֽב (Mishlei 20:19), do not join with one who draws you on with his lips, which Radak explains as the man who inclines toward you with his lips and speaks smooth things to you while his heart is not right with you.

more.h: Why a fool is called פתי
more.t: The simpleton is called פתי because he inclines to whatever comes, as פֶּתִי יַֽאֲמִין לְכָל־דָּבָר (Mishlei 14:15), a simpleton believes every word. So too כְּיוֹנָה פוֹתָה אֵין לֵב (Hoshea 7:11), like a silly dove with no heart: as the dove leans toward the food and has no heart to see that the net is spread to take her, so Ephraim leaned after what his desire drew him to, help from Egypt and Ashur, with no heart to know that the Maker of all will trip them up in going to seek help from any but him.

From this same sense and stem Radak derives פתאום, the alef standing in place of the hei of the root: וּפִתְאֹם יָבוֹא אֶל־הֵֽיכָלוֹ (Malachi 3:1), and suddenly he will come to his Heichal, and עַל־כֵּן פִּתְאֹם יָבוֹא אֵידוֹ (Mishlei 6:15), therefore his ruin will come suddenly. The sense is speed, and a thing a man does not notice until it is upon him, since the פתי does what he does in haste.

To press the suddenness further the word is doubled with פתע: בְּפֶתַע פִּתְאֹם (Bamidbar 6:9), in an instant, all at once, and אֲשֶׁר־ פִּתְאֹם לְפֶתַע (Yeshayahu 30:13), which comes suddenly, in a moment.

Turned on somebody else the verb is one man talking another round: פִּתֵּיתִי אֵת הַנָּבִיא הַהוּא (Yechezkel 14:9), I enticed that prophet, מִי יְפַתֶּה אֶת־אַחְאָב (Melachim I 22:20), who will entice Achav, and הִנֵּה אָֽנֹכִי מְפַתֶּיהָ (Hoshea 2:16), behold I will draw her on.

יַפְתְּ אֱלֹהִים לְיֶפֶת (Bereishis 9:27), Hashem will make wide for Yefes, is another sense of the root, and Radak brings the Targum, which renders כִּֽי־יַרְחִיב (Devarim 12:20), when Hashem widens your border, with אֲרֵי יַפְתֵּי. On that reading some explain וּלְפֹתֶה שְׂפָתָיו (Mishlei 20:19) of the man who opens his lips wide for empty talk and for insults, or of the one who opens his lips and uncovers a secret, whom you should not join.

more.h: His brother on a false witness
more.t: His brother Rabbi Moshe takes וַֽהֲפִתִּיתָ בִּשְׂפָתֶֽיךָ (Mishlei 24:28) from here, the hei standing for im, as if it said, and if you have enticed. Radak explains the pasuk so: אַל־תְּהִי עֵֽד־חִנָּם בְּרֵעֶךָ, be not a witness against your fellow without cause, and though you talked him round with your lips and he bore false witness for you, do not bear false witness for him in return.

פלט.sense: Getting out alive: to escape and to bring out to safety, a פליט being one who got away; in a nearby sense it is a casting off, even a miscarriage.

more.h: Escape, and the one who escaped
more.t: וּפָֽלְטוּ פְּלִיטֵיהֶם (Yechezkel 7:16), their fugitives will get away, and as a description וַיָּבֹא הַפָּלִיט (Bereishis 14:13), the fugitive came, and וְזָֽכְרוּ פְלִֽיטֵיכֶם (Yechezkel 6:9), your escaped ones will remember. Radak says the whole of it is rescue and getting away.

more.h: פליטי אפרים, the lowly of them
more.t: On כִּי אָמְרוּ פְּלִיטֵי אֶפְרַיִם (Shoftim 12:4), for the fugitives of Ephraim said, Radak explains that these are the lesser men of Ephraim, who were saying to Gilead, what are you reckoned among Ephraim and among Menasheh; and the lesser are called פלטים because they are as the leavings of the great and the honoured. In his own view פְּלִיטֵי הַגּוֹיִם (Yeshayahu 45:20) likewise means the lowly among them.

פַּלְּטָה נַפְשִׁי מֵרָשָׁע חַרְבֶּֽךָ (Tehillim 17:13), deliver my soul from the wicked, your sword, and תְּפַלְּטֵנִי מֵרִיבֵי עָם (Tehillim 18:44), you deliver me from the strivings of the people. רָנֵּי פַלֵּט תְּסוֹבְבֵנִי סֶֽלָה (Tehillim 32:7) Radak reads as songs of praise and thanks for the rescue: when I am saved from the enemy I will sing and give thanks to you.

Close to it is a throwing off: וְתַסֵּג וְלֹא תַפְלִיט (Michah 6:14), you will conceive and not bring forth, which Radak takes as the casting out of what miscarries at birth, and עַל־אָוֶן פַּלֶּט־לָמוֹ (Tehillim 56:8), a casting away and a putting far from them. The Chachamim use the word so, נדה שפלטה שכבת זרע, of a woman who casts out what she received, and the Targum renders וַיָּקֵא אֶת־יוֹנָה (Yonah 2:11), and the fish threw up Yonah, with וּפְלֵט יַת יוֹנָה.

For the last of them Radak says the right reading in his eyes is the first sense, escape, and that the pasuk is put as a question, on which reading it asks whether they are to get away for their wrongdoing.

שֹרד.sense: A survivor: those of them left over, a sense he calls plain and known; the same letters also carry a carpenter's marking line and the בִּגְדֵי הַשְּׂרָד.

more.h: Those left when the rest are gone
more.t: וְהַשְּׂרִידִים שָֽׂרְדוּ מֵהֶם (Yehoshua 10:20), the survivors who were left of them, פָּלִיט וְשָׂרִיד (Eichah 2:22), a fugitive or a survivor, and שְׂרִידֵי חָרֶב (Yirmiyahu 31:1), those left over from the sword. Radak says the sense is known and gives no gloss of his own.
יְתָֽאֲרֵהוּ בַשֶּׂרֶד (Yeshayahu 44:13), he marks it out with a שרד, is the coloured cord with which the carpenter marks off what he wants to cut away from the wood.

וְאֵת בִּגְדֵי הַשְּׂרָד (Shemos 31:10) are the garments of the service, and Radak says they are not priestly garments at all but cloths made to cover the mizbeach, the shulchan and the menorah when the camp travelled. Rashi wrote that they are called בגדי שרד because they are made like netting, which the Targum renders סרדין.

קלט.sense: Taking in and holding fast: the cities of refuge take in whoever flees there, a hoof called קלוט is closed up, and dye is taken up and held by the wool.

more.t: שָׂרוּעַ וְקָלוּט (Vayikra 22:23), the limb overgrown and the limb drawn in: Radak says the קלוט is one whose foot is gathered in and narrow, and the Chachamim explained (Bechoros 40a) that its hooves are closed like the feet of a horse or a donkey.

more.h: The cities that take a man in
more.t: עָרֵי מִקְלָט (Bamidbar 35:11), cities of refuge, are so called because they took in and gathered within them those who fled there.
From the Mishnah he brings כדי שיקלוט את העין, enough for the colour to be taken up, which Radak explains as taking the dye and gathering it in.

עיף.sense: Weary: he gives two pesukim, faint and weary and my soul faints, and says he has already set the word down under the root עוף, so nothing is explained here.

more.t: עָיֵף וְיָגֵעַ (Devarim 25:18), faint and weary, and כִּי־ עָֽיְפָה נַפְשִׁי (Yirmiyahu 4:31), for my soul faints. Radak adds only that he has already mentioned them under the root עוף, and gives no gloss here at all.

יעף.sense: Growing weary: to tire and to flag; the same letters carry a word of flying, and תועפות, which he says is strength.

more.t: לֹא יִיעַף וְלֹא יִיגָע (Yeshayahu 40:28), he neither tires nor wearies, and וְיִֽעֲפוּ נְעָרִים וְיִגָעוּ (Yeshayahu 40:30), youths will tire and weary. As a description, לִשְׁתּוֹת הַיָּעֵף (Shmuel II 16:2), for the weary man to drink; Radak says the sense of weariness is known.

more.h: The weary man thirsty to hear
more.t: לָעוּת אֶת־ יָעֵף דָּבָר (Yeshayahu 50:4), to hold up the weary with a word, and Radak says this is the man thirsty to hear the word of Hashem.

more.h: מֻעָף בִּיעָף is flight, not fatigue
more.t: מֻעָף בִּיעָף (Daniel 9:21) belongs rather to the sense of flying: Gavriel, whom Daniel had seen in the earlier vision flying above, he now saw touching him.

Another sense again: וְתֽוֹעֲפוֹת הָרִים לֽוֹ (Tehillim 95:4), the strength of the mountains is his, כְּתֽוֹעֲפֹת רְאֵם לֽוֹ (Bamidbar 23:22), like the strength of a re'em, and וְכֶסֶף תּֽוֹעָפוֹת לָֽךְ (Iyov 22:25), silver of strength will be yours. Radak says their sense is strength.

יגע.sense: Wearing oneself out with labour: the toiling, what the toil earns, and the man worn out by it; a sense he says is close to plain weariness.

more.h: Toil that wears a man out
more.t: יָגַעְתִּי בְקָרְאִי נִחַר גְּרוֹנִי (Tehillim 69:4), I am worn out with calling, my throat is dry, עַד כִּי־ יָגְעָה יָדוֹ (Shmuel II 23:10), until his hand gave out, and לֹא יִֽיגְעוּ לָרִיק (Yeshayahu 65:23), they will not labour for nothing. Radak says the sense of toil is known, like the sense of weariness.

Turned on another the verb is tiring him out: הֽוֹגַעְתַּנִי בַּֽעֲוֹנֹתֶֽיךָ (Yeshayahu 43:24), you have wearied me with your sins, and אַל־ תְּיַגַּע ־שָׁמָּה אֶת־כָּל־הָעָם (Yehoshua 7:3), do not weary the whole people by sending them there.
As a noun it is the labour and what it brings in: יְגִיעַ מִצְרַיִם (Yeshayahu 45:14), the labour of Egypt, and וְכָל־ יְגִיעֲךָ (Devarim 28:33), and all your toil.

more.h: Things that weary whoever deals in them
more.t: עָיֵף וְיָגֵעַ (Devarim 25:18), faint and weary, and כָּל־הַדְּבָרִים יְגֵעִים (Koheles 1:8), all things are wearying: Radak says they are put in the language of toil because there is labour and weariness for anyone occupied with them. So too וְשָׁם יָנוּחוּ יְגִיעֵי כֹֽחַ (Iyov 3:17), there those worn out of strength are at rest.

דנג.sense: Wax: כַּדּוֹנַג מִפְּנֵי הָאֵשׁ (Michah 1:4), like wax before the fire, and the whole of his entry is that דונג is the wax.

קיר.sense: A wall: the wall of the mizbeach or of a house, and by borrowing the walls of the heart; the doubled verb from it is tearing a wall down.

more.t: קִיר הַמִּזְבֵּֽחַ (Vayikra 1:15), the wall of the mizbeach, and נֹגַעַת בַּקִּיר הַשֵּׁנִי (Melachim I 6:27), touching the second wall; Radak says it is the כותל known from the Mishnah. In the feminine plural, בְּקִירוֹת הַבָּֽיִת (Melachim I 6:6), in the walls of the house, and וְקִֽירֹתָיו עֵץ (Yechezkel 41:22), and its walls of wood.

more.h: An upper room built of stone
more.t: On נַֽעֲשֶׂה־נָּא עֲלִיַּת־ קִיר (Melachim II 4:10), let us make a walled upper room, Radak says the upper room is joined to קיר to tell that it is to be built with walls, a building of stones, and not with partitions of reeds.
By way of borrowing, קִירוֹת לִבִּי הֹֽמֶה־לִּי (Yirmiyahu 4:19), the walls of my heart moan within me; Radak says it is said of the heart because a heart has sides and hollows.

The doubled verb is the pulling down of a wall: וְקַרְקַר כָּל־בְּנֵי־שֵֽׁת (Bamidbar 24:17), and he will break down all the sons of Shes, and מְקַרְקַר קִר (Yeshayahu 22:5). As מְשָׁרֵשׁ is taking out the root, so מקרקר is pulling down the wall, and קִר is added only for clearness, since מקרקר alone would have done, as in לִצְבֹא צָבָא (Bamidbar 4:23), to serve the service, and וַיִּקְסְמוּ קְסָמִים (Melachim II 17:17), and they divined divinations.

נכת.sense: A thing to be desired: he reads נכאת, one of the goods of Bereishis 37:25, as something precious; others say carob fruit, and Bereishis Rabbah says wax.

more.t: נְכֹאת וּצְרִי וָלֹט (Bereishis 37:25), nechos, tzari and lot, where Radak says נכאת is a desirable thing, the alef standing in for a lengthening vav. So too אֶת־בֵּית נְכֹתֹה (Yeshayahu 39:2), the house of what he treasured, which the Targum renders יַת כֹּל בֵּית גִנְזוֹהִי, the whole house of his treasuries.
Some explain נכאת וצרי ולט as the fruit of the carob tree. Bereishis Rabbah, at the end of parashah 91, explains נכאת as שעוה, wax, and Radak says that this is well known.

more.h: Verbs that may share the stem
more.t: Radak holds it possible that וַיַּכּוּם וַֽיַּכְּתוּם (Bamidbar 14:45), and they struck them and beat them down, is of this root, the form being shortened as in וַיַּדְבְּקוּ גַם־הֵמָּה (Shmuel I 14:22), and they too clung on; so also וָֽאֶכֹּת אֹתוֹ טָחוֹן (Devarim 9:21), and I beat it fine by grinding. Their sense, he says, he set out under the root כָּתַת.

הלל.sense: Praise: the sense is השבח וההודאה, praise and thanks; the same letters also carry the joy of a wedding, raving madness, and the shining of light.

more.h: Praise, and thanks along with it
more.t: שֶׁבַע בַּיּוֹם הִלַּלְתִּיךָ (Tehillim 119:164), seven times a day I praise you; the noun is תְּהִלָּה לְדָוִד (Tehillim 145:1), a praise of David, and in the plural יוֹשֵׁב תְּהִלּוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵֽל (Tehillim 22:4), he who sits enthroned on the praises of Yisrael. The reflexive is בִּקְדוֹשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל תִּתְהַלָּֽל (Yeshayahu 41:16), in the Holy One of Yisrael you will glory.

more.h: Wedding joy is close to praise
more.t: Some explain לְהִתְהַלֵּל עִם־נַֽחֲלָתֶֽךָ (Tehillim 106:5), to glory with your inheritance, from rejoicing, as קֹדֶשׁ הִלּוּלִים (Vayikra 19:24), a holy thing of rejoicing. Radak says there is no need to take them out of the sense of praise, since rejoicing is near to it: וּבְתוּלֹתָיו לֹא הוּלָּֽלוּ (Tehillim 78:63), his maidens had no wedding song, means they never came to the time of rejoicing, that is, they were not married, and the Chachamim call the wedding chamber בי הלולא (Bava Metzia 36a).

more.h: הוללות, going out of one's mind
more.t: A second sense is madness: אָמַרְתִּי לַֽהוֹלְלִים אַל־ תָּהֹלּוּ (Tehillim 75:5), I said to the raving, do not rave, כִּי הָעֹשֶׁק יְהוֹלֵל חָכָם (Koheles 7:7), oppression drives a wise man mad, and the nouns וְדַעַת הֹֽלֵלוֹת וְשִׂכְלוּת (Koheles 1:17), the knowing of madness and folly. Radak says they are all madness, the going out from the mind's understanding and from the way of what is right and straight.

מְהוֹלָלַי בִּי נִשְׁבָּֽעוּ (Tehillim 102:9), those mad against me swear by me, Radak explains as those who are mad in his own eyes; and on בִּי נִשְׁבָּֽעוּ, they swear by me, Rabbi Yonah wrote that out of how low he stood in their eyes they would say, may Hashem set me like so-and-so if such and such comes about.

יִתְהֽוֹלְלוּ הָרֶכֶב יִשְׁתַּקְשְׁקוּן בָּֽרְחֹבוֹת (Nachum 2:5), the chariots rave and clatter in the open places: Radak says that from the greatness of their running in joy it is as though they were mad with much joy. So too עַל־כֵּן יִתְהֹֽלְלוּ גוֹיִֽם (Yirmiyahu 51:7), therefore the nations rave, at the sight of Bavel's fall.

בְּהִלּוֹ נֵרוֹ עֲלֵי רֹאשִׁי (Iyov 29:3), when his lamp shone over my head, and לֹא יָהֵלּוּ אוֹרָם (Yeshayahu 13:10), they will not let their light shine. Radak notes that יהל sets the shining on the light itself and יהלו on the stars, and that from this sense the morning star is called הֵילֵל בֶּן־שָׁחַר (Yeshayahu 14:12); all of them are brightness and light.

שׁבח.sense: Praising: to laud and to be lauded, a sense he calls known; in a second sense the same verb is stilling, the quieting of a raging sea.

more.t: יְשַׁבַּח מַֽעֲשֶׂיךָ (Tehillim 145:4), he will praise your works, and שְׂפָתַי יְשַׁבְּחֽוּנְךָ (Tehillim 63:4), my lips will praise you; with the reflexive, לְהִשְׁתַּבֵּחַ בִּתְהִלָּתֶֽךָ (Tehillim 106:47), to glory in your praise. Radak says the sense is known and adds nothing to it.

בְּשׂוֹא גַלָּיו אַתָּה תְשַׁבְּחֵֽם (Tehillim 89:10), when its waves rise you still them, וְחָכָם בְּאָחוֹר יְשַׁבְּחֶֽנָּה (Mishlei 29:11), a wise man holds it back and quiets it, and מַשְׁבִּיחַ שְׁאוֹן יַמִּים (Tehillim 65:8), who stills the roaring of the seas. Radak says the sense of all of these is stilling and settling.

פאר.sense: Glory: to take glory or to give it, תפארת being splendour; a פאר is a headdress that adorns, and a פארה a bough, which is the tree's own glory.

more.t: הֲיִתְפָּאֵר הַגַּרְזֶן עַל הַחֹצֵב בּוֹ (Yeshayahu 10:15), shall the axe take glory over the one hewing with it, and אֲשֶׁר־בְּךָ אֶתְפָּאָֽר (Yeshayahu 49:3), in whom I will be glorified. On הִתְפָּאֵר עָלַי (Shemos 8:5) Radak says it is: take the glory and the praise to yourself over me, that you should say when I am to entreat for you, and so I will do.

וְאֶת־ פַּֽאֲרֵי הַמִּגְבָּעֹת (Shemos 39:28), the ornaments of the caps, פַּֽאֲרֵי פִשְׁתִּים יִֽהְיוּ עַל־רֹאשָׁם (Yechezkel 44:18), linen headdresses will be on their head, and הַפְּאֵרִים וְהַצְּעָדוֹת (Yeshayahu 3:20), the headdresses and the ankle chains. These are the caps that are a glory to a man while they are on his head, and Radak says the sense of all of them is praise and beauty.

On כָּל־פָּנִים קִבְּצוּ פָארֽוּר (Yoel 2:6), all faces gather a פארור, Menachem explains that they gathered in their glory so that none was left them, in the way of וְכֽוֹכָבִים אָסְפוּ נָגְהָֽם (Yoel 2:10), the stars gathered in their brightness. Dunash explains it from וּבִשְּׁלוּ בַּפָּרוּר (Bamidbar 11:8), and they cooked it in the pot, the alef added, so that they gathered all the blackness of the pot.

His father holds that Menachem cannot be right, since there is a difference between אסיפה and קיבוץ: gathering, קיבוץ, is said only of scattered things brought to one place, so it cannot be said of a glory that is not seen, while אסיפה can, as וַיֶּֽאֱסֹף רַגְלָיו (Bereishis 49:33), he gathered in his feet, and אֱסֹף יָדֶֽךָ (Shmuel I 14:19), draw back your hand; and one does not say קְבוֹץ ידיך, gather your hands.

It may be from this root that a branch is called so: מְסָעֵף פֻּארָה (Yeshayahu 10:33), lopping off a bough, and וַתֶּאֱרַכְנָה פֹארֹתָו (Yechezkel 31:5), its boughs grew long, like סעיף and סעפותיו. Radak says the great high branch may be called פארה because it is the glory and the beauty of the tree.

more.h: Not stripping the boughs behind you
more.t: לֹא תְפַאֵר אַֽחֲרֶיךָ (Devarim 24:20), you shall not go over the boughs after you, is pointed so as to mark the sense off, and it means that you shall not take what is left in the boughs. The Chachamim explained (Chullin 131a) it as the language of פאר, that you shall not take its glory from it.

Rabbi Yehudah wrote that the root of פֻּארָה and פֹֽארֹתָיו may be פרה, the alef before the resh standing as a lengthening vav. Radak answers that there is no proof of it, since in only a few of them does the alef come before the resh, as against וַתְּשַׁלַּח פֹּארֽוֹת (Yechezkel 17:6), and it sent out boughs, where the resh comes first.

קלס.sense: Mockery: derision and contempt, a thing made a byword; sometimes the same word is praise, which is why Kaddish says ויתקלס and one Gaon objected to it.

more.t: לַעַג וָקֶלֶס (Tehillim 44:14), derision and scorn, לְחֶרְפָּה וּלְקֶלֶס כָּל־הַיּֽוֹם (Yirmiyahu 20:8), a reproach and a mocking all the day, and in another form וְקַלָּסָה לְכָל־הָֽאֲרָצֽוֹת (Yechezkel 22:4), a mockery to all the lands. Radak says the sense is mocking and contempt.

more.h: The form that falls on the mocker
more.t: The reflexive falls on the one doing the mocking and is bound with a bet: יִתְקַלְּסוּ ־בָךְ (Yechezkel 22:5), they will mock at you, and וַיִּתְקַלְּסוּ ־בוֹ וַיֹּאמְרוּ לוֹ עֲלֵה קֵרֵחַ (Melachim II 2:23), they mocked at him and said to him, go up, baldhead. Radak says that since the mocking is kept up against them, the form shows the mocker taken up with it.

more.h: The same word used for praise
more.t: Sometimes this word falls on praise: כַּזּוֹנָה לְקַלֵּס אֶתְנָֽן (Yechezkel 16:31), like a harlot praising the hire she takes. Radak allows that וְהוּא בַּמְּלָכִים יִתְקַלָּס (Chavakuk 1:10) may be of this sense, that he glories in kings, though from what follows it, וְרֹזְנִים מִשְׂחָק לוֹ, and rulers are a laughing matter to him, it looks more like the first sense; and Targum Yonasan renders it וְהוּא עַל מַלְכַיָא מִתְלַעַב, and he mocks at kings.

more.h: ויתקלס in Kaddish, and an objection
more.t: In the sense of praise, Radak says, they said in Kaddish ויתעלה ויתקלס, may he be exalted and praised; but Rav Amram Gaon wrote in the siddur of prayers that he composed that it is not fitting to say ויתקלס.

Radak also allows explaining לְקַלֵּס אֶתְנָֽן from mocking and contempt, so that the whole word stays in one sense: the harlot mocks at the hire once she has taken it, and mocks at the man who comes after her and despises him in her heart for letting himself be drawn on by her words and by the sweetness of her lips. Or she mocks at the hire itself before him, and despises it, so that he will raise it for her.

אפס.sense: Coming to an end: the money or the thing is spent and gone. The noun is the want of a thing, 'there is none', and אַפְסֵי אָרֶץ, the ends of the earth.

more.t: אָפֵס הַמֵּץ (Yeshayahu 16:4) and כִּי אָפֵס כָּֽסֶף (Bereishis 47:15) are a past verb, and Radak glosses them כלה המץ, the מץ is finished, and כלה הכסף, the money is finished. So too הֶאָפֵס לָנֶצַח חַסְדּוֹ (Tehillim 77:9), has His kindness ceased for ever. Radak says their sense is known.

more.h: The noun: none of it, without it
more.t: בְּאֶפֶס עֵצִים תִּכְבֶּה־אֵשׁ (Mishlei 26:20) is with no wood the fire goes out; הַאֶפֶס עוֹד אִישׁ (Shmuel II 9:3), Radak: הלא עוד איש, is there not still a man; עַד אֶפֶס מָקוֹם (Yeshayahu 5:8), until there is no room; and בְּאֶפֶס עֲשָׁקֽוֹ, which Radak glosses בחנם בלא משפט, for nothing, with no justice done.

Radak says it comes in place of בלתי, 'but', 'only': אֶפֶס כִּֽי־נִאֵץ נִאַצְתָּ (Shmuel II 12:14), only that you have greatly blasphemed; אֶפֶס כי עז העם (Bamidbar 13:29), only that the people is strong; and אֲנִי וְאַפְסִי עוֹד (Tzefaniah 2:15), which he glosses אני ואין בלתי עוד, I am, and there is none besides me.

אַפְסֵי אָרֶץ (Shmuel I 2:10) is קצות הארץ, the ends of the earth. Radak says they are all near one idea, כליון ודבר שאינו, a finishing and a thing that is not, only that each is explained by the sense nearest its own place.

Radak reads מֵי אָפְסָֽיִם (Yechezkel 47:3) as מי כליון, water of ending, with only a little in it. Rabbi Yonah read it מי פסים with an added alef, water of palms, since in Aramaic the palm of the hand is called פס ידא, meaning the water covered only the soles of his feet. Radak brings Chachamim in Shekalim, that a man crosses it up to his ankles, and Targum Yonasan, who renders מֵי קַרְסוּלִין, ankle water.

תהה.sense: Desolation: הָֽיְתָה תֹהוּ וָבֹהוּ (Bereishis 1:2) is waste, and Radak says he has already explained the word at his root בָּהָה.

בלם.sense: To muzzle and stop up: עֶדְיוֹ לִבְלוֹם is to muzzle it, and Radak takes בְּלִימָה as two words, the earth hanging upon nothing.

more.t: Radak glosses עֶדְיוֹ לִבְלוֹם (Tehillim 32:9) לחסום, to muzzle. In the words of Chachamim on תֹּלֶה אֶרֶץ עַל־בְּלִימָֽה (Iyov 26:7), the world stands only in the merit of one who is בולם עצמו at a time of strife, closing his mouth, keeping silent, hearing himself shamed and giving no answer.

more.h: The plain sense: hung on nothing
more.t: By the plain sense Radak takes בלימה as two words, that the earth is תלויה על לא דבר, hung upon no thing, since it hangs in the middle of the spheres at a great distance from them on every side.

כתר.sense: Crown, כֶּתֶר; and because a crown goes round about, the verb is to encircle. In one place Radak takes it as waiting.

more.t: כֶּֽתֶר מַלְכוּת (Esther 2:17) is a royal crown. בִּי יַכְתִּרוּ צַדִּיקִים, Radak: יחשבוני עליהם לכתר, the righteous will count me a crown upon themselves. וַֽעֲרוּמִים יַכְתִּרוּ דָּעַת (Mishlei 14:18), they set knowledge as a crown on their head.

הַכֹּתֶרֶת הָאֶחָת (Melachim I 7:16), the one capital, and וּשְׁתֵּי כֹֽתָרֹת עָשָׂה, and two capitals he made. Radak says they were called so because they sat on the head of the pillars like a crown.

Since a crown is round about, Radak says the word was used for encircling: אַבִּירֵי בָשָׁן כִּתְּרֽוּנִי (Tehillim 22:13), the mighty of Bashan surrounded me; כִּתְּרוּ אֶת־בִּנְיָמִן (Shoftim 20:43), they ringed him about so that he could not flee this way or that; and כִּי רָשָׁע מַכְתִּיר אֶת־הַצַּדִּיק (Chavakuk 1:4), the wicked man encircles the righteous and closes him in.
But כַּֽתַּר ־לִי זְעֵיר וַֽאֲחַוֶּךָּ (Iyov 36:2) is another matter, and Radak says that by its place it is המתן לי מעט, wait for me a little and be still until I show you.

Targum Yonasan renders וּלְתוֹרָתוֹ אִיִּים יְיַחֵֽילוּ (Yeshayahu 42:4) with יְכַתְּרוּן, they will wait. From this Radak's father explained כִּתְּרוּ אֶת־בִּנְיָמִן as waiting for them until they came out and then giving chase, and Radak adds that the pasuk says הִרְדִיפֻהוּ, they made him give chase, and not רדפוהו, they pursued him, since Binyamin fled by their own will so that Israel would run after them.

עטר.sense: Crown, עֲטָרָה; the plain verb is to ring a man round, and the heavier forms are to crown someone or to give him a crown.

more.t: לַֽעֲטֶרֶת צְבִי (Yeshayahu 28:5), a crown of beauty; וְהָרִים הָֽעֲטָרָה (Yechezkel 21:31), take off the crown; תָּשִׁית לְרֹאשׁוֹ עֲטֶרֶת פָּֽז (Tehillim 21:4), You set a crown of fine gold on his head; and the plural וְעָשִׂיתָ עֲטָרוֹת (Zechariah 6:11), you shall make crowns. Radak says the sense is known.
עֹֽטְרִים אֶל־דָּוִד וְאֶל־אֲנָשָׁיו (Shmuel I 23:26), which Radak explains as מסובבים אותו, surrounding him and lying in wait about him like a crown, to seize them.

עַל־צֹר הַמַּֽעֲטִירָה (Yeshayahu 23:8) is Tyre that gives a crown and honour to her men. Radak says רָצוֹן תַּעְטְרֶֽנּוּ (Tehillim 5:13) may be of this, as though תעטירנו, on the pattern of יַעְשְׁרֶנּוּ הַמֶּלֶךְ (Shmuel I 17:25), and means תסובבנו רצון, favour will surround him about like a shield, which is round like a crown. He says it may also be of the plain form.

עִטַּרְתָּ שְׁנַת טוֹבָתֶךָ, You have crowned the year of Your goodness, is printed with a book it cannot belong to, so it is left uncited here. בָּֽעֲטָרָה שֶׁעִטְּרָה־לּוֹ אִמּוֹ (Shir HaShirim 3:11), the crown his mother crowned him with; הַֽמְעַטְּרֵכִי חֶסֶד וְרַֽחֲמִֽים (Tehillim 103:4), who crowns you with kindness and mercy; וְכָבוֹד וְהָדָר תְּעַטְּרֵֽהוּ (Tehillim 8:6), You crown him with honour and splendour.

נזר.sense: Holding back and keeping apart: the nazir who withholds himself from wine, and his unshorn hair; and נֵזֶר is also a crown.

more.t: אֲשֶׁר נָזֹרוּ מֵֽעָלַי בְּגִלּֽוּלֵיהֶם כֻּלָּֽם (Yechezkel 14:5) and נָזֹרוּ אָחֽוֹר (Yeshayahu 1:5 in his edition), they have all turned away from Me and turned backward; Radak says he has written them at the root זוּר, and that they may be of this root. הַנָּזֵר כַּֽאֲשֶׁר עָשִׂיתִי זֶה כַּמֶּה שָׁנִֽים (Zechariah 7:3) he explains as אם אנזר, shall I hold myself back from food, from drink and from pleasures as I have done these many years.

כֹּל יְמֵי נִזְרוֹ (Bamidbar 6:4), all the days of his abstinence, and the growth of hair is itself called נֶזֶר, שְׂעַר רֹאשׁ נִזְרוֹ (Bamidbar 6:18). Radak says that because the nazir does not shave his head, long hair was called גָּזִּי נִזְרֵךְ (Yirmiyahu 7:29), shear your hair and cast it away.

מִיַּיִן וְשֵׁכָר יַזִּיר (Bamidbar 6:3), which Radak explains יזיר עצמו, he holds himself back, for this verb too takes an object; כָּל־יְמֵי הַזִּירוֹ (Bamidbar 6:6). All of them, he says, are the matter of הפרישות, keeping apart. So וְאֶת־עִנְּבֵי נְזִירֶךָ (Vayikra 25:5) are the grapes you have kept apart from and done no work upon.

Another matter: צִיץ נֶֽזֶר ־הַקֹּדֶשׁ (Shemos 39:30), the plate of the holy crown, and נֵזֶר שֶׁמֶן מִשְׁחַת אֱלֹהָיו (Vayikra 21:12), the crown of his God's anointing oil, which Radak glosses נזר עטרה, a crown. וּלְקָדְקֹד נְזִיר אֶחָֽיו (Bereishis 49:26) is the head of his brothers and the one crowned, and מִנְּזָרַיִךְ כָּֽאַרְבֶּה (Nachum 3:17) are the princes who wear the crowns. Radak adds that נזיר אחיו may belong to the first sense, one set apart from them.

כלל.sense: Whole and complete: כָּלִיל is entire, a bride is כַּלָּה, and Radak files כֹּל, 'all', here, as this root with its doubled letter missing.

more.t: כְּלִילַת יֹפִי (Eichah 2:15) is an adjective, that she is wholly beauty; מִכְלַל ־יֹפִי (Tehillim 50:2) a noun, that Tzion is the perfection of beauty, the beauty of all the lands; and the verb כָּֽלְלוּ יָפְיֵֽךְ (Yechezkel 27:11), they made your beauty complete.

From this sense too אַֽהֲבַת כְּלוּלֹתָיִךְ (Yirmiyahu 2:2) and כַּלָּה קִשֻּׁרֶיהָ (Yirmiyahu 2:32), for Radak says a woman under her chuppah has all her beauty and all her ornaments upon her then. She is called כַּלָּה to her father in law and mother in law even after the chuppah, עֶרְוַת כַּלָּֽתְךָ (Vayikra 18:15).

וְהָאֱלִילִים כָּלִיל יַֽחֲלֹֽף (Yeshayahu 2:18), He will cut them all off; כָּלִיל תָּקְטָֽר (Vayikra 6:15) is the olah, which is burnt whole; כְלִיל ־הָעִיר (Shoftim 20:40) Radak explains as the smoke of the burning of the whole city; and כְּלִיל תְּכֵֽלֶת (Shemos 28:31) is wholly blue. The Targum renders the word גְּמִיר, entire.

Radak says the word כֹּל everywhere belongs to this root, missing its doubled letter, and that the suffixed forms prove it: כֻּלּוֹ and כֻּלָּם carry a dagesh for the letter that is gone. It is a word that gathers the particulars, and sometimes it comes as a great overstatement of number, וְכָל ־הָאָרֶץ בָּאוּ מִצְרַיְמָה (Bereishis 41:57), all the earth came to Egypt.

וְלָרָשׁ אֵֽין־ כֹּל (Shmuel II 12:3), which Radak glosses מאומה, nothing whatever, and so אֵין לְשִׁפְחָֽתְךָ כֹל בַּבַּיִת (Melachim II 4:2), your maidservant has nothing in the house. In these places, he says, the word means not even one thing out of the whole.

רקד.sense: Skipping and dancing: the mountains skip like rams, and the heavier form is to make another skip.

more.t: הֶהָֽרִים רָקְדוּ כְאֵילִים (Tehillim 114:4), the mountains skipped like rams, and עֵת סְפוֹד וְעֵת רְקֽוֹד (Koheles 3:4), a time to mourn and a time to dance. In the heavier form וּשְׂעִירִים יְרַקְּדוּ ־שָֽׁם (Yeshayahu 13:21), the שעירים will skip there; עַל־רָאשֵׁי הֶֽהָרִים יְרַקֵּדוּן (Yoel 2:5), they skip on the mountain tops; and וּמֶרְכָּבָה מְרַקֵּדָֽה (Nachum 3:2), a chariot that leaps.
וַיַּרְקִידֵם כְּמוֹ־עֵגֶל (Tehillim 29:6), He makes them skip like a calf; Radak notes that this heavier form takes an object.

כרכר.sense: Dancing: מְכַרְכֵּר is dancing, and the swift beasts called כִּרְכָּרוֹת are named for it, since they look as though they dance.

more.t: מְכַרְכֵּר בְּכָל־עֹז (Shmuel II 6:14), which Radak glosses מרקד, dancing, with all his might.

From this, Radak says, camels, or the beasts light in their going, were called כרכרות: וּבַצַּבִּים וּבַפְּרָדִים וּבַכִּרְכָּרוֹת (Yeshayahu 66:20), with litters, with mules and with כרכרות, since in their great lightness and speed they seem to be dancing.
Targum Yonasan renders מְכַרְכֵּר as מְשַׁבַּח, praising, and וּבַכִּרְכָּרוֹת as וּבְתוּשְׁבְּחָן, with songs of praise.

פזז.sense: Growing strong: וַיָּפֹזּוּ is 'they grew strong', a dancer braces himself, and פָּז is refined gold, which is the stronger for being refined.

more.t: Radak glosses וַיָּפֹזּוּ זְרֹעֵי יָדָיו (Bereishis 49:24) ויתחזקו, his arms grew strong, and מְפַזֵּז וּמְכַרְכֵּר (Shmuel II 6:16) מתחזק ורוקד, bracing himself and dancing, since dancers bind the girdle of their loins tight when they dance.

תָּשִׁית לְרֹאשׁוֹ עֲטֶרֶת פָּֽז (Tehillim 21:4), a crown of פז on his head, which Radak says is the good refined gold, since the refined is the stronger. The verb from it is זָהָב מוּפָֽז (Melachim I 10:18), gold refined and made hard, and with an added alef כֶּתֶם אוּפָֽז (Daniel 10:5). Radak adds that וַיָּפֹזּוּ זְרֹעֵי יָדָיו may be explained from this.

רצד.sense: תְּרַצְּדוּן of Tehillim 68:17: some read it as skipping, some as lowering yourselves, and Rabbeinu Hai as looking out and hoping.

more.t: On לָמָּה תְּֽרַצְּדוּן הָרִים גַּבְנֻנִּים (Tehillim 68:17), Radak reports that some explain it like תרקדון, why do you skip; or, by its place, תשפילו עצמכם, why do you lower yourselves.

Under the letter dalet, Radak says, Rabbeinu Hai explains it as לשון עיון ותוחלת, a matter of looking and hoping, as though to say why are you looking to this and hoping for it; and Radak notes that it is close to the Arabic, where looking at a thing is called אלרצ"ד.

עפר.sense: Dust, and any finely ground thing; Radak sets it beside אֲדָמָה, אֶרֶץ and תֵּבֵל, and the same letters carry lead and the young of a deer.

more.h: Dust, and the dust of gold
more.t: עָפָר מִן־הָאֲדָמָה (Bereishis 2:7), dust from the ground; עַד אֲשֶׁר־דַּק לְעָפָר (Devarim 9:21), until it was ground fine as dust. וְעַפְרֹת זָהָב לֽוֹ (Iyov 28:6) Radak explains as the dusts out of which the gold is taken, or else the ground gold is itself called dust, as Chachamim said. Ash too is called dust, מֵֽעֲפַר שְׂרֵפַת הַֽחַטָּאת (Bamidbar 19:17).

The four are one matter and are set beside one another, as עַפְרוֹת תֵּבֵל and אַדְמַת־עָפָר (Daniel 12:2), yet Radak says there is a small difference between them. עפר is mostly what is fine, and so is אדמה, though אדמה is seldom said of the fine, as וַֽאֲדָמָה עַל־רֹאשֽׁוֹ (Shmuel I 4:12). ארץ takes in the whole, settled land and wilderness together, and תבל takes in the settled part only.

Radak says fine things are named by dust: וַיָּדֶק לְעָפָר (Melachim II 23:6), he ground it to dust, and וְנָשָׂא אֶת־עֲפָרָם (Melachim II 23:4), he carried away their dust. The heavier verb taken from it is וְעִפַּר בֶּעָפָֽר (Shmuel II 16:13), dusting with dust.

צָֽלֲלוּ כַּֽעוֹפֶרֶת (Shemos 15:10), they sank like lead, which Radak says is the metal, as the Targum has it, and it is rightly named for dust, since dust eats away all metals and lessens them when they lie in it, while lead only gains in dust. And לְעֹפֶר הָֽאַיָּלִים (Shir HaShirim 2:9) and כִּשְׁנֵי עֳפָרִים (Shir HaShirim 4:5) are the young of the hart or of the deer.

אפר.sense: Ash: עָפָר וָאֵֽפֶר is dust and ash. The same letters carry a covering worn as a disguise, and Ofir, a place of gold.

more.t: וְאָֽנֹכִי עָפָר וָאֵֽפֶר (Bereishis 18:27), I am dust and ash, which Radak glosses דשן, ash.

וַיִּתְחַפֵּשׂ בָּֽאֲפֵר (Melachim I 20:38), which Radak glosses בצעיף, he disguised himself with a headcloth, the letters turned about from the פאר of וְאֶת־פַּֽאֲרֵי הַמִּגְבָּעֹת (Shemos 39:28), the headgear of the caps.

וְאֶת־ אוֹפִר וְאֶת־חֲוִילָה (Bereishis 10:29) are men's names, Radak says, and their places were called after them. They are the places of the gold, as it says אֵת כָּל־אֶרֶץ הַֽחֲוִילָה אֲשֶׁר־שָׁם הַזָּהָֽב (Bereishis 2:11), all the land of Chavilah where the gold is, and זָהָב מֵֽאוֹפִיר (Melachim I 10:11), gold from Ofir. וּבְצוּר נְחָלִים אוֹפִֽיר (Iyov 22:24) means the gold of Ofir.

אבק.sense: Fine dust: אָבָק וְעָפָר (Devarim 28:24), and ground spices are אַבְקַת רוֹכֵל; to wrestle is to raise the dust underfoot.

more.t: אָבָק וְעָפָר (Devarim 28:24) and וּפִרְחָם כָּאָבָק יַּֽעֲלֶה (Yeshayahu 5:24), their blossom goes up like dust. Radak says fine dust is called אבק, and that כאבק means fine things generally, since it does not mean dust alone.

more.h: Against Ibn Ezra on the pointing
more.t: Radak says כָּאָבָק of Yeshayahu 5:24 is wholly with kamatz and is not in the construct, against what the sage Rabbi Avraham Ibn Ezra wrote there, and that Ibn Ezra confused it with כְּאָבָק דַּק (Yeshayahu 29:5), which in some books has the alef with sheva and patach and is in the construct.

In most books, Radak says, that word too has a kamatz under the alef but the kaf with sheva, and the Mesorah notes on it לית, that it stands alone. Another note he found on וְהָיָה לְאָבָק (Shemos 9:9) says every אבקא has a kamatz, and Radak says it forgot וְעָנָן אֲבַק רַגְלָֽיו (Nachum 1:3), the cloud is the dust of His feet, unless they counted it in with the prefixed letter.

מִכֹּל אַבְקַת רוֹכֵֽל (Shir HaShirim 3:6) is the merchant's spices, ground fine. And of וַיֵּֽאָבֵק אִישׁ עִמּוֹ (Bereishis 32:25) Radak says they raised dust with their feet as each strove with the other.

דשׁן.sense: Being fat and full of sap; the noun דֶּשֶׁן is richness, and in another sense the ash of the altar that is poured out.

more.t: וְאָכַל וְשָׂבַע וְדָשֵׁן (Devarim 31:20) is a past verb, he ate and was full and grew fat; וְהָיָה דָשֵׁן וְשָׁמֵן (Yeshayahu 30:23) is an adjective, it will be rich and fat; דְּשֵׁנִים וְרַֽעֲנַנִּים יִהְיֽוּ (Tehillim 92:15), they will be full of sap and fresh. The noun is וְתִתְעַנַּג בַּדֶּשֶׁן נַפְשְׁכֶֽם (Yeshayahu 55:2), your soul will delight in richness.

דִּשַּׁנְתָּ בַשֶּׁמֶן רֹאשִׁי (Tehillim 23:5), You have made my head rich with oil, and שְׁמוּעָה טוֹבָה תְּדַשֶּׁן ־עָֽצֶם (Mishlei 15:30), good news puts fat on the bone. Where the doer is not named, נֶֽפֶשׁ־בְּרָכָה תְדֻשָּׁן (Mishlei 11:25), a soul that blesses will be made fat, and וַֽעֲפָרָם מֵחֵלֶב יְדֻשָּֽׁן (Yeshayahu 34:7), their dust will be made fat with fat.

Another matter: אֶל־שֶׁפֶךְ הַדֶּשֶׁן (Vayikra 4:12) is the ash, and so וְכָל־הָעֵמֶק הַפְּגָרִים וְהַדֶּשֶׁן (Yirmiyahu 31:39). Radak explains that this is the place where the ash was poured out, which lay outside Yerushalayim, and that the pasuk says the place will be added to the city in time to come, the whole valley up to Nachal Kidron.

Targum Yonasan renders וְכָל־הָעֵמֶק הַפְּגָרִים as the plain where the corpses of the camp of Ashur fell. Radak says he either did not render וְהַדֶּשֶׁן at all, or rendered it by משרית אתורא, since they were fat and rich, as it says of him וּמִשְׁמַן בְּשָׂרוֹ יֵרָזֶֽה (Yeshayahu 17:4), the fat of his flesh will grow lean.

וְדִשְּׁנוּ אֶת־הַמִּזְבֵּחַ (Bamidbar 4:13), which Radak glosses יסירו דשנו, they take away its ash, and וְעָשִׂיתָ סִּֽירֹתָיו לְדַשְּׁנוֹ (Shemos 27:3), its pots for taking away the ash. וְעוֹלָתְךָ יְדַשְּׁנֶה סֶֽלָה (Tehillim 20:4) he reads as ישימה דשן, He will turn it to ash, meaning that He will send His fire down from heaven to consume it and to accept it willingly.

כרב.sense: A keruv, the winged figure of the mishkan. Ibn Ezra makes the word cover any form; Chazal read the kaf as "like", a child's face.

more.t: כְּרוּב אֶחָד מִקָּצָה מִזֶּה (Shemos 25:19), one keruv at this end, and וְהָיוּ הַכְּרֻבִים פֹּֽרְשֵׂי כְנָפַיִם (Shemos 25:20), the keruvim were spreading their wings.

more.h: Ibn Ezra: the word covers any form
more.t: Ibn Ezra holds that keruv takes in every figure. The keruvim of the Torah were explained as a human form, while the face of the keruv in Yechezkel's visions looks to be the ox: in one pasuk וּפְנֵי־שׁוֹר מֵֽהַשְּׂמֹאול לְאַרְבַּעְתָּן (Yechezkel 1:10), the face of an ox on the left for all four, and in another פְּנֵי הָֽאֶחָד פְּנֵי הַכְּרוּב (Yechezkel 10:14), the face of the one being the face of the keruv, where the first had said the face of an ox.

more.h: Chazal: the kaf is a prefix
more.t: Chazal took the kaf as the prefix "like" (Chagigah 13b), keruv being כרביא, and the figures like the likeness of young children. They asked from the pesukim in Yechezkel and answered that Yechezkel begged mercy over the ox face and it was turned into a keruv, saying אין קטיגור נעשה סניגור, a prosecutor is not made a defender. They asked further from פְּנֵי הָֽאֶחָד פְּנֵי הַכְּרוּב וּפְנֵי הַשֵּׁנִי פְּנֵי אָדָם, the face of the one the face of the keruv and the face of the second the face of a man, since a man and a keruv are then two different things, and answered אפי רברבי ואפי זוטרי, large faces and small faces.
יַֽעֲשֶׂה אֹתָהּ כְּרֻבִֽים (Shemos 26:31) is that the paroches be made embroidered with the figures of keruvim.
The king is called a keruv by way of borrowed speech, for greatness: אַתְּ־ כְּרוּב מִמְשַׁח הַסּוֹכֵךְ (Yechezkel 28:14), you are the anointed covering keruv.

אפן.sense: A wheel: the wheel of a chariot, and the ofanim of Yechezkel's vision. A word spoken on its wheels is one settled in its place.

more.t: וַיָּסַר אֵת אֹפַן מַרְכְּבֹתָיו (Shemos 14:25), he removed the wheel of his chariots; כַּֽאֲשֶׁר יִהְיֶה הָֽאוֹפַן (Yechezkel 10:10), as the ofan would be; לָאֽוֹפַנִּים לָהֶם (Yechezkel 10:13), to the ofanim was said of them. The sense of them all is a wheel.

דָּבָר דָּבֻר עַל־ אָפְנָֽיו (Mishlei 25:11), a word spoken upon its wheels, is another vowel pattern and is said as a figure: the word sits settled in its place. Its pattern is that of חָפְנָיו, his two handfuls, which is one of the pairs whose single is חֹפֶן, a handful; so the single here is אֹפֶן, and the word carries both the hidden and the open.

more.h: Rabbi Yonah: the alef is added
more.t: Rabbi Yonah read it as על פניו, upon its face, the alef being an addition. He assigned to this root also נָשָׂאתִי אֵמֶיךָ אָפֽוּנָה (Tehillim 88:16), I have borne your terrors a long while, since time is called in Arabic אִפַּא"ן, with a chirik under the alef and a dagesh in the peh. Radak notes that the word is entered as well under the root פון, in the pattern of אָקוּמָה, I shall arise, as Rabbi Yehudah set it down.

אראל.sense: Erelam of Yeshayahu: their angel, arel being a name of greatness. Others read it as a compound, "I will show them", or as Yerushalayim.

more.h: Their angel, and a name of greatness
more.t: הֵן אֶרְאֶלָּם צָֽעֲקוּ חֻצָה (Yeshayahu 33:7), behold their erelam cried outside, is their angel; arel is a name of greatness, as Radak explained at the word אריאל. He is close to saying that it is all one root, even though the yud has dropped out in אֶרְאֶלָּם.

Chazal also named the holy angels with this term for their great standing (Kesubos 104a): אראלים ומצוקים אחזו בארון הקדש, the arelim and the metzukim seized the holy ark, and נצחו אראלים את המצוקים, the arelim prevailed over the metzukim. Arelim is said of the angels for their greatness, metzukim of men of weight and standing, as in מְצֻקֵי אֶרֶץ וַיָּשֶׁת עֲלֵיהֶם תֵּבֵֽל (Shmuel I 2:8), the pillars of the earth, and He set the world upon them, which Chazal expounded (Yoma 38b) of the pious and the great, upon whom the world stands.

Rabbi Adonim read אֶרְאֶלָּם as a word compounded of אֶרְאֶה לָהֶם, I will show them, as בִּשְּׁלָם הַבָּשָׂר (Melachim I 19:21) stands for בשל להם, he cooked for them. Radak's father wrote the same and explained it so: the navi says, I will show Yisrael troubles, so that they cry outside, and the messengers of peace who used to come with words of peace מר יבכיון נשמו מסילות, weep bitterly, the highways lie desolate.
Ibn Ezra took it as Yerushalayim, which is called הוֹי אֲרִיאֵל אֲרִיאֵל (Yeshayahu 29:1), woe, Ariel, Ariel. The sense is then that when they see their arel torn down, they cry outside.

חשׁמל.sense: The chashmal of Yechezkel's vision: an angel of that name, or, as Radak allows, the name of a hue close to the look of fire.

more.t: כְּעֵין הַֽחַשְׁמַל (Yechezkel 1:4), like the look of the chashmal, is an angel so called, and it was the like of his colour that the navi saw out of the fire.

more.h: Chazal: the child and the fire
more.t: So Chazal said (Chagigah 13a) of the child who was expounding the workings of the merkavah and understood the chashmal, and fire came out of the chashmal and consumed him.

They further said (Chagigah 13b) that the word is a compound, חש מל, silent and speaking. Rabbi Yehudah said חיות אש ממללות, creatures of fire that speak. A beraisa taught עתים חשות עתים ממללות, at times they are silent and at times they speak: silent when the word goes out from the mouth of Hakadosh Baruch Hu, speaking when it does not, that is, praising and lauding Hashem.

more.h: Radak: the name of a colour
more.t: Radak allows that chashmal is the name of the hue itself, one close to the hue of fire, since the pasuk says כְּעֵין הַֽחַשְׁמַל מִתּוֹךְ הָאֵשׁ, like the look of the chashmal out of the midst of the fire; and כְּעֵין חַשְׁמַל כְּמַרְאֵה־אֵשׁ בֵּֽית־לָהּ סָבִיב (Yechezkel 1:27), like the look of chashmal, like the appearance of fire with a housing round about it; and in the second vision כְּמַרְאֵה־זֹהַר כְּעֵין הַחַשְׁמַֽלָה (Yechezkel 8:2), like the appearance of brightness, like the look of the chashmalah.

חזק.sense: To be strong, and to be stronger than another; to strengthen, or to repair what is broken; and, joined to a bet, to take hold of a thing and grip it.

more.t: וַיְהִי כִּֽי־ חָזַק יִשְׂרָאֵל (Shoftim 1:28), when Yisrael grew strong; אִם־ תֶּחֱזַק אֲרָם מִמֶּנִּי (Shmuel II 10:11), if Aram is too strong for me; חֲזַקְתַּנִי וַתּוּכָל (Yirmiyahu 20:7), which Radak glosses as you were stronger than I and prevailed. The describing form is הֶֽחָזָק הוּא הֲרָפֶה (Bamidbar 13:18), whether it is strong or weak, and בְּחָזָק יָבוֹא (Yeshayahu 40:10), he comes with a strong force, his force being his arm.

more.h: Achaz and the king of Ashur
more.t: וַיָּצַר לוֹ וְלֹא חֲזָקֽוֹ (Divrei HaYamim II 28:20), he distressed him and did not strengthen him. Radak offers that it may mean he was not stronger than him, or was not strong before him, with Achaz the one spoken of; or, if the verb passes to an object, that Hashem did not strengthen Achaz before him; or that the king of Ashur did not strengthen him, for Achaz had sent to the kings of Ashur to help him, and not only did he not strengthen him, he came against him and pressed him. Radak holds this last reading the right one.

חִזְּקוּ פְנֵיהֶם מִסֶּלַע (Yirmiyahu 5:3), they made their faces harder than rock; לֹֽא־ חִזְּקוּ הַכֹּֽהֲנִים אֶת־בֶּדֶק הַבָּֽיִת (Melachim II 12:7), the kohanim did not repair the breach of the house.

more.h: Where the object is left unsaid
more.t: וְעַל־יָדָם הֶֽחֱזִיקוּ (Nechemiah 3:5), at their hand they took firm hold, meaning they took hold of the work; הַֽחֲזִיקִי מַלְבֵּֽן (Nachum 3:14), take firm hold of the brick mould, that is, of the work of the mould; כִּי הֶֽחֱזִיק עַד־לְמָֽעְלָה (Divrei HaYamim II 26:8), for he grew strong to a height, meaning he strengthened his kingship.

Where it is bound to a bet the sense is that a man fastens himself on a thing to hold it fast, and it is the sense of seizing: וְהַֽחֲזִיקִי אֶת־יָדֵךְ בּוֹ (Bereishis 21:18), hold your hand fast on him; וַיַּֽחֲזִיקוּ הָֽאֲנָשִׁים בְּיָדוֹ (Bereishis 19:16), the men took hold of his hand; אֲשֶׁר הֶחֱזַקְתִּיךָ מִקְצוֹת הָאָרֶץ (Yeshayahu 41:9), whom I took hold of from the ends of the earth. It also comes without the bet, as הַֽחֲזֵק מָגֵן וְצִנָּה (Tehillim 35:20), take hold of shield and buckler, and once with a lamed in the bet's place, וְהֶחֱזִיק לוֹ וְנָשַׁק־לֽוֹ (Shmuel II 15:5), he took hold of him and kissed him.

There is also the sense of what a vessel contains, מַֽחֲזִיק בַּתִּים שְׁלֹשֶׁת אֲלָפִים יָכִֽיל, holding three thousand bath in capacity. Chazal made this usage common (Berachos 40a): כלי ריקן מחזיק מלא אינו מחזיק, an empty vessel holds, a full one does not hold.

עזז.sense: To be strong and to prevail; oz, might, and maoz, a stronghold; az as a describing word, fierce or bold.

more.h: The verb, and a dispute over it
more.t: וַתָּעָז יַד־מִדְיָן (Shoftim 6:2), the hand of Midyan grew strong. On הַֽחָכְמָה תָּעֹז לֶחָכָם (Koheles 7:19), wisdom gives strength to the wise, Rabbi Yehudah wrote that the verb stands alone, meaning wisdom will be strong and ruling for him; Rabbi Yonah holds that it passes to an object.

עוּזָּה אֱלֹהִים (Tehillim 68:29), written with a vav and a dagesh, is a command: be strong for our sake against the enemy, as You have wrought for us many times. The word זוּ there is as in זוּ חָטָאנוּ לוֹ (Yeshayahu 42:24), against whom we have sinned, either in the sense of "which" or in the sense of "this".

עֹז לְעַמּוֹ יִתֵּן (Tehillim 29:11), He will give strength to His people; עָזִּי וְזִמְרָת יָהּ (Shemos 15:2), my strength and song is Kah; and in the fuller form וֶעֱזוּז מִלְחָמָה (Yeshayahu 42:25), the might of war, and וֶעֱזוּז נוֹרְאֹתֶיךָ יֹאמֵרוּ (Tehillim 145:6), they shall tell the might of Your awesome deeds.

With an added mem and the doubled letter dropped: לָעוֹז בְּמָעוֹז פַּרְעֹה (Yeshayahu 30:2), to take refuge in the stronghold of Pharaoh, and עַל רֹאשׁ הַמָּעוֹז הַזֶּה (Shoftim 6:26), on the top of this stronghold, said of the rock, since a rock is a place of strength.
וּמֶלֶךְ עַז יִמְשָׁל־בָּם (Yeshayahu 19:4), a fierce king shall rule over them; כִּי־ עַז הָעָם (Bamidbar 13:28), the people is strong; חֵמָה עַזָּֽה (Mishlei 21:14), fierce wrath.

From this sense also וְאֶת־הַפֶּרֶס וְאֵת הָֽעָזְנִיָּֽה (Vayikra 11:13), the peres and the ozniyah, so named for its great fierceness. It is found in the Mishnah called עוז, in חוץ מכנף העוז, except for the wing of the oz, which they explained as the ozniyah. Rabbi Yonah traced עֲזָאזֵל here too, as a place hard and fierce.

כבר.sense: Kabir: great and mighty, in quantity or in quality. Under the same letters a sieve, a cushion, a stretch of land, and kevar, already.

more.t: הֶן־אֵל כַּבִּיר וְלֹא יִמְאָס (Iyov 36:5), Hashem is mighty and does not reject; וּשְׁאָר מְעַט מִזְעָר לוֹא כַבִּֽיר (Yeshayahu 16:14), the remnant shall be small and slight, not great; כִּשְׁאוֹן מַיִם כַּבִּירִים (Yeshayahu 17:12), like the roaring of mighty waters. The sense of them all is force and magnitude, whether of amount or of quality. So too יִֽתֶּן־אֹכֶל לְמַכְבִּֽיר (Iyov 36:31), He gives food in abundance, and בִּבְלִי־דַעַת מִלִּין יַכְבִּֽר (Iyov 35:16), without knowledge he multiplies words.
In וְאוֹרִיד כַּאבִּיר (Yeshayahu 10:13), and I brought down, the alef is an addition, or else the word is compounded of כַּבִּיר and אַבִּיר, mighty and strong, and this for magnification.

כַּֽאֲשֶׁר יִנּוֹעַ בַּכְּבָרָה (Amos 9:9), as it is shaken in a sieve, is a sifting sieve, and so in another pattern וְעָשִׂיתָ לּוֹ מִכְבָּר (Shemos 27:4), you shall make for it a grating. כְּבִיר הָֽעִזִּים (Shmuel I 19:13) is a cushion of goats' wool, and so וַיִּקַּח הַמַּכְבֵּר וַיִּטְבֹּל בַּמַּיִם (Melachim II 8:15), he took the cushion and dipped it in water. Targum Yonasan renders it גוּנְבָא, as he renders וַתְּכַסֵּהוּ בַּשְּׂמִיכָֽה (Shoftim 4:18), she covered him with a rug, and it is a thick cloth.

וַיֵּלֶךְ מֵֽאִתּוֹ כִּבְרַת ־אָֽרֶץ (Melachim II 5:19), he went from him a stretch of land, and בְּעוֹד כִּבְרַת ־אֶרֶץ לָבֹא אֶפְרָתָה (Bereishis 48:7), while there was yet a stretch of land to come to Efras. It was explained as a mil, since they say the way from Rachel's burial place to Efras is a mil. Radak's own view, as he wrote at the root ברה, is that the kaf here is a prefix and not part of the root.

שֶׁכְּבָר מֵתוּ (Koheles 4:2), who already died; כְּבָר הָיָה לְעֹֽלָמִים (Koheles 1:10), it has already been in the ages before us; מַה־שֶּֽׁהָיָה כְּבָר נִקְרָא שְׁמוֹ (Koheles 6:10), what has already been, its name was called. Everywhere this word is of time gone by, and he gives its word in the vernacular. On בְּשֶׁכְּבָר הַיָּמִים הַבָּאִים הַכֹּל נִשְׁכָּח (Koheles 2:16) Radak explains that neither in what has already been nor in the days to come is there remembrance of the wise man with the fool, though over length of days all is forgotten; and some read it as in what has already been and what will be in days to come, all is forgotten, the memory of the fool.

תקף.sense: To overpower and prevail over; tokef, force; takif, strong, which is what the Targum gives for chazak.

more.t: וְאִֽם־ יִתְקְפוֹ הָֽאֶחָד (Koheles 4:12), if one overpowers him. The noun is אֶת־כָּל־ תֹּקֶף (Esther 9:29), all the force, and וְכָל־מַֽעֲשֵׂה תָקְפּוֹ (Esther 10:2), every act of his power; the describing form שֶׁהתַּקִּיף, the one stronger, in Koheles 6:10. The Targum for חָזָק (Shemos 10:19), strong, is תָּקִיף.
תִּתְקְפֵהוּ לָנֶצַח (Iyov 14:20), You overpower him forever, and תִּתְקְפֵהוּ כְּמֶלֶךְ עָתִיד לַכִּידֽוֹר (Iyov 15:24), which Radak glosses as You take hold of him.

פסל.sense: To hew and carve: the verb of cutting the second luchos, and pesel and pesilim, the carved image, mostly of stone but of wood too.

more.t: פְּסָל ־לְךָ שְׁנֵֽי־לֻחֹת אֲבָנִים (Shemos 34:1), hew for yourself two tablets of stone, and וַיִּפְסֹל שְׁנֵֽי־לֻחֹת (Shemos 34:4), he hewed two tablets. The noun is פְּסִילֵי אֱלֹֽהֵיהֶם (Devarim 7:25), the carved images of their gods, and in another pattern פֶסֶל וּמַסֵּכָה (Devarim 27:15), a carved and a molten image.

The term falls for the most part on the hewing of stones, and likewise on wood: הַנֹּֽשְׂאִים אֶת־עֵץ פִּסְלָם (Yeshayahu 45:20), who carry the wood of their carved image, and וּשְׁאֵרִיתוֹ לְאֵל עָשָׂה לְפִסְלוֹ (Yeshayahu 44:17), the rest of it he made into a god, into his carved image. וְהוּא עָבַר אֶת־ הַפְּסִילִים (Shoftim 3:26), he passed the pesilim, is a place where they used to hew stones.

חרת.sense: Engraved: charus on the luchos is cut in, the same sense he gives to charushah, engraved on the tablet of their heart.

more.t: חָרוּת עַל־הַלֻּחֹֽת (Shemos 32:15), engraved upon the tablets, is of the sense of חקוק, cut in, as Radak explained at חֲרוּשָׁה עַל־לוּחַ לִבָּם (Yirmiyahu 17:1), engraved upon the tablet of their heart.

חרט.sense: Cheret, a scribe's stylus, and the tool the egel was formed with; and charitim, pouches or bags.

more.t: וַיָּצַר אֹתוֹ בַּחֶרֶט (Shemos 32:4), he formed it with a cheret, and וּכְתֹב עָלָיו בְּחֶרֶט אֱנוֹשׁ (Yeshayahu 8:1), write upon it with a man's stylus. It is a scribes' pen. Some explain the first as done with a mould.

Targum Yonasan renders בְּחֶרֶט אֱנוֹשׁ as כְּתַב מְפָרַשׁ, plain script that any man can read. Radak holds the right sense to be that the pasuk says a man's stylus to show that the deed was to be done in fact, and that the navi should not think this writing he was commanded to write was in the vision of prophecy alone, as most of the acts shown to the nevi'im are: עָרוֹם וְיָחֵֽף (Yeshayahu 20:2), barefoot and naked, commanded to Yeshayahu; אֵשֶׁת זְנוּנִים (Hoshea 1:2), a wife of harlotry, to Hoshea; the shaving of the head and beard to Yechezkel (Yechezkel 5:1); and the like, none of which were other than in the vision of prophecy.

בִּשְׁנֵי חֲרִטִים (Melachim II 5:23) is in two bags, and so וְהַמִּטְפָּחוֹת וְהָֽחֲרִיטִֽים (Yeshayahu 3:22), the cloaks and the pouches. A purse is called in Arabic כרט"ה, the ches standing in for the Arabic kaf, as it does in many places.

רשׁם.sense: Rashum, written down and set on record; the word is of the sense of a mark and a sign, and the Aramaic carries it.

more.t: אֶת־ הָֽרָשׁוּם בִּכְתָב אֱמֶת (Daniel 10:21), what is set down in the writing of truth, is of the Aramaic tongue, as כְתָבָא דִּי רְשִׁים (Daniel 5:25), the writing that was inscribed; and the term has the sense of a mark, which is as much as to say a token and a sign.

רחב.sense: To be wide or broad, and to widen and give room; rochav, breadth; rechov, an open square; and merchav, open ground.

more.h: The verb, and a heart made broad
more.t: רָחַב פִּי עַל־אוֹיְבַי (Shmuel I 2:1), my mouth is opened wide over my enemies. On וּפָחַד וְרָחַב לְבָבֵךְ (Yeshayahu 60:5), your heart shall fear and grow broad, Radak explains that they will fear the honoured Name when they see the abundance of good, as at Hoshea 3:5, where they come trembling to Hashem and to His goodness; and broad after the troubles they were in at first, for now the heart will be broad and glad.

וְרֹחַב לֵב כַּחוֹל (Melachim I 5:9), breadth of heart like the sand: in everything that needs understanding he had a broad heart for it. Radak argues that sand is not something compared to breadth of heart as a count, since what is compared to breadth is a thing of measure, as וּרְחָבָה מִנִּי־יָֽם (Iyov 11:9), broader than the sea; rather the sand answers to all the things needing understanding, which are as the sand on the seashore, and Shlomo had breadth of heart for them all. So too לִתְבוּנָתוֹ אֵין מִסְפָּֽר (Tehillim 147:5), His understanding is beyond number, meaning the things He understands are beyond number, since what pairs with understanding is searching out, as אֵין חֵקֶר לִתְבוּנָתֽוֹ (Yeshayahu 40:28), His understanding is past searching.

וְחָמֵשׁ אַמּוֹת רֹחַב (Shemos 27:1), five amos broad; לְאָרְכָּהּ וּלְרָחְבָּהּ (Bereishis 13:17), to its length and to its breadth. וְאֶתְהַלְּכָה בָרְחָבָה (Tehillim 119:45), I shall walk in a wide place, is a name for the broad ground; כִּי בָֽרְחוֹב נָלִֽין (Bereishis 19:2), we shall spend the night in the square; the plural בְּתוֹךְ רְחֹבוֹת אֵֽרָצֵֽחַ (Mishlei 22:13), I shall be slain in the streets; and וַיּוֹצִיאֵנִי לַמֶּרְחָב (Tehillim 18:20), He brought me out to open ground.

more.h: Broad of hands, broad of soul
more.t: וּרְחַב יָדָיִם (Tehillim 104:25), broad of hands; רְחַב ־נֶפֶשׁ יְגָרֶה מָדוֹן (Mishlei 28:25), the broad of soul stirs up strife; for the feminine רְחָבָה מִצְוָתְךָ מְאֹֽד (Tehillim 119:96), Your mitzvah is exceedingly broad, and וְהָאָרֶץ רַֽחֲבַת יָדַיִם (Divrei HaYamim I 4:40), the land was broad of hands.

הִרְחִיבָה שְּׁאוֹל נַפְשָׁהּ (Yeshayahu 5:14), she'ol has widened her appetite; בַּצָּר הִרְחַבְתָּ לִּי (Tehillim 4:2), in straits You gave me room; הַרְחֶב ־פִּיךָ וַֽאֲמַלְאֵֽהוּ (Tehillim 81:11), open your mouth wide and I shall fill it.

צָרוֹת לְבָבִי הִרְחִיבוּ (Tehillim 25:17), the straits of my heart have made themselves broad, is a verb passing to an object: the troubles have widened their own place and border within the heart by their number, so that they press the heart and take more room in it. Radak notes that the pasuk speaks with elegance, joining the two terms in one matter, the one being the opposite of the other.

נתב.sense: Nasiv and nesivah, a path; its sense is that of derech, a way.

more.t: יְפַלֵּס נָתִיב לְאַפּוֹ (Tehillim 78:50), He levelled a path for His anger; נָתִיב לֹֽא־יְדָעוֹ עָיִט (Iyov 28:7), a path the bird of prey has not known; הַדְרִיכֵנִי בִּנְתִיב מִצְוֹתֶיךָ (Tehillim 119:35), lead me in the path of Your mitzvos.

וְדֶרֶךְ נְתִיבָה אַל־מָֽוֶת (Mishlei 12:28), and the way of her path is no death, where the heh is weak though it should have carried a mappik. With the feminine heh: וּבְמַיִם עַזִּים נְתִיבָֽה (Yeshayahu 43:16), a path in mighty waters, and מְנַע רַגְלְךָ מִנְּתִֽיבָתָֽם (Mishlei 1:15), keep your foot from their path. The plural is בִּנְתִיבוֹת לֹא־יָדְעוּ אַדְרִיכֵם (Yeshayahu 42:16), in paths they have not known I shall lead them. Its sense is as a way.

סלל.sense: To raise up: lifting the stones off a road, which gives both the mesillah and the siege mound; and exalting a man or Hashem.

more.t: Rabbi Yonah set down under this root several different senses: one for סֹלּוּ סֹלּוּ הַֽמְסִלָּה (Yeshayahu 62:10), clear, clear the highway; another for סֹלּוּ לָרֹכֵב בָּֽעֲרָבוֹת (Tehillim 68:5), extol Him who rides in the plains, and עֽוֹדְךָ מִסְתּוֹלֵל (Shemos 9:17), you still exalt yourself; and another for the mesillos of the house of Hashem (Divrei HaYamim II 9:11). Radak holds that they are all one sense, that of raising and lifting high.

more.h: Lifting the stones off a road
more.t: On his own reading, סֹלּוּ סֹלּוּ הַֽמְסִלָּה is lift the stones and the stumbling blocks out of the way; and because it is usual to clear the stones and lift the obstacles from a road, the road itself came to be called מְסִלָּה. So דֶּרֶךְ לֹא סְלוּלָֽה (Yirmiyahu 18:15), a way not cleared, is one whose obstacles have not been lifted from it.

more.h: His father: a road built up
more.t: Radak's father explains מְסִלָּה as a road raised with stones laid into it, and so סַקְּלוּ מֵאֶבֶן (Yeshayahu 62:10), clear it of stone, is that they built it of hard stones, as it says וּמְסִלֹּתַי יְרֻמֽוּן (Yeshayahu 49:11), and My highways shall be raised.

The timber on which stones are lifted and thrown into a city is called a sollelah: כִּרְתוּ עֵצָה וְשִׁפְכוּ עַל־יְרֽוּשָׁלַם סֹֽלְלָה (Yirmiyahu 6:6), cut down her trees and pour out a mound against Yerushalayim, and הַסֹּֽלְלוֹת בָּאוּ הָעִיר לְלָכְדָהּ (Yirmiyahu 32:24), the mounds have reached the city to take it. Targum Yonasan renders וְצָבְרִין מִלֵיתָא, and they heap up a mound, מליתא being a heap of earth in the tongue of Chazal (Bava Basra 54a). On that rendering the townsmen would pull down the houses and make heaps of the stones against the wall from within to strengthen it, and Radak says his explanation is right. Of the same matter is וַיִּצְבֹּר עָפָר וַיִּלְכְּדָֽהּ (Chavakuk 1:10), he heaped up earth and took it.

סֹלּוּ לָרֹכֵב בָּֽעֲרָבוֹת is extol Him and magnify Him. So too the fourfold word with its peh doubled, סַלְסְלֶ֥הָ וּתְרֽוֹמְמֶ֑ךָּ (Mishlei 4:8), exalt her and she will raise you, and מִסְתּוֹלֵל בְּעַמִּי (Shemos 9:17), lifting himself up over my people and taking pride against them so as not to send them out.

more.h: The mesillos of the Beis Hamikdash
more.t: Of the mesillos of the house of Hashem (Divrei HaYamim II 9:11) Radak offers ceilings, called so for their height, or steps, called so because men tread them as they tread a road. But since Melachim has מסעד, a support, where this has מְסִלּוֹת, he explains מסילות in the sense of a support, the ceiling itself being a support, or else some other structure of pillars made for support and strength.
Another sense altogether is סִלּוֹן מַמְאִיר (Yechezkel 28:24), a pricking brier, and כִּי סָֽרָבִים וְסַלּוֹנִים (Yechezkel 2:6), briers and thorns, whose sense is a thorn.

more.h: Casting a way against a man
more.t: וַיָּסֹלּוּ עָלַי דַּרְכָּם (Iyov 19:12), they cast up their way against me, and וַיָּסֹלּוּ עָלַי אָרְחוֹת אֵידָֽם (Iyov 30:12), they cast up against me the paths of their ruin. Radak had said at the outset that this second may be another matter, but Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Yonah brought it under this root, and so wrote Ibn Ezra, Rabbi Yehudah ben Balaam, and Radak's father.

רכל.sense: A merchant who travels about with his goods; the noun from it is the merchandise, and the word for a talebearer is filed here too.

more.t: בְּעִיר רֹֽכְלִים שָׂמֽוֹ (Yechezkel 17:4), he set it in a city of merchants, and בְּנֵי דְדָן רֹֽכְלַיִךְ (Yechezkel 27:15), the sons of Dedan your traders: these are the merchants. The noun for the merchandise is רכלה, as in בְּרֹב רְכֻלָּֽתְךָ (Yechezkel 28:16), in the abundance of your trading, and וּבָֽזְזוּ רְכֻלָּתֵךְ (Yechezkel 26:12), they plundered your merchandise. Another measure of the same noun is וַֽאֲרֻזִים בְּמַרְכֻלְתֵּֽךְ (Yechezkel 27:24), and cedars in your place of trade.

more.h: Targum Yonasan on Ashur and Kilmad
more.t: On אַשּׁוּר כִּלֽמַד רֹֽכַלְתֵּֽךְ (Yechezkel 27:23), Ashur and Kilmad your traders, Targum Yonasan has מְדִינַן אַתּוּר וּמָדַי אִינוּן תַּגָרֵיךְ, the provinces of Ashur and Madai, they are your merchants.

Some use the word of the spice seller alone, one sort among the merchants: מִכֹּל אַבְקַת רוֹכֵֽל (Shir HaShirim 3:6), from every powder of the merchant, and הֶֽחֱזִיקוּ הַצֹּֽרְפִים וְהָרֹֽכְלִֽים (Nechemiah 3:32), the goldsmiths and the merchants made the repairs. Radak allows that וַיָּלִינוּ הָרֹֽכְלִים וּמֹֽכְרֵי כָל־מִמְכָּר (Nechemiah 13:20), the merchants and the sellers of every sort of ware lodged, may be of that kind.

רָכִיל is a name for slander: לֹֽא־תֵלֵךְ רָכִיל (Vayikra 19:16), you shall not go about as a talebearer; הֹֽלְכֵי רָכִיל (Yirmiyahu 6:28), goers of slander; אַנְשֵׁי רָכִיל הָיוּ בָךְ (Yechezkel 22:9), men of slander were in you. The word shares in the sense of walking, since the slanderer walks into his fellow's house and then goes and tells another what he heard there.

The slanderer is like the peddling merchant who holds several kinds of goods in his hand, and like the spice seller called רוכל who holds several kinds of spices, מִכֹּל אַבְקַת רוֹכֵֽל, from every powder of the merchant. The slanderer too gathers words from this one and that one and tells them to this one and that one; or, as the trader moves goods along, buying from one and selling to another, so the slanderer moves words along, hearing from one and telling another.

כנע.sense: To be brought low, and to bring another low; the same letters carry the trader and his merchandise, and the Canaanite.

more.t: כִּֽי־ נִכְנַע אַחְאָב (Melachim I 21:29), that Achav humbled himself; וַיִּכָּנַע מִדְיָן לִפְנֵי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (Shoftim 8:28), Midyan was subdued before Bnei Yisrael; כְּהִכָּנַע מְנַשֶּׁה אָבִיו (Divrei HaYamim II 33:23), as Menasheh his father humbled himself. Where the word acts on another it is to subdue: הוּא יַשְׁמִידֵם וְהוּא יַכְנִיעֵם לְפָנֶיךָ (Devarim 9:3), He will destroy them and He will subdue them before you; וַיַּכְנַע אֱלֹהִים בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא (Shoftim 4:23), Hashem subdued on that day; וַיַּכְנַע בֶּעָמָל לִבָּם (Tehillim 107:12), He brought their heart low with toil. All of them are the matter of lowering.

more.h: Gather your humbling from the land
more.t: אִסְפִּי מֵאֶרֶץ כִּנְעָתֵךְ (Yirmiyahu 10:17), gather your humbling from the land, which Radak explains as: gather in from the world the humbling you used to work on them, for you are destined to sit under siege. אִסְפִּי here is like אֱסֹף יָדֶֽךָ (Shmuel I 14:19), withdraw your hand.

כְּנַעַן בְּיָדוֹ מֹֽאזְנֵי מִרְמָה (Hoshea 12:7 in his edition), a trader in whose hand are scales of deceit, and וַיְבִיאֵהוּ אֶל־אֶרֶץ כְּנַעַן בְּעִיר רֹֽכְלִים שָׂמֽוֹ (Yechezkel 17:4), he brought it to a land of trade, in a city of merchants he set it; the nun of the word is an added letter. So too וַֽחֲגוֹר נָֽתְנָה לַֽכְּנַֽעֲנִֽי (Mishlei 31:24), she gave a belt to the merchant, and in another measure כִּנְעָנֶיהָ נִכְבַּדֵּי־אָֽרֶץ (Yeshayahu 23:8), her traders are the honoured of the earth, which he explains as her merchants.

אִסְפִּי מֵאֶרֶץ כִּנְעָתֵךְ can be read from this second sense, of trade, and so the Targum says: כְּנוּשִׁי מֵאַרְעָא סְחוֹרְתִּיךְ, gather your merchandise from the land. By the Targum's view so too וַיַּרְא־שָׁם יְהוּדָה בַּת־אִישׁ כְּנַֽעֲנִי (Bereishis 38:2), Yehudah saw there the daughter of a merchant, and יֶחֱצוּהוּ בֵּין כְּנַֽעֲנִֽים (Iyov 40:30), they will divide him among merchants.

כִּי נִדְמָה כָּל־עַם כְּנַעַן (Tzefaniah 1:11), all the people of Canaan are cut off, may be from this sense as well: the rich men who hold the trade, as the pasuk goes on, נכרתו כל נטילי כסף, all who are laden with silver are cut off. And so וְלֹֽא־יִהְיֶה כְנַֽעֲנִי עוֹד (Zechariah 14:21), there will be no merchant any more: so many will dedicate vessels to the Beis Hamikdash that they will have no need of a trader to sell to them.

His father writes that the כנעני there is a Canaanite in fact, from the nation of Canaan. Since the hewers of wood and drawers of water were Canaanites, the Chivim whom Yehoshua made hewers of wood and drawers of water for the Beis Hamikdash, the pasuk means that they will no longer be the hewers and the drawers, for men from among the great of the nations will come to the service of the Beis Hamikdash, as it says וְגַם־מֵהֶם אֶקַּח לַכֹּֽהֲנִים לַֽלְוִיִּם (Yeshayahu 66:21), and from them too I will take for kohanim and leviim.

רצח.sense: To murder; the noun is the murder itself, and the strengthened form gives the murderers.

more.t: וְרָצַח גֹּאֵל הַדָּם אֶת־ הָרֹצֵחַ (Bamidbar 35:27), the redeemer of the blood kills the murderer; וּרְצָחוֹ נֶפֶשׁ (Devarim 22:26), and he murders him, a life; הֲרָצַחְתָּ וְגַם־יָֽרָשְׁתָּ (Melachim I 21:19), have you murdered and also taken possession; לֹא תִרְצַח (Shemos 20:14 in his edition), you shall not murder; הֲגָנֹב רָצֹחַ (Yirmiyahu 7:9), stealing, murdering.
לִפְתֹּחַ פֶּה בְּרֶצַח (Yechezkel 21:27), to open the mouth with murder, and בְּרֶצַח בְּֽעַצְמוֹתַי (Tehillim 42:11), with murder in my bones, both pointed with a segol.

הָאִשָּׁה הַנִּרְצָחָה (Shoftim 20:4), the murdered woman, and בְּתוֹךְ רְחֹבוֹת אֵֽרָצֵֽחַ (Mishlei 22:13), I shall be murdered in the midst of the streets. The strengthened form gives דֶּרֶךְ יְרַצְּחוּ שֶׁכְמָה (Hoshea 6:9), they murder on the way to Shechem; בֶּן־ הַֽמְרַצֵּחַ הַזֶּה (Melachim II 6:32), this son of the murderer; וְעַתָּה מְרַצְּחִֽים (Yeshayahu 1:21), and now murderers.

The two of them divided over תְּרָצְּחוּ כֻלְּכֶם (Tehillim 62:4). Ben Naftali reads it with a patach under the resh, so that עַד־אָנָה תְּהֽוֹתְתוּ עַל־אִישׁ, how long will you set upon a man, means that you devise ruin against men, and you are all murderers. Ben Asher reads it with a kamatz under the resh, תְּרָצְּחוּ, which makes the word a passive of the strengthened form, and then the pasuk is put as a prayer: may you all be murdered, and be always כְּקִיר נָטוּי, a leaning wall, a pushed fence that is close to falling, so that you stand in fear continually.

הרג.sense: To kill or slay; the nouns from it are the slaughter itself and the day of killing.

more.t: כִּי הָרַג שָׁאוּל (Shmuel I 22:21), for Shaul killed; יַֽהֲרֹג בַּבָּרָד גַּפְנָם (Tehillim 78:47), He killed their vines with hail; הִרְגוּ אִישׁ אֲנָשָׁיו (Bamidbar 25:5), let each man kill his men; הָרֹג בָּקָר וְשָׁחֹט צֹאן (Yeshayahu 22:13), slaying cattle and slaughtering sheep; וְיוֹאָב וַֽאֲבִישַׁי אָחִיו הָֽרְגוּ לְאַבְנֵר (Shmuel II 3:30), Yoav and Avishai his brother killed Avner. The slain are הֲרֻגֵי מָוֶת (Yirmiyahu 18:21), slain of death, and בַּֽהֲרוּגִים הָאֵלֶּה (Yechezkel 37:9), these slain ones.

עֵת לַֽהֲרוֹג וְעֵת לִרְפּוֹא (Koheles 3:3), a time to kill and a time to heal. Although healing is not the opposite of killing, the pasuk says healing because the reviving of the dead is not a time that runs by the way of the world as the other times do, even though it comes by way of a miracle and is destined to be. Some explain לַֽהֲרוֹג as like לִמְחוֹץ, to smite.

גֵּיא הַֽהֲרֵגָה (Yirmiyahu 7:32), the valley of the killing, and לְיוֹם הֲרֵגָֽה (Yirmiyahu 12:3), for a day of slaughter. Without the feminine hei: בְּיוֹם הֶרֶג רָב (Yeshayahu 30:25), on a day of great slaughter, pointed with segols, and מַכַּת־חֶרֶב וְהֶרֶג וְאַבְדָן (Esther 9:5), a blow of the sword and killing and destruction.

אִם־ כְּהֶרֶג הֲרֻגָיו הֹרָֽג (Yeshayahu 27:7), was he slain as his slain were slain, and כִּֽי־עָלֶיךָ הֹרַגְנוּ כָל־הַיּוֹם (Tehillim 44:23), for Your sake we are killed all the day. The passive is בַּחֶרֶב תֵּֽהָרַגְנָה (Yechezkel 26:6), they shall be killed by the sword, and בֵּהָרֵג הֶרֶג בְּתוֹכֵךְ (Yechezkel 26:15), when slaughter is done in your midst, which stands in the measure of בֵּֽעָטֵף עוֹלֵל וְיוֹנֵק (Eichah 2:11), when infant and suckling faint, though by rule the two would be בְּהֵהָרֵג and בְּהֵעָטֵף.

קטל.sense: To kill, in two pesukim; the noun from it is slaughter, and he says plainly that their matter is killing.

more.t: אִם־ תִּקְטֹל אֱלוֹהַּ רָשָׁע (Tehillim 139:19), if You would slay the wicked, and הֵן יִקְטְלֵנִי (Iyov 13:15), though He slay me. The noun is מֵהַר עֵשָׂו מִקָּֽטֶל (Ovadiah 1:9), from the mount of Esav, by slaughter, whose kamatz stands because of the pause. Their matter is killing.

רסן.sense: The bridle put in a beast's mouth to guide it; a bridle thrown off is a figure for fear and shame cast away.

more.t: וְרֶסֶן מַתְעֶה (Yeshayahu 30:28), a bridle that leads astray, and וְרֶסֶן מִפָּנַי שִׁלֵּֽחוּ (Iyov 30:11), they have cast off the bridle before me, pointed with segols.

Radak explains וְרֶסֶן מִפָּנַי שִׁלֵּֽחוּ to mean that they showed no fear and no shame before him, as though until then he had been stopping their mouths with a bridle the way it is done to animals, as the pasuk says בְּמֶתֶג וָרֶסֶן עֶדְיוֹ לִבְלוֹם (Tehillim 32:9), with bit and bridle to curb his trappings, which is set in the mouths of beasts to lead them as the rider wishes; and now they have sent the bridle away from before him, meaning that they do not fear him.
בְּכֶפֶל רִסְנוֹ מִי יָבֽוֹא (Iyov 41:5), who can come within his double bridle, is said by way of likeness.

מתג.sense: The bit or the goad used on a beast; the same word names Meseg HaAmah that David took from the Pelishtim.

more.t: בְּמֶתֶג וָרֶסֶן עֶדְיוֹ לִבְלוֹם (Tehillim 32:9), with bit and bridle to curb his trappings; מֶתֶג לַֽחֲמוֹר (Mishlei 26:3), a goad for the donkey; וּמִתְגִּי בִּשְׂפָתֶיךָ (Yeshayahu 37:29), my bit in your lips: all three are one matter. מֶתֶג לַֽחֲמוֹר is the iron goad fixed in the end of a stick, with which the donkey is pricked to hurry him. In the other two it is the long iron put in the beast's mouth to lead her, called in the foreign tongue פְּרֵי"ן, and it is like the bridle except that it is not made in its fashion.

וַיִּקַּח דָּוִד אֶת־ מֶתֶג הָֽאַמָּה מִיַּד פְּלִשְׁתִּֽים (Shmuel II 8:1), David took Meseg HaAmah from the hand of the Pelishtim, which Targum Yonasan renders תִּקוּן אַמְתָא, the setting in order of the amah. In Divrei HaYamim, in its place, the pasuk runs וַיִּקַּח אֶת־גַּת וּבְנֹתֶיהָ מִיַּד פְּלִשְׁתִּֽים (Divrei HaYamim I 18:1), he took Gat and her daughter towns from the hand of the Pelishtim; Radak offers that Meseg HaAmah may be a name covering Gat and her daughter towns together.

זמם.sense: To think or to plan, and the noun is the thought or the scheme; a second sense of these letters is lewdness and abomination.

more.t: אֲשֶׁר זָמָם (Eichah 2:17), what He planned, and כַּֽאֲשֶׁר זָמַם לַֽעֲשׂוֹת לְאָחִיו (Devarim 19:19), as he schemed to do to his brother. עַל כִּֽי־דִבַּרְתִּי זַמֹּתִי (Yirmiyahu 4:28), because I have spoken, I have planned, is accented on the syllable before the last, while זַמֹּתִי בַּל־יַֽעֲבָר־פִּֽי (Tehillim 17:3), my thought shall not pass my mouth, is accented on the last.

זְמָמוֹ אַל־תָּפֵק (Tehillim 109:9 in his edition), do not let his scheme come about; in another measure, זִמֹּתַי נִתְּקוּ (Iyov 17:12 in his edition), my thoughts are torn away; and with an added mem, מְזִמָּה תִּשְׁמֹר עָלֶיךָ (Mishlei 20:11 in his edition), thought will guard over you. All of these and their like are the matter of thinking.

זִמַּת אִוֶּלֶת חַטָּאת (Mishlei 24:9), the scheming of folly is sin: whoever thinks upon matters of folly, it brings him to sin. וְתֽוֹעֲבַת לְאָדָם לֵֽץ, and the scorner is an abomination to man: one who thinks upon the words of the scorner, who is no fool but mocks people and whose dealings are evil, and who runs after him, is brought to be an abomination to man, that people loathe him.

more.h: Not setting your heart to it
more.t: אֶת־ הַזִּמָּה עַל כָּל־תּֽוֹעֲבֹתָֽיִךְ (Yechezkel 16:43), the scheming upon all your abominations, Radak reads as: you did not set your heart to it and did not think what you had done upon all your abominations.

In another sense: כִּי זִמָּה עָשֽׂוּ (Hoshea 6:9), for they did lewdness, and זִמָּה הִֽוא (Vayikra 18:17), it is lewdness. The plural is הוּא זִמּוֹת יָעָץ (Yeshayahu 32:7), he counsels lewd schemes, and with an added mem, אֲשֶׁר יֹאמְרֻךָ לִמְזִמָּה (Tehillim 139:20), who speak of You for scheming, and עֲשׂוֹתָהּ הַֽמְזִמָּתָה הָֽרַבִּים (Yirmiyahu 11:15), the many who carry out their scheming. Their matter is filth and abomination and evil deed.
Some say that they are all one matter, since every זמה is a thought, whether for good or for evil, and each one is explained according to its place.

נוא.sense: To hold back or turn away, breaking words and plans and voiding them.

more.t: וְאִם־ הֵנִיא אָבִיהָ אֹתָהּ (Bamidbar 30:6), and if her father holds her back; וְלָמָּה תְנִואוּן (Bamidbar 32:7), and why would you turn away the heart of Bnei Yisrael; שֶׁמֶן רֹאשׁ אַל־ יָנִי רֹאשִׁי (Tehillim 141:5), let fine oil not refuse my head, where the word is written without an alef.

וִֽידַעְתֶּם אֶת־ תְּנֽוּאָתִֽי (Bamidbar 14:34), you shall know My opposition, and תְּנוּאוֹת עָלַי יִמְצָא (Iyov 33:10), He finds occasions of opposition against me. Their matter is the breaking of words and thoughts and the voiding of them.

פרר.sense: Under these letters his entry is the cooking pot alone: פָּרוּר is the cauldron in which food is boiled.

more.t: וּבִשְּׁלוּ בַּפָּרוּר (Bamidbar 11:8), and they cooked it in the pot, and אוֹ בַפָּרוּר (Shmuel I 2:14), or in the cauldron: it is the pot in which one cooks. Some explain כָּל־פָּנִים קִבְּצוּ פָארֽוּר (Yoel 2:6), all faces have gathered פארור, from this word, taking it to mean blackness; Radak has treated that word under the root פָּאַר.

בטל.sense: One line only: the grinders of Koheles 12:3, glossed in a single word, with the note that Chachamim use this word a great deal.

more.t: וּבָטְלוּ הַטֹּֽחֲנוֹת (Koheles 12:3), and the grinders ceased. His whole gloss is one word, printed ושבחו, and they praised, which does not answer to the pasuk and reads as a slip of the press. Radak adds that Chachamim used this word a great deal, the light form where it stands of itself and the strengthened form where it acts upon something else.

אות.sense: A sign, that is a mark or token; he sets it beside מופת, a wonder, and treats the pair under the headword יפת.

more.t: וְנָתַן אֵלֶיךָ אוֹת אוֹ מוֹפֵֽת (Devarim 13:2), and he gives you a sign or a wonder; וּבָא הָאוֹת וְהַמּוֹפֵת (Devarim 13:3), and the sign or the wonder comes; זֹאת אוֹת ־הַבְּרִית (Bereishis 9:12), this is the sign of the covenant; וְהָיָה הַדָּם לָכֶם לְאֹת (Shemos 12:13), the blood shall be a sign for you; אִישׁ עַל־דִּגְלוֹ בְאֹתֹת (Bamidbar 2:2), each man by his banner with signs. Its explanation is a mark, and Radak writes further on it under the root יפת.

יפת.sense: The headword under which he treats מופת, a wonder: it is like a sign, but a sign can be a bare mark and a wonder cannot.

more.t: תְּנוּ לָכֶם מוֹפֵת (Shemos 7:9), give yourselves a wonder; אֲנִי מֽוֹפֶתְכֶם (Yechezkel 12:11), I am your wonder; אֶת־כָּל־ הַמֹּֽפְתִים הָאֵלֶּה (Shemos 11:10), all these wonders. Its matter is like אוֹת, a sign, except that אוֹת falls in places where מוֹפֵת cannot: אִישׁ עַל־דִּגְלוֹ בְאֹתֹת (Bamidbar 2:2), each man by his banner with signs, and וְהָֽיְתָה לְאוֹת בְּרִית (Bereishis 9:13), and it shall be for a sign of a covenant. In those places and their like מוֹפֵת does not fall, for a מוֹפֵת is a thing shown so that one may believe through it in something of its kind that is destined to be shown; אוֹת comes in that sense too, except that at times it comes for a mark alone, and מוֹפֵת does not.

פלא.sense: Wondrous, and too wondrous for a man to reach; the nouns are a wonder and wonders, and a nearby sense is setting apart, as in a vow.

more.t: כִּי יִפָּלֵא מִמְּךָ דָבָר (Devarim 17:8), if a matter is too hard for you; לֹֽא־ נִפְלֵאת הִוא מִמְּךָ (Devarim 30:11), it is not too wondrous for you; נִפְלְאַתָה אַֽהֲבָֽתְךָ לִי (Shmuel II 1:26), your love to me was wondrous, carrying two feminine endings, like כִּי הֶחְבְּאַתָה (Yehoshua 6:17), for she hid; נִפְלָאִים מַֽעֲשֶׂיךָ (Tehillim 139:14), Your works are wondrous; בִּגְדֹלוֹת וּבְנִפְלָאוֹת מִמֶּֽנִּי (Tehillim 131:1), in great things and in things too wondrous for me; שִׂיחוּ בְּכָל־ נִפְלְאוֹתָֽיו (Tehillim 105:2), speak of all His wonders. It is written once as though from a root ending in hei: נוֹרָאוֹת נִפְלֵיתִי (Tehillim 139:14), I am made fearfully wondrous.

עֹשֵׂה פֶֽלֶא (Shemos 15:11), doer of wonder, pointed with segols; וַתֵּרֶד פְּלָאִים (Eichah 1:9), she came down wondrously. The feminine plural is פְּלָאוֹת עֵדְוֹתֶיךָ (Tehillim 119:129), Your testimonies are wonders, and קֵץ הַפְּלָאֽוֹת (Daniel 12:6), the end of the wonders; with an added mem, מִפְלְאוֹת תְּמִים דֵּעִֽים (Iyov 37:16), the wonders of Him who is perfect in knowledge. The adjective is פְּלִאָֽיה (Tehillim 139:6), wondrous, said of דַעַת מִמֶּנִּי, knowledge that is beyond me, formed as שְֹרִידָה is from שָֹרִיד and פְּלִיטָה from פָּלִיט; and in another measure, פֶּלֶא יוֹעֵץ (Yeshayahu 9:5), wonder of a counsellor.

הִפְלִיא עֵצָה (Yeshayahu 28:29), He made counsel wondrous; כִּֽי־ הִפְלִיא חַסְדּוֹ לִי (Tehillim 31:22), for He made His kindness wondrous to me; אֲשֶׁר־עָשָׂה עִמָּכֶם לְהַפְלִיא (Yoel 2:26), who dealt wondrously with you; הַפְלֵא וָפֶלֶא (Yeshayahu 29:14), wonder upon wonder; and וְתָשֹׁב תִּתְפַּלָּא ־בִֽי (Iyov 10:16), and again You show Yourself wondrous against me. The matter of wonder is well known.

וְהוּא־ פֶֽלִאי (Shoftim 13:18), and it is wondrous, is an adjective for the wondrous name, as though to say: my name is wondrous and too lofty to be made known to you. So too with Yaakov Avinu, where the angel did not wish to make his name known to him and said לָמָּה זֶּה תִּשְׁאַל לִשְׁמִי (Bereishis 32:30), why is it that you ask my name.
