This was because the angels appeared to them in the likeness of men and did not reveal that they were angels, and so did not mention their names. So too פְּלֹנִי אַלְמֹנִי (Melachim II 6:8), the man whose name is hidden from the one who mentions him; and even where he is known to the one who mentions him, if he does not wish to call him by name he says פלוני of him. Chachamim are accustomed to this usage in their language.

A sense close to this one: כִּי יַפְלִא לִנְדֹּר נֶדֶר נָזִיר (Bamidbar 6:2), when a man sets himself apart to vow the vow of a nazir, and לְפַלֵּא ־נֶדֶר (Bamidbar 15:3), to set apart a vow. Their matter is separating, and in this sense the root is פָּלָה with a hei.

פתע.sense: Suddenly, which he glosses as all at once and without intent.

more.t: פֶּתַע יִשָּׁבֵר (Mishlei 6:15), suddenly he will be broken, the pei pointed with a segol; בְּפֶתַע פִּתְאֹם (Bamidbar 6:9), in sudden suddenness; וְאִם־ בְּפֶתַע בְּלֹֽא־אֵיבָה (Bamidbar 35:22), and if suddenly, without enmity. His gloss is: suddenly, without intent.

אגד.sense: Gathering things and tying them into one bundle; from there, a single band of men, and a single settled counsel.

more.t: אֲגֻדַּת אֵזוֹב (Shemos 12:22), a bundle of hyssop, and הַתֵּר אֲגֻדּוֹת מוֹטָה (Yeshayahu 58:6), to loose the bands of the yoke: these and their like are the gathering of things and the tying of them together.
For the hyssop Chazal teach that the mitzvah of hyssop is שלשה קלחין, three stalks, ובהם שלשה גבעולין, with three stems in them.

וַיִּֽהְיוּ לַֽאֲגֻדָּה אֶחָת (Shmuel II 2:25), they became one band, means one gathering and one agreement; so וַֽאֲגֻדָּתוֹ עַל־אֶרֶץ יְסָדָהּ (Amos 9:6), He founded His band upon the earth, is His counsel and His agreement.

In his own view the three elements that rest upon the earth are what is called an agudah, since they are one bundle laid one upon the other upon the earth, and that is why the pasuk says He founded His bundle upon the earth.

עוד.sense: Three things under one root: to plunder, and the spoil taken; to testify, a witness and his testimony; and duration, still, while, again and for ever.

more.t: חֶבְלֵי רְשָׁעִים עִוְּדֻנִי (Tehillim 119:61) is that they plundered me and despoiled me. The noun is יֹאכַל עַד (Bereishis 49:27), he devours spoil, and אָז חֻלַּק עַד ־שָׁלָל מַרְבֶּה (Yeshayahu 33:23), then plunder and much spoil were divided, which he reads as spoil and plunder, two nouns side by side.
לְיוֹם קוּמִי לְעַד (Tzefaniah 3:8) and its like were brought under the root עד, but Radak holds the right filing is here, since we find עודונו.

הַֽעִידֹתִי בָכֶם הַיּוֹם (Devarim 4:26), I call you to witness this day, and הָעֵד הֵעִד בָּנוּ הָאִישׁ לֵאמֹר (Bereishis 43:3), the man warned us solemnly. Some of them are close to warning, and are put in the language of testimony because one who warns a man warns before witnesses, so that he cannot deny it afterwards.

The Torah and the mitzvos are called תעודה and עדות, testimony, because Israel took His mitzvos upon themselves: לְתוֹרָה וְלִתְעוּדָה (Yeshayahu 8:20), to the Torah and to the testimony. So אֲרוֹן הָֽעֵדֻת (Shemos 25:22), the ark of the testimony, is named for the luchos within it, which are testimony to Israel.

בְּעוֹד שְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים (Bereishis 40:19), within three days, he reads as at the end of that time; כִּֽי־כָל־ עוֹד נִשְׁמָתִי בִי (Iyov 27:3) is as long as the soul is in me; and עוֹלָם וָעֶד (Tehillim 104:5) is all the days the world endures.

more.h: Not yet, and what it implies
more.t: אֲשֶׁר לֹא זְכַרְתָּם עוֹד (Tehillim 88:6) he reads as whom You have not yet remembered, and takes it as a sign that a time will come when the dead are remembered.

Rabbi Yehudah separates מָֽה־ אֲעִידֵךְ מָה אֲדַמֶּה־לָּךְ (Eichah 2:13), what shall I take to witness for you, what shall I liken to you, from this sense. Radak holds it can be read within it: what nation can I bring to testify to you, to show you one stricken as you were.

פנג.sense: Pannag, a food named beside wheat and honey; some take it for a place name, the Targum for a field herb, and Yosef ben Gurion for balsam.

more.t: בְּחִטֵּי מִנִּית וּפַנַּג וּדְבַשׁ (Yechezkel 27:17), with wheat of Minnis and pannag and honey. Some say pannag is the name of a place, and so is מִנִּית, Minnis.
The Targum gives וְקוֹלְיָא, kulya, and kulya in the words of Chazal is a herb among the field greens that are eaten, as they say מערבין בקוליא, that an eruv may be made with kulya.
Yosef ben Gurion said that pannag is balsam, and that it was found in Yericho. Radak notes that the same pasuk says וצרי, and tzori, balm, is explained as the oil of afarsemon, which is the balsam.

צרה.sense: Tzori, the balm of Gilad: a resin that drips from the ketaf tree, and one of the spices of the ketores.

more.t: מְעַט צֳרִי (Bereishis 43:11), a little balm, הַצֳרִי אֵין בְּגִלְעָד (Yirmiyahu 8:22), is there no balm in Gilad, and עֲלִי גִלְעָד וּקְחִי צֳרִי (Yirmiyahu 46:11), go up to Gilad and take balm.
In וָצֹרִי, and balm, the vowel is a cholam; in the three above it is a kamatz chataf; and in וּצְרִי וָלֹט (Bereishis 37:25), balm and ladanum, it carries a sheva alone.
Radak identifies it with the נטף, the dripping gum that the pasuk names among the spices of the ketores.

Chazal bring Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: הצרי אינו אלא שרף הנוטף מעצי הקטף, tzori is nothing but the sap that drips from the ketaf trees, which are scored so that the tzori runs out of them. In la'az it is called balsam.

נטף.sense: Dripping and flowing: hands that drip myrrh and mountains that drip wine; by transfer, speech that drops, and so to preach.

more.t: וְיָדַי נָֽטְפוּ ־מוֹר (Shir HaShirim 5:5), my hands dripped myrrh, and יִטְּפוּ הֶֽהָרִים עָסִיס (Yoel 4:18), the mountains shall drip sweet wine. The noun is נִטְפֵי ־מָיִם (Iyov 36:27), drops of water. Radak sums the whole of it as flowing and melting.

By way of borrowing, of speech: וְעָלֵימוֹ תִּטֹּף מִלָּתִֽי (Iyov 29:22), my word dropped upon them, as in תִּזַּל כַּטַּל אִמְרָתִי (Devarim 32:2), my speech shall distil as the dew. In the causative it is to preach: אַטִּף לְךָ לַיַּיִן וְלַשֵּׁכָר (Michah 2:11), I will preach to you of wine and strong drink. In אַל־ תַּטִּפוּ יַטִּיפוּן (Michah 2:6) it is Israel preaching at the true prophets and telling them not to preach.

הַנְּטִיפוֹת וְהַשֵּׁירוֹת (Yeshayahu 3:19) and וְהַנְּטִפוֹת (Shoftim 8:26) are הענקים, neck pendants; and they say that clear bdolach is called by this name in Arabic. Some explain the first instead as the vessels in which the tzori is kept.

נָטָף וּשְׁחֵלֶת (Shemos 30:33 in his edition), nataf and shecheles: they say the nataf is the tzori, so called because it drips from the ketaf trees, as Chazal say that tzori is nothing but the sap that drips from them.

בשֹם.sense: Spice, the fragrant kind. His entry glosses nothing, and sets out only the word's three vowel patterns and the plural gathered from them.

more.t: וּקְנֵה־ בֹשֶׂם (Shemos 30:23), sweet cane of spice, and לֹא־בָא כַבֹּשֶׂם הַהוּא (Melachim I 10:10), no such spice ever came again; a second pattern in וְקִנְּמָן־ בֶּשֶׂם מַֽחֲצִיתוֹ (Shemos 30:23), and of fragrant cinnamon half as much; a third in אָרִיתִי מוֹרִי עִם־ בְּשָׂמִי (Shir HaShirim 5:1), I have gathered my myrrh with my spice.
The plural is בְּשָׂמִים רֹאשׁ (Shemos 30:23), chief spices, and it is gathered from one of the three patterns; which of them, he leaves to his chapter on the grammar of nouns.

להב.sense: A flame, and then the blade of a sword or spear, which is called a lahav because it flashes as a flame does.

more.t: וַיְהִי בַעֲלוֹת הַלַּהַב (Shoftim 13:20), as the flame went up; in the feminine לֶֽהָבָה מִקִּרְיַת סִיחֹן (Bamidbar 21:28), a flame from the city of Sichon; and in the construct plural לַֽהֲבוֹת אֵֽשׁ (Tehillim 29:7), flames of fire.

Since the sword resembles a flame in its flashing, it too is called a lahav: וַיָּבֹא גַם־הַנִּצָּב אַחַר הַלַּהַב (Shoftim 3:22), the haft went in after the blade. So the pasuk likens it to flame and to lightning together, וְלַהַב חֶרֶב וּבְרַק חֲנִית (Nachum 3:3), the flame of the sword and the lightning of the spear; and in the feminine וְלַהֶבֶת חֲנִיתוֹ (Shmuel I 17:7) is the iron of his spear.
פְּנֵי לְהָבִים פְּנֵיהֶֽם (Yeshayahu 13:8), their faces are faces of flames, he takes as the plural of the flame. No other word stands under these letters in his entry.

אור.sense: Light, and to give light: the luminaries, and light as a figure for abundant good. He finds five further senses under these letters.

more.t: רְאוּ־נָא כִּי־ אֹרוּ עֵינַי (Shmuel I 14:29), see how my eyes have brightened, and קוּמִי אוֹרִי (Yeshayahu 60:1), arise and shine. Of making something else light: הֵאִירוּ בְרָקָיו תֵּבֵל (Tehillim 97:4), His lightnings lit up the world, and יָאֵר פָּנָיו אִתָּנוּ סֶֽלָה (Tehillim 67:2), may He make His face shine with us.

The noun: בְּאֽוֹר ־פְּנֵי־מֶלֶךְ חַיִּים (Mishlei 16:15), in the light of a king's face is life; the plural לְעֹשֵׂה אוֹרִים גְּדֹלִים (Tehillim 136:7), who made the great lights; and with a mem set in front, כָּל־ מְאוֹרֵי אוֹר בַּשָּׁמַיִם (Yechezkel 32:8), all the bright lights of heaven.

Some of them stand for abundant good: אֽוֹר ־צַדִּיקִים יִשְׂמָח (Mishlei 13:9), the light of the righteous rejoices, and לַיְּהוּדִים הָֽיְתָה אוֹרָה (Esther 8:15), the Jews had light. Darkness in the same way stands for abundant trouble.

אֵי־זֶה הַדֶּרֶךְ יִשְׁכָּן־ אוֹר (Iyov 38:19), where is the way where light dwells: Rav Saadiah Gaon explained it of a place on earth that is light the whole year but for one day, and its opposite, a place all darkness but for one day, which is וחשׁך אי זה מקומו, and darkness, where is its place.

Some derive אֶת ־הָֽאוּרִים וְאֶת־הַתֻּמִּים (Vayikra 8:8), the Urim and the Tumim, from light. Radak writes that what they are has not become clear to us, since the pesukim make them something other than the stones of the choshen. Rashi explained them as the writing of the Shem HaMeforash set within the folds of the choshen, by which it lit up its words and made them whole; Radak closes that the truth is not known.

וְלֹֽא־ תָאִירוּ מִזְבְּחִי חִנָּם, you shall not light My altar for nothing, he glosses ולא תלהיבו, you shall not set it ablaze. So לְכוּ בְּאוּר אֶשְׁכֶם (Yeshayahu 50:11), walk in the flame of your fire, and נָשִׁים בָּאוֹת מְאִירוֹת אוֹתָהּ (Yeshayahu 27:11), which he reads of men weak as women who come and burn it.

more.h: A hollow, a valley, a hole
more.t: אֲשֶׁר הֽוֹצֵאתִיךָ מֵאוּר כַּשְׂדִּים, who brought you out of Ur Kasdim, is fire according to the reading Chazal gave it, or else אוּר כַּשְׂדִּֽים is the valley of the Kasdim, as עַל־כֵּן בָּֽאֻרִים כַּבְּדוּ (Yeshayahu 24:14) is glossed בעמקים, in the valleys. So too מְאוּרַת צִפְעוֹנִי (Yeshayahu 11:8) is חור צפעוני, the viper's hole.

לְלַקֵּט אֹרֹת (Melachim II 4:39), to gather orot, he glosses ירקות, greens, and the Targum renders יֵרוֹקָנִין, greens. Chazal ask what orot are and answer that it is gargir, rocket, called so because it lights up the eyes. Some read טַל אוֹרֹת טַלֶּךָ (Yeshayahu 26:19), the dew of orot is Your dew, in this sense, dew fit for greens, or else as the light of day.

כְּחֹם צַח עֲלֵי־ אוֹר (Yeshayahu 18:4), like clear heat upon rain, and יָפִיץ עֲנַן אוֹרֽוֹ (Iyov 37:11), He scatters the cloud of His rain. Chazal hold that every orah said in Elihu's words is the coming down of rain, and some say rain is called or on account of the lesser luminary, since by its movements the rain comes at the Creator's command.
וַֽעֲדָרִים לַֽאֲוֵרֽוֹת (Divrei HaYamim II 32:28) are the mangers, the letters turned about from אֻרְוֹת סוּסִים (Melachim I 5:6), stalls for horses.

שׁלהב.sense: A blaze, the flame at full strength; where Scripture attaches the Name to a word it magnifies it, and shalheves-yah is a great flame.

more.t: יֹֽנַקְתּוֹ תְּיַבֵּשׁ שַׁלְהָבֶת (Iyov 15:30), the blaze shall dry up his branch, and לֹֽא־תִכְבֶּה לַהֶבֶת שַׁלְהֶבֶת (Yechezkel 21:3), the flaming blaze shall not be quenched.

שַׁלְהֶבֶתְיָֽה (Shir HaShirim 8:6) is written as one word but carries the sense of two, a great flame. Scripture magnifies a thing by attaching it to the Name, as in מַאְפֵּלְיָה (Yirmiyahu 2:31), a deep darkness, and the like, which he treats under the root אפל.
שלהבת, blaze, is like להבת, flame, and flame is set in construct to blaze in the manner of אַדְמַת־עָפָר (Daniel 12:2), the dust of the earth, and מִטִּיט הַיָּוֵן (Tehillim 40:3), the miry clay.

The Targum renders פְּנֵי לְהָבִים פְּנֵיהֶֽם (Yeshayahu 13:8), their faces are faces of flame, as אַפֵּי שַׁלְהוֹבִין אַפֵּיהוֹן, faces of blazes are their faces, and בְּלַבַּת־אֵשׁ (Shemos 3:2), in a flame of fire, as בְּשַׁלְהוֹבִית אֶשָּׁתָא, in a blaze of fire.

לפד.sense: A torch, meaning the burning wood itself; torch and lightning are close in sense, and wood is called a torch only once it is alight.

more.t: כְּלַפִּיד יִבְעָֽר (Yeshayahu 62:1), it shall burn like a torch, and לַפִּיד בּוּז (Iyov 12:5), a torch of contempt: a lapid is the wood that is alight.
אֵשֶׁת לַפִּידוֹת (Shoftim 4:4) is אשת ברק, the wife of Barak, and Radak holds barak, lightning, and lapid, torch, close to one another in sense.

וַיַּבְעֶר־אֵשׁ בַּלַּפִּידִים (Shoftim 15:5), he set fire to the torches, names them for their end, since before he set the fire in them they were not torches but wood. So too וְטַֽחֲנִי קָמַח (Yeshayahu 47:2), grind meal, and אָפִיתִי עַל־גֶּחָלָיו לֶחֶם (Yeshayahu 44:19), I baked bread on its coals.
אֶת־הַקּוֹלֹת וְאֶת־ הַלַּפִּידִם, the thunder and the torches, is said by way of likeness, as though they saw torches burning.

פרשֹ.sense: Spreading a thing out flat: a cloud spread for a covering, hands spread in tefillah, a net spread; and from there, scattering to the winds.

more.t: פָּרַשׂ עָנָן לְמָסָךְ (Tehillim 105:39), He spread a cloud for a covering, וּפָרַשׂ כַּפָּיו אֶל־הַבַּיִת (Melachim I 8:38), he spreads his hands toward the House, and פָּרְשׂוּ רֶשֶׁת לְיַד מַעְגָּל (Tehillim 140:6), they spread a net beside the path: all of them are spreading flat. The noun is מִפְרְשֵׂי ־עָב (Iyov 36:29), the spreading of the clouds.

Close to it: וְהַנִּשְׁאָרִים לְכָל־רוּחַ יִפָּרֵשׂוּ (Yechezkel 17:21), the rest shall be scattered to every wind, and כִּי כְּאַרְבַּע רוּחוֹת הַשָּׁמַיִם פֵּרַשְׂתִּי אֶתְכֶם (Zechariah 2:10), which he reads: as the four winds of heaven are far one from another, so will I set you far apart in scattering you.

A further sense in וּפָֽרְשׂוּ כַּֽאֲשֶׁר בַּסִּיר (Michah 3:3) and פֹּרֵשׂ אֵין לָהֶֽם (Eichah 4:4), none breaks bread for them, and פֵּֽרְשָׂה צִיּוֹן בְּיָדֶיהָ (Eichah 1:17); Radak says he treated these in his root פרס. Some read בְּפָרֵשׂ (Tehillim 68:15), when He spread out, in this sense as well.

פרשׁ.sense: To make a thing plain, and so a full account of it; also the horseman, named for pricking his horse on, and separately the dung of an animal.

more.t: לִפְרשׁ לָהֶם (Vayikra 24:12), to make it plain to them, and לֹא פֹרַשׁ מַה־יֵּֽעָשֶׂה לֽוֹ (Bamidbar 15:34), it had not been made plain what was to be done with him: the sense throughout is explanation and clarification. The noun is וְאֵת פָּרָשַׁת הַכֶּסֶף (Esther 4:7), the full account of the money, and וּפָרָשַׁת גְּדֻלַּת מָרְדֳּכַי (Esther 10:2), the full account of Mordechai's greatness.
Close to it, נִפְרָשׁוֹת (Yechezkel 34:12), said of a flock, means נפרדות, ones that have been separated off.
וּכְצִפְעֹנִי יַפְרִֽשׁ (Mishlei 23:32), it strikes like an adder, is the striking that Chazal call טריקה, as in חויא טרקיא, a snake that strikes.

more.h: Why a rider is a parash
more.t: From that sense the horseman is called a parash, as in בְּרִכְבּוֹ וּבְפָֽרָשָֽׁיו (Shemos 14:17), with his chariot and his horsemen, since he pricks the horse with the spurs on his feet to make it run. In פָּרָשׁ מַֽעֲלֶה (Nachum 3:3) Radak reads the horseman as raising the flame of the sword and the lightning of the spear, the vav of ולהב being an added one; or the phrase is short of a word, meaning raising a spear or a javelin.
Some take סוּסִים וּפָֽרָשִׁים (Yechezkel 27:14), horses and horsemen, as a named breed of horse. Radak holds there is no need for that, and the word is as it sounds.

A separate word: וְזֵרִיתִי פֶרֶשׁ עַל־פְּנֵיכֶם (Malachi 2:3), I will scatter dung upon your faces, and עַל־ פִּרְשָׁהּ יִשְׂרֹֽף (Bamidbar 19:5), its dung shall be burnt: it is the dung in the animal's belly.

באר.sense: Two words under one set of letters: to set a thing out plainly, and a well, one whose waters well up from below.

more.t: בֵּאֵר אֶת־הַתּוֹרָה הַזֹּאת (Devarim 1:5), he set this Torah out plainly, בַּאֵר הֵיטֵֽב (Devarim 27:8), set it out very plainly, and וּבָאֵר עַל־הַלֻּחוֹת (Chavakuk 2:2), set it plainly upon the tablets. Radak glosses the first two: he explained the Torah, he explained well.

The other sense: בְּאֵר מַיִם חַיִּים (Shir HaShirim 4:15), a well of living water, חָפַרְתִּי אֶת־ הַבְּאֵר הַזֹּֽאת (Bereishis 21:30), I dug this well, and the plural וְכָל־ הַבְּאֵרֹת אֲשֶׁר חָֽפְרוּ (Bereishis 26:15), all the wells they had dug. A well is one whose waters well up.
In construct the plural sometimes keeps its vowels, בְּאֵרֹת הַמַּיִם (Bereishis 26:18), the wells of water, and sometimes changes them, בֶּֽאֱרֹת חֵמָר (Bereishis 14:10), wells of clay.

פשׁר.sense: The solving of a matter, which he glosses as pisron, the interpreting of it; the word itself stands in Koheles alone.

more.t: וּמִי יוֹדֵעַ פֵּשֶׁר דָּבָר (Koheles 8:1), who knows the interpretation of a thing, pointed with a tzere, though there are seforim that point it with a segol. Its sense is פתרון דבר, the solving of a matter.

The Targum renders אִישׁ כְּפִתְרוֹן חֲלֹמוֹ (Bereishis 41:11), each man according to the interpretation of his dream, as גְּבַר כְּפִשְׁרַן חֶלְמֵהּ, each man according to the solving of his dream, which is this word.

פתר.sense: To interpret a dream: the verb and its noun pisron are the explaining and clarifying of what a dream holds.

more.t: כַּֽאֲשֶׁר פָּֽתַר ־לָנוּ (Bereishis 41:13), as he interpreted for us, וּפֹתֵר אֵין אֹתוֹ, and there was none to interpret it, and תִּשְׁמַע חֲלוֹם לִפְתֹּר אֹתֽוֹ, you understand a dream to interpret it. The noun is אִישׁ כְּפִתְרוֹן חֲלֹמוֹ, each man according to the interpretation of his dream. The sense of them all is the explanation and clarification of a dream.
His entry stops in the middle of a sentence, as he begins to turn to the words of four letters under these letters, and what he meant to say of them is not in it.

הבל.sense: A thing that is nothing at all: emptiness, and the verb of going after it and becoming empty oneself.

more.t: הֶבֶל הֵמָּה (Yirmiyahu 10:15), they are nothing, and הֲבֵל הֲבָלִים (Koheles 1:2), emptiness of emptinesses: Radak glosses hevel as a thing that is nothing at all.
וַיֵּלְכוּ אַֽחֲרֵי הַהֶבֶל וַיֶּהְבָּלוּ (Yirmiyahu 2:5), they went after emptiness and became empty themselves, and מַהְבִּלִים הֵמָּה אֶתְכֶם (Yirmiyahu 23:16), they are making you empty.
Chazal use the word of the vapour that leaves the mouth, הבל פיו, the breath of his mouth, and הבל תינוקות, the breath of schoolchildren, since it is a thing that ceases and is gone at once.

שׁעל.sense: The hollow of the hand and what it holds, a fistful; from it a narrow vineyard path; and under the same letters, the fox.

more.h: A fistful of water or of dust
more.t: מִֽי־מָדַד בְּשָׁעֳלוֹ מַיִם (Yeshayahu 40:12), who measured the waters in the hollow of his hand. In another form לִשְׁעָלִים לְכָל־הָעָם (Melachim I 20:10), handfuls for all the people, and בְּשַֽׁעֲלֵי שְׂעֹרִים (Yechezkel 13:19), handfuls of barley. Radak glosses these as a fist, that is, a fistful.

more.h: The narrow way through the vineyards
more.t: בְּמִשְׁעוֹל הַכְּרָמִים (Bamidbar 22:24) is a path, and Radak says the vineyard way is called משעול because it is a narrow road with no more width to it than the measure that lets a man walk along it.

more.h: Yonasan on the dust on their feet
more.t: Targum Yonasan renders לִשְׁעָלִים לְכָל־הָעָם אֲשֶׁר בְּרַגְלָֽי, handfuls for all the people who are at my feet, as לְמֵיסַב בִּשְׁעוֹלֵי פַרְסַת רִגְלֵי עַמָא דְעִמִי, to take up in the hollows of the hoofs of the feet of the people who are with me. Radak explains this as the dust that clings to the soles of their feet.

more.h: The fox under the same letters
more.t: אִם־יַֽעֲלֶה שׁוּעָל וּפָרַץ (Nechemiah 3:35), if a fox goes up he will breach it, and שֽׁוּעָלִים קְטַנִּים (Shir HaShirim 2:15), little foxes. Radak says the animal is known, and gives it no further gloss.

אבה.sense: To be willing, to desire. From it the pauper, who lacks all and craves all; and filed here too is the word for father, and so an elder or a chief.

more.t: וְלֹא־אָבָה (Devarim 23:6) is Hashem not being willing, and אִם־יְפַתּוּךָ חַטָּאִים אַל־תֹּבֵֽא (Mishlei 1:10), if sinners entice you, do not consent. Radak takes the alef as standing for a hei and the first root letter as hidden, and the sense of the root as one of will and desire.

וְתָפֵר הָֽאֲבִיּוֹנָה (Koheles 12:5) belongs here, the yud of the third root letter standing for a hei. Radak glosses אֲבִיּוֹנָה as the one that has the will and the craving, the soul that desires, so that the pasuk says the soul breaks its covenant with the body. Others say the word is a name for the organ of relations.

more.h: Why the very poor man is אביון
more.t: The very poor man is called אביון because he lacks everything and his craving and his will go out to all. Radak brings Vayikra Rabbah, that the אביון sees a thing and does not eat it, sees a thing and does not drink it, and craves everything, and that he is harder pressed than the עני, the poor man.

more.h: אָבִי יִבָּחֵן, my wish or my Father
more.t: אָבִי יִבָּחֵן אִיּוֹב עַד־נֶצַח (Iyov 34:36) Radak first takes as: my wish and my will is that Iyov be tested. Further on he reports that some read the word instead as father, a calling out to Hashem.

חָֽלְפוּ עִם־אֳנִיּוֹת אֵבֶה (Iyov 9:26) is, on his reading, ships whose will and desire is to reach the place, so that they hurry; as they pass, so his days passed quickly. Some make it the name of a place or a river, and some take it from איב, enmity, ships of plunderers. Only two words of these letters fall outside the sense of will. One is לְמִי אוֹי לְמִי אֲבוֹי (Mishlei 23:29), who has woe, who has sorrow, which is like אוי, woe, though some take it from אביון, meaning who has poverty.

more.h: אב the father and the chief
more.t: The second word outside that sense is אָב וָאֵם (Esther 2:7), father and mother, whose meaning Radak calls known. The great man and the man who comes first is called by it too: וַיְשִׂימֵנִי לְאָב לְפַרְעֹה (Bereishis 45:8), meaning an officer and a great man, as a father is officer over a son, and וֶֽהְיֵה־לָנוּ לְאָב וּלְכֹהֵן (Shoftim 18:19), be to us a father and a kohen.

Pupils are called sons, בְנֵֽי־הַנְּבִיאִים (Melachim II 2:15), the sons of the prophets, and so אֲבִי כָּל־תֹּפֵשׂ כִּנּוֹר וְעוּגָֽב (Bereishis 4:21) and אֲבִי ישֵׁב אֹהֶל וּמִקְנֶֽה (Bereishis 4:20) mean that he was first and a teacher to everyone who holds harp and pipe, and to everyone who dwells in a tent and keeps cattle, as a father comes before a son.

דלל.sense: To run low or be brought low: waters dried up, a man grown poor, honour made small, a man sick; and in one place, eyes lifted high.

more.t: דָּלְלוּ וְחָֽרְבוּ (Yeshayahu 19:6) Radak glosses as they dried up, and he puts דַּלּוּ מֵאֱנוֹשׁ נָֽעוּ (Iyov 25:4), they dried up away from men and wandered off, with it.

וְאִם־דַּל הוּא וְאֵין יָדוֹ מַשֶּׂגֶת (Vayikra 14:21) is a poor man. The plural is הֹֽלְכִים וְדַלִּֽים (Shmuel II 3:1), going and growing ever weaker, the feminine is דַּלּוֹת וְרָעוֹת תֹּאַר (Bereishis 41:19), thin and ill in form, and the noun is וּמִדַּלַּת הָאָרֶץ, the poorest of the land, which Radak says may instead be a description of the community. The plural of that noun is וּמִדַּלֹּות הָעָם (Yirmiyahu 52:15), the poorest of the people.

מַדּוּעַ אַתָּה כָּכָה דַּל בֶּן־הַמֶּלֶךְ (Shmuel II 13:4) is sick, and so אַשְׁרֵי מַשְׂכִּיל אֶל־ דָּל (Tehillim 41:2), happy is he who considers the sick man, since Radak says that mizmor was made over his illness. מִדַּלָּה יְבַצְּעֵנִי (Yeshayahu 38:12) he explains as: I thought that this sickness of mine would finish me, that I would die of it.

דַּלּוּ עֵינַי לַמָּרוֹם (Yeshayahu 38:14), my eyes are lifted to the height, he sets apart: here the sense is that they were raised. Rabbi Yonah joined נִצְּרָה עַל־ דַּל שְׂפָתָֽי (Tehillim 141:3), guard the door of my lips, to this sense, and Radak says he will take that word up again under the root דָּלַת.
וְדַלַּת רֹאשֵׁךְ כָּאַרְגָּמָן (Shir HaShirim 7:6), and the hair of your head like purple, is the tresses of hair.

מכך.sense: To sink low. He reckons with it the brother who grows poor and the roof that sags, all of them a sense of lowness.

more.t: וַיָּמֹכּוּ בַּֽעֲוֹנָֽם (Tehillim 106:43), they were brought low in their sin, opens the entry, and Radak thinks וְכִי־יָמוּךְ אָחִיךָ (Vayikra 25:25), when your brother grows poor, comes from it, a shuruk standing in for a cholam as in יָרוּן וְשָׂמֵֽחַ (Mishlei 29:6), he sings and rejoices. So too וּמָךְ אָחִיךָ עִמּוֹ (Vayikra 25:47), your brother grows poor beside him, where the kamatz is not the way of the doubled roots, and he suggests the resting letter came in place of the doubled one.

יִמַּךְ הַמְּקָרֶה (Koheles 10:18), the rafters sink, is the form in which the thing itself is brought low, and וְֽהֻמְּכוּ כַּכֹּל יִקָּפְצוּן (Iyov 24:24), they are brought low and gathered in like all, is the form of being brought low by another. Radak says the word should by rights have been וְהֻמַּכּוּ, and that all of them carry a sense of lowness.

His father writes that the root of וְֽהֻמְּכוּ is נָמַך, and brings as proof the Chachamim's מקום נָמוֹךְ, a low place (Berachos 10b), on the pattern of גָּדוֹל; and further, that it should have said והמכו with a dagesh in the kaf were its root מָכַך.

more.h: Radak's answer on the doubled roots
more.t: Radak says there is no proof from יִדְּמוּ כָּאָבֶן (Shemos 15:16), they are still as a stone, or וַֽיִּתְּמוּ יְמֵי בְכִי אֵבֶל (Devarim 34:8), the days of weeping for the mourning came to an end, for on his father's view their roots are נָדַם and נָתַם, while on Radak's own account they belong with the doubled roots, and so does וְֽהֻמְּכוּ along with them. He adds that the low place in the words of the Chachamim may itself be of the doubled roots, like נָגוֹזּוּ וְעָבָר (Nachum 1:12), they were shorn and he passed away.

תכך.sense: A sense of breaking, of the man who breaks whoever trusts in him and cheats him with his mouth; Rav Saadiah Gaon makes him a man of middling means.

more.t: רָשׁ וְאִישׁ תְּכָכִים (Mishlei 29:13), a poor man and a man of oppressions, with תֹּךְ וּמִרְמָֽה (Tehillim 55:12), oppression and deceit, and מִתּוֹךְ וּמֵחָמָס (Tehillim 72:14), from oppression and from violence, all carry a sense of breaking. Radak explains תוך ומרמה as breaking the man who trusts in him and does not guard himself against him, and deceiving him with his mouth.
Radak says he has already written this word under the root תוּך, except that Rabbi Yehudah Chayuj brought it together with אִישׁ תְּכָכִים, a man of oppressions, under one sense.

The Gaon Rav Saadiah explained תככים from תּוֹךְ הַבַּיִת (Shmuel II 4:6), the middle of the house, which is the middling sort. He said that רָשׁ וְאִישׁ תְּכָכִים, a poor man and a man of middling means, are fit to be shown kindness, since there are middling people who hide their poverty and keep up their standing so as to remain in honour; the pasuk therefore puts the two at one rank, and says that both need pity.

ירד.sense: To go down, and in the form that acts on a thing, to bring down. From it the slope of a hill, and eyes that run down with tears.

more.t: יָרֹד יָרַדְנוּ בַּתְּחִלָּה (Bereishis 43:20), we came down at the first, and רְדוּ־שָׁמָּה וְשִׁבְרוּ־לָנוּ מִשָּׁם (Bereishis 42:2), go down there and buy us food from there. The form that brings a thing down gives הוֹרַדְנוּ בְיָדֵנוּ (Bereishis 43:22), we brought it down in our hand, and וּבִנְסֹעַ הַמִּשְׁכָּן יוֹרִידוּ אֹתוֹ הַֽלְוִיִּם (Bamidbar 1:51), when the Mishkan travels the Leviim take it down.

עֵינִי עֵינִי יֹרְדָה מַּיִם (Eichah 1:16) he reads as running down with water, and וְתֵרַדְנָה עֵינֵינוּ דִּמְעָה (Yirmiyahu 9:17) as running down with tears. Radak adds that it may be read with no letter missing: because tears pour down from the eyes so freely, the going down is ascribed to the eyes themselves, as in וְהַגְּבָעוֹת תֵּלַכְנָה חָלָב (Yoel 4:18), the hills shall flow with milk.

more.h: The ephod that came down in his hand
more.t: Some read אֵפוֹד יָרַד בְּיָדֽוֹ (Shmuel I 23:6) as though it said he brought it down. Radak finds that hard, since the plain form of this root is not found taking an object. He offers that Evyasar, when he came down, came down with the ephod in his hand, and that Evyasar in fleeing took his vessels and his clothes, and it was caused by Hashem that the ephod was among them without his noticing, so that he did not know of it until he came to David. That is why the pasuk does not say he brought it down but that the ephod came down in his hand by chance, and Radak holds that reading the right one.

more.h: Rabbi Yonah's reading, and the answer
more.t: Rabbi Yonah explains וְיָרַדְתִּי עַל־הֶֽהָרִים (Shoftim 11:37) as and I will go up, and likewise וְלֹא־יֵרֵד עִמָּנוּ בַּמִּלְחָמָה (Shmuel I 29:4), he will not go up with us to the war. Radak says there is no sense in it, since going up is the opposite of going down, and that going down to war is the plain meaning, war being fought in the valley and not on the mountain. He reads Yiftach's daughter as saying: I will go down from the Mitzpeh to walk on the hills, for Yiftach's house was in the Mitzpeh and the Mitzpeh stood higher than the hills, and she said, I will go down and part from people and be alone there and weep over my maidenhood.

מַֽעֲשֵׂה מוֹרָֽד (Melachim I 7:29) he takes as beaten work, which is near to the sense of going down. Targum Yonasan renders it עוֹבַד כִּבּוּשׁ, work of pressing, as Onkelos rendered עַד רֶדֶת חֹֽמֹתֶיךָ (Devarim 28:52), until your walls come down. Radak adds that the word may instead be of the root רָדַד, and then it fits its sense well.

גדר.sense: To wall up or fence in, and the fence itself: the low wall of a garden or vineyard and the sheepfold, the whole root a sense of stopping up and closing off.

more.t: גָּדַר דְּרָכַי בְּגָזִית (Eichah 3:9), He walled my ways with hewn stone, גָּדַר בַּֽעֲדִי וְלֹא אֵצֵא (Eichah 3:7), He fenced me about and I cannot go out, and אָרְחִי גָדַר וְלֹא אֶעֱבוֹר (Iyov 19:8), He fenced my path and I cannot pass. Radak sums the root as stopping up and closing off.

The noun is גָּדֵר מִזֶּה וְגָדֵר מִזֶּֽה (Bamidbar 22:24), a fence on this side and a fence on that, and פָּרֹץ גְּדֵרוֹ (Yeshayahu 5:5), breaking down its fence. In the plural לָמָּה פָּרַצְתָּ גְדֵרֶיהָ (Tehillim 80:13), why have You broken down her fences, and יוֹם לִבְנוֹת גְּדֵרָיִךְ (Michah 7:11), a day for building your fences. Another form is וְגֶדֶר אֲבָנָיו נֶֽהֱרָֽסָה (Mishlei 24:31), its stone wall was thrown down.

Radak says that every wall made for gardens and for vineyards, and every wall that is not strong building of the kind houses and city walls are, is called a גדר, as in גֶּדֶר הֶֽחָצֵר (Yechezkel 42:10), the wall of the courtyard.

The closing in made for a sheep pen bears the word too: גִּדְרֹת צֹאן נִבְנֶה לְמִקְנֵנוּ (Bamidbar 32:16), we will build sheepfolds here for our cattle, and וּגְדֵרֹת לְצֹנַֽאֲכֶם (Bamidbar 32:24), folds for your flocks. Radak says this is what the Chachamim call a דיר, in their words about animals entering the pen to be tithed (Bava Metzia 6b).

more.h: Rashi and Yonasan on the folds
more.t: Rashi explained וְהִתְשׁוֹטַטְנָה בַּגְּדֵרֹות (Yirmiyahu 49:3) from this, that is, they will make sport in the dung of the sheepfolds by way of contempt. Targum Yonasan renders it וְאִתְהַמְמוּן בְּסִיָען, and they shall be struck dumb in their hedges.

קוה.sense: To hope and wait; a second sense of gathering, as waters gather to one place; and a third, the measuring line and the cord.

more.t: אֲשֶׁר לֹֽא־יֵבֹשׁוּ קוָֹֽי (Yeshayahu 49:23), those who hope in Me shall not be ashamed. In the strengthened form קִוְּתָה נַפְשִׁי (Tehillim 130:5), my soul hoped, וַיְקַו לַֽעֲשׂוֹת עֲנָבִים (Yeshayahu 5:2), he hoped it would make grapes, and יְקַו־לְאוֹר וָאַיִן (Iyov 3:9), let it hope for light and there be none. Radak gives all of them as expectation and waiting.

The noun is מִקְוֵה יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yirmiyahu 14:8), the hope of Yisrael, and in another form וַיִּכְלוּ בְּאֶפֶס תִּקְוָֽה (Iyov 7:6), they came to an end without hope, and וְתִקְוָתִי מִי יְשׁוּרֶֽנָּה (Iyov 17:15), and my hope, who shall see it.

וְנִקְוּוּ אֵלֶיהָ כָל־הַגּוֹיִם (Yirmiyahu 3:17), all the nations shall be gathered to her, and יִקָּווּ הַמַּיִם (Bereishis 1:9), let the waters be gathered. The noun is מִקְוֵה־מַיִם (Vayikra 11:36), a gathering of water, and in the feminine וּמִקְוָה עֲשִׂיתֶם בֵּין הַחֹמֹתַיִם (Yeshayahu 22:11), you made a reservoir between the two walls. Radak gives their sense as gathering.

more.h: The third sense, the measuring line
more.t: קַו־קָו וּמְבוּסָה (Yeshayahu 18:2) he explains as: little by little they will trample him down, the way a builder stretches out the line a little at a time. So too קַו לָקָו (Yeshayahu 28:10) is building after building, the prophets charging them command after command and they building themselves building after building, since a command and a statute are like a building. And בְּכָל־הָאָרֶץ יָצָא קַוָּם (Tehillim 19:5) he glosses as their building.

אֶת־תִּקְוַת חוּט הַשָּׁנִי (Yehoshua 2:18), the line of scarlet thread, is another form, joined to the word for thread as אַדְמַת־עָפָר (Daniel 12:2) is joined. Targum Yonasan renders it תּוֹרָא דְחוּט זְהוֹרִיתָא, the border of the scarlet thread, and the Targum on the hem at the opening of the garment (Shemos 28:32) gives תּוֹרָא יְהֵא מַקַּף לְפוּמֵהּ, a border shall go round its mouth. Radak draws from this that the Targum takes תקות חוט השני as the hem of a red garment.

וּמִקְוֵה סֹֽחֲרֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ יִקְחוּ מִקְוֵה בִּמְחִֽיר (Melachim I 10:28), and the king's traders took the מקוה at a price. Radak explains that Shlomo's traders brought horses out of Mitzrayim, and that the מקוה is the linen work of Mitzrayim, brought out at a price. Pharaoh had granted Shlomo the export of the horses, so that the horses went out without payment while the linen went out for money. In Divrei HaYamim II 1:16 the word is written מִקְוֵא with an alef.

זנח.sense: To cast off and reject; and in the form that acts on a thing, to put a vessel out of use.

more.t: זָנַח (Eichah 2:7) is Hashem casting off His mizbeach, and כִּי לֹא יִזְנַח לְעוֹלָם (Eichah 3:31), for He will not cast off for ever. The form that takes no object is וַתִּזְנַח מִשָּׁלוֹם נַפְשִׁי (Eichah 3:17), my soul is put far from peace.

more.h: Putting a thing out of use
more.t: The form that acts on a thing gives וְאֵת כָּל־הַכֵּלִים אֲשֶׁר הִזְנִיחַ הַמֶּלֶךְ אָחָז (Divrei HaYamim II 29:19), all the vessels that King Achaz cast aside, and וְהֶֽאֶזְנִיחוּ נְהָרוֹת (Yeshayahu 19:6), the rivers shall be cast off.

more.h: Rabbi Yonah on the added alef
more.t: Rabbi Yonah wrote that in this word the Hebrews followed the way of Aramaic, which adds an alef, as in אִשְׁתִּיו חַמְרָא (Daniel 5:4), they drank wine, and אֶתְכְּרִיַּת רוּחִי (Daniel 7:15), my spirit was grieved; and that they wrote in it the hei of the form as well. Radak says he has already set out its grammar in the grammar part of his work.

נבט.sense: To look and gaze at; the noun is the thing one looks to, and he gives the whole root the sense of watchful attention.

more.t: וְנִבַּט לָאָרֶץ (Yeshayahu 5:30), one looks to the earth, he takes as a past form of the strengthened kind, though some say it is the form in which a thing happens of itself. The commoner form is לֹא־הִבִּיט אָוֶן בְּיַֽעֲקֹב (Bamidbar 23:21), He has not looked on iniquity in Yaakov, וְהִבִּיטוּ אַֽחֲרֵי מֹשֶׁה (Shemos 33:8), they looked after Moshe, and הַבֶּט־נָא הַשָּׁמַיְמָה (Bereishis 15:5), look now toward the heavens.

וְהַבִּיט אֶל־עָמָל לֹא תוּכָל (Chavakuk 1:13), You cannot look upon wrong, מֵֽהַבִּיט אֶל־הָֽאֱלֹהִֽים (Shemos 3:6), from looking toward Hashem, and אַל־תַּבִּיט אַֽחֲרֶיךָ (Bereishis 19:17), do not look behind you.

more.h: The noun, and the sense of the root
more.t: The noun is הִנֵּה־כֹה מַבָּטֵנוּ (Yeshayahu 20:6), see, such is what we looked to, and מִכּוּשׁ מַבָּטָם (Yeshayahu 20:5), Kush was what they looked to, with a patach under the mem; and וְעֶקְרוֹן כִּֽי־הוֹבִישׁ מֶבָּטָהּ (Zechariah 9:5), Ekron, for what she looked to has withered, with a segol under the mem. Radak gives their sense as watchful attention.

שׁקף.sense: To look out from above, and so to watch over; from it the lintel, and windows framed in a wall.

more.t: וְצֶדֶק מִשָּׁמַיִם נִשְׁקָֽף (Tehillim 85:12), righteousness looks down from heaven, בְּעַד אֶשְׁנַבִּי נִשְׁקָֽפְתִּי (Mishlei 7:6), I looked out through my lattice, and כִּי רָעָה נִשְׁקְפָה מִצָּפוֹן (Yirmiyahu 6:1), for evil looks out from the north. Radak gives their sense as watching and gazing.

more.h: Why the word is used passively
more.t: Radak says the word is used in the form of being acted upon because a man who stands in a high place and looks out is himself looked at by those who look toward him. That is why it says הַשְׁקִיפָה מִמְּעוֹן קָדְשְׁךָ מִן־הַשָּׁמַיִם (Devarim 26:15), look down from Your holy dwelling from the heavens, in the active form, since the Holy One looks out and is not looked at.

וַיַּשְׁקֵף אֲבִימֶלֶךְ (Bereishis 26:8) is so put because he was in a place where he saw them and they did not see him; and וַתַּשְׁקֵף בְּעַד הַחַלּֽוֹן (Melachim II 9:30) likewise, for she saw them and they did not see her until Yehu drew near the gate.

On חַלּוֹנֵי שְׁקֻפִים אֲטֻמִֽים (Melachim I 6:4), windows broad and narrow, the Targum says פְּתִיחָן מִלְגָיו וּסְתִימָן מִלְבָרָא, open within and closed without. Radak notes that in the words of the Chachamim the reverse is found (Menachos 86b): open outside and closed inside, unlike other windows, to show that He has no need of light.

אֶל־הַמַּשְׁקוֹף וְאֶל־שְׁתֵּי הַמְּזוּזֹת (Shemos 12:22) is the upper threshold above the doorpost of the gate, so called, Radak says, because it is always looked out from, or because the door strikes against it continually. Ibn Ezra wrote that the משקוף is a window made above the doorway, from which they look out when a man calls at the gate to see who is calling, a thing known in the land of Yishmael, where windows are made above the doorways to look out from.

וּשְׁקֻפִים שְׁלֹשָׁה טוּרִים (Melachim I 7:4), three rows of beams set one facing the other, Targum Yonasan renders וּכְלֵנְסָא תְּלַת סִדְרִין, three rows of poles; and וְכָל־הַפְּתָחִים וְהַמְּזוּזוֹת רְבֻעִים שָׁקֶף (Melachim I 7:5), all the doorways and doorposts squared with a beam, is rendered מְרַבְּעִין וַחֲפָן כְּלֵנְסָא, squared and covered with poles. Radak points to the poles of cedar the Chachamim speak of bringing (Rosh Hashanah 22b).

צפה.sense: To look out and keep watch, and so to wait for; and a second sense, overlaying a thing with metal.

more.t: צֹפֶה נְתַתִּיךָ (Yechezkel 3:17), I have set you as a watchman, עֵינָיו בַּגּוֹיִם תִּצְפֶּינָה (Tehillim 66:7), His eyes keep watch on the nations, and צָפֹה הַצָּפִית (Yeshayahu 21:5), set the watch. Radak says הַצָּפִית may be a description of the watchman, the tav standing for the hei of the third root letter, or else the tav is added to the word.

וְהִשְׁקֵיתִי אֶרֶץ צָפָֽתְךָ מִדָּמְךָ (Yechezkel 32:6) he glosses as the land of your looking out and your gazing, meaning that even the high places will be watered from your blood. Radak notes that he gave another explanation of the word under the root צוּף.

In the strengthened form בְּצִפִּיָּתֵנוּ צִפִּינוּ (Eichah 4:17), in our watching we watched, בֹּקֶר אֶֽעֱרָךְ־לְךָ וַֽאֲצַפֶּֽה (Tehillim 5:4), in the morning I set it before You and wait, and צַפֵּה־דֶרֶךְ (Nachum 2:2), watch the road. Radak says that in this form it comes near the sense of hoping, since one who waits on another looks out for him.

more.h: Why a high place is a מצפה
more.t: The noun is וַיִּקְרָא אַרְיֵה עַל־מִצְפֶּה (Yeshayahu 21:8), a lion called out upon the watchtower. Radak says a high place is called a מצפה because a man looks out from it far off, and he sums this whole sense as looking.

וְצִפָּה רָֽאשֵׁיהֶם (Shemos 36:38), he overlaid their tops, וְצִפִּיתָ אֹתָם (Shemos 27:6), and you shall overlay them, and מְצֻפֶּה עַל־חָרֶשׂ (Mishlei 26:23), laid over earthenware. The noun is צִפּוּי לַמִּזְבֵּֽחַ (Bamidbar 17:4), an overlay for the mizbeach.

Radak allows that וְהַצֶּפֶת אֲשֶׁר־עַל־רֹאשׁוֹ אַמּוֹת חָמֵֽשׁ (Divrei HaYamim II 3:15), and the capital that was on its top was five cubits, is of this root and this sense, the capital being so called because it was an overlay for the pillar. He adds that he will write צֶפֶת as a root of its own, as Rabbi Yonah did, who said in the name of Rav Saadiah Gaon that the word means a צנצנת, a jar.

שׁגח.sense: To gaze with close attention: three places only, looking out from a dwelling, in through windows, and at a fallen king.

more.t: מִֽמְּכֽוֹן־שִׁבְתּוֹ הִשְׁגִּיחַ (Tehillim 33:14), from His dwelling place He gazed out, רֹאֶיךָ אֵלֶיךָ יַשְׁגִּיחוּ (Yeshayahu 14:16), those who see you gaze at you, and מַשְׁגִּיחַ מִן־הַֽחֲלֹּנוֹת (Shir HaShirim 2:9), gazing in through the windows. Radak gives their sense as looking with close attention.

אסף.sense: To gather in: the harvest, a man gathered to his people at death, the metzora taken back; and a second sense of removal and making an end.

more.t: וְאָסַף אִישׁ טָהוֹר (Bamidbar 19:9), a clean man shall gather up, וַיַּֽאַסְפוּ אֶת־הַשְּׂלָו (Bamidbar 11:32), they gathered the quail, and אָסֹף אֶאֱסֹף יַֽעֲקֹב כֻּלָּךְ (Michah 2:12), I will surely gather all of you, Yaakov. Radak gives their sense as gathering, but says there is a difference between this word and קבץ, which he will set out under that root.

more.h: Why the festival is חַג הָאָסִיף
more.t: וְחַג הָֽאָסִיף (Shemos 34:22), the festival of ingathering, is so called, he says, because then they gather the grain harvest and the vintage and all the fruit into the houses on account of the rains.

בַּֽעֲלֵי אֲסֻפּוֹת (Koheles 12:11), masters of collections, means the words of the masters of collections. Radak says the wise are called masters of compilations because they gather the words of the wisdoms into their books.

more.h: The crowd that gathered to them
more.t: וְהָֽאסַפְסֻף אֲשֶׁר בְּקִרְבּוֹ (Bamidbar 11:4) doubles the second and third root letters, the alef resting, and the doubling strengthens the sense. Radak takes it as the great crowd that had gathered to them, and points to וְגַם־עֵרֶב רַב עָלָה אִתָּם (Shemos 12:38), and a great mixed multitude went up with them.

כַּֽאֲשֶׁר נֶֽאֱסַף אַֽהֲרֹן אָחִֽיךָ (Bamidbar 27:13), as Aharon your brother was gathered in, and אֲנִי נֶֽאֱסָף אֶל־עַמִּי (Bereishis 49:29), I am being gathered to my people. Radak says the word is used of dying because the dead man has gone the way his fathers went, as though he were gathered to them.

וְאָסַף הַמְּצֹרָֽע (Melachim II 5:11), and he will gather the metzora in, and עַד־הֵֽאָסֵף מִרְיָֽם (Bamidbar 12:15), until Miriam was taken back. Radak explains that the metzora's way is to sit outside the camp or the city, parted from people, and when he is healed he is gathered back to them and comes in among them.

Radak explains עָשִׁיר יִשְׁכַּב וְלֹא יֵאָסֵף (Iyov 27:19) so: if a rich man lies down in sickness he will not die rich, for before he dies they plunder all that he has, since once he has fallen to his bed they no longer fear him. That is why the pasuk says עֵינָיו פָּקַח וְאֵינֶֽנּוּ, he opened his eyes and he is not, meaning that he is no longer in his wealth.

more.h: The other sense, making an end
more.t: אָסֹף אָסֵף כֹּל מֵעַל פְּנֵי הָֽאֲדָמָה (Tzefaniah 1:2), I will utterly make an end of everything from off the face of the earth, and אָסֹף אֲסִיפֵם (Yirmiyahu 8:13), I will make a full end of them, whose root Radak gives as סוף. So too פֶּן־אֹסִֽפְךָ עִמּוֹ (Shmuel I 15:6), lest I sweep you away with him. All of these he gives as removal and destruction.

קבץ.sense: To gather together. His father's rule is that this word is said only of what is scattered, while the word for taking in is said even of what is not.

more.t: וַיִּקְבֹּץ אֶת־כָּל־אֹכֶל (Bereishis 41:48), he gathered all the food, וְקֹבֵץ עַל־יָד יַרְבֶּֽה (Mishlei 13:11), one who gathers little by little increases it, and שְׁלַח קְבֹץ אֵלַי אֶת־כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל (Melachim I 18:19), send and gather all Yisrael to me. The noun is קְבֻצַת כֶּסֶף וּנְחשֶׁת (Yechezkel 22:20), a gathering of silver and copper.

In the strengthened form וְקִבַּצְתִּים מִיַּרְכְּתֵי־אָרֶץ (Yirmiyahu 31:7), I will gather them from the ends of the earth, and כָּל־צֹאן קֵדָר יִקָּבְצוּ לָךְ (Yeshayahu 60:7), all the flocks of Kedar shall be gathered to you. The noun is בְּזַֽעֲקֵךְ יַצִּילֻךְ קִבּוּצַיִךְ (Yeshayahu 57:13), when you cry out let your gatherings save you, which Radak glosses as your assemblies.

more.h: Rabbi Yonah on קִבָּצָה, and Radak
more.t: On כִּי מֵֽאֶתְנַן זוֹנָה קִבָּצָה (Michah 1:7), for she gathered it from a harlot's hire, Rabbi Yonah wrote that the chirik stands in place of a shuruk, as in וּפִתְּחוּ שְׁעָרַיִךְ תָּמִיד (Yeshayahu 60:11), and your gates shall be open continually. Radak holds it right that קבצה is of the strengthened form, and reads the pasuk as: what Shomron had, she gathered from a harlot's hire, וְעַד־אֶתְנַן זוֹנָה יָשֽׁוּבוּ, and to a harlot's hire they shall return.

more.h: His father on the two words
more.t: His father writes in the Chibbur HaLeket that gathering is said only of what is scattered, while taking in is said even of what is not scattered. One says אסוף ידיך, draw in your hand, and does not say קבוץ ידיך; one says ויאסוף רגליו, he drew in his feet, and ואין איש מאסף אותי, and no man takes me into his house, but one does not say מקבץ אותי.

זלזל.sense: The shoots of a vine: וְכָרַת הַזַּלְזַלִּים (Yeshayahu 18:5) is the cutting away of the young branches, a word he glosses in Old French.

רמח.sense: A spear: וַיִּקַּח רֹמַח בְּיָדֽוֹ (Bamidbar 25:7), he took a spear in his hand. He says the meaning of the word is known.

more.t: מִרְקוּ הָֽרְמָחִים (Yirmiyahu 46:4), polish the spears, is the plural built as בֹּקֶר, morning, gives בקרים, mornings. עִם־חַרְבֹֽתֵיהֶם רָמְחֵיהֶם וְקַשְּׁתֹֽתֵיהֶֽם (Nechemiah 4:7), with their swords, their spears and their bows, may stand on a pattern of its own.

more.h: A kamatz in the careful sefarim
more.t: In some exact sefarim רָמְחֵיהֶם is pointed with a kamatz under the resh, holding to the base form, the way חָדְשֵׁיכֶם וּמֽוֹעֲדֵיכֶם (Yeshayahu 1:14), your new moons and your appointed times, is pointed. Rabbi Yonah wrote the same.

כיד.sense: A kidon, the spear that carries the banner, and perhaps the spear alone; but a kidon of bronze between the shoulders is armour and not a weapon.

more.h: The spear that carries the banner
more.t: נְטֵה בַּכִּידוֹן אֲשֶֽׁר־בְּיָֽדְךָ (Yehoshua 8:18), stretch out the kidon that is in your hand, is the spear on which the banner is set. So too וְיִשְׂחַק לְרַעַשׁ כִּידֽוֹן (Iyov 41:21), it laughs at the rattling of a kidon, though this one may be the spear by itself without the banner, and the rattling is the noise the spear makes as it is carried along.
לַהַב חֲנִית וְכִידֽוֹן (Iyov 39:23), the flash of spear and kidon, he reads as the blade of a spear and the blade of a kidon.

more.h: Where it is not a spear
more.t: וְכִידוֹן נְחשֶׁת בֵּין כְּתֵפָֽיו (Shmuel I 17:6), a bronze kidon between his shoulders, is no spear but a guard for the shoulders, and the Targum renders it וּמְסַחֲפָא דִנְחָשָׁא, a covering of bronze. At קֶשֶׁת וְכִידוֹן יַֽחֲזִיקוּ (Yirmiyahu 6:23), they take hold of bow and kidon, the Targum has קַשְׁתָּן וּתְרֵיסִין, bows and shields.
כִּידוֹ (Iyov 21:20), what his own eyes are to see, he reads as though it were אידו, his ruin.

שׁפט.sense: To judge and to pass sentence; the noun is both the judgment given and the settled rule, the law and the proper order of a thing.

more.h: Judging a man and his cause
more.t: אֲשֶׁר שָׁפַט הַמֶּלֶךְ (Melachim I 3:28), the judgment the king gave; וּשְׁפָטָנוּ מַלְכֵּנוּ (Shmuel I 8:20), our king shall judge us; וְשָֽׁפְטוּ אֶת־הָעָם (Shemos 18:22), they shall judge the people; וּשְׁפַטְתֶּם צֶדֶק (Devarim 1:16), judge righteously. and כִּי שְׁפָטוֹ (Shmuel II 18:19), that Hashem judged him, the pasuk going on מִיַּד אֹיְבָיו, from the hand of his enemies.

כַּֽאֲשֶׁר נִשְׁפַּטְתִּי אֶת־אֲבוֹתֵיכֶם (Yechezkel 20:36), as I came to judgment with your fathers; הִנְנִי נִשְׁפָּט אוֹתָךְ (Yirmiyahu 2:35), I am bringing you to judgment; נִשָּֽׁפְטָה יָחַד (Yeshayahu 43:26), let us be judged together; בְּהִשָּׁפְטוֹ יֵצֵא רָשָׁע (Tehillim 109:7), when he is judged let him come out guilty. הִיא שֹֽׁפְטָה אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל (Shoftim 4:4), she was judging Israel, and לִמְשֹֽׁפְטִי אֶתְחַנָּֽן (Iyov 9:15), I would plead with the one who judges me, are the heavier form of the same word.

The noun also stands for the punishment done: חֶרֶב שְׁפוֹט וְדֶבֶר (Divrei HaYamim II 20:9), sword, judgment and plague; וּשְׁפוּטִים עָשׂוּ בָֽהּ (Yechezkel 23:10), they carried out judgments upon her; שְׁפָטִֽים (Bamidbar 33:4), the judgments Hashem executed.

more.h: The rule, the law, the manner
more.t: A second sense is what is fixed and proper: וְזֶה יִהְיֶה מִשְׁפַּט הַכֹּֽהֲנִים (Devarim 18:3), this shall be the kohanim's due; כַּמִּשְׁפָּט הָֽרִאשׁוֹן (Bereishis 40:13), after the former manner; מִשְׁפַּט הַמֶּלֶךְ אֲשֶׁר יִמְלֹךְ עֲלֵיכֶם (Shmuel I 8:11), the way of the king who will reign over you; וַיָּסֹבּוּ אֶת־הָעִיר כַּמִּשְׁפָּט הַזֶּה (Yehoshua 6:15), they went round the city in this same manner; וְאַרְמוֹן עַל־ מִשְׁפָּטוֹ יֵשֵֽׁב (Yirmiyahu 30:18), the palace shall sit in its own proper place; יְכַלְכֵּל דְּבָרָיו בְּמִשְׁפָּֽט (Tehillim 112:5), he orders his affairs by rule. All of these are the fixed rule, the law and the right order.

At יַסְּרֵנִי (Yirmiyahu 10:24), chasten me, he takes בְּמִשְׁפָּט to mean by a measure I can bear, which is why the pasuk goes on אַל־בְּאַפְּךָ פֶּן־תַּמְעִטֵֽנִי, not in your anger, lest you make me few.

חקק.sense: To cut in and engrave, and so to set a thing down in writing; a man's written due is his חֹק, his portion, and from there a fixed law or custom.

more.h: Cut into rock, book and wall
more.t: הוֹי הַחֹֽקְקִים חִקְקֵי־אָוֶן (Yeshayahu 10:1), woe to those who inscribe decrees of wrong; חֹֽקְקִי בַסֶּלַע מִשְׁכָּן לֽוֹ (Yeshayahu 22:16), carving himself a dwelling in the rock, where the yud is an addition, as it is in חֹֽצְבִי, hewing, in that same pasuk; חֲקֻקִים בַּשָּׁשַֽׁר (Yechezkel 23:14), cut in and coloured with vermilion; וְחַקּוֹתָ עָלֶיהָ עִיר (Yechezkel 4:1), engrave a city upon it; בְּחוּקוֹ חוּג עַל־פְּנֵי תְהֽוֹם (Mishlei 8:27), when he cut a circle on the face of the deep; בְּחוּקוֹ מוֹסְדֵי אָֽרֶץ (Mishlei 8:29), when he cut out the foundations of the earth.

עַל־לוּחַ אִתָּם וְעַל־סֵפֶר חֻקָּהּ (Yeshayahu 30:8), on a tablet with them and in a book, has the heh with a mappik and means engrave it; בַּסֵּפֶר וְיֻחָֽקוּ (Iyov 19:23), that they were graven in a book; וְיִשְׁכַּח מְחֻקָּק (Mishlei 31:5), and he forgets what has been decreed.
חִקְקֵי ־לֵֽב (Shoftim 5:15), the engravings of the heart, are what the heart cuts into itself and turns over: why they never came out to the war.

more.h: Mechokek as the one who writes
more.t: בִּמְחֹקֵק בְּמִשְׁעֲנֹתָם (Bamidbar 21:18), with the mechokek, with their staves; וּמְחֹקֵק מִבֵּין רַגְלָיו (Bereishis 49:10), and a mechokek from between his feet; חֶלְקַת מְחֹקֵק (Devarim 33:21), the portion of a mechokek; יָֽרְדוּ מְחֹקְקִים (Shoftim 5:14), mechokekim came down. All of these he takes as writing, and the ruler's way is that his scribe sits at his feet. חֶלְקַת מְחֹקֵק he takes as the Targum does.

It can also be read that the mechokek is the ruler himself, so called because he sets the laws of his land. Then וּמְחֹקֵק מִבֵּין רַגְלָיו is that a ruler shall not depart from his seed, מִבֵּין רַגְלָיו as in הַיּוֹצֵת מִבֵּין רַגְלֶיהָ (Devarim 28:57), what comes out from between her feet; and חֶלְקַת מְחֹקֵק goes with the opening of the pasuk, וירא ראשית לו, he saw a first portion for himself, that he looked and chose first to take his share across the Yarden, seeing that the portion of kings and rulers was there, בתים ספונים וטובים, houses panelled and good. So too מְחֹֽקְקֵנוּ (Yeshayahu 33:22), the one who gave us our laws.

כִּֽי־ חָקְךָ וְחָק־בָּנֶיךָ נִתְּנוּ (Vayikra 10:13), your due and your sons' due are given; כִּי חֹק לַכֹּֽהֲנִים מֵאֵת פַּרְעֹה (Bereishis 47:22), the kohanim had an allowance from Pharaoh; הַטְרִיפֵנִי לֶחֶם חֻקִּֽי (Mishlei 30:8), feed me my allotted bread. At כִּי יַשְׁלִים חֻקִּי (Iyov 23:4) he takes the blows and sores that pain him day after day as though they were the portion set for him, and מֵחֻקִּי צָפַנְתִּי אִמְרֵי־פִֽיו (Iyov 23:12) as: it was my practice to store his words in my heart. לִבְלִי־ חֹק (Yeshayahu 5:14) is the opposite of rule and of custom.

חֻקָּה אַחַת לָכֶם (Bamidbar 15:15), one statute for you; זֹאת חֻקַּת הַתּוֹרָה (Bamidbar 19:2), this is the statute of the Torah; חֻקּוֹת עוֹלָם תָּמִֽיד (Yechezkel 46:14), lasting statutes always; וְאֶת־ חֻקֹּתַי תִּשְׁמְרוּ (Vayikra 18:4), and you shall keep my statutes.

פלל.sense: To judge, to give a ruling and to carry one out; prayer is called תְּפִלָּה because the one who prays asks to be judged in mercy.

more.t: רְאֹה פָנֶיךָ לֹא פִלָּלְתִּי (Bereishis 48:11), I did not reckon on seeing your face, he reads as: I did not make the judgment in myself that I could ever see your face again.
וַיַּֽעֲמֹד פִּֽינְחָס וַיְפַלֵּל (Tehillim 106:30), Pinchas stood up and did judgment, is the judgment he carried out when he ran Zimri and Kozbi bas Tzur through.

more.h: The judge, and the man judged
more.t: On וּפִֽלְלוֹ (Shmuel I 2:25) he says: if a man sins against a man, the judge judges him and brings him out clear of his fellow's hand, ordering what is fitting or making a settlement between the two; but if a man sins against Hashem, who is there to enter into judgment with him. The judge is spoken of in the form that turns the act back on the doer though the act is his own, as at וְנִשְׁפַּטְתִּי אִתּוֹ בְּדֶבֶר וּבְדָם (Yechezkel 38:22), I will come to judgment with him with plague and with blood, since a judge goes back over the pleadings and sets each man's claim before the other, as though he himself were the one being judged.

אֲשֶׁר פִּלַּלְתְּ לַֽאֲחוֹתֵךְ (Yechezkel 16:52), that you gave judgment on your sister: the pasuk says גַּם־אַתְּ שְׂאִי כְלִמָּתֵךְ, you too bear your shame, for you sat in judgment on her when she first began to do wrong, and now you have done worse than she did, so that by your own sins you have made her out the righteous one.

עָוֹן פְּלִילִי (Iyov 31:28), a wrong for the judges; עָוֹן פְּלִילִֽים (Iyov 31:11), a wrong the judges must deal with; וְנָתַן בִּפְלִלִֽים (Shemos 21:22), he shall pay as the judges assess; פְלִילָה (Yeshayahu 16:3), give a ruling; פָּקוּ פְּלִֽילִיָּֽה (Yeshayahu 28:7), they stumbled in giving judgment. All of them are judgment and law. Rabbi Yehudah holds that וְנִפְֽלַל חָלָל (Yechezkel 28:23), and the slain shall fall, is the passive of this root.

וַיִּתְפַּלֵּל אַבְרָהָם (Bereishis 20:17), Avraham prayed; וְהִתְפַּלֵּל אֶל־הַבַּיִת (Melachim I 8:42), and he prays toward this house; וְיִתְפַּלֵּל בַּֽעַדְךָ וֶֽחְיֵה (Bereishis 20:7), he will pray for you and you will live; and the noun תְּפִלָּה לְמֹשֶׁה (Tehillim 90:1), a prayer of Moshe, and שָׁמַעְתִּי אֶת־ תְּפִלָּֽתְךָ (Melachim I 9:3), I have heard your prayer. Prayer is a request, and it belongs to this root because the one who prays asks that he be judged in mercy and that the many wrongs he has done not be looked at, the judgment he wants being that they be left him and not called to mind against him, as the navi said יַסְּרֵנִי (Yirmiyahu 10:24), chasten me, but by measure.

בקשׁ.sense: To look for something, and to require it of a man; the noun is a request. He says their meaning is known.

more.t: בִּקַּשְׁתִּיהוּ וְלֹא מְצָאתִיהוּ (Shir HaShirim 5:6), I sought him and did not find him; יְבַקֵּשׁ אֶת־נַפְשִׁי (Shmuel I 22:23), he seeks my life; מִיָּדִי תְּבַקְשֶׁנָּה (Bereishis 31:39), you would require it at my hand; and at Shmuel I 20:16 the demand is made מִיַּד אֹֽיְבֵי דָוִֽד, at the hand of David's enemies.

וַיְבֻקַּשׁ הַדָּבָר וַיִּמָּצֵא (Esther 2:23), the matter was looked into and found out; וּֽתְבֻקְשִׁי וְלֹֽא־תִמָּצְאִי עוֹד (Yechezkel 26:21), you will be sought and never found again; and the noun, וְלַֽעֲשׂוֹת אֶת־ בַּקָּשָׁתִי (Esther 5:8), and to grant my request.
The kuf of בִּקֵּשׁ carries no strengthening point, and through most of this pattern it takes a sheva and stays light.

מאן.sense: To refuse: מֵאֵן בִּלְעָם הֲלֹךְ עִמָּֽנוּ (Bamidbar 22:14), Bilam refused to go with them.

more.t: מֵֽאֲנוּ קַחַת מוּסָר (Yirmiyahu 5:13), they refused to take correction; אִם־ מָאֵן יְמָאֵן אָבִיהָ (Shemos 22:16), if her father altogether refuses.

וְאִם־ מָאֵן אַתָּה לְשַׁלֵּחַ (Shemos 7:27), if you are one who refuses to let them go, is the form that describes rather than tells, on the pattern of וְשַׁבֵּחַ אֲנִי אֶת־הַמֵּתִים (Koheles 4:2), and I praise the dead. A second pattern gives הַמֵּֽאֲנִים לִשְׁמוֹעַ אֶת־דְּבָרַי (Yirmiyahu 13:10), those who refuse to hear my words.

סרב.sense: To refuse and to be obstinate; he reads סָֽרָבִים as men who refuse and rebel, and says the word is common in the language of Chazal.

more.h: What the Targum does with it
more.t: כִּי סָֽרָבִים וְסַלּוֹנִים (Yechezkel 2:6), for they are sarabim and thorns, he glosses ממאנים וממרים, men who refuse and rebel. The Targum of וַיְמָאֵן (Bereishis 37:35), and he refused, is וְסָרֵיב, and the Targum of עַם מְרִי (Yeshayahu 30:9), a rebellious people, is סַרְבָן, a refuser.
Chazal use the word, as in ולא יהיה סרבן באותה שעה (Berachos 34a), that he should not be one who refuses at that hour, and Radak says there is a great deal more of it.

חסל.sense: To make an end of a thing and eat it away; the locust that consumes most is called חָסִיל, and from here the word for finishing a seder.

more.t: כִּי יַחְסְלֶנּוּ הָֽאַרְבֶּֽה (Devarim 28:38), the locust will consume it, he glosses יכרתנו ויכלנו, it cuts it off and finishes it. That is why the kind of locust that destroys most is called חָסִיל, as in וְהֶֽחָסִיל וְהַגָּזָם (Yoel 2:25), the chasil and the gazam.

Chazal asked why it is called חָסִיל and answered שהוא חוסל הכל, that it makes an end of everything; and of another of its names, גובי דהוא גבי דינא דמריה, that it collects its Master's due. From this comes the way of saying that a thing is done and complete, חסלת סדר פלוני או מסכת פלונית, such a seder is finished, or such a masechta.

חגב.sense: A chagav, one of the kinds of locust: וַנְּהִי בְעֵינֵינוּ כַּֽחֲגָבִים (Bamidbar 13:33), we were like chagavim in our own eyes.

more.t: וְאֶת־ הֶֽחָגָב לְמִינֵֽהוּ (Vayikra 11:22), and the chagav after its kind, is one of the kinds of locust.

וְיִסְתַּבֵּל הֶֽחָגָב (Koheles 12:5), the chagav shall be a burden, has been read (Shabbos 152a) as though the word were עגב, as in וַתַּעְגְּבָה (Yechezkel 23:16), she lusted, so that it hints at the organ of relations. Radak holds the plain meaning is the right one, and says he will explain the word at the root סבל.

צלל.sense: Shade, and the shadow that passes; and in other senses a ringing in the ears, cymbals and bells, and sinking down like lead.

more.t: יָמָיו כְּצֵל עוֹבֵֽר (Tehillim 144:4), his days are like a passing shadow, is the shadow that goes by quickly as the sun moves on, or else the shadow of a bird passing overhead in flight, which is how the Midrash read it: כהדין עופא דעבר בטוליה וטוליה עבר עמיה, like that bird which passes by with its shadow, and its shadow passes along with it. So כִּי יִנָּטוּ צִלְלֵי ־עָֽרֶב (Yirmiyahu 6:4), for the shadows of evening stretch out; יְסֻכֻּהוּ צֶאֱלִים צִלְלוֹ (Iyov 40:22), the shade trees cover him with their shadow; וְלֹֽא־יַֽאֲרִיךְ יָמִים כַּצֵּל (Koheles 8:13), he will not lengthen his days like a shadow; בְּצֵל קֹֽרָתִֽי, in the shade of my roof; סָר צִלָּם מֵֽעֲלֵיהֶם (Bamidbar 14:9), their shadow has turned away from them; וְנָסוּ הַצְּלָלִים (Shir HaShirim 2:17), and the shadows flee.

more.h: In the shade of wisdom and of money
more.t: בְּצֵל הַֽחָכְמָה בְּצֵל הַכָּסֶף (Koheles 7:12), in the shade of wisdom, in the shade of money, he reads as: a man rests in the shade of wisdom when he is also in the shade of money and has enough for his needs, since he is better received by others when he has no need of them, and can hold to his learning when he has what to live on. So the other pasuk, טוֹבָה חָכְמָה עִם־נַֽחֲלָה (Koheles 7:11), wisdom is good with an inheritance; and even so the advantage is knowledge, for wisdom by itself keeps its owner alive.

הוֹי אֶרֶץ צִלְצַל כְּנָפָיִם (Yeshayahu 18:1), a land shadowing with wings, he takes of a land that casts shade over the world with the great number of its wings, a figure for the quantity of goods and wares that go out from it to other lands. Targum Yonasan rendered it דְאָתָן לָהּ בִּסְפִינָן מֵאַרְעָא רְחִיקָא וְקִלְעֵיהוֹן פְּרִיסָן כְּנִשְׁרָא דְטָאִיס בְּכַנְפוֹהִי, that they come to it in ships from a far land, their sails spread like an eagle flying with its wings.

כַּֽאֲשֶׁר צָֽלְלוּ שַֽׁעֲרֵי יְרֽוּשָׁלַם (Nechemiah 13:19), when the gates of Yerushalayim grew shadowed, is that the sun had gone down; and וְחֹרֶשׁ מֵצַל (Yechezkel 31:3), a thicket casting shade, is the form that makes another do the thing, or else a word of description.

more.h: A sound that shakes the ear
more.t: A second sense is noise: לְקוֹל צָֽלְלוּ שְׂפָתַי (Chavakuk 3:16), at the sound my lips quivered; תִּצַּלְנָה שְׁתֵּי אָזְנָֽיו (Melachim II 21:12), both his ears will ring; תִּצַּלְנָה אָזְנָֽיו (Yirmiyahu 19:3), his ears will ring; תְּצִלֶּינָה שְׁתֵּי אָזְנָֽיו (Shmuel I 3:11), both his ears will ring. The sense is the movement of a shaking noise, which he names in Old French. So צְלִיל (Shoftim 7:13) is the noise of a לֶחֶם שְׂעֹרִים, a barley loaf, which he heard and then saw turning over in the camp of Midian.

מְצִלּוֹת הַסּוּס (Zechariah 14:20), the bells of the horse, are the jingles hung on a horse that knock against each other. וּבִמְנַֽעַנְעִים וּבְצֶלְצֶלִֽים (Shmuel II 6:5), with rattles and with cymbals, and בְצִֽלְצְלֵי ־שָׁמַע (Tehillim 150:5), sounding cymbals, are two bronze vessels struck one against the other to make a noise, as the Mishnah has it, הקיש בן ארזא בצלצל, ben Arza struck the cymbal; but בְּֽצִלְצְלֵי תְרוּעָֽה (Tehillim 150:5), cymbals of blasting, he takes of the trumpets. בַּֽמְצִלְתַּיִם (Ezra 3:10), with cymbals, and בִּמְצִלְתַּיִם נְחֹשֶׁת לְהַשְׁמִֽיעַ (Divrei HaYamim I 15:19), with bronze cymbals to sound out, drop the doubled letter, and the word stands in the form of two because they are a pair struck together.

A further sense is going down: צָֽלֲלוּ כַּֽעוֹפֶרֶת (Shemos 15:10), they sank like lead. Rabbi Yehudah brought כַּֽאֲשֶׁר צָֽלְלוּ שַֽׁעֲרֵי יְרֽוּשָׁלַם (Nechemiah 13:19) along with it, reading that the gates of Yerushalayim were sunk away from being entered, which is to say that evening had come. Radak holds the right reading of that one is the one he wrote above, from צֵל, shade.

וּבְצִלְצַל דָּגִים רֹאשֽׁוֹ (Iyov 40:31), and his head with a fish tziltzal, is a tool with which a fish is speared in the water and lifted out, which he names in Old French; and there are those who say it is a vessel made of rods that the fish's head goes into and is caught in.

ישׁע.sense: Rescue and deliverance; the noun is salvation, the verb is to save a man, and from it comes the word for one who saves.

more.t: יָצָאתָ לְיֵשַׁע עַמֶּךָ (Chavakuk 3:13), you went out for the deliverance of your people, has a tzere; כִּֽי־כָל־ יִשְׁעִי וְכָל־חֵפֶץ כִּי־לֹא יַצְמִֽיחַ (Shmuel II 23:5), for all my deliverance and all my desire, though he does not make it grow, has a chirik under the yud; and וְיֶשְֽׁעֲךָ תִּתֶּן־לָֽנוּ (Tehillim 85:8), and grant us your deliverance, has a segol.

וַֽיְהִי־לִי לִֽישׁוּעָה (Shemos 15:2), he became my salvation; אֱמֹר לְנַפְשִׁי יְֽשֻֽׁעָתֵךְ אָֽנִי (Tehillim 35:3), say to my soul, I am your salvation. With a tav added in front and the first letter of the root falling away: תְּשׁוּעָה גְדוֹלָה (Shmuel I 19:5), a great deliverance; הַנּוֹתֵן תְּשׁוּעָה לַמְּלָכִים (Tehillim 144:10), who gives deliverance to kings; וּתְשׁוּעָה בְּרֹב יוֹעֵֽץ (Mishlei 11:14), and deliverance in many counsellors; שֶׁקֶר הַסּוּס לִתְשׁוּעָה (Tehillim 33:17), a horse is a false thing for deliverance; and הַתְּשׁוּעָֽה (Mishlei 21:31), the deliverance, which is Hashem's.

more.h: His father on a word in Iyov
more.t: His father explains אִם־בְּפִידוֹ לָהֶן שֽׁוּעַ (Iyov 30:24) from this sense: in the פיד, which is the day of death, there is deliverance for those worn out of strength in life, as it says וְשָׁם יָנוּחוּ יְגִיעֵי כֹֽחַ (Iyov 3:17), and there the weary of strength are at rest. On that reading שֽׁוּעַ is from יָשַׁע with the first letter of the root missing, as בוּל הָרִים (Iyov 40:20), the produce of the hills, stands for יְבוּל with its first letter gone.

הוֹשִׁיעַ (Tehillim 20:7), he has saved; וַיְהִי לָהֶם לְמוֹשִֽׁיעַ (Yeshayahu 63:8), and he became a savior to them; הוֹשַׁע (Yirmiyahu 31:6), save; הֽוֹשִׁיעֵנוּ (Divrei HaYamim I 16:35), save us; and the noun מוֹשָׁעָה, deliverance, with the plural לְֽמוֹשָׁעוֹת (Tehillim 68:21), for deliverances.

יִשְׂרָאֵל נוֹשַׁע (Yeshayahu 45:17), Israel is saved, and עַם נוֹשַׁע (Devarim 33:29), a people saved, take a patach, since they tell of something done; אֵין הַמֶּלֶךְ נוֹשָׁע בְּרָב־חָיִל (Tehillim 33:9), the king is not saved by a great army, takes a kamatz, since it stands as a description. וְנֽוֹשַׁעְתֶּם מֵאֹֽיְבֵיכֶֽם (Bamidbar 10:9), and you will be saved from your enemies.

נצל.sense: To be rescued and to rescue; underneath it is taking away, since a rescue takes a man out of the hand of the one who had hold of him.

more.t: וַֽאֲמַרְתֶּם נִצַּלְנוּ (Yirmiyahu 7:10), and you say, we are saved; אֲשֶׁר־ יִנָּצֵל אֵלֶיךָ (Devarim 23:16), who escapes to you; לְהִנָּצֵל מִפְּנֵי מֶלֶךְ אַשּׁוּר (Yeshayahu 20:6), to be delivered from the king of Ashur; הֵמָּה בְצִדְקָתָם יְנַצְּלוּ נַפְשָׁם (Yechezkel 14:14), they by their righteousness will deliver their own soul.

וְהַצֵּל לֹֽא־ הִצַּלְתָּ אֶת־עַמֶּֽךָ (Shemos 5:23), and you have not delivered your people at all; וְהִצַּלְתֶּם אֶת־נַפְשֹׁתֵינוּ (Yehoshua 2:13), and you shall save our lives; לְמַעַן הַצִּיל אֹתוֹ (Bereishis 37:23), in order to save him; כְּאוּד מֻצָּל מִשְּׂרֵפָה (Amos 4:11), like a brand pulled out of the burning; הֲלוֹא זֶה אוּד מֻצָּל מֵאֵֽשׁ (Zechariah 3:2), is this not a brand pulled out of the fire; and the noun רֶוַח וְהַצָּלָה (Esther 4:14), relief and deliverance.

אֲשֶׁר הִצִּיל (Bereishis 31:16), what he took away, and אֶת־מִקְנֵה אֲבִיכֶם (Bereishis 31:9), your father's cattle, are this taking. וְהִצִּיל עֵינֵֽנוּ (Shmuel II 20:6) he reads as his taking our sight away, by getting inside one of the towns and out of view; and וְאַל־ תַּצֵּל מִפִּי דְבַר־אֱמֶת עַד־מְאֹד (Tehillim 119:43), and do not take the word of truth out of my mouth utterly.

more.h: Stripping, and the root of it all
more.t: A near sense is stripping what another has: וְנִצַּלְתֶּם אֶת־מִצְרָֽיִם (Shemos 3:22), and you will strip Egypt, and וַיְנַצְּלוּ לָהֶם לְאֵין מַשָּׂא (Divrei HaYamim II 20:25), they stripped for themselves more than they could carry. So too וַיִּתְנַצְּלוּ בְנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת־עֶדְיָם מֵהַר חוֹרֵֽב (Shemos 33:6), the children of Israel stripped themselves of their ornaments from Mount Chorev, which he reads as their taking the ornaments off and wearing them no more. The sense is removal and stripping away, and the first sense falls under it too, since a rescue is a removal from the one who had taken him.

פרק.sense: To break off and tear away: a yoke from the neck, rings from the ear; and a rescue too, which tears a man out of his enemy's hand.

more.t: וּפָֽרַקְתָּ עֻלּוֹ מֵעַל צַוָּארֶֽךָ (Bereishis 27:40), you will break his yoke off your neck; פֹּרֵק וְאֵין מַצִּֽיל (Tehillim 7:3), tearing with none to rescue; פָּֽרְקוּ נִזְמֵי הַזָּהָב (Shemos 32:2), break off the golden rings; וּפַרְסֵיהֶן יְפָרֵֽק (Zechariah 11:16), he will tear off their hooves; מְפָרֵק הָרִים (Melachim I 19:11), breaking the mountains. All of it is breaking, and the parting of one thing from another.

הִתְפָּרָקוּ וַיִּתְּנוּ־לִי (Shemos 32:24), they took them off and gave them to me, and וַיִּֽתְפָּֽרְקוּ כָּל־הָעָם (Shemos 32:3), and all the people took them off, are said of their stripping off the golden rings in their ears. The form that turns the act back on the doer is used because they did it with a will, wanting to be rid of their rings and have them no longer. So too הִתְפָּרְקוּ וְיָבֵשׁוּ (Yechezkel 19:12), they were broken off and dried up.

The noun is a breaking: כַּחַשׁ פֶּרֶק מְלֵאָה (Nachum 3:1), full of lying and of tearing. On וְאַֽל־תַּֽעֲמֹד עַל־ הַפֶּרֶק in Ovadiah, do not stand at the perek, he says you should not have stood over the breaking that came upon Israel but should have saved them if you could, in the way of לֹא תַֽעֲמֹד עַל־דַּם רֵעֶךָ (Vayikra 19:16), do not stand by your fellow's blood. Others take על הפרק as the head of the roads, the place where the roads part, and there you stood telling the Bavliim which way the fugitive had gone.

וַתִּשָּׁבֵר מַפְרַקְתּוֹ (Shmuel I 4:18), his mafreketh was broken, is the bone of the neck. Chazal speak of it, ודילמא בעצם המפרקה איפגים (Chullin 10b), perhaps it was the neck bone that was nicked; and it carries that name because it is made of joint upon joint.

Close to the first sense is rescue: וַיִּפְרְקֵנוּ מִצָּרֵינוּ (Tehillim 136:24), he tore us free from our foes; פֹּרֵק אֵין מִיָּדָֽם (Eichah 5:8), there is none to tear us out of their hand; and the Targum of וַיּוֹשַׁע (Shemos 14:30), and he saved, is וּפְרַק.

עקד.sense: To bind, to tie; and the marked sheep called עֲקֻדִּים, named from the place where foreleg is bound to hind leg.

more.t: וַיַּעֲקֹד אֶת יִצְחָק בְּנוֹ (Bereishis 22:9), and he bound Yitzchak his son, he glosses plainly as tying.

עֲקֻדִּים נְקֻדִּים (Bereishis 30:39), the ringed and the speckled, and עָקֹד (Bereishis 30:40): their markings fall at the spot where the foreleg is bent onto the hind leg and tied, and from that spot of binding they take the name.

בֵּית עֵקֶד הָרֹעִים (Melachim II 10:12): Targum Yonasan renders בֵּית כְּנִישַׁת רַעֲיָא, the shepherds' gathering place. His father takes it as the house where the shepherds sheared their flocks, since at the shearing they tie the animals by the legs, at the very place of binding.

חבשׁ.sense: To bind: a turban bound on the head, a wound bound up, a donkey saddled; and, of a ruler, holding men bound under his rule.

more.t: וְחָבַשְׁתָּ לָהֶם מִגְבָּעֹת (Shemos 29:9), you shall bind turbans on them; פְּאֵרְךָ חֲבוֹשׁ עָלֶיךָ (Yechezkel 24:17), bind your headdress upon yourself; סוּף חָבוּשׁ לְרֹאשִׁי (Yonah 2:6), weed bound about my head; פְּנֵיהֶם חֲבֹשׁ בַּטָּמוּן (Iyov 40:13), bind their faces in the hidden place. He glosses the group as tying and girding.

It is also the binding of a wound and the wrapping laid over it: וְלַנִּשְׁבֶּרֶת לֹא חֲבַשְׁתֶּם (Yechezkel 34:4), the broken you did not bind up; כִּי הוּא יַכְאִיב וְיֶחְבָּשׁ (Iyov 5:18), He wounds and He binds up; וּמְחַבֵּשׁ לְעַצְּבוֹתָם (Tehillim 147:3), binding up their sorrows; and of the wound left alone, לֹא זֹרוּ וְלֹא חֻבָּשׁוּ (Yeshayahu 1:6), not pressed out and not bound up.

Because a ruler confines and holds bound whoever breaks his commands, the word serves for rule itself: לֹא אֶהְיֶה חֹבֵשׁ (Yeshayahu 3:7), I will not be a ruler, and הַאַף שׂוֹנֵא מִשְׁפָּט יַחֲבוֹשׁ (Iyov 34:17), shall one who hates justice govern.

It is fastening the beast's girth too: וַיַּחֲבֹשׁ אֶת חֲמֹרוֹ (Bereishis 22:3), he saddled his donkey; חִבְשׁוּ לִי הַחֲמוֹר (Melachim I 13:13), saddle me the donkey; צֶמֶד חֲמוֹרִים חֲבוּשִׁים (Shoftim 19:10), a pair of saddled donkeys. He closes that all of them from this root are one sense.

חתל.sense: To swaddle or wrap about; he glosses it as binding up and enwrapping.

more.t: וַעֲרָפֶל חֲתֻלָּתוֹ (Iyov 38:9), thick cloud its swaddling band; וְהָחְתֵּל לֹא חֻתָּלְתְּ (Yechezkel 16:4), you were not swaddled at all; לָשׂוּם חִתּוּל (Yechezkel 30:21), to put on a binding.

שׁאג.sense: The lion's roar; and carried over to a man crying out and raising his voice over his troubles.

more.t: אַרְיֵה שָׁאָג (Amos 3:8), a lion has roared; שֹׁאֵג לִקְרָאתוֹ (Shoftim 14:5), roaring toward him; שֹׁאֲגִים לַטָּרֶף (Tehillim 104:21), roaring after prey; עָלָיו יִשְׁאֲגוּ כְפִרִים (Yirmiyahu 2:15), young lions roared over him; שָׁאֹג יִשְׁאַג עַל נָוֵהוּ (Yirmiyahu 25:30), he shall surely roar over his dwelling.

שָׁאַגְתִּי מִנַּהֲמַת לִבִּי (Tehillim 38:9), I have roared from the groaning of my heart, and וַיִּתְּכוּ כַמַּיִם שַׁאֲגֹתָי (Iyov 3:24), my roarings pour out like water: the lion's word set to a man moaning and giving voice to his troubles.
שְׁאָגָה לוֹ כַּלָּבִיא (Yeshayahu 5:9), he has a roar like a lioness, and in construct שַׁאֲגַת אַרְיֵה וְקוֹל שָׁחַל (Iyov 4:10), the roar of the lion and the voice of the fierce lion.

נהם.sense: To growl or groan; he makes it the same matter as שְׁאָגָה, roaring.

more.t: וְנָהַמְתָּ בְאַחֲרִיתֶךָ (Mishlei 5:11), you will groan at your end, and וּנְהַמְתֶּם אִישׁ אֶל אָחִיו (Yechezkel 24:23), you shall groan one to another; so too מִנַּהֲמַת לִבִּי (Tehillim 38:9), from the groaning of my heart.

יִשְׁאַג כַּכְּפִירִים וְיִנְהֹם (Yeshayahu 5:29), he roars like the young lions and growls; the noun נַהַם כַּכְּפִיר אֵימַת מֶלֶךְ (Mishlei 20:2), the dread of a king is a growl like a young lion's; and of water, כְּנַהֲמַת יָם (Yeshayahu 5:30), like the roaring of the sea.

הגה.sense: Sounding with the mouth: muttering, murmuring, the dove's moan and the lion's growl; and in another sense, removing a thing.

more.t: כִּי אֱמֶת יֶהְגֶּה חִכִּי (Mishlei 8:7), my palate speaks truth; וּלְשׁוֹנִי אִם יֶהְגֶּה רְמִיָּה (Iyov 27:4), nor shall my tongue utter deceit; יֶהְגּוּ רִיק (Tehillim 2:1), they mutter emptiness; לֹא יֶהְגּוּ בִּגְרוֹנָם (Tehillim 115:7), they make no sound in their throat; וְהָגִיתִי בְכָל פָּעֳלֶךָ (Tehillim 77:11), I will murmur over all Your work. He sums the whole of it as speech and the sound the mouth makes.

כַּאֲשֶׁר יֶהְגֶּה הָאַרְיֵה (Yeshayahu 31:4), as the lion growls; וְכַיּוֹנִים הָגֹה נֶהְגֶּה (Yeshayahu 59:11), we moan and moan like doves; and הַמְצַפְצְפִים וְהַמַּהְגִּים (Yeshayahu 8:19), those who chirp and mutter.

וְהֶגֶה מִפִּיו יֵצֵא (Iyov 37:2), a sound goes out from his mouth; כִּלִּינוּ שָׁנֵינוּ כְמוֹ הֶגֶה (Tehillim 90:9), we spend our years like a sigh; קִנִים וָהֶגֶה וָהִי (Yechezkel 2:10), lamentations, moaning and woe. In other forms הִגָּיוֹן (Tehillim 9:17), הֶגְיוֹן לִבִּי (Tehillim 19:15), my heart's murmuring, הֲגִיגִי (Tehillim 5:2), and וְהָגוּת לִבִּי תְבוּנוֹת (Tehillim 49:4), my heart's musing is of understanding.

more.h: A form pointed to match its neighbour
more.t: הֹרוֹ וְהֹגוֹ מִלֵּב דִּבְרֵי שָׁקֶר (Yeshayahu 59:13), putting forth and uttering words of falsehood from the heart, is an infinitive. His father writes that הֹרוֹ carries its cholam by rule, being from יָרָה, as at וּלְהוֹרֹת אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (Vayikra 10:11), to teach Bnei Yisrael, and that וְהֹגוֹ was given a cholam only so the two words should match, as a written and a read form are matched at Shmuel II 3:25.

more.h: His father on what it is not
more.t: His father holds the whole root a mumbling and a chirping, with no sense of reading or speaking in it. וּבְתוֹרָתוֹ יֶהְגֶּה (Tehillim 1:2) is therefore not the reading itself: a man reads in Torah so much that at every hour, even when he is not reading, the words come out of his mouth and rise to his lips. The proof he gives is וְכַיּוֹנִים הָגֹה נֶהְגֶּה (Yeshayahu 59:11), which is chirping and is like a sound of wailing, and so קִנִים וָהֶגֶה (Yechezkel 2:10).

הָגוֹ סִיגִים מִכָּסֶף (Mishlei 25:4), take the dross away from the silver, and הָגוֹ רָשָׁע לִפְנֵי מֶלֶךְ (Mishlei 25:5), take the wicked man away from before the king; so too הָגָה בְּרוּחוֹ הַקָּשָׁה (Yeshayahu 27:8). His father puts כַּאֲשֶׁר הֹגָּה מִן הַמְסִלָּה (Shmuel II 20:13), when he was moved off the highway, in this root and this sense.

שׁוק.sense: Several words carry these letters: longing and desire, a vat brimming over, the street, and the leg.

more.t: וְאֶל אִישֵׁךְ תְּשׁוּקָתֵךְ (Bereishis 3:16), your longing shall be toward your husband; וְאֵלֶיךָ תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ (Bereishis 4:7), its longing is toward you; וְעָלַי תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ (Shir HaShirim 7:11), his desire is upon me. He glosses them as craving and desire, and takes וְנַפְשׁוֹ שׁוֹקֵקָה (Yeshayahu 29:8), his soul is craving, as likely the same and its root.

פָּקַדְתָּ הָאָרֶץ וַתְּשֹׁקְקֶהָ (Tehillim 65:10) he reads two ways: You visited the land and longed for it, to sate it; or, as a transitive verb, You had already made it long, decreeing that it crave the rain, and only afterward did You visit it.

וְהֵשִׁיקוּ הַיְקָבִים תִּירוֹשׁ וְיִצְהָר (Yoel 2:24), the vats shall overflow with wine and oil. He sets the form beside וְהֵצִיפוּ, the making of water flood over, as at הֵצִיף אֶת מֵי יַם סוּף (Devarim 11:4), He made the waters of the Sea of Reeds flood over them.

The Chachamim use the word of water brought into contact with a mikveh (Pesachim 34b): water of the Chag that became tamei, if he dipped it and then sanctified it, it is tahor; sanctified first and dipped after, it is tamei. He explains the dipping as sinking the vessel into the mikveh water until that water floats above it.
וְסָבְבוּ בַשּׁוּק (Koheles 12:5), they go about in the street, and בַּשְּׁוָקִים וּבָרְחֹבוֹת (Shir HaShirim 3:2), in the streets and in the squares. He calls this sense known and does not gloss it.

שׁוֹק הַיָּמִין (Shemos 29:22), the right leg; עַל הַבִּרְכַּיִם וְעַל הַשֹּׁקַיִם (Devarim 28:35), on the knees and on the legs; שׁוֹקָיו עַמּוּדֵי שֵׁשׁ (Shir HaShirim 5:15), his legs are pillars of marble. At אֶת הַשּׁוֹק וְהֶעָלֶיהָ (Shmuel I 9:24) he reads what is upon it as the thigh that sits above the leg. From it he takes the reflexive form יִשְׁתַּקְשְׁקוּן בָּרְחֹבוֹת (Nachum 2:5), in the squares, which he again calls known and leaves unglossed.

וַיַּךְ אוֹתָם שׁוֹק עַל יָרֵךְ (Shoftim 15:8) he explains as felling them with the blow: a man falling before his pursuer buckles at the knees and drops on his face, so that his leg lies upon his thigh. His father reads it otherwise, שׁוֹק the foot soldier and יָרֵךְ the man riding the horse, and Targum Yonasan renders פָּרָשִׁין עִם רִגְלָאִין, horsemen with footmen.

נהק.sense: To bray, the cry of the wild donkey; he glosses it as a moaning noise.
