קְצוּצֵי פֵאָה (Yirmiyahu 9:25) he takes as those cut off and scattered to every side, and from it אָמַרְתִּי אַפְאֵיהֶם (Devarim 32:26), I said I would scatter them, which he glosses as I will scatter them into every corner.

more.h: The corner of head and beard
more.t: On לֹא תַקִּפוּ פְּאַת רֹאשְׁכֶם (Vayikra 19:27), do not round off the corner of your head, Chachamim explained (Makkos 20b) that it is the end of the head, the line that levels his temples with the back of his ears and with his forehead. פְּאַת זְקָנֶךָ in the same pasuk, the corner of your beard, he glosses as שבולת הזקן, the tip of the beard.
פָּתְהֵן יְעָרֶה (Yeshayahu 3:17) may be explained from this root, he says, giving it no rendering here, and adds that more is written under the root פות.

קצע.sense: To scrape a surface clean, as plaster off a wall; and the מִקְצוֹעַ, a corner of a building.

more.t: וְאֶת־הַבַּיִת יַקְצִעַ מִבַּיִת (Vayikra 14:41), he shall scrape the house from within. The Targum renders יְקַלְפוּן, they shall peel, and he takes it to mean that the plaster is removed.

יַעֲשֵׂהוּ בַּמַּקְצֻעוֹת (Yeshayahu 44:13), he shapes it with the מַקְצֻעוֹת, the tool with which a craftsman peels wood and smooths it. He says מקצעות in the plural because they are two tools for this work, one called simant and one plana. Targum Yonasan renders בְּאִזְמֵילַיָא, and this tool, he says, is like a blade.

בְּמִקְצֹעַ הֶחָצֵר (Yechezkel 46:21), at the corner of the court, לִשְׁנֵי הַמִּקְצֹעֹת (Shemos 26:24), for the two corners, and לִמְקֻצְעֹת הַמִּשְׁכָּן (Shemos 26:23), for the corners of the Mishkan; their sense, he says, is פנות, corners. The verb from it is מְהֻקְצָעוֹת (Yechezkel 46:22), having corners.

מֹר וַאֲהָלוֹת קְצִיעוֹת (Tehillim 45:9), myrrh and aloes and cassia. The Targum of קִדָּה (Shemos 30:24) is קְצִיעֲתָא, which he has already written is the קשט, the costus, and so Rav Saadiah Gaon explained. But in the compounding of the ketores, in the passage at Kerisos 6a, מר וקציעה, myrrh and cassia, and הקשט, the costus, are counted as two separate kinds. Mar Rav Chafetz explained that the קשט is what Arabic calls kost, and קציעה he explained as amber.

קצה.sense: The end or edge of a thing, and the far reach of it; as a verb, to cut off.

more.t: מְקַצֶּה רַגְלַיִם (Mishlei 26:6), cutting off feet, and לְקַצּוֹת בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל (Melachim II 10:32), to cut away at Yisrael. The simple form gives קְצוֹת עַמִּים רַבִּים (Chavakuk 2:10), the cutting off of many peoples; the sense is severing and cutting. Chazal use it so in לקצות עמו בתאנים (Maasros 2:6), to cut up a cake of figs.

The end of a place and its border is called קָצֶה: מִן־הַקָּצֶה אֶל־הַקָּצֶה (Shemos 36:33), from end to end, and קְצֵה גְבוּלֶךָ (Bamidbar 20:16), the edge of your border. In the feminine, עַל־שְׁנֵי קְצוֹת הַחֹשֶׁן (Shemos 28:26), on the two ends of the choshen, and עַל אַרְבַּע קְצוֹתָיו (Shemos 27:4), on its four ends. Another form is וּמִקְצָת יָמִים עֲשָׂרָה (Daniel 1:15), at the end of ten days.

more.h: One who sends by a fool
more.t: He explains מְקַצֶּה רַגְלַיִם (Mishlei 26:6) of the man who sends a message by a fool: it is as though his feet were cut off and he cannot walk, so that he must send the fool, who is of no use to him; and the pasuk adds חמס שותה, he drinks violence.

אֶת־הֶעָפָר אֲשֶׁר הִקְצוּ (Vayikra 14:41), the dust that they scraped off, he takes to mean that they moved it to the edge of the house to clear it away and carry it outside the city; so הִקְצוֹת אֶת־הַבַּיִת (Vayikra 14:43). Targum Yonasan renders it in the sense of peeling, like יַקְצִעַ.
וְאֵין קֵצֶה לְמַרְכְּבֹתָיו (Yeshayahu 2:7), there is no end to his chariots, he puts in this root and this sense, and it is like קֵץ; he allows it may instead be from קָצַץ, with an added heh.

נתק.sense: To tear a thing loose from what holds it, to pull away and uproot; and נֶתֶק, a nega in a place of hair.

more.t: וְלֹא נִתַּק שְׂרוֹךְ נְעָלָיו (Yeshayahu 5:27), the strap of his shoes is not broken, נִתְּקוּ כַּפּוֹת רַגְלֵי הַכֹּהֲנִים (Yehoshua 4:18), the soles of the kohanim's feet were drawn away, and כַּאֲשֶׁר יִנָּתֵק פְּתִיל־הַנְּעֹרֶת (Shoftim 16:9), as a thread of tow snaps. The stronger forms carry the same: נִתְּקוּ מוֹסֵרוֹת (Yirmiyahu 5:5), they have burst the bonds, and הֲלוֹא אֶת־שָׁרָשֶׁיהָ יְנַתֵּק (Yechezkel 17:9), will he not tear up its roots. So too of men drawn out of a city, עַד הַתִּיקֵנוּ אוֹתָם מִן־הָעִיר (Yehoshua 8:6) and הָנְתְּקוּ מִן־הָעִיר (Shoftim 20:31). All of them, he says, are the sense of removing and uprooting.

וְנָתוּק וְכָרוּת (Vayikra 22:24), torn and cut, he explains of one whose testicles have been torn by hand until the cords they hang by are severed, though they are still inside the sac and the sac itself is not torn away.
נֶתֶק הוּא (Vayikra 13:30), it is a nesek: the name of a nega in a place of hair, and he reports that it has been explained as a black spot.

He allows that אַתִּיק אֶל־פְּנֵי־אַתִּיק (Yechezkel 42:3), one אתיק set before another, may come from this root, the dagesh in the tav standing for the nun that has fallen away; so too כִּי־יוֹכְלוּ אַתִּיקִים (Yechezkel 42:5) and וְאַתִּיקֶיהָא מִפּוֹ וּמִפּוֹ (Yechezkel 41:15), its אתיקים on this side and on that. He gives the word no English of his own, and reports that Targum Yonasan renders it זִיוְיָתָהָא, corners.

חטב.sense: To cut wood; and of a thing shaped by cutting, hewn and dressed straight.

more.t: וְלֹא יַחְטְבוּ מִן־הַיְּעָרִים (Yechezkel 39:10), they shall not cut wood out of the forests, and מֵחֹטֵב עֵצֶיךָ (Devarim 29:10), from the hewer of your wood; the sense is cutting.

Rabbi Yonah takes חֲטֻבוֹת אֵטוּן מִצְרָיִם (Mishlei 7:16) in another sense, and reads כזויות מחטבות (Tehillim 144:12), like hewn corners, as high and lifted up. He brings the Targum of הֶאֱמִירְךָ הַיּוֹם (Devarim 26:18), which is חָטְבָךְ, using these very letters.

Radak holds the word should not be taken out of the first sense. חֲטֻבוֹת אֵטוּן מִצְרָיִם he refers to the bed: its poles are hewn and set right with the adze and the compass and the like, the tools with which beds are made. And כזויות מחטבות, because it is the way of the world to build the corners of a house of hewn ashlar stone even where the rest of it is built of rough stones; the corner stones are cut so well and so straight that they all look like one stone, and the pasuk likens daughters even and straight in their stature to those corners.

נאם.sense: An utterance, a saying pronounced: נְאֻם, a declaration, with the verb וַיִּנְאֲמוּ, to declare.

more.t: וַיִּנְאֲמוּ נְאֻם (Yirmiyahu 23:31), they declare a declaration, and נְאֻם־פֶּשַׁע לָרָשָׁע (Tehillim 36:2), the utterance of transgression to the wicked; their sense is a saying. He holds נְאֻם a noun, and allows it may be a verb in the construct, but in וַיִּנְאֲמוּ נְאֻם it is a noun, on the pattern of זְבוּל.
From this he takes מֵסִיר שָׂפָה לְנֶאֱמָנִים (Iyov 12:20), He removes the speech of the נֶאֱמָנִים, whom he explains as those clear of tongue and skilled in the art of speech.

חוה.sense: To tell, to declare what one knows.

more.t: אֲחַוֶּה דֵּעִי אַף־אָנִי (Iyov 32:10), I too will declare my opinion, and כַּתַּר־לִי זְעֵיר וַאֲחַוֶּךָּ (Iyov 36:2), wait for me a little and I will tell you; with the noun וְאַחֲוָתִי בְּאָזְנֵיכֶם (Iyov 13:17), and my telling in your ears, whose alef is added. All of it, he says, is the sense of telling.
חַוֹּת יָאִיר (Bamidbar 32:41) he does not explain here; he says it will be explained in the root חיה.

נבע.sense: To well up, as water out of its source; and of speech, to pour words out of the mouth.

more.t: נַחַל נֹבֵעַ (Mishlei 18:4), a flowing brook. The noun is מַבּוּעַ: וְצִמָּאוֹן לְמַבּוּעֵי מָיִם (Yeshayahu 35:7), the thirsty ground shall become springs of water, and וְעַל־מַבּוּעֵי מַיִם יְנַהֲלֵם (Yeshayahu 49:10), by springs of water He shall lead them. The welling of water, he says, is its coming out from its source.

וְתִשָּׁבֶר כַּד עַל־הַמַּבּוּעַ (Koheles 12:6), the pitcher is broken at the fountain, he reads of the body: the כַּד is the gall, and the מַבּוּעַ the liver on which the gall rests. The liver is called מַבּוּעַ because it is the source of the blood.

Speech is called by this word because it comes out of the mouth as water from its source: יוֹם לְיוֹם יַבִּיעַ אֹמֶר (Tehillim 19:3), day to day pours out speech, אַבִּיעָה חִידוֹת (Tehillim 78:2), I will pour out riddles, and תַּבַּעְנָה שְׂפָתַי תְּהִלָּה (Tehillim 119:171), my lips shall pour out praise.

more.h: The fly in the perfumer's oil
more.t: יַבְאִישׁ יַבִּיעַ שֶׁמֶן רוֹקֵחַ (Koheles 10:1), it makes the perfumer's oil stink and sends the stench up. Radak says the stench never stops, since the fly keeps making it well up and bringing it out. Rabbi Yonah reads יַבִּיעַ here as speech, as though from the strength of its stink the oil cried its own stench abroad, in the way of וְשֶׁמֶן יְמִינוֹ יִקְרָא (Mishlei 27:16). Rabbi Yitzchak ibn Giat takes it from אבעבועות, blisters, and its root, holding it a doubled verb in the heavy form, since oil that goes bad raises blisters.

שֹוח.sense: To speak and muse aloud; and the noun שִׂיחַ, a man's talk, and in places his business.

more.t: לָשׂוּחַ בַּשָּׂדֶה, to go out and talk in the field, he takes as the speech of prayer, and בְּפִקֻּדֶיךָ אָשִׂיחָה, I will muse on Your precepts. אָרִיד בְּשִׂיחִי (Tehillim 55:3), I am restless in my complaint, is the speech of troubles and the recounting of hardships; so אֶשְׁפֹּךְ לְפָנָיו שִׂיחִי (Tehillim 142:3), I pour out my complaint before Him, and מֵרֹב שִׂיחִי (Shmuel I 1:16), out of the abundance of my complaint.

וַהֲקִיצוֹתָ הִיא תְשִׂיחֶךָ (Mishlei 6:22), and when you awake it shall talk with you, he explains: it will be to you like a companion speaking with you. So יָשִׂיחוּ בִי יֹשְׁבֵי שָׁעַר (Tehillim 69:13), those who sit in the gate talk of me, and עַל־דֶּרֶךְ שִׂיחוּ (Shoftim 5:10), you who walk on the way, speak.

אַתֶּם יְדַעְתֶּם אֶת־הָאִישׁ וְאֶת־שִׂיחוֹ (Melachim II 9:11), you know the man and his שִׂיחַ, he explains as his doings; so וּמַגִּיד לְאָדָם מַה־שֵּׂחוֹ (Amos 4:13), which has a tzeirei. And כִּי־שִׂיחַ וְכִי־שִׂיג לוֹ (Melachim I 18:27) he takes as: he has business and an affair with another, or the overtaking of his enemies in war.

שׁוח.sense: A pit dug in the ground; and שַׁחַת, the pit a man goes down to, whose sense he says is that of a grave.

more.t: שׁוּחָה עֲמֻקָּה (Mishlei 22:14), a deep pit, and כִּי־כָרוּ שׁוּחָה לְנַפְשִׁי (Yirmiyahu 18:20), they have dug a pit for my soul. Another form takes a chirik: כָּרוּ לְפָנַי שִׁיחָה (Tehillim 57:7), they dug a pit before me, and כָּרוּ־לִי זֵדִים שִׁיחוֹת (Tehillim 119:85), the insolent have dug pits for me. He allows that these too may be from the root שָׁחַח.

more.h: שַׁחַת, the pit of the grave
more.t: לַשַּׁחַת יוֹרִדוּךָ (Yechezkel 28:8), they bring you down to the pit, וְלֹא־יָמוּת לַשַּׁחַת (Yeshayahu 51:14), he shall not die and go down to the pit, לִבְאֵר שַׁחַת (Tehillim 55:24), the well of the pit, and בְּשַׁחְתָּם נִתְפָּשׂ (Yechezkel 19:4), he was caught in their pit; their sense, he says, is that of a grave. He allows that they come from the root יָשַׁח, as דַּעַת comes from יָדַע.

כִּי שָׁחָה אֶל־מָוֶת בֵּיתָהּ (Mishlei 2:18), for her house sinks down to death, Rabbi Yonah filed in this root. Radak allows that the word is from שָׁחַח, which is why Rabbi Yehudah did not bring it here, except that most books have it with a kamatz, and a doubled verb would take a patach, as is the rule with a ches.
בְּאֶרֶץ עֲרָבָה וְשׁוּחָה (Yirmiyahu 2:6), in a land of desert and שׁוּחָה, whose sense here he gives as desolation and ruin; and so Targum Yonasan renders בַּאֲרַע מֵישַׁר וְחָרוֹב.

בגד.sense: To betray, to break faith with one who trusted you; and, in the same letters, בֶּגֶד, a garment.

more.t: כָּל־רֵעֶיהָ בָּגְדוּ בָהּ (Eichah 1:2), all her friends have betrayed her, and וּבְאֵשֶׁת נְעוּרֶיךָ אַל־יִבְגֹּד (Malachi 2:15), let none betray the wife of his youth. The nouns are בֹּגְדֵי בָגֶד (Yirmiyahu 12:1), traitors who betray, and אַנְשֵׁי בֹּגְדוֹת (Tzefaniah 3:4), men of treacheries. The sense, he says, is one who transgresses his fellow's covenant and deals falsely with him when he had trusted him.

מַדּוּעַ נִבְגַּד אִישׁ בְּאָחִיו (Malachi 2:10), why do we deal falsely each man with his brother. Rabbi Yaakov ben Elazar wrote that the form is a passive one; Radak holds that wrong, since verbs of this kind yield no passive, and points to אכן בָּגְדָה אשה מרעה (Yirmiyahu 3:20), surely a woman betrays her companion.

וּבֶגֶד לִלְבֹּשׁ (Bereishis 28:20), a garment to wear, וְלָבַשׁ בְּגָדִים אֲחֵרִים (Vayikra 6:4), he shall put on other garments, and בְּכָל־עֵת יִהְיוּ בְגָדֶיךָ לְבָנִים (Koheles 9:8), let your garments always be white. There is a feminine plural too, כָּל־בִּגְדֹתֶיךָ (Tehillim 45:9), all your garments. He gives this word no gloss, saying its sense is known.

לבשׁ.sense: To put on a garment and to be clothed in it; and, of another, to clothe him.

more.t: אֲשֶׁר לָבַשׁ־בּוֹ הַמֶּלֶךְ (Esther 6:8), which the king has worn, יִלְבַּשׁ עַל־בְּשָׂרוֹ (Vayikra 6:3), he shall put on over his flesh, and צֶדֶק לָבַשְׁתִּי וַיִּלְבָּשֵׁנִי (Iyov 29:14), I put on righteousness and it clothed me. Of a man dressed: הָיָה לָבֻשׁ בְּגָדִים צוֹאִים (Zechariah 3:3), he was clothed in filthy garments, and לָבֻשׁ שָׁנִים (Mishlei 31:21), clothed in scarlet.

more.h: Why the word works both ways
more.t: Once a man has put a garment on, he is לָבוּשׁ from the garment and the garment is לָבוּשׁ upon him, so that one form serves for both. He shows the same in חוֹגֵר and חָגוּר, one who girds and one girded, in אֲחֻזֵי חֶרֶב (Shir HaShirim 3:8), holders of the sword, and in וְאַתָּה תֶּאְזֹר מָתְנֶיךָ (Yirmiyahu 1:17), gird your loins, beside אָזוּר בְּמָתְנָיו (Melachim II 1:8), girded about his loins.

וַיַּלְבֵּשׁ אֹתָם אֶת־אֶלְעָזָר בְּנוֹ (Bamidbar 20:28), he clothed Elazar his son in them, הִלְבִּישַׁנִי בִּגְדֵי־יֶשַׁע (Yeshayahu 61:10), He has clothed me in garments of salvation, and וְהַלְבֵּשׁ אֹתְךָ מַחֲלָצוֹת (Zechariah 3:4), and I will clothe you in fine robes.

לְבוּשׁ, the clothing, as in וְנָתוֹן הַלְּבוּשׁ וְהַסּוּס (Esther 6:9), let the clothing and the horse be given; מַלְבּוּשׁ נָכְרִי (Tzefaniah 1:8), foreign dress; and תִּלְבֹּשֶׁת, as in בִּגְדֵי נָקָם תִּלְבֹּשֶׁת (Yeshayahu 59:17), garments of vengeance for clothing.

שֹמל.sense: The left hand and the left side; and from these same letters, he says without doubt, שִׂמְלָה, a garment.

more.t: שְׂמֹאול בַּעֲשֹׂתוֹ וְלֹא־אָחַז (Iyov 23:9), on the left where He works, and I do not grasp Him; the alef stands in place of a vav of lengthening. The verb: מַיְמִינִים וּמַשְׂמִאלִים (Divrei HaYamim I 12:2), using the right hand and the left, and without the alef לְהֵמִין וּלְהַשְׂמִיל (Shmuel II 14:19), to turn right or left, and הָשִׂימִי הַשְׂמִילִי (Yechezkel 21:21), set yourself right, go left. The adjective is הַשְּׂמָאלִי (Divrei HaYamim II 3:17), the left-hand one, and הַשְּׂמָאלִית (Vayikra 14:16), the left hand.

He holds, and says it is right in his eyes, that the word is of four letters, since no added letter carrying a vowel is found among the letters of a root except in לְדַרְיוֹשׁ הַדָּבָר (Ezra 10:16); and perhaps, he says, it is a compound word.

What comes from this root without doubt, he says, is שִׂמְלָה: אֶת־הַשִּׂמְלָה (Bereishis 9:23), the garment, שִׂמְלָתְךָ לֹא בָלְתָה (Devarim 8:4), your garment did not wear out, and וּכְלֵי זָהָב וּשְׂמָלֹת (Shemos 3:22), vessels of gold and garments. Their sense he leaves as known.

מדד.sense: To measure; and the noun מִדָּה, a measure, and of a man, great size.

more.t: מִי־מָדַד בְּשָׁעֳלוֹ מַיִם (Yeshayahu 40:12), who measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, וּמַדֹּתֶם מִחוּץ לָעִיר (Bamidbar 35:5), you shall measure outside the city, and וַיָּמֹדּוּ בָעֹמֶר (Shemos 16:18), they measured with the omer. Of what cannot be measured, אִם־יִמַּדּוּ שָׁמַיִם (Yirmiyahu 31:36), if the heavens can be measured; and with a cord, וַיְמַדְּדֵם בַּחֶבֶל (Shmuel II 8:2), he measured them with the line.
וַיִּתְמֹדֵד עַל־הַיֶּלֶד (Melachim I 17:21), he stretched himself over the child, which he glosses: he laid himself out flat upon him.

more.h: His father on עמד וימדד ארץ
more.t: עָמַד וַיְמֹדֶד אֶרֶץ (Chavakuk 3:6), his father explains so: the Aron stood in Gilgal and the land was divided to them by measure. וַיַּתֵּר גּוֹיִם (Chavakuk 3:6) is that He drove the nations out of their land, taking וַיַּתֵּר from לְנַתֵּר בָּהֵן עַל־הָאָרֶץ (Vayikra 11:21), to leap with them upon the ground, whose Targum is לְקַפָּצָא, from מְקַפֵּץ עַל־הַגְּבָעוֹת (Shir HaShirim 2:8), leaping over the hills; and it is a verb that takes an object.

אֲרֻכָּה מֵאֶרֶץ מִדָּהּ (Iyov 11:9), longer than the earth is its measure: the heh takes a mapik though the form should be מִדָּתָהּ, as פִּנָּהּ (Mishlei 7:8) stands for פִּנָּתָהּ. Rabbi Yaakov ben Elazar wrote that these are masculine nouns, מד and בז.

אִישׁ מִדָּה (Divrei HaYamim I 11:23) he explains as great in stature, and so אַנְשֵׁי מִדּוֹת (Bamidbar 13:32), men of great size, and אֶבְנֶה־לִּי בֵּית מִדּוֹת (Yirmiyahu 22:14), I will build myself a house of large measures. From this too וַיְהִי אִישׁ מָדֹין (Shmuel II 21:20), read מָדוֹן, since in its place in Divrei HaYamim I 20:6 he is called אִישׁ מִדָּה; and Targum Yonasan renders וַהֲוָה גְבַר דְמִשְׁחָן, he was a man of measures.

Rabbi Yonah divided the root into two senses, as the wise Rabbi Yehudah had divided them. Radak sees no need for it: though one is the measure of a surface and the other the measure of what fills a vessel, it is all one sense of measuring.

לְמִדַּת הַמֶּלֶךְ (Nechemiah 5:4) he keeps out of this root: its proper form is מִנְדַת with an added mem, and it belongs with מִנְדָּה בְלוֹ וַהֲלָךְ (Ezra 4:13). Chazal explained (Nedarim 62b) that מנדה is the king's portion, בלו head money, and הלך the arnona, the king's portion being the gift made to a king when he passes through.

עטה.sense: To wrap oneself in a covering, to put a garment about one; and in a second sense, to turn aside.

more.t: וְעָטָה אֶת־אֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם (Yirmiyahu 43:12), he shall wrap himself in the land of Mitzrayim כַּאֲשֶׁר־יַעְטֶה הָרֹעֶה אֶת־בִּגְדוֹ, as a shepherd wraps himself in his garment; עֹטֶה אוֹר כַּשַּׂלְמָה (Tehillim 104:2), wrapped in light as in a cloak; כְּבֶגֶד יַעְטֶה (Tehillim 109:19), he puts it about him as a garment; and וְעַל־שָׂפָם יַעְטֶה (Vayikra 13:45), he shall cover over his moustache. Their sense is being wrapped in a covering.

more.h: Shame put on like a cloak
more.t: הֶעֱטִיתָ עָלָיו בּוּשָׁה סֶלָה (Tehillim 89:46), You have wrapped him about with shame, with מְעֻטָּה לְטָבַח (Yechezkel 21:20), wrapped for the slaughter, and the noun מַעֲטֵה תְהִלָּה (Yeshayahu 61:3), a wrapping of praise.

In a second sense, where the root's last letter shows: שַׁלָּמָה אֶהְיֶה כְּעֹטְיָה (Shir HaShirim 1:7), why should I be as one who turns aside, which is how he explains it, turning away and straying by the flocks of your companions. So וַיַּעַט הָעָם (Shmuel I 14:32), the people turned upon the spoil, and וַתַּעַט אֶל־הַשָּׁלָל (Shmuel I 15:19), you turned upon the spoil; their yud and tav carry a patach, which puts them in this root. But וַיָּעַט בָּהֶם (Shmuel I 25:14), whose yud carries a kamatz, he keeps for the root עיט.

קשׁר.sense: To tie one thing to another, to bind and join; and of men, to bind themselves together in a conspiracy.

more.t: וּקְשַׁרְתָּם לְאוֹת, you shall bind them for a sign, and וַתִּקְשֹׁר עַל־יָדוֹ שָׁנִי, she tied a scarlet thread on his hand. Of love, וְנַפְשׁוֹ קְשׁוּרָה בְנַפְשׁוֹ (Bereishis 44:30), his soul is bound up with his soul, which he explains of the greatness of his love, as though the one soul were tied to the other and joined to it; so וְנֶפֶשׁ יְהוֹנָתָן נִקְשְׁרָה בְּנֶפֶשׁ דָּוִד (Shmuel I 18:1).

וַתִּקָּשֵׁר כָּל־הַחוֹמָה עַד־חֶצְיָהּ (Nechemiah 3:38), the whole wall was joined together to half its height, which he explains: the whole building of the wall was knit together and complete, with no breach left in it.

כַּלָּה קִשֻּׁרֶיהָ (Yirmiyahu 2:32), a bride her attire, and וְהַקִּשֻּׁרִים וּבָתֵּי הַנֶּפֶשׁ (Yeshayahu 3:20), which he explains of the ornaments and necklaces a woman ties on her head or about her throat; so וּתְקַשְּׁרִים כַּכַּלָּה (Yeshayahu 49:18), you shall bind them on as a bride does.

Where matters are joined and men gathered into one agreement: כִּי קְשַׁרְתֶּם כֻּלְּכֶם עָלַי (Shmuel I 22:8), you have all conspired against me, אֲחִיתֹפֶל בַּקֹּשְׁרִים עִם־אַבְשָׁלוֹם (Shmuel II 15:31), Achitofel is among the conspirators with Avshalom, and קָשַׁר עָלֶיךָ עָמוֹס (Amos 7:10), Amos has conspired against you. The noun is לֹא־תֹאמְרוּן קֶשֶׁר (Yeshayahu 8:12), you shall not call it a conspiracy, and וַיְהִי הַקֶּשֶׁר אַמִּץ (Shmuel II 15:12), the conspiracy was strong.

וְהַקְּשֻׁרִים לְיַעֲקֹב (Bereishis 30:42) and הַצֹּאן הַמְקֻשָּׁרוֹת (Bereishis 30:41) the Targum renders בַכִּירַיָּא, the firstlings. They are the ones born in Nisan, he says, stronger and healthier than the rest, and they are called by a word of tying because a knot is strong.

הַתְקַשֵּׁר מַעֲדַנּוֹת כִּימָה (Iyov 38:31), can you bind the chains of כִּימָה, he has already treated in the root כִּימָה. His father takes תקשור here from וְהַקְּשֻׁרִים לְיַעֲקֹב, the early-born, so that כִּימָה is what ripens the fruit early, while משכות כסיל תפתח is what ripens it last.

קטר.sense: To burn incense, and to send an offering up in smoke; and in Aramaic, in these same letters, to tie a knot.

more.t: אֲשֶׁר קִטְּרוּ־שָׁמָּה הַכֹּהֲנִים (Melachim II 23:8), where the kohanim burned offerings, וְקַטֵּר מֵחָמֵץ תּוֹדָה (Amos 4:5), burn a thanksgiving offering of what is leavened, וְהִקְטִירָם הַכֹּהֵן (Vayikra 3:16), the kohen shall turn them into smoke, and כָּלִיל תָּקְטָר (Vayikra 6:15), it shall be wholly burned. The noun is הֲלוֹא אֶת־הַקִּטֵּר אֲשֶׁר קִטַּרְתֶּם (Yirmiyahu 44:21), the burning that you burned.

מְקֻטֶּרֶת מוֹר וּלְבוֹנָה (Shir HaShirim 3:6), perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, which he explains of her garments being smoked with spices. The nouns for the incense itself are קְטוֹרָה, as in יָשִׂימוּ קְטוֹרָה בְּאַפֶּךָ (Devarim 33:10), they shall set incense before You, and with a tav וְשַׁמְנִי וּקְטָרְתִּי (Yechezkel 16:18), my oil and my incense.

וּקְטָרְתִּי (Yechezkel 16:18) carries a kamatz chatuf by the reading of Ben Asher, which is the rule, and by the reading of Ben Naftali it is וּקְטַרְתִּי with a patach; and at וּקְטָרְתִּי וְשַׁמְנִי (Yechezkel 23:41) the two are divided.

מֻקְטָר מֻגָּשׁ לִשְׁמִי (Malachi 1:11), incense offered to My name: Radak reads it that in every place incense is offered to His name, with a pure mincha, had He commanded them so. Ibn Ezra reads גָּדוֹל שְׁמִי בַּגּוֹיִם (Malachi 1:11) as: from the rising of the sun to its setting they magnify My name, and He reckons it to them as though they were bringing a pure mincha and burning incense before Him, not as you do, who offer defiled bread and profane My name. His father reads that though they serve idols there, it is in Hashem's name that they serve and their intent is to Heaven. Radak adds that מֻקְטָר may be a passive form, the burning said of the spice incense, the offering of the korbanos, and the mincha of the fine flour.

קִיטֹר הָאָרֶץ (Bereishis 19:28), the smoke of the land, כְּקִיטֹר הַכִּבְשָׁן (Bereishis 19:28), like the smoke of a furnace, and שֶׁלֶג וְקִיטוֹר (Tehillim 148:8), snow and vapour, which he explains as the vapour rising off the earth that looks like smoke. At כִּי־הָיִיתִי כְּנֹאד בְּקִיטוֹר (Tehillim 119:83), for I am become like a skin bottle in smoke, he says the skin of his flesh is likened to a bottle in smoke because it is dried out.

The pan in which the ketores is put: וּבְיָדוֹ מִקְטֶרֶת לְהַקְטִיר (Divrei HaYamim II 26:19), and in his hand a pan to burn incense, and וְאִישׁ מִקְטַרְתּוֹ בְּיָדוֹ (Yechezkel 8:11), each man his pan in his hand. And the altar they burn upon is מִקְטַר קְטֹרֶת (Shemos 30:1).

חֲצֵרוֹת קְטֻרוֹת (Yechezkel 46:22) he explains as קשורות, tied together: the Targum of וַתִּקְשֹׁר (Bereishis 38:28) is וּקְטָרַת, and in Aramaic וּמְשָׁרֵא קִטְרִין (Daniel 5:12) is one who unties knots, and וְקִטְרֵי חַרְצֵהּ מִשְׁתָּרַיִן (Daniel 5:6) the knots of his loins coming loose. So the courts are joined and tied at the corners, one to this corner and one to that, in the way of וַתִּקָּשֵׁר כָּל־הַחוֹמָה עַד־חֶצְיָהּ (Nechemiah 3:38). Targum Yonasan renders דָרָתָא מְקַטְרָן. In Maseches Middos (2:5) they said that קטורות means only that they were not roofed.

ישׁן.sense: To sleep, and the sleep itself; in another sense old, ישן being last year's produce and נושן what has stood three years.

more.t: יָשַׁנְתִּי אָז יָנוּחַ לִי (Iyov 3:13), "I would have slept, then it would be restful for me", and וְיָשְׁנוּ שְׁנַת־עוֹלָם וְלֹא יָקִיצוּ (Yirmiyahu 51:39), "and they shall sleep an everlasting sleep and not awake".

more.h: The noun, and שֵׁנָא with an alef
more.t: אַל־תֶּאֱהַב שֵׁנָה פֶּן־תִּוָּרֵשׁ (Mishlei 20:13), "do not love sleep lest you be dispossessed"; in כֵּן יִתֵּן לִידִידוֹ שֵׁנָא (Tehillim 127:2), "so He gives His beloved sleep", the alef stands in place of a heh. Without smichus it takes a tav: אִם־אֶתֵּן שְׁנָת לְעֵינָי (Tehillim 132:4), "if I give sleep to my eyes".
The adjective in וַיִּקַץ כְּיָשֵׁן (Tehillim 78:65), of one awaking as a sleeper does, and אֲנִי יְשֵׁנָה וְלִבִּי עֵר (Shir HaShirim 5:2), "I am asleep but my heart is awake".
The heavy form is transitive: וַתְּיַשְּׁנֵהוּ עַל־בִּרְכֶיהָ (Shoftim 16:19), "and she put him to sleep on her knees".

Another sense entirely: וַאֲכַלְתֶּם יָשָׁן (Vayikra 26:10), "and you shall eat what is old", and חֲדָשִׁים גַּם־יְשָׁנִים (Shir HaShirim 7:14), "new ones and also old". יָשָׁן נוֹשָׁן (Vayikra 26:10) means very old: ישן is of last year, נושן of three years.

עתק.sense: Thick and strong, so also much and great; in another sense to move off and be uprooted from a place, which is how a copyist copies.

more.t: עָתְקוּ גַּם־גָּבְרוּ חָיִל (Iyov 21:7), "they have grown thick and strong in wealth"; and the word is said of thick, strong speech, so וְהַדְּבָרִים עַתִּיקִים (Divrei HaYamim I 4:22), words that are weighty.
Another form of the word: יֵצֵא עָתָק מִפִּיכֶם (Shmuel I 2:3), "let hard speech go out of your mouth", and הַדֹּבְרוֹת עַל־צַדִּיק עָתָק (Tehillim 31:19), "that speak hard words against a tzaddik".

הוֹן עָתֵק וּצְדָקָה (Mishlei 8:18), "lasting wealth and righteousness", which he glosses much and great; and וְלִמְכַסֶּה עָתִיק (Yeshayahu 23:18), "and for costly covering", a covering thick and of worth.

וְצוּר יֶעְתַּק מִמְּקֹמֽוֹ (Iyov 14:18), "and a rock moves from its place", meaning it turns aside and is torn out; הַמַּעְתִּיק הָרִים וְלֹא יָדָעוּ (Iyov 9:5), "who removes mountains and they know not", uprooting them from their place; וַיַּעְתֵּק מִשָּׁם הָהָרָה (Bereishis 12:8) means he moved his tent from there; הֶעְתִּיקוּ מֵהֶם מִלִּים (Iyov 32:16), "words were taken from them", they had nothing left to answer.

אֲשֶׁר הֶעְתִּיקוּ אַנְשֵׁי חִזְקִיָּה (Mishlei 25:1), "which the men of Chizkiyahu copied": one who writes from book to book is called מעתיק because he uproots the words from one book into another, and though the first book is not stripped of them, the scribe is as though he uprooted them.

עַתִּיקֵי מִשָּׁדָיִם (Yeshayahu 28:9), which he takes as those torn away from the breasts to suckle no more, like גְּמוּלֵי מֵחָלָב, "weaned from milk", in that same pasuk. His father held it is from the first sense: thick and fat from the milk they drank, and without understanding.

עָתְקָה בְּכָל־צוֹרְרָי (Tehillim 6:8): it has grown old because of all my adversaries who anger me, and from much weeping over that anger it has aged. In Aramaic likewise וְעַתִּיק יוֹמִין יְתִב (Daniel 7:9), and the Targum for ישן is עתיק, so וְהַדְּבָרִים עַתִּיקִים may be explained from this.

דגה.sense: To teem as fish do; and the fish itself, דג and דגה, which he ties to this root, noting the word is used in two roots at once.

more.t: וְיִדְגּוּ לָרֹב בְּקֶרֶב הָאָרֶץ (Bereishis 48:16), "and let them teem greatly in the midst of the land": its sense is let them increase, as the fish do.

The plural in smichus proves it, since it has a sheva: דְּגֵי הַיָּם (Bamidbar 11:22), "the fish of the sea", as בְּנֵי comes from בָּנִים and שְׁנֵי from שְׁנַיִם; and so דְגַת־יְאֹרֶיךָ (Yechezkel 29:4), "the fish of your rivers", and תִּבְאַשׁ דְּגָתָם (Yeshayahu 50:2), "their fish shall stink". Had דגה been from the roots whose middle letter is a heh it would not change in smichus, as קָמָה does not in בְּקָמַת רֵעֶךָ (Devarim 23:26).

מְבִיאִים דָּאג (Nechemiah 13:16), "bringing fish", is written with an alef as the middle root letter, and so דִיגוּם (Yirmiyahu 16:16) and the fishermen דַּוָּגִים (Yechezkel 47:10) and דַיָּגִים (Yirmiyahu 16:16). Radak says he will write them again under דוג, and that the truth is the word was used in both roots, as many are.

כור.sense: The smith's crucible for melting silver and gold; a kor, which is the chomer, thirty se'ah; and the land a man comes from.

more.t: מִכּוּר הַבַּרְזֶל (Devarim 4:20), "from the iron crucible", and מַצְרֵף לַכֶּסֶף וְכוּר לַזָּהָב (Mishlei 17:3), "a refining pot for silver and a crucible for gold": the vessel in which the smith melts the silver and the gold.
כֹּרִים עֶשְׂרִים אֶלֶף (Divrei HaYamim II 2:9), "twenty thousand kor": the kor is the chomer, and it is thirty se'ah.

מְכֹרֹתַיִךְ וּמֹלְדֹתַיִךְ (Yechezkel 16:3), "your origin and your birth", with a cholam; with a shuruk under the kaf, בְּאֶרֶץ מְכֻרוֹתַיִךְ (Yechezkel 21:35), which is like מגורותיך, the land where you dwelt, and so עַל־אֶרֶץ מְכוּרָתָם (Yechezkel 29:14), "to the land of their origin".

תנן.sense: The tannin: on dry land a kind of snake, in the water a kind of great fish shaped like a snake; תנים is the same word with a mem.

more.h: On land and in the water
more.t: וַיְהִי לְתַנִּין (Shemos 7:10), "and it became a tannin", and the plural אֶת־הַתַּנִּינִם הַגְּדֹלִים (Bereishis 1:21), "the great tanninim". Those spoken of on dry land are one of the kinds of snake, and those spoken of in the water one of the kinds of great fish shaped like snakes.

more.h: A mem in place of the nun
more.t: הַתַּנִּים הַגָּדוֹל הָרֹבֵץ בְּתוֹךְ יְאֹרָיו (Yechezkel 29:3), "the great tannim crouching in the midst of his rivers", and כַּתַּנִּים בַּיַּמִּים (Yechezkel 32:2), "like a tannim in the seas": it is the way of the language for mem and nun to come one for the other, as מוֹף and נוֹף, כְּמֹהֶם and כְּמֹהֶן.

In Eichah 4:3 the tannim חָלְצוּ שַׁד, "have drawn out the breast", and so מְעוֹן תַּנִּים (Yirmiyahu 9:10), "a lair of tannim". The feminine plural is לְתַנּוֹת מִדְבָּר (Malachi 1:3), "to the tannos of the wilderness", and the Targum renders תנים as ירודין.

more.h: Why it draws out the breast
more.t: On חָלְצוּ שַׁד, "they have drawn out the breast", he brings the Targum in Eichah, that these creatures have breasts up to their faces, and when they suckle their young, so that the young should not see them, they choke them and eat them. From Midrash Tanchuma he brings that when the tannin comes to suckle, its mother sees it from afar and draws out her breasts, so that it should suckle and not see them covered and refuse.

נין.sense: נין is a descendant: he glosses the word as בן, a son, and pairs it with נכד as the line that comes after a man.

more.t: וְנִין וָנֶכֶד (Yeshayahu 14:22), "offspring and posterity", וּלְנִינִי וּלְנֶכְדִּי (Bereishis 21:23), "to my son and to my grandson", נִינָם יָחַד (Tehillim 74:8): their sense is like בן.
Another form of the word is וְאַחֲרִיתוֹ יִהְיֶה מָנוֹן (Mishlei 29:21), and the passive from it stands in Tehillim 72:17, where לִפְנֵי שֶׁמֶשׁ, "before the sun", his name is carried on.
Radak notes that he has already written נִינָם יָחַד (Tehillim 74:8) under the root ינה.

תישׁ.sense: The he-goat, which he calls a known thing; his one point of grammar is whether או in Mishlei means "and" or a plain "or".

more.t: זַרְזִיר מָתְנַיִם אוֹ־תָיִשׁ (Mishlei 30:31), "a girt greyhound or a he-goat": the או stands in place of a vav, "and"; or it is או in its plain sense, this one or that one, each of them stepping and walking well.
וּתְיָשִׁים עֶשְׂרִים (Bereishis 32:15), "and twenty he-goats", of which he says only that it is known.

גדה.sense: The גדי, the young of the flock, which he allows may be of sheep as well as goats; and in another sense גדות, a river's banks.

more.t: וַיִּשְׁלַח יְהוּדָה אֶת־גְּדִי הָעִזִּים (Bereishis 38:20), "and Yehudah sent the kid of the goats": the young is called גדי whether of goats or of sheep, since the pasuk attaches גדי to עזים, so it seems there is a גדי that is not of goats.

He explained that nothing is called גדי except from the goats, and that גדי עזים means a little one that still needs the goats, as שְׂעִיר־עִזִּים (Bamidbar 7:16); and he said that in Arabic it is likewise called גדי.

אֶחָד נֹשֵׂא שְׁלֹשָׁה גְדָיִים (Shmuel I 10:3), "one carrying three kids", and שְׁנֵי גְּדָיֵי עִזִּים (Bereishis 27:9), "two kids of the goats"; in the feminine, וּרְעִי אֶת־גְּדִיֹּתַיִךְ (Shir HaShirim 1:8), "and pasture your kids".

more.h: Why the pasuk names a kid
more.t: לֹא־תְבַשֵּׁל גְּדִי בַּחֲלֵב אִמּוֹ (Shemos 34:26), "do not cook a kid in its mother's milk": the same law holds for the flesh of any animal, and the pasuk spoke of what is usual, since people ate kids more than lambs. It named the smallest of the animals because large flesh is not cooked in milk, milk cooking quickly and flesh not, unless it is the flesh of the young, which is near to being cooked.

Goats' milk is the most plentiful, and the pasuk spoke of what is common, as וְדֵי חֲלֵב עִזִּים (Mishlei 27:26), "and enough goats' milk". So too our Rabbis spoke of what is found most, saying a goat is for its milk (Shabbos 19b), and what my goats give in milk I sell you (Bava Metzia 64a).

So too וְאֵת בַּת הַיַּעֲנָה (Vayikra 11:16), "and the daughter of the ostrich": the same law holds for the ostrich itself, and the pasuk speaks as the world does, since it is eaten only while small and tender, its flesh being very hard when grown and unfit to eat. The young female's flesh is softer than the male's, so the pasuk says בת.

more.h: One that has a mother's milk
more.t: Our Rabbis expounded (Chullin 113a) that בחלב אמו was said of one that has a mother's milk, since fowl in milk is forbidden not from the Torah but from the words of the Soferim.

Another sense: מָלֵא עַל־כָּל־גְּדוֹתָיו (Yehoshua 3:15), "full over all its banks", and וְהָלַךְ עַל־כָּל־גְּדוֹתָיו (Yeshayahu 8:7), "and it shall go over all its banks", meaning over all its edges on this side and that. Rabbi Yaakov ben Elazar wrote that אֲשֶׁר בְּתוֹךְ־הַנַּחַל הַגָּד (Shmuel II 24:5) is one of these banks, and Yonasan rendered it as the valley of the tribe of Gad.

רחל.sense: The ewe: his whole entry is two pesukim and the gloss כבשות, female sheep.

more.t: וּכְרָחֵל לִפְנֵי גֹזְזֶיהָ נֶאֱלָמָה (Yeshayahu 53:7), "and as a ewe before her shearers is dumb", and רְחֵלִים מָאתַיִם (Bereishis 32:15), "two hundred ewes": he glosses them כבשות, female sheep, and says no more.

איל.sense: Strength is the root sense: from it the mighty and the powerful, and under the same letters the ram, the hart, the great tree and the doorpost.

more.t: כְּגֶבֶר אֵין־אֱיָל (Tehillim 88:5), "like a man without strength": אֱיָל is power, and so אֱיָלוּתִי לְעֶזְרָתִי חוּשָׁה (Tehillim 22:20), "my strength, hasten to my help", which stands in the feminine like עזרתי. Sometimes the middle root letter is quiescent: יֶשׁ־לְאֵל יָדִי (Bereishis 31:29), "it is in the power of my hand", and כִּי יֶשׁ־לְאֵל יָדָם (Michah 2:1). Another form is אוֹל, on the pattern of אוֹר: וּבָרִיא אוּלָם (Tehillim 73:4), their strength is sound.

הָאֵל (Yeshayahu 42:5) means the mighty One, and מִי־כָמֹכָה בָּאֵלִם (Shemos 15:11), "who is like You among the mighty". הָבוּ לַי"י בְּנֵי אֵלִים (Tehillim 29:1) are the kings, בְּנֵי not being in smichus, as בְּנֵי שִׁלֵּשִׁים (Bereishis 50:23); or they are the stars, with בני in smichus, the stars called בני and the angels אלים, as בְּרָן־יַחַד כּוֹכְבֵי בֹקֶר (Iyov 38:7), "when the morning stars sang together". And וּמִצְרַיִם אָדָם וְלֹא־אֵל (Yeshayahu 31:3), "and Mitzrayim are men and not אל", means not an angel.

וְאֶתְּנֵהוּ בְּיַד אֵיל גּוֹיִם (Yechezkel 31:11), "and I gave him into the hand of the mighty one of the nations", is written with a yud for the easterners, and the Mesorah notes it the only one full in a non-sacred sense; it means the mighty one of the nations, Nevuchadnetzar. So וְאֶת־אֵילֵי הָאָרֶץ לָקָח (Yechezkel 17:13), "and he took the mighty of the land", written with a yud, while יְדַבְּרוּ־לוֹ אֵלֵי גִבּוֹרִים (Yechezkel 32:21) is without a yud, and the Mesorah notes it the only one lacking.

Rabbi Yehudah wrote that the adjective is written with a yud at אֵלֵי גִבּוֹרִים. Radak holds the copyist may have erred and dropped words, and that Rabbi Yehudah wrote it of אֵיל גּוֹיִם, then listed אֵילֵי הָאָרֶץ and אֵלֵי גִבּוֹרִים without marking which is full and which lacking. Radak adds that such a man deserves to be judged favourably in every way we can, since he lit the eyes of all who came after him in grammar and the language of Mikra; and although some books have אילי גבורים with a yud, we rely on the Mesorah in the books, which we found lacking.

וְקֹרָא לָהֶם אֵילֵי הַצֶּדֶק (Yeshayahu 61:3), "and they shall be called the mighty of righteousness"; or אֵלֵי there is from אלה and אלים, trees, since the pasuk says מַטַּע י"י לְהִתְפָּאֵר, "the planting of Hashem, to be glorified".

אַיָּל וּצְבִי (Devarim 14:5), "hart and gazelle", אַיָּלָה שְׁלֻחָה (Bereishis 49:21), "a hind let loose", and גַּם־אַיֶּלֶת בַּשָּׂדֶה (Yirmiyahu 14:5), "even the hind in the field". In כְּאַיָּל תַּעֲרֹג עַל־אֲפִיקֵי־מָיִם (Tehillim 42:2), "as the hart longs for brooks of water", the verb comes in the feminine because אַיָּל is a general name covering male and female, like וַיְהִי־לִי שׁוֹר וַחֲמוֹר (Bereishis 32:6); the feminine means the herd of harts, for they go together in many droves.

אַיֶּלֶת הַשַּׁחַר (Tehillim 22:1) is the morning star. Some explain it from the first sense, the strength of the dawn's rising. Radak holds the right reading is that it is a mashal for Knesses Yisrael, as Shir HaShirim likens them to hinds, and the dawn likewise, מִי־זֹאת הַנִּשְׁקָפָה כְּמוֹ־שָׁחַר (Shir HaShirim 6:10), "who is she that looks forth like the dawn"; the whole mizmor is about Knesses Yisrael in their galus.

אַיִל תָּמִים מִן־הַצֹּאן (Vayikra 5:15), "an unblemished ram from the flock": a lamb older than a year is called איל. In וּמֵאָה אֶלֶף אֵילִים צָמֶר (Melachim II 3:4) the governed word is missing and it means אלי צמר, rams with their wool, that had not been shorn.

אֵיל פָּארָן (Bereishis 14:6), עִם־אֵלוֹן מֻצָּב אֲשֶׁר בִּשְׁכֶם (Shoftim 9:6) and בְּאֵלֹנֵי מַמְרֵא (Bereishis 18:1) he takes as the Targum has it, מֵשְׁרֵי, a plain. אֵלוֹן מֻצָּב means that in that plain stood something set up, a stone or the like, and the plain was called after it so that the place could be known.

הָאַיִל מְזוּזוֹת חֲמִשִׁית (Melachim I 6:31), וְאֶל־אַיִל תִּמֹרִים (Yechezkel 40:16), and וּמִדָּה אַחַת לָאֵילִם מִפֹּה וּמִפּוֹ (Yechezkel 40:10), "and one measure for the posts on this side and that": their sense is doorposts. וְאֵלַמָּיו (Yechezkel 40:29) means arches.

כשֹב.sense: כשב is the lamb, the same word as כבש with its letters turned: to a year old it is כשב or כבש, and older than a year it is איל.

more.h: כשב and כבש are one word
more.t: אִם־כֶּשֶׂב הוּא־מַקְרִיב (Vayikra 3:7), "if he brings a lamb", and וְהַכְּשָׂבִים הִפְרִיד יַעֲקֹב (Bereishis 30:40), "and Yaakov separated the lambs": it is known that כשב is like כבש reversed, and the two are one.
While it is a year old it is called כשב and כבש; older than a year it is called איל.

ארר.sense: To curse; and the מארה he takes as the lack of good, the opposite of a blessing, which is an addition of good.

more.t: וַיֹּאמֶר אָרוּר כְּנָעַן (Bereishis 9:25), "and he said, cursed be Canaan", אֹרוּ אָרוֹר יֹשְׁבֶיהָ (Shoftim 5:23), "curse her inhabitants bitterly", and וְאָרוֹתִי אֶת־בִּרְכוֹתֵיכֶם (Malachi 2:2), "and I will curse your blessings".
אֲשֶׁר אֵרְרָהּ י"י (Bereishis 5:29), "which Hashem cursed", and הַמַּיִם הַמְאָרְרִים (Bamidbar 5:22), "the water that brings the curse".
Rabbi Yehudah wrote that אָרָה־לִּי (Bamidbar 22:6), "curse for me", is of the heavy form; Radak holds it may well be of the light one.

אֶת־הַמְּאֵרָה (Malachi 2:2), "the curse": by rule it would carry a dagesh but for the resh, on the pattern of מְחִתָּה and מְגִנָּה. It is a curse and a lack of good, the opposite of blessing, since a blessing is an addition of good and a מארה the lack of it.

more.h: A tefillah that anger be lessened
more.t: אָרוּר אַפָּם כִּי עָז (Bereishis 49:7), "cursed be their anger for it was fierce", is a tefillah that their anger be made less.

וַאֲשֶׁר תָּאֹר יוּאָר (Bamidbar 22:6), "and whom you curse is cursed". בַּמְּאֵרָה אַתֶּם נֵאָרִים (Malachi 3:9), "you are cursed with the curse", may be from this root too, the vowel under the nun changed because the resh could not take a dagesh; Rabbi Yehudah put it with נִאֵר מִקְדָּשׁוֹ (Eichah 2:6), and Radak says it is written there.

קלל.sense: Light and swift, and from lightness both contempt and cursing; under the same letters קלל of burnished copper and קלקל of what is spoiled.

more.t: הֵן קַלֹּתִי מָה אֲשִׁיבֶךָּ (Iyov 40:4), "behold I am of small account, what shall I answer You", וּנְקַלֹּתִי עוֹד מִזֹּאת (Shmuel II 6:22), "and I shall be yet lighter than this", וּבֹזַי יֵקָלּוּ (Shmuel I 2:30), "and those who despise Me shall be despised", and וַתֵּקַל גְּבִרְתָּהּ (Bereishis 16:4), "and her mistress was light in her eyes". So too וּמַדּוּעַ הֲקִלֹּתַנִי (Shmuel II 19:44) and לְהָקֵל כָּל־נִכְבַּדֵּי־אָרֶץ (Yeshayahu 23:9), "to bring low all the honoured of the earth": all of them carry the sense of contempt. עַל־נְקַלָּה (Yirmiyahu 6:14) he explains as על אמירה נקלה, a slight saying.
קַל־הוּא עַל־פְּנֵי־מַיִם (Iyov 24:18), "he is swift upon the face of the waters", and קַלִּים הָיוּ רֹדְפֵינוּ (Eichah 4:19), "our pursuers were swift": near in sense to the first.
בַּלֶּחֶם הַקְּלֹקֵל (Bamidbar 21:5), with the first root letter doubled: our Rabbis explained (Yoma 75b; Avodah Zarah 5a) that they called the mon so because it was absorbed in the limbs.

מִקֹּל זְנוּתָהּ (Yirmiyahu 3:9), which he files under lightness, and the Mesorah notes it the only one lacking, reading it as lightness. Our Rabbis in the Yerushalmi in Challah explain it as it sounds, the voice, and said that a woman's voice is ervah, bringing this very phrase as the reason.

אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ קִלֵּל (Vayikra 20:9), "he has cursed his father and his mother", וּמְקַלֵּל אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ (Shemos 21:17), לֹא־תְקַלֵּל חֵרֵשׁ (Vayikra 19:14), "do not curse the deaf", and וְקִלֵּל בְּמַלְכּוֹ (Yeshayahu 8:21), "and he curses his king". The passive is תְּקֻלַּל חֶלְקָתָם בָּאָרֶץ (Iyov 24:18), "their portion in the land is cursed", and the noun בְּרָכָה וּקְלָלָה (Devarim 11:26), "blessing and curse". כִּי־מְקַלְלִים לָהֶם בָּנָיו (Shmuel I 3:13) he also allows to be from contempt, as וּבֹזַי יֵקָלּוּ.

כִּי־קִלְלַת אֱלֹהִים תָּלוּי (Devarim 21:23) means he hangs for having cursed Hashem. It may also be taken from the first sense: the hanged man is a disgrace to Hashem, since whoever sees him says he hangs for having blasphemed. There are two reasons in the matter, he says, and they do not reach equally far: this one is the reason for the blasphemer and the idolater, who were the men hanged, and the other, וְלֹא תְטַמֵּא אֶת־אַדְמָתְךָ (Devarim 21:23), "and you shall not defile your land", is a reason for everyone hanged in Eretz Yisrael, since a body left unburied is tumah to the land.

So Yehoshua did with the king of Ai and the five kings, commanding that they be taken down at evening and a heap of stones made over them (Yehoshua 10:27); and so Yisrael are to do with the slain of Gog and Magog, וּקְבָרוּם בֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל לְמַעַן טַהֵר אֶת־הָאָרֶץ, "and the house of Yisrael shall bury them in order to cleanse the land". As for the sons of Shaul, left from Nisan until Tishrei עַד נִתַּךְ־מַיִם עֲלֵיהֶם (Shmuel II 21:10), "until water was poured upon them", our Rabbis explained (Yevamos 79a) that though it is written לֹא־תָלִין נִבְלָתוֹ עַל־הָעֵץ (Devarim 21:23), better one letter of the Torah be uprooted and Heaven's name sanctified in public, since passers-by asked what these were and were told they were kings' sons who laid hands on converts, and said no nation is fit to cleave to like this one.

קִלְקַל בַּחִצִּים (Yechezkel 21:26) and וְכָל־הַגְּבָעוֹת הִתְקַלְקָלוּ (Yirmiyahu 4:24), "and all the hills were shaken", with the first root letter doubled as well. They are of the sense of קלקול in the words of our Rabbis, which is ruin and destruction, as they said (Shabbos 13:3; 108b) that all who spoil are exempt. Rabbi Yonah explained them as movement, in the sense of lightness, and Radak’s father wrote the same: קִלְקַל בַּחִצִּים means he commanded the arrows be shot upward, and if the arrow falls toward Bnei Ammon he will go there. So Yonasan holds, rendering it קְשַׁת בְּגִרְרַיָּא.

נְחֹשֶׁת קָלָל (Yechezkel 1:7) means copper polished and bright, and from this וְהוּא לֹא־פָנִים קִלְקַל (Koheles 10:10), that the face of the iron was not honed. Menachem joined קִלְקַל בַּחִצִּים to this sense.

אלה.sense: An oath, and so a curse, since a curse comes with an oath and Hashem's name; the same letters carry a lament, the terebinth, אולי and אל.

more.t: וְאַתְּ אָלִית וְגַם אָמַרְתְּ בְּאָזְנַי (Shoftim 17:2), "and you swore and also said in my ears", which is transitive and means you adjured; אָלֹה וְכַחֵשׁ (Hoshea 4:2), "swearing and lying", and אָלוֹת שָׁוְא (Hoshea 10:4), "false oaths", which are intransitive. The heavy form is וְנָשָׁא־בוֹ אָלָה לְהַאֲלֹתוֹ (Melachim I 8:31), "and an oath is laid upon him to make him swear".

תְּהִי נָא אָלָה בֵּינוֹתֵינוּ (Bereishis 26:28), "let there now be an oath between us", בְּשָׁמְעוֹ אֶת־דִּבְרֵי הָאָלָה (Devarim 29:19), "when he hears the words of the curse", and in another form תַּאֲלָתְךָ לָהֶם (Eichah 3:65), the tav added as in תַּאֲנָתָהּ מִי יְשִׁיבֶנָּה (Yirmiyahu 2:24). All of them are an oath, since the curse comes with an oath and with mention of Hashem's name.

Another sense: אֱלִי כִּבְתוּלָה חֲגֻרַת־שָׂק (Yoel 1:8), which he explains as קונני, lament; and so the Targum renders שָׂא קִינָה (Yechezkel 19:1) as טוּל אִלְיָא and וַיְקֹנֵן הַמֶּלֶךְ (Shmuel II 3:33) as וַאֲלָא מַלְכָּא.
הָאַלְיָה תְמִימָה (Vayikra 3:9), "the whole fat tail": the yud is the last root letter and the heh the feminine ending, and its sense is known.

תַּחַת הָאֵלָה אֲשֶׁר עִם־שְׁכֶם (Bereishis 35:4), "under the terebinth that is by Shechem", and with a dagesh תַּחַת הָאַלָּה אֲשֶׁר בְּמִקְדַּשׁ י"י (Yehoshua 24:26), the dagesh standing in place of the quiescent letter. The plural is כִּי יֵבֹשׁוּ מֵאֵילִים אֲשֶׁר חֲמַדְתֶּם (Yeshayahu 1:29), "for they shall be ashamed of the terebinths you desired", and הַנֶּחָמִים בָּאֵלִים (Yeshayahu 57:5); they say it is called in the vernacular אולמו. It may also be a general name for any tree.
Although it was in Shechem, it appears that they brought the aron of Hashem there, as it says וַיִּתְיַצְּבוּ לִפְנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים (Yehoshua 24:1), "and they stood before Hashem".

more.h: Yonasan and Rabbi Yonah on the tree
more.t: Yonasan renders אלה and אלים as בּוּטְמָא, but וַיּוֹצֵא אֵלָיו אֶל־תַּחַת הָאֵלָה (Shoftim 6:19) he rendered אִילָנָא, while the earlier וַיֵּשֶׁב תַּחַת הָאֵלָה (Shoftim 6:11) he rendered בּוּטְמָא. Rabbi Yonah wrote that in Arabic it is called בט"ם. Radak adds that they may all be from the root איל.

אוּלַי יְמֻשֵּׁנִי אָבִי (Bereishis 27:12), "perhaps my father will feel me", אוּלַי נָטְתָה מִפָּנַי (Bamidbar 22:33) and אוּלַי יַעֲשֶׂה (Hoshea 8:7): they are said of a doubtful matter, in the sense of שמא, perhaps. עַל־אוּבַל אוּלָי (Daniel 8:2) is a place name, its yud the last root letter in place of a heh.

Since the pasuk says וַתֵּט לְפָנַי, which means she turned off the road and stood before me, the sense is: had she turned away from me and gone off, גַּם־אֹתְכָה הָרַגְתִּי (Bamidbar 22:33), "you too I would have killed". Radak says he does not know why the commentators explained אולי there as לולי, and that מפני is the opposite of לפני, the mem showing what is far and the lamed what is near.

וַיֹּאמֶר י"י אֶל־אַבְרָם (Bereishis 12:1) and the like, whose sense is known. It also stands for other words: for מן in לִשְׁבֹּר אֶל־יוֹסֵף (Bereishis 41:57), from Yosef; for על in וַיַּךְ אֶת־הַפְּלִשְׁתִּי אֶל־מִצְחוֹ (Shmuel I 17:49), on his forehead; for עם in קִבְרוּ אֹתִי אֶל־אֲבֹתָי (Bereishis 49:29), with my fathers; for a beis in הִנֵּה־הוּא נֶחְבָּא אֶל־הַכֵּלִים (Shmuel I 10:22), among the baggage; for את in וַיִּרְדְּפוּ אֶל־מִדְיָן (Shoftim 7:25); and for בעבור in וַיֹּאמֶר אַבְרָהָם אֶל־שָׂרָה אִשְׁתּוֹ (Bereishis 20:2), concerning Sarah his wife.

Another word in this root marks a plural as זה marks a single one: הָאֲרָצֹת הָאֵל (Bereishis 26:3), "these lands", and לָאֲנָשִׁים הָאֵל (Bereishis 19:8), "these men". With a heh added, וְאֵלֶּה שְׁמוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (Shemos 1:1), "and these are the names of the sons of Yisrael", and אֵלֶּה הַדְּבָרִים (Devarim 1:1). It may be that this word has a quiescent middle letter, or that it is of two letters.

קבב.sense: To curse; and under the same letters הַקֻּבָּה, which is a tent or chamber, and קֳבָתָהּ, which he ties to the maw of a beast.

more.t: וְקַבֹּתוֹ לִי מִשָּׁם (Bamidbar 23:27), "and curse him for me from there", מָה אֶקֹּב לֹא קַבֹּה אֵל (Bamidbar 23:8), "how shall I curse whom Hashem has not cursed", and וְקָבְנוֹ־לִי מִשָּׁם (Bamidbar 23:13): their sense is cursing.
וַיָּבֹא אַחַר אִישׁ־יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶל־הַקֻּבָּה (Bamidbar 25:8), "and he came after the man of Yisrael into the chamber", which is like אל האהל, into the tent.

In that same pasuk וְאֶת־הָאִשָּׁה אֶל־קֳבָתָהּ comes without the dagesh. It may be of the sense of הַזְּרֹעַ וְהַלְּחָיַיִם וְהַקֵּבָה (Devarim 18:3), "the shoulder, the cheeks and the maw", which the Targum renders לִמְעָהָא: the pouch in the animal's innards where the milk it sucks is gathered, said of a person by way of borrowing; or it is so in a person's innards too. Our Rabbis explained (Sanhedrin 82b; Chullin 134b) קבתה as the place of ervah in a woman.

Radak says no root can be settled for קבה. Rabbi Yonah put it under the root קבה, on the pattern of חֵמָה, and Radak says he has already written what is good and right at חֵמָה, whose root is יחם. From the way the Mishnah reads it in smichus (Chullin 8:5), קיבת הנכרי with a tzeirei under the kuf, and with the possessive, a kosher animal that suckled from a tereifah, its maw is forbidden, it would appear the root is קוב; then ואל האשה אל קבתה is of another form, from the roots whose middle letter is weak, the separate form being קֹבָה, the cholam turning to a kamatz katan when joined. Or it is from those whose last letter is weak, the separate form being קֹבֶת, on the pattern of שֹׁקֶת.

מאר.sense: He glosses מַמְאִיר as מכאיב, causing pain: the pricking brier, and the tzaraas that is מַמְאֶרֶת.

more.t: סִלּוֹן מַמְאִיר (Yechezkel 28:24), "a pricking brier", whose sense is like מכאיב, one that causes pain; and so צָרַעַת מַמְאֶרֶת (Vayikra 13:51), a tzaraas that pains.

דחף.sense: Driving and thrusting away: the runners go out driven in haste, Haman is driven off, and the noun goes with them.

more.t: הָֽרָצִים יָצְאוּ דְחוּפִים (Esther 3:15), the runners went out driven in haste, and in the passive form וְהָמָן נִדְחַף (Esther 6:12), Haman was driven off.
יְצוּדֶנּוּ לְמַדְחֵפֹֽת (Tehillim 140:12), it shall hunt him to thrustings down. He puts all of them under the one sense of thrusting away.

הדף.sense: Shoving and thrusting: a man pushed without enmity, the weak shouldered aside, a man thrust from his post, enemies driven out.

more.h: Pushing a man, pushing with shoulder
more.t: וְאִם־בְּפֶתַע בְּלֹֽא־אֵיבָה הֲדָפוֹ (Bamidbar 35:22), if he pushed him suddenly without enmity, and יַעַן בְּצַד וּבְכָתֵף תֶּהְדֹּפוּ (Yechezkel 34:21), because you shove with side and shoulder.

more.h: Thrust from a post and from the land
more.t: וַֽהֲדַפְתִּיךָ מִמַּצָּבֶךָ (Yeshayahu 22:19), I will thrust you from your station, and לַֽהֲדֹף אֶת־כָּל־אֹֽיְבֶיךָ (Devarim 6:19), to thrust out all your enemies. All of them are the one sense of pushing.

more.h: A vowel the precise books split on
more.t: וְהַוַּת רְשָׁעִים יֶֽהְדֹּֽף (Mishlei 10:3), the craving of the wicked He thrusts away. He found the yud pointed with segol in some of the precise books and with patach in others.

דפק.sense: Driving and knocking: flocks driven too hard, men battering at a door, the beloved knocking, one sense of thrusting and striking.

more.t: וּדְפָקוּם יוֹם אֶחָד (Bereishis 33:13), if they drive them hard a single day, which he takes in the sense of thrusting.

more.h: Beating and knocking at a door
more.t: מִֽתְדַּפְּקִים עַל־הַדָּלֶת (Shoftim 19:22), battering at the door, and קוֹל דּוֹדִי דוֹפֵק (Shir HaShirim 5:2), the sound of my beloved knocking. These too are the thrusting and the striking upon the door.

כבס.sense: Laundering: washing garments, and by extension washing a heart clean of sin. The כובס is the man who launders clothes.

more.t: אֶל־מְסִלַּת שְׂדֵה כוֹבֵֽס (Yeshayahu 7:3), to the highway of the launderer's field: a noun for one who launders clothes, and Chazal use it too, אשתייר ההוא כובס (Kesubos 103b), that one launderer was left.

more.h: Why it is the launderer's field
more.t: It is the field where the launderers would spread their clothes out in the sun, and Yonasan renders it חֲקַל מַשְׁטַח קְצִירַיָא, the field where the launderers spread things out.

כִּבֵּס בַּיַּיִן לְבֻשׁוֹ (Bereishis 49:11), he washes his clothing in wine, וְכִבַּסְתֶּם בִּגְדֵיכֶם (Bamidbar 31:24), you shall wash your garments, and of a person כַּבְּסִי מֵֽרָעָה לִבֵּךְ (Yirmiyahu 4:14), wash your heart clean of evil, כַּבְּסֵנִי מֵֽעֲוֹנִי (Tehillim 51:4), wash me of my sin.

more.h: The washed garment, the washed mark
more.t: וְכֻבַּס שֵׁנִית וְטָהֵֽר (Vayikra 13:58), it shall be washed a second time and be clean, and אַֽחֲרֵי הֻכַּבֵּס אֶת־הַנֶּגַע (Vayikra 13:55), after the mark has been washed. He closes that the sense is well known.

רחץ.sense: Washing, of the body above all: Aharon and his sons wash, a daughter of Pharaoh bathes at the river, and Moav is called a washing pot.

more.t: וְרָֽחֲצוּ אַֽהֲרֹן וּבָנָיו (Shemos 30:19), Aharon and his sons shall wash, וְרָֽחַצְתָּ אֹתָם בַּמָּֽיִם (Shemos 29:4), you shall wash them in water, and לִרְחֹץ עַל־הַיְאֹר (Shemos 2:5), to bathe at the river.
וְרָחַצְתְּ וָסַכְתְּ (Rus 3:3), wash and anoint, means wash your flesh, and where the kohanim wash with water (Shemos 30:20) he supplies that they wash their hands and their feet in it.
Radak holds all of these to be verbs that take an object, someone washing something. His father explained some of them as intransitive, the washer washing himself.

וּמִצֹּֽאָתוֹ לֹא רֻחָֽץ (Mishlei 30:12), not washed of its filth, רֻחַצְתְּ לְמִשְׁעִי (Yechezkel 16:4), washed smooth, said in the negative of the newborn, and שֶׁעָלוּ מִן־הָרַחְצָה (Shir HaShirim 4:2), that came up from the washing.

מוֹאָב סִיר רַחְצִי (Tehillim 60:10), Moav is my washing basin, the noun without the heh; its singular would be רַחַץ, on the pattern of נַעַר, a lad, and נַעַל, a shoe. The sense of washing, he says, is well known.

שׁטף.sense: Rinsing with force and sweeping away: hands rinsed in water, a chariot washed down, a river that floods the land and carries it off.

more.t: וְיָדָיו לֹֽא־שָׁטַף בַּמָּיִם (Vayikra 15:11), he did not rinse his hands in water, וַיִּשְׁטֹף אֶת־הָרֶכֶב (Melachim I 22:38), they washed down the chariot, and וְכָל־כְּלִי־עֵץ יִשָּׁטֵף בַּמָּֽיִם (Vayikra 15:12), every wooden vessel shall be rinsed in water. All of them are washing with force and scouring off.

וְיִשְׁטְפוּ אֶרֶץ וּמְלוֹאָהּ (Yirmiyahu 47:2), they flood the land and its fullness, וּנְהָרוֹת לֹא יִשְׁטְפוּהָ (Shir HaShirim 8:7), rivers shall not sweep it away, שָׁטַף וְעָבַר (Yeshayahu 8:8), it sweeps through and passes on, and the noun לְשֵׁטֶף מַיִם רַבִּים (Tehillim 32:6), the flood of many waters.

He likens a horse in full run to a flooding stream, כְּסוּס שׁוֹטֵף בַּמִּלְחָמָֽה (Yirmiyahu 8:6), like a horse rushing into battle, and trouble crossing the world, שׁוֹט שׁוֹטֵף כִּי יַֽעֲבֹר (Yeshayahu 28:18), when the sweeping scourge passes through.

דוח.sense: Two things under one heading: being thrust down and unable to rise, and rinsing off, as the olah is rinsed before it is offered.

more.t: דֹּחוּ וְלֹא־יָכְלוּ קֽוּם (Tehillim 36:13), they are thrust down and cannot rise, which he reads as though נִדְחוּ. The Chacham Rabbi Yehudah holds this and its neighbour to be two roots of one sense, and files them with the roots weak in the middle letter.
יָדִיחַ מִקִּרְבָּהּ (Yeshayahu 4:4), He will rinse away from within her, and שָׁם יָדִיחוּ אֶת־הָֽעֹלָֽה (Yechezkel 40:38), there they rinse the olah.

מִלָּא כְרֵשֹׂו מֵֽעֲדָנָי (Yirmiyahu 51:34), he filled his belly with my delights, and the verb that follows is this rinsing out. Chazal use the word often, מדיח ומולח ומדיח (Chullin 113a), he rinses and salts and rinses again.

מרק.sense: Scouring clean and polishing: spears burnished, a vessel scoured and rinsed, the women's ointments, and the broth that scours the meat.

more.t: מִרְקוּ הָֽרְמָחִים (Yirmiyahu 46:4), polish the spears, נְחֹשֶׁת מָרֽוּק (Divrei HaYamim II 4:16), burnished copper, and וּמֹרַק וְשֻׁטַּף בַּמָּֽיִם (Vayikra 6:21), which he explains as scouring it and rinsing it thoroughly.

more.h: Hot water and cold in Chazal
more.t: Chazal (Zevachim 96a) put the scouring in hot water and the rinsing in cold, and some of them hold the scouring and the rinsing are in cold water and the purging in hot.

וְנָתוֹן תַּמְרוּקֵיהֶֽן (Esther 2:3), their ointments given them, and וּבְתַמְרוּקֵי הַנָּשִֽׁים (Esther 2:12), with the ointments of the women: what women adorn themselves with is called תמרוק because it scours the grease off the flesh and cleans it.
וְאֶת־הַמָּרַק שְׁפוֹךְ (Shoftim 6:20), pour out the broth: the water meat is cooked in is called מרק because the scouring of the meat is in it.

בטח.sense: Trusting and resting secure, whether in Hashem or in wealth, a mountain or a brother; and the confidence itself, in several nouns.

more.t: שֹׁקֵט וּבֹטֵחַ (Shoftim 18:7), quiet and secure, אֶבְטַח וְלֹא אֶפְחָד (Yeshayahu 12:2), I will trust and not be afraid, and the adjective כִּי בְךָ בָּטֽוּחַ (Yeshayahu 26:3), because he trusts in You.

more.h: What Yirmiyahu was told to trust
more.t: וּבְאֶרֶץ שָׁלוֹם אַתָּה בוֹטֵחַ (Yirmiyahu 12:5), in a land of peace you are secure: the men of Anasos, whom he ought to have been able to trust, are themselves the danger, and they seek his life. וְאֵיךְ תַּֽעֲשֶׂה בִּגְאוֹן הַיַּרְדֵּֽן (Yirmiyahu 12:5), how then will you do in the swelling of the Yarden, is the sending to Yerushalayim. So too כִּי גַם־אַחֶיךָ וּבֵית־אָבִיךָ גַּם־הֵמָּה בָּגְדוּ בָךְ, even your brothers and your father's house have betrayed you.

וְהַבֹּֽטְחִים בְּהַר שֹֽׁמְרוֹן (Amos 6:1), those secure in the mountain of Shomron, הַבֹּטְחִים עַל־חֵילָם (Tehillim 49:7), those who trust in their wealth, אַל־תִּבְטְחוּ לָכֶם אֶל־דִּבְרֵי הַשֶּׁקֶר (Yirmiyahu 7:4), do not trust in words of falsehood, and וְעַל־כָּל־אָח אַל־תִּבְטָחוּ (Yirmiyahu 9:3), put no trust in any brother.

וַיָּבֹאוּ עַל־הָעִיר בֶּטַח (Bereishis 34:25), they came upon the city while it sat secure, מָה הַבִּטָּחוֹן הַזֶּה (Yeshayahu 36:4), what is this confidence, מִבְטָח בּוֹגֵד (Mishlei 25:19), a traitor relied upon, מִבֵּית אֵל מִבְטֶחָֽם (Yirmiyahu 48:13), Beis El their reliance, and בְּהַשְׁקֵט וּבְבִטְחָה (Yeshayahu 30:15), in quiet and in confidence.

וְאַתָּה הִבְטַחְתָּ אֶת־הָעָם הַזֶּה (Yirmiyahu 28:15), you made this people rely, וְאַל־יַבְטַח אֶתְכֶם חִזְקִיָּהוּ (Yeshayahu 36:15), let Chizkiyahu not make you rely, and מַבְטִיחִי עַל־שְׁדֵי אִמִּֽי (Tehillim 22:10), who set me secure at my mother's breasts.
וְאֵת הָֽאֲבַטִּחִים (Bamidbar 11:5), and the melons: he says the alef may be an addition here, or the word may be one of four letters, and he gives its name in the vernacular.

חסה.sense: Taking refuge and sheltering under something: in the shadow of wings, in the shade of a tree, in the crags, and the shelter itself.

more.h: Sheltering in the shadow of wings
more.t: אֶֽחֱסֶה בְסֵתֶר כְּנָפֶיךָ (Tehillim 61:5), I will shelter in the covert of Your wings, and בְּצֵל כְּנָפֶיךָ יֶחֱסָיֽוּן (Tehillim 36:8), in the shadow of Your wings they take shelter.

בֹּאוּ חֲסוּ בְצִלִּי (Shoftim 9:15), come and shelter in my shade, וּבָהּ יֶחֱסוּ עֲנִיֵּי עַמּֽוֹ (Yeshayahu 14:32), in her the poor of His people shelter, בְךָ חָסָיָה נַפְשִׁי (Tehillim 57:2), in You my soul shelters, and מוֹשִׁיעַ חוֹסִים (Tehillim 17:7), who saves those who shelter in Him.

מַחְסֶה מִזֶּרֶם צֵל מֵחֹרֶב (Yeshayahu 25:4), a shelter from the downpour and a shade from the heat, סְלָעִים מַחְסֶה לַֽשְׁפַנִּֽים (Tehillim 104:18), the crags are a shelter for the hyraxes, and וְהֶֽחָסוּת בְּצֵל־מִצְרַיִם לִכְלִמָּֽה (Yeshayahu 30:3), sheltering in Mitzrayim's shade turns to disgrace. He puts the whole of it as taking shelter, and gives the word for it in the vernacular.

more.h: A masorah against his own pointing
more.t: He sets אֶֽחֱסֶה בְסֵתֶר כְּנָפֶיךָ, pointed with shva alone, against וּבְצֵֽל־כְּנָפֶיךָ אֶחְסֶה (Tehillim 57:2), with shva and segol, and then reports another masorah he found, by which every מַֽחֲסֶה, מַֽחֲסִי and לַֽחֲסוֹת is soft, and every אֶחֱסֶה soft but one, that same וּבְצֵֽל־כְּנָפֶיךָ אֶחְסֶה. Radak says that if so, it is the reverse of what he had written.

יחל.sense: Waiting in hope: waiting as for rain, hope given to another, hope drawn out long, and Noach waiting out the seven days.

more.t: וְיִֽחֲלוּ כַמָּטָר לִי (Iyov 29:23), they waited for me as for rain, כַּֽאֲשֶׁר יִחַלְנוּ לָֽךְ (Tehillim 33:22), as we have waited for You, and וְלֹא יְיַחֵל לִבְנֵי אָדָֽם (Micha 5:6), he does not wait upon men.

עַל אֲשֶׁר יִֽחַלְתָּֽנִי (Tehillim 119:49), because You gave me hope: the verb carries over to a third party, You put hope in me by telling me to hope in You. So too וְיִֽחֲלוּ לְקַיֵּם דָּבָֽר (Yechezkel 13:6), they give the people hope that their prophecy will stand, and it is empty and false.

וַיָּחֶל עוֹד (Bereishis 8:10), he waited again, whose proper form he gives as וַיִּיָחֶל; or it may be from the root חיל, as he wrote there. וַיִּיָּחֶל עוֹד שִׁבְעַת יָמִים (Bereishis 8:12) is his standing in hope through the first seven days and seven more besides.

more.h: His father on hope that fails
more.t: וַתֵּרֶא כִּי נֽוֹחֲלָה אָֽבְדָה תִּקְוָתָהּ (Yechezkel 19:5): Radak reads it as her standing many days in hope and then her hope being lost. His father read נֽוֹחֲלָה as hope's reverse, that her hope was lost, and held that וַיִּיָּחֶל is not the passive form but the reflexive, since one binyan does not carry a thing and its opposite. Radak answers that the yud is pointed with kamatz, as the passive form requires.

more.h: Waiting for words, and not waiting
more.t: הֵן הוֹחַלְתִּי לְֽדִבְרֵיכֶם (Iyov 32:11), I waited for your words, and לֹא־כֵן אֹחִילָה לְפָנֶיךָ (Shmuel II 18:14), which he reads as: it is no good that I draw it out before you and wait for you to go and strike him, I will go myself; and he took three rods.

מֵעַי מֵעַי (Yirmiyahu 4:19): the verb may be of the sense of חִיל כַּיּֽוֹלֵדָֽה (Tehillim 48:7), writhing like a woman in labour, so that יחל and חיל are one sense, I give trembling to my innards out of my worry; or it is that I am pained; or it is from this root itself, I said I would give my innards hope that good is still to come, though they are now in evil.
תּוֹחֶלֶת מְמֻשָּׁכָה (Mishlei 13:12), hope drawn out long, and הֵן־תֹּחַלְתּוֹ נִכְזָבָה (Iyov 41:1), his hope proves a lie.

חכה.sense: Waiting and hoping: those who wait for Hashem, those who wait for a death that does not come, and the band that lies in wait.

more.h: Waiting for what has not come
more.t: אַשְׁרֵי כָּל־חוֹכֵי לֽוֹ (Yeshayahu 30:18), fortunate are all who wait for Him, אַשְׁרֵי הַֽמְחַכֶּה (Daniel 12:12), fortunate is the one who waits, and הַֽמְחַכִּים לַמָּוֶת וְאֵינֶנּוּ (Iyov 3:21), who wait for death and it does not come.

more.h: Waiting out a man, lying in wait
more.t: חִכָּה אֶת־אִיּוֹב בִּדְבָרִים (Iyov 32:4), he waited out Iyov's words, and וּכְחַכֵּי אִישׁ גְּדוּדִים (Hoshea 6:9), as bands lie in wait for a man. He puts the whole sense with hope.

Of Yeshayahu 30:18, that Hashem waits to be gracious to you, he gives two readings: that He lengthens the time of the favour, like one who waits and does not pass on; or that the verb takes an object, as at עַל אֲשֶׁר יִֽחַלְתָּֽנִי (Tehillim 119:49), so that He assures you that you may wait for Him to favour you, for so He will do. Radak holds the second correct.

סמך.sense: Leaning and holding up: hands laid on a man, a heart propped steady, a people leaning on a king's word; and a second sense of drawing near.

more.t: כִּֽי־סָמַךְ מֹשֶׁה אֶת־יָדָיו עָלָיו (Devarim 34:9), Moshe leaned his hands upon him, וְהַֽלְוִיִּם יִסְמְכוּ אֶת־יְדֵיהֶם (Bamidbar 8:12), the Leviim lean their hands, and וְסָמַךְ יָדוֹ עַל־הַקִּיר (Amos 5:19), he rests his hand on the wall.

סָמוּךְ לִבּוֹ לֹא יִירָא (Tehillim 112:8), his heart is propped and he does not fear, and יֵצֶר סָמוּךְ תִּצֹּר שָׁלוֹם שָׁלוֹם (Yeshayahu 26:3), which he reads as a mind that leans and rests on You, which You guard, and it is at peace because it trusts in You.

עָלֶיךָ נִסְמַכְתִּי מִבֶּטֶן (Tehillim 71:6), on You I have leaned from the womb, and וַיִּסָּֽמְכוּ הָעָם עַל־דִּבְרֵי יְחִזְקִיָּהוּ (Divrei HaYamim II 32:8), the people leaned on Yechizkiyahu's words. The sense of all of them is support, as Chazal say (Bava Kamma 100a) חזי דעלך קא סמיכנא, see that it is on you I lean, my prop and my reliance.

סָמַךְ מֶלֶךְ־בָּבֶל אֶל־יְרוּשָׁלַם (Yechezkel 24:2), the king of Bavel closed in on Yerushalayim, עָלַי סָמְכָה חֲמָתֶךָ (Tehillim 88:8), Your wrath presses upon me, and סַמְּכוּנִי בָּֽאֲשִׁישׁוֹת (Shir HaShirim 2:5), stay me with cakes: here the sense is nearness and encircling, as Chazal say erev Shabbos סמוך לחשיכה (Shabbos 11a), close to nightfall.

more.h: Grain and wine near him always
more.t: וְדָגָן וְתִירשׁ סְמַכְתִּיו (Bereishis 27:37), with grain and wine I have sustained him, meaning they be near and at hand to him always, and so וְרוּחַ נְדִיבָה תִסְמְכֵֽנִי (Tehillim 51:14), that a willing spirit be near me always.

וַתְּכַסֵּהוּ בַּשְּׂמִיכָֽה (Shoftim 4:18), she covered him with a שמיכה, written with a sin: the thick covering with tufts of wool coming out of it, which Chazal call גלופקר (Shabbos 51a), and which the vernacular names too. Chazal call a thick thing סמיכתא, as in סמיכתא וקלישתא (Chullin 55b), thick and thin. He says he will set it out under the letter sin.

כסל.sense: The fool and his folly; in a second sense confidence and hope; also the star Kesil, and the flanks at the roots of the thighs.

more.t: הַכְּסִיל חֹבֵק אֶת־יָדָיו (Koheles 4:5), the fool folds his hands, וְהַכְּסִיל בַּחֹשֶׁךְ הוֹלֵךְ (Koheles 2:14), the fool walks in darkness, and as a verb וּבְאַחַת יִבְֽעֲרוּ וְיִכְסָלוּ (Yirmiyahu 10:8), in one thing they are brutish and foolish. The nouns go with it: זֶה דַרְכָּם כֵּסֶל לָמוֹ (Tehillim 49:14), this is their way, their folly, and אֵשֶׁת כְּסִילוּת הֹֽמִיָּה (Mishlei 9:13), the woman of folly is loud.

אִם־שַׂמְתִּי זָהָב כִּסְלִי (Iyov 31:24), if I made gold my confidence, אֲשֶׁר־יָקוֹט כִּסְלוֹ (Iyov 8:14), whose confidence is cut off, and הֲלֹא יִרְאָֽתְךָ כִּסְלָתֶךָ (Iyov 4:6), is your fear not your confidence: these he puts with trust and hope.

more.h: Rabbeinu Saadiah on the rich man
more.t: Rabbeinu Saadiah read מֵֽעִקֵּשׁ שְׂפָתָיו וְהוּא כְסִֽיל (Mishlei 19:1), crooked of lips and a כסיל, in this sense: he trusts in his wealth, set against the poor man, as the crooked lips are set against walking in integrity. When the pasuk comes again it reads וְהוּא עָשִׁיר (Mishlei 28:6), and he is rich, where here it has והוא כסיל.

more.h: Rabbi Yonah and Ibn Ezra on the star
more.t: עָשׁ כְּסִיל וְכִימָה (Iyov 9:9): Rabbi Yonah wrote that it is a great star, called in Arabic Suhail, and the stars joined to it are named after it, as at כִּֽי־כֽוֹכְבֵי הַשָּׁמַיִם וּכְסִילֵיהֶם (Yeshayahu 13:10), the stars of heaven and their Kesilim. The Chacham Rabbi Avraham Ibn Ezra explained that they are two stars, one of them called Kesil, the red one, which kills camels if they catch sight of it. Radak adds that וכסיליהם is close in derivation to the loins.

וַיַּעַשׂ פִּימָה עֲלֵי־כָֽסֶל (Iyov 15:27), he put fat upon his flank, and אֲשֶׁר עַל־הַכְּסָלִים (Vayikra 3:4), the fat that is upon the flanks, which he says wants a vav, ואשר על הכסלים. The כסלים are beside the kidneys, below the waist, at the roots of the thighs, and the Targum renders them גססיא. Chazal (Niddah 48b) speak of poor girls carrying their brothers on their flanks.

נחשׁ.sense: Divining by omens; the snake; and copper, whether the burnished vessel, the fetter, or a forehead of brass for hardness.

more.t: מְעוֹנֵן וּמְנַחֵשׁ (Devarim 18:10), a soothsayer and a diviner, וְהָֽאֲנָשִׁים יְנַֽחֲשׁוּ (Melachim I 20:33), the men took it for an omen, כִּי לֹא־נַחַשׁ בְּיַֽעֲקֹב (Bamidbar 23:23), there is no divining in Yaakov, and לִקְרַאת נְחָשִׁים (Bamidbar 24:1), going out toward omens.

Chazal (Sanhedrin 68b) set out the forbidden divining: one who says his bread fell from his mouth, his staff fell from his hand, his son calls after him, a raven calls to him, a deer cut across his path, a snake at his right and a fox at his left, do not begin, for it is morning, it is Rosh Chodesh, it is Motzaei Shabbos. They count there too those who divine by weasel, by birds and by stars.

הֲלוֹא יְדַעְתֶּם כִּֽי־נַחֵשׁ יְנַחֵשׁ אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר כָּמֹֽנִי (Bereishis 44:15), did you not know that a man like me surely divines: Radak reads it as asking diviners on his behalf by means of it, and there are those who explain that he divines by it himself, taking the loss of the cup he drank from as a bad omen for himself.

וְהַנָּחָשׁ הָיָה עָרוּם (Bereishis 3:1), the snake was cunning, and נָחָשׁ שָׂרָף (Devarim 8:15), a burning snake, called so because it burns with the breath of its mouth. נְחָשִׁים צִפְעֹנִים (Yirmiyahu 8:17), snakes and vipers, wants its vav, like שֶׁמֶשׁ יָרֵחַ (Chavakuk 3:11), sun and moon.

more.h: His father on the copper snake
more.t: נְחַשׁ נְחשֶׁת (Bamidbar 21:9): his father wrote that the physicians say a man bitten by a snake who then sees copper dies at once, and therefore Hashem told Moshe to make a snake of copper, and everyone who was bitten looked at it and lived, against the nature of the world, to make the miracle greater. So too the cake of figs for Chizkiyahu (Yeshayahu 38:21), and the tree Hashem showed Moshe at the waters (Shemos 15:25), which the Yalkut in the name of the Mechilta says was a bitter tree.

נָחָשׁ בָּרִחַ, the barred serpent, and נָחָשׁ עֲקַלָּתוֹן, the twisting serpent, are Livyasan, named so for its likeness to a snake; it is called tannin as well, it and the great fish, as the snakes of the dry land are also called tanninim. He takes the two names as a mashal for the kings of the nations. Others explain נָחָשׁ בָּרִחַ as the celestial dragon, twisting because it is bent, and barring because it reaches from end to end.

נְחֹשֶׁת קָלָֽל (Yechezkel 1:7), burnished copper, נְחֹשֶׁת מְמֹרָֽט (Melachim I 7:45), polished copper, and וַיִּשְׂאוּ אֶת־כָּל־נְחֻשְׁתָּם בָּבֶֽלָה (Yirmiyahu 52:17), they carried all their copper off to Bavel. אִם־בְּשָׂרִי נָחֽוּשׁ (Iyov 6:12), is my flesh copper, וְאֶֽת־אַרְצְכֶם כַּנְּחֻשָֽׁה (Vayikra 26:19), your land like copper, and וּמִצְֽחֲךָ נְחוּשָֽׁה (Yeshayahu 48:4), your forehead copper: every נחשת and נחושה spoken this way is a matter of hardness.

כֻּלָּם סָרֵי סֽוֹרְרִים הֹֽלְכֵי רָכִיל נְחשֶׁת וּבַרְזֶל (Yirmiyahu 6:28): as copper is mixed with iron so that it cuts well, so are they mixed with one another in talebearing to do harm, and Yonasan renders it that they walk in guile as copper is mixed with iron. He reads סָרֵי as though written with a sin, lords of the rebellious: the servants are rebellious and evil and carry tales to their masters, as neither copper nor iron does the cutting work without the other.

הִכְבִּיד נְחָשְׁתִּֽי (Eichah 3:7), he made my fetter heavy, and וַיַּֽאַסְרֵהוּ בַּֽנְחֻשְׁתַּיִם (Yirmiyahu 39:7), they bound him in fetters: these are the shackles, named so because they are made of copper, and the Targum renders them chains of copper. יַעַן הִשָּׁפֵךְ נְחֻשְׁתֵּךְ (Yechezkel 16:36) he reads as your lower part, a way of speaking of nakedness, and the Targum has it that her shame was uncovered; so too וְחָרָה נְחֻשְׁתָּהּ (Yechezkel 24:11), its bottom grows hot, and the נחשת of an oven in the Mishnah (Keilim 8:3) is its underside.
וַיִּקְרָא־לוֹ נְחֻשְׁתָּֽן (Melachim II 18:4): the added letters make the thing small, that is, that it had no use at all, and so אֲמִינוֹן (Shmuel II 13:20), where the addition likewise belittles.

צפע.sense: The viper that comes out of the snake's root; and in the same letters cattle dung, and the offshoots of a house, its sons and daughters.

more.t: כִּֽי־מִשֹּׁרֶשׁ נָחָשׁ יֵצֵא צֶפַע (Yeshayahu 14:29), from the root of a snake comes out a viper.
נְחָשִׁים צִפְעֹנִים (Yirmiyahu 8:17) he reads as snakes and vipers, the vav wanting; or צפעונים describes the snakes, the צפעוני being the hard and fierce one.

צְפִיעֵי הַבָּקָר (Yechezkel 4:15) he explains as the cattle's dung, and in the same sense הַצֶּֽאֱצָאִים וְהַצְּפִעוֹת (Yeshayahu 22:24), which he takes as the sons and the daughters, as though it said הצאצאים והצאצאות; the Targum renders them sons and sons of sons.

נוס.sense: To flee; in the causative to make others flee to safety, and the nouns are the flight itself and the refuge fled to.

more.t: "And he fled outside" (Bereishis 39:13), "and we shall flee before them" (Yehoshua 8:5), "if we indeed flee they will not set their heart upon us" (Shmuel II 18:3), "when they fled from before Israel" (Yehoshua 10:11).

more.h: Ransom and the city of refuge
more.t: "You shall take no ransom for him that flees to his city of refuge" (Bamidbar 35:32) means that from one who has cause to flee no ransom is taken to let him come back and settle in the land before the Kohen Gadol dies; he flees to his city of refuge as the law requires. The Sifri reads the pasuk of one who killed deliberately, that he may not pay money and be exiled. Rabbeinu Shlomo took the word as a description of the man who has fled, on the pattern of "the backslider in heart" (Mishlei 14:14), and Radak says he explained it well.

"Nor had his moisture fled" (Devarim 34:7) is borrowed speech, that his moisture had not gone. His father in Sefer HaGaluy read it "his moisture had not dried", from the Arabic used of bread drying out, and Radak says he explained it well, for what sense is there in flight said of moisture?

"And you shall flee to the valley of my mountains" (Zecharyah 14:5) is read on the pattern of "and you shall return", "and you shall arise". Yonasan rendered it as though the valley of the mountains were stopped up, which looks as though he read it as a passive of the root meaning to stop up. Some say it is found so in a few precise books, but Radak says he has not seen it; Ibn Ezra wrote that the people of the East read it that way.

"We will flee on horses" (Yeshayahu 30:16) was taken by Rabbi Yonah in the sense of height and elevation, as in "lifted as an ensign upon His land" (Zecharyah 9:16). Radak holds there is no need to take it from its plain sense, as Rabbi Yehudah also wrote. Hashem had said they would be saved in their own land "in stillness and quiet" (Yeshayahu 30:15); they refused, and said they would flee to Ashur and Mitzrayim for help, so they will flee here and there and not be saved by that flight.

more.h: Making others flee, and the nouns
more.t: The causative is "he made his servants and his cattle flee" (Shemos 9:20), "to bring it to safety from Midian" (Shoftim 6:11). The nouns all mean flight: "in flight they fled and did not turn" (Yirmiyahu 46:5), "refuge is lost from them" (Iyov 11:20), "my refuge in the day of trouble" (Yirmiyahu 16:19), "you shall not go out in flight" (Yeshayahu 52:12), "they shall flee the flight of the sword" (Vayikra 26:36).

ברח.sense: To flee from danger; in the causative to drive another off; a separate sense is the bar that runs through from end to end.

more.t: "And David fled and escaped" (Shmuel I 19:18), "for he was fleeing" (Bereishis 31:20), "and Yaakov fled" (Hoshea 12:13), "and they fled into hiding" (Daniel 10:7). The causative drives another away: "they drove out the inhabitants of Gas" (Divrei HaYamim I 8:13), "one who despoils his father and drives off his mother" (Mishlei 19:26), "and I drove him from me" (Nechemyah 13:28), "an arrow will not put him to flight" (Iyov 41:20).

His father held that "Yonah rose to flee to Tarshish" (Yonah 1:3) and "for he was fleeing from before Hashem" (Yonah 1:10) are not flight proper, since flight proper is only from danger to life, but hastening the errand. He hastened so that Hashem should not give him a sign and a wonder, which would cause the people of Nineveh to repent, and their repentance would bring destruction on Israel. So too "therefore I hastened to flee to Tarshish" (Yonah 4:2).

more.h: The sign given him in the sea
more.t: Hashem, knowing his intent, gave him his sign in the sea, and none is greater: they cast him into the sea, the men of the ship were on their way to Nineveh, and when they saw him there they recognised him. The matter reached the king of Nineveh, and they believed at once, since the men of the ship testified that it was they who had thrown him in.

His father read "from before" as meaning at the command of the one who sends, as in "messengers shall go out from before Me in ships" (Yechezkel 30:9); and David said "where shall I flee from You" (Tehillim 139:7) and not "from before You". On that reading "go out from Bavel, flee from the Kasdim" (Yeshayahu 48:20) and "and the Leviim and the singers fled each to his field" (Nechemyah 13:10) can be taken the same way.

Another sense is running through: "to pass through in the midst of the boards" (Shemos 36:33), and in the causative "passing through from end to end" (Shemos 26:28). Hence the middle bar and the five bars of the Mishkan. The phrase "Livyasan the fleeing serpent" is a description on this sense, since it bars the sea from one end to the other, and it is a mashal for the powerful kings. Some read "I will bring down all of them as fugitives" (Yeshayahu 43:14) from here too, bound in an iron bar.

רוץ.sense: To run, and the runner who runs; a second and separate sense is to crush and to break.

more.t: "The lad ran" (Shmuel I 20:36), "if I run after him" (Melachim II 5:20), "I did not send the prophets, yet they ran" (Yirmiyahu 23:21), "runner runs to meet runner" (Yirmiyahu 51:31), "and Esav ran" (Bereishis 33:4).
