The nouns: "the race is not to the swift" (Koheles 9:11), "like the running of Achimaatz" (Shmuel II 18:23), "and their course is evil" (Yirmiyahu 23:10).

"For by You I run at a troop" (Shmuel II 22:30) he explains as running at the troop of his enemies and pursuing them. Rabbi Yonah took it from the sense of crushing, and Radak holds the first sense nearer.

"Fifty men running before him" (Melachim I 1:5). With a nun in place of a mem, "the sound of the runners, the people" (Melachim II 11:13) stands for the runners, as "to the end of the days" (Daniel 12:13) stands for the days. He explains that sound as the sound of rejoicing, for they were rejoicing and saying long live the king.

The causative: "Kush shall hasten her hands to God" (Tehillim 68:32), "in a moment I will make him run from her" (Yirmiyahu 49:19), "and they rushed him from the pit" (Bereishis 41:14), "and run this to the camp for your brothers" (Shmuel I 17:17), "and they brought it quickly to all the people" (Divrei HaYamim II 35:13). The intensive: "like the lightnings they dart" (Nachum 2:5).

"He shall not grow dim nor be crushed" (Yeshayahu 42:4), which he says he explained at the root of growing dim, and "and the golden bowl is shattered" (Koheles 12:6). "And she crushed his skull" (Shoftim 9:53) has chirik under the resh. The noun is "and upon the oppression and upon the violence done" (Yirmiyahu 22:17). Also "and they oppressed and crushed" (Shoftim 10:8), "and the children struggled within her" (Bereishis 25:22), "and the wheel is broken at the pit" (Koheles 12:6), "when they grasped you by the hand you broke" (Yechezkel 29:7).

"The king pulled down and smashed from there" (Melachim II 23:12) is transitive, that he overcame them and broke them from there. Yonasan rendered it "and removed from there", and on his view it belongs with "and Esav ran" (Bereishis 33:4), except that this one is transitive and means he made them run from there. Radak adds that "and the wheel is broken at the pit" (Koheles 12:6) may belong to the first sense.

ערק.sense: Those who flee, which is how the Targum renders fleeing; and by a second sense the sinews.

more.t: "Those who flee to the parched land" (Iyov 30:3) are the ones fleeing. The Targum of "and he fled" (Bereishis 39:12) uses this word.

"And my sinews do not rest" is the second sense, the sinews. The Targum of "wrought iron" (Yechezkel 27:19) renders it sinews of iron, as is said elsewhere, "and your neck an iron sinew". In Arabic the sinews are called by this word.

גבע.sense: A hill, which is like a mountain but not as high; by other senses the cap worn on the head, and the goblet.

more.t: "In Geva of Binyamin" (Shmuel I 13:16) has a segol. With the feminine heh it is givah, and in construct "the hill of Shaul" (Shmuel I 15:34), "the hill of the foreskins" (Yehoshua 5:3); in the plural "the mountains and the hills" (Yeshayahu 55:12). A hill is like a mountain but is not as high as a mountain.
Another sense is in "and caps you shall make for them", which are the hats set on the head for splendour.

Another sense again: "and the goblet was found" (Bereishis 44:12), "and my goblet, the silver goblet" (Bereishis 44:2), "the man in whose hand the goblet was found" (Bereishis 44:17), "three cups shaped like almonds" (Shemos 25:33), "and in the menorah four cups" (Shemos 25:34). It is like a cup but made on another pattern, and that is the force of "bowls full of wine, and cups" (Yirmiyahu 35:5).

צנף.sense: To wind round about; the turban wound on the head, and the headwrap the women wore.

more.t: "He will surely wind you round with a winding" (Yeshayahu 22:18) means He will overturn you and turn you about, the way a turban is turned round the head.

"And with a linen turban he shall be wound" (Vayikra 16:4), "remove the turban and lift off the crown" (Yechezkel 21:31), "turban and sash" (Shemos 28:4), "the pure turban" (Zecharyah 3:5), "like a robe and a turban" (Iyov 29:14), and in the feminine plural "and the headwraps and the veils" (Yeshayahu 3:23). He adds nothing further, saying only that the word is known.

כבע.sense: The helmet, the gear that shields the head.

more.t: "And a helmet of salvation on His head" (Yeshayahu 59:17), "and a helmet of copper on his head" (Shmuel I 17:5), "shield and helmet they hung upon you" (Yechezkel 27:10), "all of them with shield and helmet" (Yechezkel 38:5), "and stand forth in helmets" (Yirmiyahu 46:4). It is an implement that shields the head, and he gives a la'az for it.

In "and a helmet of salvation on His head" (Yeshayahu 59:17) and "and a helmet of copper on his head" (Shmuel I 17:5) the stress is on the earlier syllable; in "shield and helmet they hung upon you" (Yechezkel 27:10) and the rest it falls on the last.

אזר.sense: To gird and to brace oneself with strength; the belt one girds with; and on a second sense, of firebrands, the authorities differ.

more.t: "They were girded with strength" (Shmuel I 2:4), "and you, gird your loins" (Yirmiyahu 1:17), "girded with a belt at his loins" (Melachim II 1:8). In the intensive, "I gird you though you did not know Me" (Yeshayahu 45:5), "and You girded me with strength" (Tehillim 18:40). The passive is "girded with might" (Tehillim 65:7), and the reflexive "Hashem is clothed, He has girded Himself with strength" (Tehillim 93:1), "gird yourselves and be shattered" (Yeshayahu 8:9). All of them mean girding and bracing.
The thing one girds with is the ezor: "and He binds a belt on their loins" (Iyov 12:18), "and behold, the belt was ruined" (Yirmiyahu 13:7), "nor the belt of his loins undone" (Yeshayahu 5:27).

For "those who gird firebrands" (Yeshayahu 50:11) Rabbi Yonah gave "kindlers of fire". Some explain "bringers out of fire", meaning those who carve wood and stone and by the force of their carving bring fire out of them. His father explained it from the first sense, gatherers of firebrands.

רדם.sense: To fall into heavy sleep; the noun tardemah is that strong sleep.

more.t: "I fell into a deep sleep on my face to the ground" (Daniel 8:18), "and he was fast asleep and weary" (Shoftim 4:21), which is past tense; "chariot and horse fell fast asleep" (Tehillim 76:7), which is a participle; "and he lay down and slept heavily" (Yonah 1:5).
"And Hashem God caused a deep sleep to fall" (Bereishis 2:21) is the noun, and it is the strong sleep.

נום.sense: To slumber; slumber is not strong the way sleep is, but comes only a little at a time.

more.t: "Your shepherds slumber, king of Ashur" (Nachum 3:18); "they slumbered their sleep", which he explains as slumbering in their sleep; "behold, He neither slumbers nor sleeps" (Tehillim 121:4).

"And slumber clothes a man in rags" (Mishlei 23:21); with an added tav, "nor slumber to your eyelids" (Mishlei 6:4); in the plural, "a little slumber" (Mishlei 6:10), "in slumberings upon the bed" (Iyov 33:15). Slumber is not strong like sleep but comes a little at a time, and he gives a la'az for it.

פצר.sense: To press a man hard and urge him past his will; the whole of it is the overriding of a man's will, and compulsion.

more.t: "And he pressed them greatly" (Bereishis 19:3), "and he urged him to take it, and he refused" (Melachim II 5:15 in his edition), "and his father-in-law pressed him" (Shoftim 19:7), "and they pressed him until he was ashamed" (Melachim II 2:17), "and they pressed hard upon the man, upon Lot" (Bereishis 19:9).
The causative gives "and iniquity and terafim is pressing" (Shmuel I 15:23). All of it is the sense of overriding what a man wills, and compulsion.

דחה.sense: To push over and thrust away; the passive is the one thrust out and scattered, and the nouns are the stumble and the ruin.

more.t: "You pushed me hard" (Tehillim 118:13), "who planned to thrust aside my steps" (Tehillim 140:5), "and the angel of Hashem thrusting" (Tehillim 35:5), "a wall pushed over" (Tehillim 62:4).

The passive: "the wicked man is thrust down" (Mishlei 14:32), "they shall be thrust and fall in it" (Yirmiyahu 23:12), which has a pasach and the stress on the earlier syllable, against the usual, and "He gathers the outcasts of Israel" (Tehillim 147:2). He allows that the last might be from the roots that drop a nun and would then have wanted a dagesh, but holds the right view to be that it is a passive of this root.

more.h: Thrust down and unable to rise
more.t: "They were thrust down and could not rise" (Tehillim 36:13), which he says he found in the precise books with the stress on the last syllable. Rabbi Yehudah wrote it among the roots whose middle letter is a heh.
The nouns are "my foot from stumbling" (Tehillim 116:8) and, on another pattern with an added mem, "and a smooth mouth works ruin" (Mishlei 26:28).

נסע.sense: To set out and to pull a thing up from its place; in the causative to move it from where it stood, and the noun is the march.

more.t: "For he had set out from Lachish" (Yeshayahu 37:8), "and a wind went forth from Hashem" (Bamidbar 11:31), "and Avram set out" (Bereishis 12:9), "and behold, Mitzrayim setting out after them" (Shemos 14:10), "and they set out from Sukkos" (Bamidbar 33:6), "let us set out and go" (Bereishis 33:12), "and we set out from the river Ahava" (Ezra 8:31), "arise, set out" (Devarim 2:24), "and it was when the aron set out" (Bamidbar 10:35). Some hold that "let us set out and go" is an imperative with an added heh.

The transitive is "and she pulled away the pin of the loom" (Shoftim 16:14) and "and he pulled them up together with the bar" (Shoftim 16:3), though these too can be read as intransitive, so that the second means he set out with them, that is with the doors. The passive: "my dwelling is pulled up and carried off" (Yeshayahu 38:12), "is not their cord pulled up" (Iyov 4:21).

The causative: "and Moshe made Israel set out" (Shemos 15:22), "and the full one you shall set aside" (Melachim II 4:4), "and they moved great stones" (Melachim I 5:31), "one who moves stones" (Koheles 10:9). "Whole stone moved" (Melachim I 6:7) means that they moved the stones whole from the mountain, and did not build with ones they found flawed but moved these from the mountain.

"And he went on his marches" (Bereishis 13:3), "their goings out by their marches" (Bamidbar 33:2), "these are the marches of Bnei Yisrael" (Bamidbar 33:1). Used as an infinitive: "and for the setting out of the camps" (Bamidbar 10:2), as if to say to set the camps moving, and "arise, go on the march before the people" (Devarim 10:11).

"The spear, the massa and the coat of mail" (Iyov 41:18) names a weapon of war, as the commentators explained it, and the Mesorah says the word occurs twice in two senses. Rabbi Yonah took it instead from setting out, like "whole stone moved" (Melachim I 6:7), meaning the spear that is carried in the hand rather than the one girded on like a sword.

חגר.sense: To gird, and so to bind and tie fast; girded for war or in sackcloth, and the belt itself.

more.t: "And you shall gird them with a sash" (Shemos 29:9). In "the remnant of wrath You shall gird" (Tehillim 76:11) it means You shall gird and bind them so that they do not act on the wrath they had against Yerushalayim, for girding is tying and binding fast.

more.h: The mizmor of the camp of Ashur
more.t: He reads that whole mizmor as prophecy about the camp of Ashur encamped over Yerushalayim: "God is known in Yehudah" (Tehillim 76:2), "and His covert was in Shalem" (Tehillim 76:3), which is Yerushalayim, since until Yerushalayim God was not known in those wars, for Ashur had conquered all of Eretz Yisrael; when he came to Yerushalayim and spoke haughtily, God was known and His name great, as in "and he struck in the camp of Ashur" (Melachim II 19:35). "For the wrath of man shall praise You" (Tehillim 76:11) means that the one whose wrath was against You and raged against You will praise You against his will, and his wrath will turn to thanks. Then the remaining kings of the nations who had wrath against Yerushalayim will have their wrath girded and bound, for they will fear from what they hear was done in the camp of Ashur. That is "He cuts off the spirit of princes, awesome to the kings of the earth" (Tehillim 76:13), matching "every mighty man of valour and leader and officer in the camp of the king of Ashur" (Divrei HaYamim II 32:21).

more.h: Or the wrath of Mitzrayim and Kush
more.t: He offers a second reading of "the wrath of man shall praise You" (Tehillim 76:11), that it is said of the Mitzrim and the men of Kush who were with Ashur in the camp and turned to the faith of the Jews when they saw that great blow. Of them it is said "the labour of Mitzrayim and the merchandise of Kush" (Yeshayahu 45:14), and "an altar to Hashem in the midst of the land of Mitzrayim" (Yeshayahu 19:19) with the whole parsha.

more.h: Girded for war, girded in sack
more.t: "Your loins girded" (Shemos 12:11), "girded with weapons of war" (Shoftim 18:11), "gird your sword on your thigh, mighty one" (Tehillim 45:4), "wail like a maiden girded in sackcloth" (Yoel 1:8), "and they shall gird on sackcloth" (Yechezkel 7:18).

"Girded with a belt on their loins" (Yechezkel 23:15), with a cholam; "she gave a girdle to the merchant" (Mishlei 31:24); "and in place of a girdle, a rope"; "in his girdle that was on his loins" (Melachim I 2:5); "and they made themselves girdles" (Bereishis 3:7); and on another pattern "a girding of sackcloth" (Yeshayahu 3:24). All of them mean a belt.

"And they come girding out of their fetters" (Shmuel II 22:46) he glosses יתנועעו מכבליהם, they move from the fetters they are in, so that from the weight of them they limp. From the words of our Rabbis, "they sat on a plank or on a bench when these are unsteady" (Zavim 3:3), which he explains as when they move, for when the legs are uneven, one shorter than another, a man sitting on it sways this way and that like a lame man. Some read the word as a transposition, from the Targum of "and from the chambers, terror" (Devarim 32:25), so that it means they shall be afraid of their strongholds; and Yonasan rendered it that they shall tremble from their fortresses.

לון.sense: To lodge the night, and from there to abide and persist; a second sense, kept apart by a dagesh, is to murmur and complain.

more.t: "And he lodged that night" (Bereishis 32:22), "and we shall lodge in Givah" (Shoftim 19:13), where the root's nun is swallowed into the dagesh of the plural nun. As a description, "why do you lodge over against the wall" (Nechemyah 13:21) and "and it shall lodge in the midst of his house" (Zecharyah 5:4), where a segol stands in place of a kamatz. Further: "and Yehoshua lodged" (Yehoshua 8:9), "and he lodged there that night" (Bereishis 32:14), "and they lodged there" (Shoftim 18:4), "for we shall lodge in the street" (Bereishis 19:2), "only do not lodge in the street" (Shoftim 19:20).

The holy tongue uses lodging for persistence: "strength lodges in his neck" (Iyov 41:14), "he shall lodge satisfied, not visited by evil" (Mishlei 19:23), "how long shall it lodge within you" (Yirmiyahu 4:14), "and it shall lodge in the midst of his house" (Zecharyah 5:4). These are not the lodging of the night but constant persistence.

"And on their provocations my eye lodges" (Iyov 17:3 in his edition) means he did not sleep because his companions provoked his words and condemned him. Some read it from persistence on a matter, taking "my eye" as his attention, that he thinks and dwells on their provocation always. Since the lodging of the night is a cessation of all business and a settling into sleep and rest, Iyov said that he was awake at night and his dwelling was on their provocations.

more.h: What does not lodge with a man
more.t: "And man in his splendour does not lodge" (Tehillim 49:13) means that what a man holds precious, namely his money, does not lodge with him at his death but is left behind; and so at the close of the mizmor, "man in his splendour who does not understand" (Tehillim 49:21), that he does not understand while still alive with his money. Rabbi Yehudah HaLevi read it that there is with a man something precious that will not lodge, meaning will not lie down and die, which is the soul, and a man who has not learned and does not understand is therefore like the beasts. Of "his soul shall lodge in goodness" Radak says that when he dies his soul will rest in goodness.

The transitive is "they cause the naked to lodge without clothing" (Iyov 24:7), "a place for us to lodge" (Bereishis 24:23); the reflexive, "he shall lodge in the shadow of Shakai" (Tehillim 91:1). The nouns: "to the lodging place" (Bereishis 43:21), "a wayfarers' lodge" (Yirmiyahu 9:1), and in the feminine "like a hut in a cucumber field" (Yeshayahu 1:8), "and it shall sway like a hut" (Yeshayahu 24:20). That is the watchman's booth, called so because it is not for dwelling but only to pass the night in.

"That you murmured against Me" (Bamidbar 14:29), "and the people murmured against Moshe" (Shemos 17:3); with a dagesh, "and they made the whole congregation murmur against him" (Bamidbar 14:36), which is causative upon a third party, "that you murmur against Him" (Shemos 16:8), "that you murmur against us" (Shemos 16:7). Most of this sense comes with a dagesh to keep it apart from the other. The noun is "I have heard the murmurings" (Shemos 16:12), where the dagesh stands in place of the quiescent letter, and the passive is "and they murmured against Moshe and against Aharon" (Bamidbar 14:2). A telunah is a grievance.

שֹושֹ.sense: To rejoice and take delight, said both of Hashem rejoicing over Israel and of a man rejoicing in what he has been given.

more.t: שש אנכי על אמרתך (Tehillim 119:162), I rejoice over Your word; and פגעת את שש ועשה צדק (Yeshayahu 64:4), which he explains as one who rejoices in Your mitzvos.

ישֻשום מדבר (Yeshayahu 35:1), the wilderness shall rejoice; he reads the ending as rejoice in them or with them, comparing בשלם הבשר (Melachim I 19:21), which is he cooked the meat for them. Some say the mem stands for a nun, so that ישֻשום is ישֻשון.

The causative forms he lists, as שישו אתה (Yeshayahu 66:10), rejoice with her, he takes as intransitive. Chazal (Megillah 10b) hold the causative transitive: He does not rejoice but makes others rejoice, the proof being that it is written ישיש and not ישוש.

more.h: Masos, the joy of a way
more.t: The noun: משוש לכל הארץ (Eichah 2:15), a joy to all the earth; and הן הוא משוש דרכו (Iyov 8:19), which he explains as the joy he took in his way and in his evil deeds, and this is his end, for he perished quickly.

גיל.sense: His entry under these letters is not joy but likeness: אשר כגילכם (Daniel 1:10) means those who are of your sort, resembling you.

more.t: He brings the language of Chazal (Megillah 11a), the brother of a head and the ben gilo of a head, that is, one who resembles him.

רנן.sense: Crying out aloud: song and gladness, or proclamation, or prayer, or weeping and wailing, each one according to its place.

more.t: He sums the root as the language of crying out: some of it for song and joy, some for proclaiming, some for prayer, and some for weeping and groaning, as וכשדים באניות רנתם (Yeshayahu 43:14), the Kasdim whose cry is in their ships.

פצחי רנה (Yeshayahu 54:1), break out in song; ויעבר הרנה במחנה (Melachim I 22:36), the cry passed through the camp; הקשיבה רנתי (Tehillim 17:1), hear my cry. The fuller form: באו לפניו ברננה (Tehillim 100:2), come before Him with song.

more.h: Ibn Ezra on the morning stars
more.t: ברן יחד כוכבי בקר (Iyov 38:7), when the morning stars sang together: Rabbi Avraham ibn Ezra writes that the morning stars are the seven planets, called also stars of light, and the bnei Elokim are the upper arrays, whose motion is their song and their shout.

הרנינו לאלהים עוזנו (Tehillim 81:2) he explains as say a song, and הרנינו גוים עמו (Devarim 32:43) as you nations who are His people, sing, for He avenges the blood of His servants. Others take הרנינו as proclaim, like חכמות בחוץ תרנה (Mishlei 1:20), wisdom cries aloud outside, so that the call is to proclaim about them wherever they are.

כגבור מתרונן מיין (Tehillim 78:65), like a man sunk in sleep from the wine he drank who now wakes from it and shouts; he says like a warrior because nothing but the wine took his strength. So Hakadosh Baruch Hu was as one asleep while He bore with Israel's sins, and when they angered Him He took His vengeance, and this is said of the destruction of the Mishkan at Shiloh.
כנף רננים (Iyov 39:13) is the name of a bird called so, perhaps because it sings and is fine of voice, or because it sings and takes delight in its wings, which are beautiful like the peacock's.

דוץ.sense: A word of gladness and joy: ולפניו תדוץ דאבה (Iyov 41:14), before him sorrow turns to dancing.

more.t: He likens it to the Targum of שישו אתה משוש (Yeshayahu 66:10), rejoice with her a rejoicing, which is rendered דוצו עמה דיץ.

חדה.sense: To rejoice: ויחד יתרו (Shemos 18:9), Yisro rejoiced; and from it the noun chedvah, gladness.

more.t: ויחד יתרו (Shemos 18:9) is formed like ויחן שם ישראל (Shemos 19:2). Its regular form would be ויחדה, and the dagesh in the dalet is to steady the reading, because the stress falls back off the last syllable.

עז וחדוה במקמו (Divrei Hayamim I 16:27), strength and gladness are in His place, and the gladness of Hashem that is your strength (Nechemiah 8:10); the causative תחדהו בשמחה (Tehillim 21:7), You gladden him with joy. The sense of all of them is joy.

He allows that אל יחד בימי שנה (Iyov 3:6), let it not rejoice among the days of the year, may come from this root and this sense. But ברזל בברזל יחד ואיש יחד פני רעהו (Mishlei 27:17), iron sharpens iron and a man sharpens the face of his fellow, belong to the sense he set out already at the root חדד.

חדק.sense: One of the kinds of thorns: כמשכת חדק (Mishlei 15:19), a hedge of thorn.

more.h: The best of them a brier
more.t: טובם כחדק (Michah 7:4), their best is like a chedek: he says the good one among them is like this thorn.

שׁאה.sense: Desolation and ruin, with a second use for a man struck dumb with wonder, and a further sense of roaring and tumult.

more.t: עד אשר אם שאו ערים (Yeshayahu 6:11), until the cities lie waste, and the nifal תשאה שממה (Yeshayahu 6:11), it be left desolate. The noun ושאיה יכת שער (Yeshayahu 24:12), which he reads as and in ruin the gate is battered; the causative להשאות גלים נצים (Yeshayahu 37:26), to lay waste ruined heaps, where the parallel in Melachim (II 19:25) prints להשות, and he has already written of it at the root נשא.
והאיש משתאה לה (Bereishis 24:21), the man stood gazing at her in astonishment: some of these are the language of wonder, as the word for desolation also gives משתומם, one who is dumbfounded.

ושאון לאמים כשאון מים כבירים ישאון (Yeshayahu 17:12), the roar of peoples like the roar of mighty waters that roar, and וירד הדרה והמונה ושאונה (Yeshayahu 5:14), her splendour and her multitude and her tumult go down: a sense of uproar. So too ועלית כשאה (Yechezkel 38:9), you will come up like a storm, water that comes in force and has the sound of a roar.

Rabbi Yonah writes that ושאננך עלה באזני (Yeshayahu 37:29) belongs to this sense, the proper form being ושאונך, your roaring, the nun doubled to intensify the uproar. Radak adds that he found in the Mesorah that every שאנן is the language of quiet except this one and its fellow, which are the language of קול שאון מעיר (Yeshayahu 66:6), a sound of uproar from the city.

more.h: Ibn Ezra and his father: quiet
more.t: Rabbi Avraham ibn Ezra explains it as it sounds, the language of quiet, joined to התרגזך אלי, your raging against Me, the verse being elliptical: your raging against Me, and the rage of your ease has come up into My ears, that is, you rage against Me because of the quiet and the rest you have. His father explains it the same way.

ברק.sense: Lightning, and from it the gleam of a gem and the flash of a blade; the barkanim are a kind of thorn.

more.t: ברוק ברק ותפיצם (Tehillim 144:6), flash lightning and scatter them; התשלח ברקים וילכו (Iyov 38:35), will you send out lightnings and they go. The thing, he says, is known.
אדם פטדה וברקת (Shemos 28:17) and וברקת וזהב (Yechezkel 28:13): a precious stone, yellow like gold, called so because it gleams like the lightning.

למען היה לה ברק (Yechezkel 21:15), that it have brightness, that is, much shine like the look of lightning; וברק ממררתו יהלך (Iyov 20:25) is the spear blade that is like lightning, and so ברק חניתך (Chabakuk 3:11), the lightning of your spear, and וברק חנית (Nachum 3:3), the flash of a spear.
Rabbi Yonah explains וברק ממררתו of the red bile, meaning the gall bladder.
ואת הברקנים (Shoftim 8:7), one of the kinds of thorns.

חרל.sense: The charul, a prickly growth; the authorities he brings differ over which plant it is.

more.t: תחת חרול יספחו (Iyov 30:7), under the charul they huddle together; ממשק חרול (Tzefaniah 2:9), a patch of charul; כסו פניו חרלים (Mishlei 24:31), its face was covered with charulim.
Some explain it as a plant resembling thorns, ortigas in the vernacular; others as the thorn with whose flower they curdle the cheese, cardon in the vernacular.

קמשׁ.sense: One of the kinds of thorns, which he glosses ortiga in the vernacular.

more.t: קמוש וחוח (Yeshayahu 34:13), kimosh and briar; והנה עלה כלו קמשנים (Mishlei 24:31), it had all grown over with kimshonim.

שֹוך.sense: To hedge a way about with thorns, and the nouns for the thorn hedge itself; in a separate sense, a bough.

more.t: הנני שך את דרכך בסירים (Hoshea 2:8), I am hedging your way with thorns; שכת בעדו (Iyov 1:10), You have hedged him about.

ישר ממסוכה (Michah 7:4), straighter than a hedge, though written with a samech, as is כל אבן יקרה מסכתך (Yechezkel 28:13), which he explains as your fence; כמשכת חדק (Mishlei 15:19) is with a sin. Because they make the fences of vineyards and gardens out of thorn and brier, the fence is called a mesuchah.
הסר משוכתו (Yeshayahu 5:5), remove its hedge, where the quiescent letter is swallowed into a dagesh; and some differ with him and read משוכתו soft.

more.h: Sikim, and his father on sakin
more.t: לשכים בעיניכם (Bamidbar 33:55), for thorns in your eyes. His father explains ושמת שכין בלעך (Mishlei 23:2), you shall put a knife to your throat, from this, the patach standing where a chirik would be, as in many words, and the nun and the mem being interchangeable as in חיים and חיין, ימים and ימין. Another form is התמלא בשכות עורו (Iyov 40:30), can you fill his hide with barbs, where the dagesh again stands in place of the quiescent letter, and he says their sense is known.
Another sense altogether: איש שוכה (Shoftim 9:49), each man his bough, and שוכת עצים (Shoftim 9:48), a bough of trees; these mean a branch.

קרע.sense: To tear and rend, of garments and of a kingdom torn away; the sense in all of them is splitting and cutting, and at times opening up.

more.t: ויקרע את בגדיו (Bereishis 37:29), he rent his garments; קרעו בגדיהם (Bamidbar 14:6), they rent their garments; קרוע כתנתו (Shmuel II 15:32), his coat rent, which comes with a kamatz in the construct like לבש הבדים (Yechezkel 9:11), clothed in linen; קרועי בגדים (Yeshayahu 36:22), with garments rent; יקרעה בתער הספר (Yirmiyahu 36:23), he would cut it with the scribe's knife.

more.h: The sense of all of them
more.t: The nifal והמזבח נקרע (Melachim I 13:5), the altar was rent, and לא יקרע (Shemos 28:32), that it not be torn: the sense in all of them is splitting and cutting.

קרעו ולא דמו (Tehillim 35:15), they tore and did not keep still, as though they tore my flesh by how they kept on speaking against me; and כי תקרעי בפוך עיניך (Yirmiyahu 4:30), that you widen your eyes with paint, as though she tears her eyes by how she keeps on painting them. He offers also that קרעו ולא דמו falls on the cutting of the tongue in words, or on the wide opening of the mouth in laughter, and Radak holds that last reading the correct one.

וקרע לו חלוני (Yirmiyahu 22:14), he cuts himself out windows: Yonasan renders ופצים ליה חרכין, that is, he opened openings for him. So too לוא קרעת שמים (Yeshayahu 63:19), had You but rent the heavens: a sense of opening.

חתך.sense: נחתך על עמך ועל עיר קדשך (Daniel 9:24), it is decreed upon your people and upon your holy city; he explains it as decreed, cut out.

more.t: Chazal made this language common, as in חתיכה של בשר (Zevachim 92b), a piece of meat, in place of the form חתך, and there are many more besides these.

בתר.sense: To cut in two: ואת הצפר לא בתר (Bereishis 15:10), the bird he did not divide; the noun is a piece cut off.

more.t: ויבתר אתם בתוך (Bereishis 15:10), he cut them through the middle; ויתן איש בתרו (Bereishis 15:10), each man set his piece; ויעברו בין בתריו (Yirmiyahu 34:18), they passed between its pieces. Also על הרי בתר (Shir Hashirim 2:17), upon the mountains of cleft. The sense is a portion.

אטד.sense: A kind of thorn bush: גרן האטד (Bereishis 50:10), the threshing floor of Atad.

more.t: קוץ ודרדר, thorn and thistle, Onkelos renders כובין ואטדין; the atad is one of the kinds of thorns, cardon in the vernacular.

נתח.sense: To cut a carcass into its pieces: ונתח אתו לנתחיו (Vayikra 1:12), he shall cut it into its pieces; the nesachim are limbs.

more.t: וינתחה לעצמיה לשנים עשר נתחים (Shoftim 19:29), he cut her limb by limb into twelve pieces; תנתח לנתחיו (Shemos 29:17), you shall cut it into its pieces; אסף נתחיה אליה (Yechezkel 24:4), gather its pieces into it.
כל נתח טוב (Yechezkel 24:4), every good piece, has the nun with a segol, and there are books that have it with a tzere.

פלח.sense: Splitting and cleaving, and the noun פֶּלַח, a piece split off: a millstone, a slice of pressed fig, a segment of pomegranate.

more.t: פֹלֵחַ וּבֹקֵעַ (Tehillim 141:7), splitting and cleaving; וַיְפַלַּח אֶל־סִיר הַנָּזִיד (Melachim II 4:39), he split them into the pot of stew; יְפַלַּח כִּלְיוֹתַי (Iyov 16:13), he splits my kidneys.

כְּפֶלַח תַּחְתִּֽית (Iyov 41:16), like a lower piece, is the nether of the pair, the two stones looking as though one had been split off from its fellow; פֶּלַח רֶכֶב (Shoftim 9:53) is a piece of the upper stone, which is the רֶכֶב of (Devarim 24:6).
פֶלַח דְּבֵלָה (Shmuel I 30:12) is a piece of pressed figs, and כְּפֶלַח הָֽרִמּוֹן (Shir HaShirim 4:3) is a split piece of the pomegranate.

קטב.sense: Destruction, and with it the sense of cutting off; the sickness that comes upon a man suddenly and kills him.

more.t: וְקֶטֶב מְרִירִי (Devarim 32:24), bitter destruction, and מִקֶּטֶב יָשׁוּד צָהֳרָֽיִם (Tehillim 91:6), the destruction that ravages at noon; on another pattern אֱהִי קָֽטָבְךָ שְׁאוֹל (Hoshea 13:14), I will be your destruction, O grave.
The word carries the sense of cutting off, and what is meant by it is the illness that falls on a man of a sudden and kills him.
Radak brings that Targum on לַחְטֹב עֵצִים (Devarim 19:5), to cut wood, which renders it לְמִקְטוֹעַ קֵיסִין, to cut logs.

פרם.sense: Tearing a garment, and by the distinction he draws from Chazal, tearing it open at the seam rather than through the cloth.

more.t: וּבְגָדָיו לֹא יִפְרֹֽם (Vayikra 21:10), he shall not tear his garments; וּבִגְדֵיכֶם לֹֽא־ תִפְרֹמוּ וְלֹא תָמֻתוּ (Vayikra 10:6), do not tear your garments and you will not die; בְּגָדָיו יִהְיוּ פְרֻמִים (Vayikra 13:45), his garments shall be torn.

Chazal say (Sotah 1:5) ואוחז בבגדיה אם נקרעו נקרעו ואם נפרמו נפרמו, he takes hold of her garments, if they tear they tear and if they come apart they come apart; from their setting the two words side by side Radak holds there is a difference between them, קריעה being in the body of the garment away from the seam and פרימה being at the seam.

גדע.sense: Cutting down and hewing off: a tree felled, an arm severed, a horn broken off.

more.t: גָּדַע בָּֽחֳרִי־אַף (Eichah 2:3), he cut down in fierce anger; וְגָֽדַעְתִּי אֶת־זְרֹֽעֲךָ (Shmuel I 2:31), I will cut off your arm; וְרָמֵי הַקּוֹמָה גְּדוּעִים (Yeshayahu 10:33), the tall of stature are hewn down.

נִגְדַּעְתָּ לָאָרֶץ (Yeshayahu 14:12), you were cut down to the ground; נִגְדְּעָה קֶרֶן מוֹאָב (Yirmiyahu 48:25), the horn of Moav is cut off; שִׁקְמִים גֻּדָּעוּ (Yeshayahu 9:10 in his edition), sycamores were cut down.

וַֽאֲשֵֽׁירֵהֶם תְּגַדֵּעוּן (Devarim 7:5), you shall cut down their asheiros; וְכָל־קַרְנֵי רְשָׁעִים אֲגַדֵּעַ (Tehillim 75:11), all the horns of the wicked I will cut off. All of it is cutting off.

קצץ.sense: Cutting and severing; and from the same root קֵץ, an end, the place where time is cut, which may be the close of a span or its start.

more.t: וְקַצֹּתָה אֶת־כַּפָּהּ (Devarim 25:12), you shall cut off her hand; קִצֵּץ עֲבוֹת רְשָׁעִֽים (Tehillim 129:4), he cut the cords of the wicked; וְקִצֵּץ פְּתִילִם (Shemos 39:3), and he cut it into threads; בְּֽהֹנוֹת יְדֵיהֶם וְרַגְלֵיהֶם מְקֻצָּצִים (Shoftim 1:7), the thumbs of their hands and the big toes of their feet cut off; וַיְקַצְּצוּ אֶת־יְדֵיהֶם וְאֶת־רַגְלֵיהֶם (Shmuel II 4:12), they cut off their hands and their feet.

more.h: The end, as a place of cutting
more.t: From this root and this sense come בָּא הַקֵּץ (Yechezkel 7:6), the end has come, and קֵץ כָּל־בָּשָׂר (Bereishis 6:13), the end of all flesh: the close of a stretch of time, as though it were a place of cutting.

more.h: Or the start of a stretch
more.t: מִקֵּץ שֶֽׁבַע־שָׁנִים תַּֽעֲשֶׂה שְׁמִטָּֽה (Devarim 15:1), at the end of seven years you shall make a release: though it is an end for the release of monies, it is a beginning for the release of land and the sending out of servants. So too מִקֵּץ שֶׁבַע שָׁנִים תְּֽשַׁלְּחוּ (Yirmiyahu 34:14), at the end of seven years you shall send out, is the start of the seventh year, for both head and end are called a קָצֶה.

וְעַל כָּל־ קְצוּצֵי פֵאָה (Yirmiyahu 9:25), all who are clipped at the corner, belongs with the cutting; and Radak holds it may belong here in the other way as well, meaning those who dwell at the end of the settled world, at the edge of it.

more.h: A nun in place of a doubled letter
more.t: עַד־אָנָה תְּשִׂימוּן קִנְצֵי לְמִלִּין (Iyov 18:2), how long will you set ends to words, has a nun standing in for the doubling. Some of the grammarians read כִּי לֹא־תָמְנוּ (Eichah 3:22), for we are not consumed, the same way, as though it were תממו. Or else קִנְצֵי and קֵץ have a root קָנַץ, and it is for the missing nun that קֵץ takes a dagesh when it joins: קִצּוֹ, קִצִּי.

כעס.sense: Anger and vexation, and in the causative the provoking of another to anger; all of it wrath and fierce anger.

more.t: רָשָׁע יִרְאֶה וְכָעָס (Tehillim 112:10), the wicked man will see and be vexed; וְכָעַס הַרְבֵּה וְחָלְיוֹ וָקָֽצֶף (Koheles 5:16), and much vexation and his sickness and wrath; וַיִּכְעַס אָסָא אֶל־הָרֹאֶה (Divrei HaYamim II 16:10), Asa was angry with the seer.

וְכִֽעֲסַתָּה צָֽרָתָהּ (Shmuel I 1:6), her rival provoked her; כִּֽעֲסוּנִי בְּהַבְלֵיהֶם (Devarim 32:21), they provoked me with their empty things; בְּגוֹי נָבָל אַכְעִיסֵֽם (Devarim 32:21), with a vile nation I will provoke them; כֵּן תַּכְעִסֶנָּה (Shmuel I 1:7), so she would provoke her; לְהַכְעִיסוֹ בְּמַֽעֲשֵׂה יְדֵיכֶֽם (Devarim 31:29), to provoke Him with the work of your hands; וְהִכְעַסְתִּי לֵב עַמִּים רַבִּים (Yechezkel 32:9), I will vex the heart of many peoples.

גַּם־ כַּעַס (Shmuel I 1:6), vexation too; כַּעַס לְאָבִיו בֵּן כְּסִיל (Mishlei 17:25), a foolish son is a vexation to his father; כִּי מֵרֹב שִׂיחִי וְכַעְסִי (Shmuel I 1:15), out of the abundance of my complaint and my vexation; and in the plural עַל כָּל־ הַכְּעָסִים אֲשֶׁר הִכְעִיסוֹ מְנַשֶּֽׁה (Melachim II 23:26), all the provocations wherewith Menashe provoked Him.

Some of them are written with a sin: כִּי לֶאֱוִיל יַֽהֲרָג־ כָּעַשׂ (Iyov 5:2), vexation kills the fool; וַתֵּכַהּ מִכַּעַשׂ עֵינִי (Iyov 17:7), my eye is dim from vexation; וְתֶרֶב כַּֽעַשְׂךָ עִמָּדִי (Iyov 10:17), you increase your indignation against me; לוּ שָׁקוֹל יִשָּׁקֵל כַּעְשִׂי (Iyov 6:2), if only my vexation were weighed.

more.h: Rabbi Yonah on the sin spelling
more.t: Rabbi Yonah wrote that the two of them, the weighing of כַּעְשִׂי in (Iyov 6:2) and כִּי מֵרֹב שִׂיחִי וְכַעְסִי (Shmuel I 1:15), are a root of their own spelled with a sin and meaning pain. Radak holds this unneeded, since when a man frets and is in pain he vexes himself; and besides, כִּי מֵרֹב שִׂיחִי וְכַעְסִי stands with a samech in every accurate book he has seen.

כִּי הִכְעִיסוּ לְנֶגֶד הַבּוֹנִֽים (Nechemiah 3:37), for they provoked before the builders, means to Radak that they provoked us before the builders, so as to hold back the builders' hearts from building. Rabbi Yonah wrote that it is a matter of mockery and scorn, and Radak holds that unneeded.

חמה.sense: Under these letters he has the father-in-law and mother-in-law and the wall חוֹמָה; wrath חֵמָה he defers to the root יָחַם, which he holds is its root.

more.t: הִנֵּה חָמִיךְ (Bereishis 38:13), behold your father-in-law, on the pattern of אָחִיךְ from אָחָה; וְהִיא שָֽׁלְחָה אֶל־ חָמִיהָ (Bereishis 38:25), and she sent to her father-in-law; כַּלָּה בַּֽחֲמֹתָהּ (Michah 7:6), a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. The singular standing alone is not found, but it is חָם and חָמוֹת as it is אָח and אָחוֹת.

This word falls only on the woman, and חוֹתֵן and חוֹתֶנֶת only on the man. In the Mishnah, though, Radak found the word used of a man too, in האוכל אצל חמיו, האוכל אצל חמותו (Kesubos 12a), one who eats at his father-in-law's and one who eats at his mother-in-law's.

חוֹמָה הָיוּ עָלֵינוּ (Shmuel I 25:16), they were a wall to us; אֲנִי חוֹמָה (Shir HaShirim 8:10), I am a wall; עַד רֶדֶת חֹֽמֹתֶיךָ (Devarim 28:52), until your walls come down; וְקָרָאת יְשׁוּעָה חוֹמֹתַיִךְ (Yeshayahu 60:18), you shall call your walls Salvation. He calls this one well known.
חֵמָה אֵין לִי, I have no wrath, he says he will write at the root יָחַם, because in his view that is its root.

חרה.sense: Anger burning; the root of the matter is heat, since it is out of great heat that a man grows angry.

more.t: עַל־הָֽרֹעִים חָרָה אַפִּי (Zecharyah 10:3), my anger burned against the shepherds; וְחָרָה אַפִּי בוֹ (Devarim 31:17), my anger will burn against him; and the infinitive בַּֽחֲרוֹת אַפָּם בָּֽנוּ (Tehillim 124:3), when their anger burned against us.

more.h: A second infinitive, not a noun
more.t: הֱשִׁיבוֹתָ מֵֽחֲרוֹן אַפֶּֽךָ (Tehillim 85:4), you turned back from the burning of your anger, is a second infinitive and not a noun: were it a noun it would read מֵחָרוֹן with a kamatz under the ches, since it is not in construct, and אַפֶּֽךָ is what the verb acts on.

בְּנֵי אִמִּי נִֽחֲרוּ ־בִי (Shir HaShirim 1:6), my mother's sons were incensed against me; כֹּל הַנֶּחֱרִים בָּךְ (Yeshayahu 41:11), all who are incensed against you; אַל־ תִּתְחַר בַּמְּרֵעִים (Tehillim 37:1), do not be incensed at evildoers; אַל־ תִּתְחַר בְּמַצְלִיחַ דַּרְכּוֹ (Tehillim 37:7), do not be incensed at the man who prospers in his way.

Radak allows that the root of תִּתְחַר may be תחר or תחרה, on the pattern of the ordinary form and not of וְאַל־ תִּתְגָּר (Devarim 2:9), do not contend, and he holds this right because of its patach, since on the pattern of תִּתְגָּר it would carry a kamatz as that word does.

הֶֽחֱרָה הֶֽחֱזִיק (Nechemiah 3:20), he heated himself to take firm hold of the work; וַיַּחַר עָלַי אַפּוֹ (Iyov 19:11), his anger burned against me. All of it is anger, and the root of the matter is heat.

כִּי חָרוֹן אֶל־כָּל־הֲמוֹנָֽהּ (Yechezkel 7:12), for burning anger is upon all her multitude; תְּשַׁלַּח חֲרֹנְךָ (Shemos 15:6 in his edition), you send out your burning anger; and on another pattern מֶה חֳרִי הָאַף הַגָּדוֹל הַזֶּֽה (Devarim 29:24 in his edition), what is this great heat of anger.

זעם.sense: Denouncing and cursing in anger; his sense for the whole of it is loathing together with rage and anger.

more.t: וְזָעַם עַל־בְּרִֽית־קוֹדֶשׁ (Daniel 11:30), he raged against the holy covenant; אֲשֶׁר זָעַמְתָּה זֶה שִׁבְעִים שָׁנָֽה (Zecharyah 1:12), which you have been indignant these seventy years; יִזְעָמוּהוּ לְאֻמִּֽים (Mishlei 24:24), peoples will curse him; וּלְכָה זֹֽעֲמָה יִשְׂרָאֵֽל (Bamidbar 23:7), come, denounce Israel.
וְאֵיפַת רָזוֹן זְעוּמָֽה (Michah 6:10), a scant measure that is accursed; וּפָנִים נִזְעָמִים (Mishlei 25:23), a face full of rage.

זַעַם מִלֵּאתָֽנִי (Yirmiyahu 15:17), you have filled me with indignation; מִזַּעַם לְשׁוֹנָם (Hoshea 7:16), because of the rage of their tongue; שְׁפָךְ־עֲלֵיהֶם זַעְמֶךָ (Tehillim 69:25), pour out your indignation upon them.

זעף.sense: Being sullen and out of temper; the sense of the whole of it is wrath and anger, and it is said of a raging sea as well.

more.t: אֶת־פְּנֵיכֶם זֹֽעֲפִים (Daniel 1:10), your faces downcast; וְהִנָּם זֹֽעֲפִֽים (Bereishis 40:6), and behold they were downcast; and the description אֶל־בֵּיתוֹ סַר וְזָעֵף (Melachim I 21:4), to his house sullen and out of temper.

וּבְזַעְפּוֹ עִם־הַכֹּֽהֲנִים (Divrei HaYamim II 26:19), in his raging with the kohanim, which he counts an infinitive; and וַיַּֽעֲמֹד הַיָּם מִזַּעְפּֽוֹ (Yonah 1:15), the sea stood still from its raging.

קצף.sense: Wrath, and the sense of it is a boiling over in anger; from that it is said of water churned up by a strong wind.

more.t: וְעַל כָּל־הָֽעֵדָה יִקְצֹף (Vayikra 10:6), and He will be wroth with the whole congregation; הַסְתֵּר וְאֶקְצֹף (Yeshayahu 57:17), I hid myself and was wroth; וְהָיָה כִֽי־יִרְעַב וְהִתְקַצַּף (Yeshayahu 8:21), and when he is hungry he will fall into a rage; וּבְחֹרֵב הִקְצַפְתֶּם (Devarim 9:8), at Chorev you stirred up wrath; מַקְצִפִים הֱיִיתֶם (Devarim 9:22), you were stirring up wrath.

כִּֽי־יָצָא הַקֶּצֶף (Bamidbar 17:11), for the wrath has gone out; עַל־אֲבֽוֹתֵיכֶם קָֽצֶף (Zecharyah 1:2), wrath against your fathers; כִּי בְקִצְפִּי הִכִּיתִיךְ (Yeshayahu 60:10), in my wrath I struck you; מִקִּצְפּוֹ תִּרְעַשׁ הָאָרֶץ (Yirmiyahu 10:10), at his wrath the earth quakes; אַל־ בְּקֶצְפְּךָ תוֹכִיחֵנִי (Tehillim 38:2), do not rebuke me in your wrath.

Because the sense is a boiling, it is said of water churned up by a strong wind: כְּקֶצֶף עַל־פְּנֵי־מָֽיִם (Hoshea 10:7), like froth on the face of the water. So Targum Yonasan renders it כְּרוּתְחָא עַל אַפֵּי מַיָא, like a boiling on the face of the water.

Some explain the word as the bark of a tree, and so read וּתְאֵנָתִי לִקְצָפָה (Yoel 1:7), and my fig tree for stripping, that it was peeled from its great dryness, as the pasuk says there חָשׂף חֲשָׂפָהּ, he has stripped it bare. Radak adds that וּתְאֵנָתִי לִקְצָפָה may also be taken in the first sense, that is, given over to a curse.

עשׁן.sense: Smoke, and what gives off smoke; and since anger is heat, he shows Scripture calling anger smoke as it calls it fire.

more.t: וְהַר סִינַי עָשַׁן כֻּלּוֹ (Shemos 19:18), and Mount Sinai was altogether smoking, which he takes as a past verb, half of it kamatz and half patach; גַּע בֶּהָרִים וְֽיֶעֱשָֽׁנוּ (Tehillim 144:5), touch the mountains and they will smoke; and as a description וְאֶת־הָהָר עָשֵׁן (Shemos 20:15), and the mountain smoking, and הָֽאוּדִים הָֽעֲשֵׁנִים (Yeshayahu 7:4), the smoking firebrands.

תַנּוּר עָשָׁן (Bereishis 15:17), a smoking oven, which he allows may be a description; כֶּעָשָׁן נִמְלָחוּ (Yeshayahu 51:6), like smoke they vanish; וְהִבְעַרְתִּי בֶֽעָשָׁן רִכְבָּהּ (Nachum 2:14), I will burn her chariots in smoke, that is, in a great fire whose smoke is seen from afar. In construct וְהִנֵּה עָלָה עֲשַׁן הָעִיר (Yehoshua 8:20), and behold the smoke of the city went up, and on another pattern כְּעֶשֶׁן הַכִּבְשָׁן (Shemos 19:18), like the smoke of the furnace.

Since anger and fury are heat, Scripture calls them fire, כִּי־אֵשׁ קָֽדְחָה בְאַפִּי (Devarim 32:22), for a fire has kindled in my anger, and calls them smoke too: עַד־מָתַי עָשַׁנְתָּ בִּתְפִלַּת עַמֶּֽךָ (Tehillim 80:5), how long have you smoked against the prayer of your people; יֶעְשַׁן אַפְּךָ בְּצֹאן מַרְעִיתֶֽךָ (Tehillim 74:1), will your anger smoke against the flock of your pasture; עָלָה עָשָׁן בְּאַפּוֹ (Shmuel II 22:9), smoke went up in his nostrils.

נאץ.sense: Spurning and holding in contempt; and the intensive forms, he says, come close to provoking to anger.

more.t: וְתוֹכַחַת נָאַץ לִבִּֽי (Mishlei 5:12), my heart spurned reproof; נָֽאֲצוּ כָּל־תּֽוֹכַחְתִּֽי (Mishlei 1:30), they spurned all my reproof; וַֽעֲצַת עֶלְיוֹן נָאָֽצוּ (Tehillim 107:11), they spurned the counsel of the Most High; וַיִנְאַץ בְּזַֽעַם־אַפּוֹ (Eichah 2:6), and He spurned in the rage of his anger.

נִֽאֲצוּ הָֽאֲנָשִׁים הָאֵלֶּה (Bamidbar 16:30), these men spurned; וְאֵת אִמְרַת קְדֽוֹשׁ־יִשְׂרָאֵל נִאֵֽצוּ (Yeshayahu 5:24), and they spurned the word of the Holy One of Israel; וְנִאֲצוּנִי וְהֵפֵר אֶת־בְּרִיתִֽי (Devarim 31:20), they will spurn me and break my covenant; עַד־אָנָה יְנַֽאֲצֻנִי (Bamidbar 14:11), how long will they spurn me; וְכָֽל־ מְנַֽאֲצַי לֹא יִרְאֽוּהָ (Bamidbar 14:23), and none who spurn me will see it; אֶפֶס כִּֽי־ נִאֵץ נִאַצְתָּ (Shmuel II 12:14), only because you have utterly spurned, where the first נאץ is an infinitive.

וְתָמִיד כָּל־הַיּוֹם שְׁמִי מִנֹּאָֽץ (Yeshayahu 52:5), and continually all the day my name is spurned, should by rule be מִתְנָאֵץ; or else, Radak says, it is a compounded form with the passive, as he set out in the section on grammar, in the chapter on the verbs.

יוֹם־צָרָה וְתוֹכֵחָה וּנְאָצָה (Yeshayahu 37:3), a day of trouble and rebuke and contempt; and on another pattern וַֽיַּֽעֲשׂוּ נֶאָצוֹת גְּדֹלֽוֹת (Nechemiah 9:18), and they committed great blasphemies, and שָׁמַעְתִּי אֶת־כָּל־ נָאָצוֹתֶיךָ (Yechezkel 35:12), I have heard all your blasphemies.
The sense of all of them is loathing, and those of the intensive are close to provoking to anger; all of them are near one another in sense.

רעם.sense: Two senses under one set of letters: a face darkened with rage, and thundering, whose sense is a loud shaking.

more.t: רָֽעֲמוּ פָּנִֽים (Yechezkel 27:35), their faces were troubled; and בַּֽעֲבוּר הַרְּעִמָהּ (Shmuel I 1:6), in order to make her fret, whose resh he says is doubled as the resh of מִקְּדָשׁ (Shemos 15:17), the Sanctuary of. The sense of these is rage in the face.

יִרְעַם הַיָּם וּמְלֹאוֹ (Tehillim 98:7), let the sea thunder and its fullness; אֵֽל־הַכָּבוֹד הִרְעִים (Tehillim 29:3), the God of glory thundered; יַרְעֵם מִן־שָׁמַיִם (Shmuel II 22:14), He thundered from heaven; וּבְקוֹל כָּמֹהוּ תַרְעֵֽם (Iyov 40:9), and can you thunder with a voice like his.

רַעַם שָׂרִים וּתְרוּעָֽה (Iyov 39:25), the thunder of captains and the shouting; הֲתַלְבִּישׁ צַוָּארוֹ רַעְמָֽה (Iyov 39:19), do you clothe his neck with thunder. Their sense is that of a loud shaking.

שׁצף.sense: He reads בְּשֶׁצֶף קֶצֶף (Yeshayahu 54:8), in a שֶׁצֶף of wrath, from its place as meaning with a little wrath.

more.t: Radak takes the word by what stands beside it: the pasuk before says בְּרֶגַע קָטֹן עֲזַבְתִּיךְ (Yeshayahu 54:7), for a small moment I forsook you, and so בְּשֶׁצֶף קֶצֶף is a small measure of wrath.

אפע.sense: A kind of snake, short and thick, its venom harsher than the male's; and in one pasuk a word for nothing (Yeshayahu 41:24).

more.t: וּפָֽעָלְכֶם מֵאָפַע (Yeshayahu 41:24), "and your work is from afa", which he glosses מאין, from nothing.

more.h: His father: a samech turned ayin
more.t: His father explained מֵאָפַע as מֵאֶפֶס, from nothing at all, the samech exchanged for an ayin.
His brother Rabbi Moshe explained it from אֶפְעֶה, the viper: you are nothing, and your work is the work of snakes, which harm those who cling to them.

תִּבָּקַע אֶפְעֶה (Yeshayahu 59:5), "a viper breaks out"; אֶפְעֶה וְשָׂרָף מְעוֹפֵף (Yeshayahu 30:6), "viper and flying saraf"; לְשׁוֹן אֶפְעֶה (Iyov 20:16), "a viper's tongue". They say it is the female of the saraf, short and thick, and its venom harsher than the male's.

פתן.sense: The venomous snake; and under the same letters the מפתן, the lower threshold that is trodden on.

more.t: עַל־חֻר פָּתֶן (Yeshayahu 11:8), "over the hole of a pesen"; מְרוֹרַת פְּתָנִים בְּקִרְבּוֹ (Iyov 20:14), "the gall of pesanim within him"; רֹאשׁ־פְּתָנִים יִינָק (Iyov 20:16), "he sucks the poison of pesanim". They are the evil snakes.
פֶתֶן חֵרֵשׁ (Tehillim 58:5), "a deaf pesen", is said for the extremity of its evil: no charm takes hold of it.

כְּרֻתוֹת אֶל־הַמִּפְתָּן (Shmuel I 5:4), "cut off at the threshold"; מִתַּחַת מִפְתַּן הַבַּיִת קָדִימָה (Yechezkel 47:1), "from under the threshold of the house eastward". It is the lower sill that is trodden on, and the Targum renders it סְקוֹפָא.

שׁפף.sense: One line: שְׁפִיפֹן עֲלֵי־אֹרַח (Bereishis 49:17), a shefifon on the path, with no meaning given, only the word's form.

more.t: He says of שְׁפִיפֹן only that it follows the pattern of ישימון, wasteland. What the creature is, his entry does not say.

זחל.sense: Creeping along the ground on the belly, and of water that flows; and at Iyov 32:6 he takes it as fear, where Rabbi Yonah differs.

more.t: עַל־כֵּן זָחַלְתִּי וָֽאִירָא (Iyov 32:6), "therefore I was afraid and feared". By what its place requires, he glosses זָחַלְתִּי as "I was afraid".
Rabbi Yonah explained זָחַלְתִּי as "I held back", comparing the Arabic.

זֹֽחֲלֵי עָפָֽר (Devarim 32:24), "creepers of the dust"; כְּזֹֽחֲלֵי אֶרֶץ (Michah 7:17), "like creepers of the earth". They are the swarming creatures that drag and move along the ground on their bellies.

Chazal call flowing water זוחלים (Mikvaos 5:5), and from this, in his view, אֶבֶן הַזֹּחֶלֶת (Melachim I 1:9) is so named because the water would flow and stream beside it, אֲשֶֽׁר־אֵצֶל עֵין רֹגֵל, "which is beside Ein Rogel".

Rabbeinu Shlomo explained אֶבֶן הַזֹּחֶלֶת as a great stone the young men would test their strength on, to shift it and drag it; Yonasan rendered אֶבֶן סְכוּתָא, a stone they stand on to watch into the distance.

רעד.sense: Trembling. He brings the verb, the noun and the causative, and says the word is known, without glossing it further.

more.t: הַמַּבִּיט לָאָרֶץ וַתִּרְעָד (Tehillim 104:32), "He looks at the earth and it trembles".
יֹֽאחֲזֵמוֹ רָעַד (Shemos 15:15), "trembling seizes them"; and with the feminine heh, רְעָדָה אֲחָזָתַם שָׁם (Tehillim 48:7), "trembling took hold of them there".
The heavier form here is a verb that stands on its own: עָמַדְתִּי מַרְעִֽיד (Daniel 10:11), "I stood trembling"; מַרְעִידִים עַל־הַדָּבָר (Ezra 10:9), "trembling over the matter".

רתת.sense: Trembling, known from the Targum's word for רעד; at Hoshea 13:1 it is the trembling Yeravam's calves brought on Israel.

more.t: The Targum renders יֹֽאחֲזֵמוֹ רָעַד (Shemos 15:15), "trembling seizes them", with רְתֵיתָא, so רְתֵת is trembling.
כְּדַבֵּר אֶפְרַיִם רְתֵת (Hoshea 13:1): when Yeravam, who was of Efrayim, spoke the matter of the calves, a great trembling was borne up in Israel.

רעשׁ.sense: To quake and shake, of earth, sea and walls, and the noun רַעַשׁ, a quaking; he glosses the sense as movement and trembling.

more.t: וְרָֽעֲשׁוּ מִפָּנַי דְּגֵי הַיָּם (Yechezkel 38:20), "the fish of the sea quake before Me"; תִּרְעַשְׁנָה חֽוֹמוֹתַיִךְ (Yechezkel 26:10), "your walls shall shake"; וַתִּרְעַשׁ הָאָרֶץ (Yirmiyahu 51:29), "and the earth quaked".
הִרְעַשְׁתִּי גוֹיִם (Yechezkel 31:16), "I made nations quake"; מַרְעִישׁ מַמְלָכֽוֹת (Yeshayahu 14:16), "who shook kingdoms".

רַעַשׁ גָּדוֹל (Yechezkel 3:12), "a great quaking"; לַחְמְךָ בְּרַעַשׁ תֹּאכֵל (Yechezkel 12:18), "you shall eat your bread in trembling". Their sense is movement and trembling, and he gives a word for it in the foreign tongue.
יִרְעַשׁ כַּלְּבָנוֹן פִּרְיוֹ (Tehillim 72:16), "his fruit shall shake like Levanon". They said it is as though יעשר reversed, that it grow rich.

Rabbi Yonah explained יִרְעַשׁ as "it will be fruitful and multiply", comparing the Arabic word used of blessing and fruitfulness, and took פִּרְיוֹ, "his fruit", as his sons: that his sons multiply as the trees of Levanon are many.
Rabbi Avraham Ibn Ezra explained it as it stands, that this fruit, which is the grain, shall shake, and it grows so great that it shakes the trees of Levanon.

געשׁ.sense: To heave and toss: the earth quaking, rivers whose waters surge, men who drink and reel. The sense of all of them is tossing and movement.

more.t: וַתִּגְעַשׁ וַתִּרְעַשׁ הָאָרֶץ (Tehillim 18:8), "the earth heaved and quaked", and the like in the reflexive at Shmuel II 22:8.
כַּנְּהָרֹות יִתְגָּֽעֲשׁוּ מֵימָֽיו (Yirmiyahu 46:7), "his waters toss like the rivers"; וְכַנְּהָרֹות יִתְגֹּעֲשׁוּ מָיִם (Yirmiyahu 46:8), "and like the rivers the waters toss".
וְשָׁתוּ וְהִתְגֹּֽעֲשׁוּ וְהִתְהֹלָלוּ (Yirmiyahu 25:16), "they shall drink and reel and act madly". The sense of them all is tossing and movement.

more.h: One address that will not carry
more.t: יְגֹֽעֲשׁוּ עָם וְיַֽעֲבֹרוּ, "a people is shaken and passes on", he brings from Iyov for the form whose doer is not named; his edition prints a chapter number that is not a chapter of Iyov, so it is left uncited here.

חרד.sense: Trembling in fear, the whole body moving when sudden fear comes; and in a set of pesukim plain movement, with no fear in it.

more.t: וְחָרַד וּפָחַד (Yeshayahu 19:16), "he shall tremble and fear"; וַיֶּֽחֱרַד יִצְחָק (Bereishis 27:33), "Yitzchak trembled". Their sense is fear together with movement of the body: when sudden fear comes upon a man, his whole body moves.

מִֽי־יָרֵא וְחָרֵד (Shoftim 7:3), "who is afraid and trembling"; לִבּוֹ חָרֵד עַל אֲרוֹן הָאֱלֹהִים (Shmuel I 4:13), "his heart trembled for the Aron of Hashem"; הַֽחֲרֵדִים אֶל־דְּבָרוֹ (Yeshayahu 66:5), "those who tremble at His word".

חֲרָדָה גְּדֹלָה (Bereishis 27:33), "a great trembling"; וַתְּהִי לְחֶרְדַּת אֱלֹהִֽים (Shmuel I 14:15), which he takes to mean a great trembling, and the like of it he treated in root אפל; חֶרְדַּת אָדָם יִתֵּן מוֹקֵשׁ (Mishlei 29:25), "the fear of man lays a snare".
וְכָל־הַֽמַּֽחֲנֶה הֶֽחֱרִֽיד (Shoftim 8:12), "he made all the camp tremble"; לְהַֽחֲרִיד אֶת־כּוּשׁ בֶּטַח (Yechezkel 30:9), "to make Kush tremble", Kush that had been secure.

חָרַדְתְּ אֵלֵינוּ אֶת־כָּל־הַֽחֲרָדָה הַזֹּאת (Melachim II 4:13): you bestirred yourself for us, moved your vessels from place to place and cleared us a place. So too וַיֶּֽחֶרְדוּ זִקְנֵי הָעִיר לִקְרָאתוֹ (Shmuel I 16:4), "the elders of the city hurried to meet him", and יֶֽחֶרְדוּ כְצִפּוֹר מִמִּצְרַיִם (Hoshea 11:11), "they shall flit like a bird from Mitzrayim". He glosses these ינועו, they move.

All those in the movement sense carry a segol under the ches, but יֶֽחְרְדוּ (Yechezkel 26:18), the isles shall tremble, has a sheva, and so וְכָל־הָעָם חָֽרְדוּ אַֽחֲרָֽיו (Shmuel I 13:7), which he reads as movement too: and all the people moved after him.

ארה.sense: He files the lion here: אַרְיֵה, and אֲרִיאֵל for the mizbeach; under the same headword also to pluck or gather, and stalls for cattle.

more.t: וְאָרוּהָ כָּל־עֹבְרֵי דָֽרֶךְ (Tehillim 80:13), "all who pass by pluck her"; אָרִיתִי מוֹרִי (Shir HaShirim 5:2), "I have gathered my myrrh". Some explain נָשִׁים בָּאוֹת מְאִירוֹת אוֹתָהּ (Yeshayahu 27:11), "women come and gather it", from this sense, though it belongs to another root: when the boughs break, the women come and gather, since it is not their way to climb the tree. He treated it in root אור.

וְאֻֽרָוֹת לְכָל־בְּהֵמָה וּבְהֵמָה (Divrei HaYamim II 32:28), "stalls for every kind of beast"; אֻרְוֹת סוּסִים (Melachim I 5:26), "stalls for horses"; with a yud in place of the last root letter, אֻרְיוֹת סוּסִים (Divrei HaYamim II 9:25). They are feeding troughs, and the Targum of אֵבוּס בְּעָלָיו (Yeshayahu 1:3), "his master's crib", is אוֹרְיָא דִמְרוֹהִי.

אַרְיֵה שָׁאָג (Amos 3:8), "a lion has roared"; without the heh, וְכַֽאֲרִי יִתְנַשָּׂא (Bamidbar 23:24), "he raises himself like a lion"; the plural אֲרָיוֹת (Melachim I 10:19) and in masculine form אֲרָיִים (Melachim I 10:20). Of the word itself he says only that it is known.
אֶת־אַרְגֹּב וְאֶת־הָאַרְיֵה (Melachim II 15:25) are the names of two warriors who came with Pekach and helped him strike the king, and fifty men of the Giladim came with him besides.

ארי joined to the word אל gives אֲרִיאֵל, the name of the mizbeach, and Yerushalayim was called by it for the mizbeach in her. הוֹי אֲרִיאֵל אֲרִיאֵל קִרְיַת חָנָה דָוִד (Yeshayahu 29:1), "woe, Ariel, Ariel, the city where David encamped": as blood is thrown on the mizbeach, so the whole city will be full of blood of those killed in her markets and streets, which is וְהָיְתָה לִּי כַּֽאֲרִיאֵֽל (Yeshayahu 29:2), "she shall be to Me like an Ariel".

more.h: Why the mizbeach is so called
more.t: Chazal said (Yoma 21b) that the holy fire that came down from heaven crouched upon it like a lion; and in Maseches Middos, that the Heichal is narrow behind and wide in front and so resembles a lion, which they learn from הוֹי אֲרִיאֵל אֲרִיאֵל.

הוּא הִכָּה אֵת שְׁנֵי אֲרִיאֵל מוֹאָב (Shmuel II 23:20), "he struck the two Ariels of Moav", meaning the two great warriors of Moav; the Targum renders תְּרֵין רַבְרְבֵי מוֹאָב. The great and mighty are called so because the lion is great and strong among beasts, and אֵל is a term of force, as יֶשׁ־לְאֵל יָדִי (Bereishis 31:29), "it is in my power". With the alef turned to heh and the yud dropped, the mizbeach is וְהַֽהַרְאֵל (Yechezkel 43:15).

לבא.sense: The lion. He glosses לָבִיא plainly as the lion, and settles its feminine and its two plurals against the forms he holds proper.

more.t: כְּלָבִיא שָׁכֵן (Devarim 33:20), "he dwells like a lavi". It is the lion.
מָה אִמְּךָ לְבִיָּא (Yechezkel 19:2), "what is your mother, a lioness". Its proper form is לְבִיאָה, the yud standing in place of the alef and the alef in place of the heh.

נַפְשִׁי בְּתוֹךְ לְבָאִם (Tehillim 57:5), "my soul is among lions"; the correct form is לְבִיאִים, as נָבִיא gives נְבִיאִים. The feminine plural is וּמְחַנֵּק לְלִבְאֹתָיו (Nachum 2:13), "and strangling for his lionesses".

לישׁ.sense: The great lion. His whole entry is two pesukim and that gloss.

more.t: לַיִשׁ אֹבֵד מִבְּלִי־טָרֶף (Iyov 4:11), "the layish perishes for lack of prey"; לָבִיא וָלַיִשׁ (Yeshayahu 30:6), "lavi and layish". It is the great lion.

שׁחל.sense: The lion; and under the same letters שְׁחֵלֶת, the spice the language of the Mishnah calls צפורן, a fingernail.

more.t: עַל־שַׁחַל וָפֶתֶן תִּדְרֹךְ (Tehillim 91:13), "you shall tread on shachal and pesen"; וָאֱהִי לָהֶם כְּמוֹ־שָׁחַל (Hoshea 13:7), "I was to them like a shachal". It is the lion.

נָטָף וּשְׁחֵלֶת (Shemos 30:34), "nataf and shecheles". It is the spice called in the language of the Mishnah צפורן, a fingernail (Kerisos 6a), being smooth and glossy like a nail; the Targum renders it וְטוּפְרָא.

שׁחץ.sense: Pride. His entry under these letters is about pride, בְּנֵי־שָׁחַץ (Iyov 41:26), and says nothing of a beast.

more.t: הוּא מֶלֶךְ עַל־כָּל־בְּנֵי־שָׁחַץ (Iyov 41:26), "he is king over all the sons of shachatz"; לֹֽא־הִדְרִיכֻוהוּ בְנֵי־שָׁחַץ (Iyov 28:8), "the sons of shachatz have not trodden it". The sense is pride.

more.h: Chazal use it the same way
more.t: Chazal too said (Shabbos 62b) that the people of Yerushalayim were אנשי שחץ, men of pride and coarseness of spirit.

גור.sense: The young of beasts while still small, גורים, lion cubs; and under the same letters to sojourn, to fear, and to gather.

more.t: גּוּר אַרְיֵה יְהוּדָה (Bereishis 49:9), "Yehudah is a lion's cub"; בְּתוֹךְ כְּפִרִים רִבְּתָה גוּרֶֽיהָ (Yechezkel 19:2), "among young lions she raised her cubs"; הֵינִיקוּ גּוּרֵיהֶן (Eichah 4:3), "they nursed their cubs"; with a cholam, כְּגוֹרֵי אֲרָיֹֽות (Yirmiyahu 51:38), "like lions' cubs"; and for the females, בְּדֵי גֹֽרוֹתָי (Nachum 2:13), "enough for his lionesses". The young of beasts while still small are called גורים.

וְגָר זְאֵב עִם־כֶּבֶשׂ (Yeshayahu 11:6), "the wolf shall sojourn with the lamb"; עִם־לָבָן גַּרְתִּי (Bereishis 32:4 in his edition), "I sojourned with Lavan"; מִי־יָגוּר בְּאָהֳלֶךָ (Tehillim 15:1), "who shall dwell in Your tent". גָּרִים יֹאכֵֽלוּ (Yeshayahu 5:17) is "those who come to sojourn shall eat", and may also be read as כרים, lambs.

לַגֵּר אֲשֶׁר־בִּשְׁעָרֶיךָ (Devarim 14:21) is the foreigner living in Eretz Yisrael who took upon himself not to serve avodah zarah, and so every ger the Torah speaks of in that way, as וְנִמְכַּר לְגֵר תּוֹשָׁב (Vayikra 25:47). One who converted outright is the ger the Torah charges with the mitzvos, as הָֽאֶזְרָח וְהַגֵּר (Vayikra 16:29), "the native and the ger".

לֹא תָגוּרוּ מִפְּנֵי־אִישׁ (Devarim 1:17), "do not fear any man"; גּוּרוּ לָכֶם מִפְּנֵי־חֶרֶב (Iyov 19:29), "fear the sword for yourselves". The nouns are כִּי אִם־מָגוֹר מִסָּבִֽיב (Yirmiyahu 20:10), "but terror all around", and מְגוֹרַת רָשָׁע הִיא תְבוֹאֶנּוּ (Mishlei 10:24), "what the wicked dreads shall come upon him". He lists לוּלֵי כַּעַס אוֹיֵב אָגוּר (Devarim 32:27) here as well, were it not for the enemy’s anger I dreaded; and the translator, he notes, took that word rather from אָֽגְרָה בַקָּצִיר (Mishlei 6:8), "she gathers in the harvest".

יָגוּרוּ עָלַי עַזִים (Tehillim 59:4), "the strong gather against me"; עַל־דָּגָן וְתִירוֹשׁ יִתְגּוֹרָרוּ (Hoshea 7:14), "over grain and wine they gather themselves". מִי־גָר אִתָּךְ (Yeshayahu 54:15) is who will gather with you to fight, said of Gog and Magog, of whom it says עָלַיִךְ יִפּֽוֹל, "he shall fall upon you", and elsewhere עַל־הָרֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל תִּפּוֹל (Yechezkel 39:4), "you shall fall on the mountains of Israel".

הַעוֹד הַזֶּרַע בַּמְּגוּרָה (Chaggai 2:19), "is the seed still in the granary", and with two mems נֶֽהֶרְסוּ מַמְּגֻרוֹת (Yoel 1:17), "the granaries are broken down". They are the place where the grain is gathered. His father wrote that the first mem is a servile letter, and that is why the second is doubled, with a pasach in place of a chirik, as לְמַבָּרִֽאשׁוֹנָה (Divrei HaYamim I 15:13).

more.h: Is there seed left in the granary
more.t: He reads הַעוֹד הַזֶּרַע בַּמְּגוּרָה as a question: have you seed left in the granary to lean on? You have only what is sown in the ground, and so you need His blessing; once they began building the Bayis they knew His blessing at once, in the seed and in the fruit of the tree. Rabbeinu Shlomo explained that they had not yet sown that year, the seed being still in the granary, and from now they would sow in a time of blessing, for building the Bayis brings blessing on the work of their hands.

סַעַר מִתְגּוֹרֵר (Yirmiyahu 30:23) may be read from this sense of gathering, and so Targum Yonasan renders עִלְעוּל מִתְכְּנַשׁ, a storm gathering itself; the Mesorah says of the word that it occurs twice in two senses.

שֹמח.sense: Joy: to rejoice, the one who rejoices, and the noun שִׂמְחָה; and by borrowing, increase.

more.t: שָׂמַח מִצְרַיִם בְּצֵאתָם (Tehillim 105:38), "Mitzrayim rejoiced when they went out"; לָכֵן שָׂמַח לִבִּי (Tehillim 16:9), "therefore my heart rejoiced"; and on another pattern, יָרוּן וְשָׂמֵֽחַ (Mishlei 29:6), "he sings and rejoices".

more.h: A command that is a taunt
more.t: שְׂמַח בָּחוּר בְּיַלְדוּתֶיךָ (Koheles 11:9), "rejoice, young man, in your youth", is spoken as a threat: rejoice, and see what will befall you in the end. So too בֹּאוּ בֵֽית־אֵל וּפִשְׁעוּ (Amos 4:4), "come to Beis El and rebel", and אִישׁ גִּלּוּלָיו לְכוּ עֲבֹדוּ (Yechezkel 20:39), "go, serve each man his idols".

וְהָיִיתָ אַךְ שָׂמֵֽחַ (Devarim 16:15), "and you shall be only joyful". In the construct it changes, שִׂמְחֵי־לֵֽב (Yeshayahu 24:7), "the glad of heart", and does not change in שְׂמֵחֵי רָעָתִי (Tehillim 35:26), "those glad at my hurt".
כִּֽי־בְשִׂמְחָה תֵצֵאוּ (Yeshayahu 55:12), "for you shall go out with joy"; וּבְיוֹם שִׂמְחַתְכֶם (Bamidbar 10:10), "and on the day of your rejoicing".

אֽוֹר־צַדִּיקִים יִשְׂמָח (Mishlei 13:9), "the light of the righteous rejoices", is said by way of borrowing, and its sense is increase. In this sense Chazal (Sukkah 7a) call the larger handbreadth a laughing one, and its opposite a sad handbreadth.

שַׂמֵּחַ שִׂמֳּחָֽהוּ (Yirmiyahu 20:15), "he gladdened him greatly"; חֲכַם בְּנִי וְשַׂמַּח לִבִּי (Mishlei 27:11), "be wise, my son, and gladden my heart"; and in the other causative, הִשְׂמַחְתָּ כָּל־אוֹיְבָֽיו (Tehillim 89:43), "You gladdened all his enemies".

Rabbi Yonah took וְשִׁבַּחְתִּֽי אֲנִי אֶת־הַשִּׂמְחָה (Koheles 8:15), "and I praised joy", in another sense, that it means contentment. Radak holds there is no need for that, though it is true that one who rejoices in his portion is the one content with what he has: the pasuk says that a man should rejoice in what he has, and eat and drink and let his soul see good in his labour.
